title: Military jet crashes in Serbia and the pilot is killed, authorities say
summary: Serbia's defense ministry says that a military jet crashed northwest of Belgrade, killing the pilot
story: Serbia's defense ministry says that a military jet crashed northwest of Belgrade, killing the pilot
BELGRADE, Serbia -- A Serbian military jet crashed on Tuesday northwest of Belgrade, killing the pilot, the defense ministry said. The ministry did not immediately give a reason for the crash.
The MIG-29 jet crashed around 8:45 a.m. into a field near the town of Stara Pazova, some 50 kilometers (30 miles) from the Serbian capital, a statement said.
Some local Serbian media published photos of the burning wreckage in the field and an ambulance and police cars parked nearby.

Serbia's defense ministry statement said a special commission will work to determine what happened. The pilot, Maj. Goran Bulajic, was born in 1973 and had joined the army in 1996, it said. No other details were immediately available.

title: How Europe decided on 'return hubs' for migrants
summary: A group of European countries has announced plans to establish a "migrant hub" in Rwanda for rejected asylum-seekers
story: A group of European countries has announced plans to establish a "migrant hub" in Rwanda for rejected asylum-seekers
BRUSSELS -- A group of European countries announced on Monday that they aim to set up a “migrant hub” in Rwanda where rejected asylum-seekers could be sent from next year.

The European Union has worked for years to tighten migration rules, push down the number of asylum-seekers coming to the 27-nation bloc and increase deportations of migrants who aren’t entitled to stay. Sending people to centers outside Europe has emerged as a central element.
Here's a timeline of events that led to this agreement:
2015: Over 1 million people — the majority from war-stricken Syria — arrive in Europe seeking asylum, in what was at the time the largest migration crisis impacting the continent since World War II.

June 2016: The U.K. votes to leave the European Union in a referendum following a campaign during which those favoring Brexit use images of lines of migrants as a warning of what staying in the EU would entail.

September 2018: Sweden joins Europe's move to the right as voters boost a party that campaigned on anti-migrant sentiment and policies. It follows similar shifts in Germany, Austria and Italy as part of a backlash to the 2015 migration crisis. Denmark floats an idea it later scraps to deport migrants to a remote island once used as a research laboratory for contagious animal diseases.

September 2020: Denmark appoints a special envoy to toughen EU migration policies including setting up migrant reception centers in one or more countries outside the EU to diminish the incentive for migrants to seek asylum in Denmark and improving the deportation of rejected asylum-seekers.

April 2021: After Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, leading a center-left Social Democratic-led government, rolls out a vision of having “zero asylum-seekers," Denmark begins revoking the residency permits of some Syrian refugees.

April 2022: Britain announces a deal with Rwanda to send some asylum-seekers thousands of miles to the East African country — a plan it says will stop people-smugglers sending desperate migrants on treacherous journeys across the English Channel.

November 2023: The U.K. Supreme Court rules that the deal with Rwanda to return asylum-seekers there is unlawful because they would not be safe there. The Conservative government says it will send migrants to the African country regardless. Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni and her Albanian counterpart, Edi Rama, strike a five-year deal for Albania to shelter up to 3,000 migrants picked up by the Italian coast guard in international waters each month.

June 2024: Far-right parties make major gains in elections to the Parliament of the European Union, rattling traditional political powers. In France, President Emmanuel Macron calls a snap election that results in a boost for the anti-migration far right, weakening his own government.
July 2024: The U.K. scraps the Rwanda migration deal shortly after the Conservatives are defeated in an election, ceding power to the Labour Party under Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer.

October 2024: Italy’s government formally opens two centers in Albania where it plans to process male migrants who are intercepted in international waters. Less than a month later, a court in Italy rules against the right-wing government’s move to detain 12 migrants at the new centers.

January 2025: An Italian appeals court refuses to approve the speedy expulsion of 43 asylum seekers detained in Albania. The migrants were among 49 people who were transferred to Albania on an Italian naval ship under the five-year agreement with Albania.

March 2025: The Meloni government approves a decree expanding the use of the Albanian fast-track processing centers to include the detention of rejected asylum-seekers with deportation orders. The Albanian centers have remained substantially inactive since their opening in October, due to legal hurdles and amid wide opposition from human rights groups.
April 2025: Italian authorities transfer 40 migrants with no permission to remain in the country to the Albanian centers.

March 2026: Rwanda tells an international arbitration panel that Britain still owes it 100 million pounds ($134 million) under the refugee resettlement deal scrapped in 2024. The court dismisses Rwanda's claim.

March 2026: European lawmakers vote to ease the setting up of new migrant detention centers outside the European Union, known as “return hubs.” Any EU nation can start negotiating on its own or in small coalitions to deport migrants not to their home countries but to facilities yet to be built outside the 27-nation bloc.

June 2026: The three main bodies of the EU, the European Parliament, the European Commission and the European Council, reach agreement over migration policy to increase deportations and to allow member nations to make deals for so-called return hubs.

August 2026: A spokesperson for the Rwandan government defends the practice of establishing return hubs, saying it is “natural” for her government to negotiate with European countries and others to potentially host asylum seekers who are not allowed to live elsewhere.
Sept. 2026: Denmark and four other European Union countries agree on a model for “return hubs” in non-EU nations and say they hope to begin sending migrants to the facilities as early as 2027.
Ciobanu reported from Warsaw, Poland.

title: Iran-backed group warns Iraqi forces against entering its stronghold near Baghdad
summary: Kataib Hezbollah, a powerful Iran-backed armed group, has vowed to confront Iraqi government forces if they enter its stronghold near Baghdad
story: Kataib Hezbollah, a powerful Iran-backed armed group, has vowed to confront Iraqi government forces if they enter its stronghold near Baghdad

JURF AL-SAKHAR, Iraq -- A powerful Iran-backed armed group in Iraq vowed on Tuesday to confront government forces if they try to enter its main stronghold near Baghdad, denying allegations that it is smuggling oil from the area.
The standoff between Kataib Hezbollah and Iraqi authorities is shaping up to be the first major test of the new government’s resolve to disarm nonstate armed groups.

Abu Taleb al-Saidi of Kataib Hezbollah made the comments a day after Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said security forces would enter Jurf al-Sakhar, south of Baghdad in Babil province, later this week. Local media reported that the group had until Friday to leave.
Kataib Hezbollah, one of Iraq’s most powerful armed groups, wields considerable influence in Jurf al-Sakhar and has maintained an armed presence there for more than a decade.

The planned move by al-Zaidi is part of his push to disarm powerful Iran-backed groups by mid-2027. The move by both rival sides raises alarms of internal Shiite fighting that has been mostly avoided since the 2003 U.S.-led invasion that removed Saddam Hussein from power.

Two officials from Kataib Hezbollah told The Associated Press that Gen. Esmail Qaani, who heads the foreign wing of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard, arrived in Baghdad on Monday to take part in mediation to end the tension. The officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly, gave no further details.

The United States backs efforts to disarm Iran-backed groups in Iraq as part of its push to reduce Tehran’s influence in the region, including in Iraq and Lebanon. Washington has described Kataib Hezbollah as an “Iran-backed terrorist organization.”

Lebanese authorities will likely be watching the standoff in Jurf al-Sakhar closely. They have made little progress in carrying out their own plan to disarm Lebanon’s Hezbollah militia, which is allied with but separate from Kataib Hezbollah.
Also Tuesday, an Iraqi judicial committee inspected Jurf al-Sakhar following allegations by authorities that Kataib Hezbollah had used the area to smuggle oil worth tens of millions of dollars.

The state news agency quoted an unnamed senior official as saying the judicial committee was accompanied by a government committee. The inspection aimed to examine the circumstances of the alleged smuggling and identify sites where violations had occurred.

The agency quoted al-Zaidi as saying that all suspects involved in the oil smuggling operations will be referred to the judiciary and that legal measures will be taken against them. He also ordered the dismissal of nine security and administrative officials in Babil governorate, including the Babil police chief, commanders and directors of security and intelligence agencies, and the director of the State Company for Oil Pipelines.

Ali al-Nheir, a member of the parliament’s investigative committee, told the state news agency that the investigation that included thermal imaging showed 25 tanker trucks each carrying 36,000 liters.
“The reports reviewed by the committee were shocking, and included evidence and documents proving the existence of smuggling operations,” al-Nheir said about Jurf al-Sakhar.

Another Kataib Hezbollah official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told journalists touring Jurf al-Sakhar on Tuesday that two facilities in the area refine oil. He said the fuel was used only to run the group’s vehicles and power generators and denied allegations of smuggling.
The official said Jurf al-Sakhar had been hit more than 35 times since the U.S. and Israel began attacking Iran in late February.
He warned that if “a war is imposed on us we will fight.”
Associated Press writer Bassem Mroue contributed to this report from Beirut.

title: Lula to govern Brazil for fourth term but faces challenges. Here’s what to know
summary: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a surprise reelection victory but faces significant challenges
story: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a surprise reelection victory but faces significant challenges

RIO DE JANEIRO -- Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a surprise reelection victory in late October, but he faces a multitude of challenges on issues ranging from the economy and public security to relations with the United States.

While Lula ultimately bested challenger Flávio Bolsonaro by 4.4 million votes after trailing him in the first round, the country remains deeply divided and many voters expressed dissatisfaction with the leftist president's most recent term, which began in 2023.

Bolsonaro refused to recognize the result of the election, declared himself the victim of electoral fraud without providing evidence and fled to Miami. He has vowed to lead a fortified opposition from the U.S.
As Lula prepares to begin his next term, here is a look at challenges ahead.

Lula is facing pressure from investors who had counted on Bolsonaro winning the election after the far-right candidate received more votes than Lula on Oct. 4. Markets did not react well to his loss. Brazil’s currency, the real, dropped by 12% against the dollar the day after the election, while the stock market tumbled nearly 14% and has not rebounded since.
Investors believed a Bolsonaro victory would rein in government spending and are concerned about Lula’s future fiscal policy, said Sergio Vale, chief economist at consultancy firm MB Associados.
“Lula and the government have vowed not to touch spending while keeping all the promises made these last few years,” said Vale. “Unfortunately, they’re not compatible with fiscal responsibility.”

Lula’s government recently unveiled plans to save up to 60 billion reais ($10.6 billion) in public funds through curbs on tax breaks and spending caps — a proposal that is currently moving through Congress.

During Lula’s third term, Brazil’s public debt grew from around 7.2 trillion reais ($1.3 trillion) in 2022 to 11.1 trillion reais ($2 trillion) this year, which analysts say spurred inflation and contributed to high interest rates ultimately remaining unchanged from 13.75% despite variations over the course of the term.
The high cost of living also left many Brazilians unhappy with the state of the economy despite record-low unemployment.

Lula will face a Congress that shifted further to the right in October's legislative elections. Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party secured the largest blocs in both houses, gaining an extra 23 seats in the lower house and nearly doubling its Senate seats, mostly at the expense of centrist parties.
Despite Bolsonaro’s departure for Miami, his party will remain a force to be reckoned with, retaining instruments to block governmental proposals and even challenge judicial authorities.

Bolsonaro’s congressional allies want, above all, to impeach Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who chaired the investigation that led to President Jair Bolsonaro serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup.

Their efforts would be helped if Rogério Marinho, Bolsonaro’s campaign coordinator, becomes Senate president. He announced his candidacy last week, promising not to focus solely on impeachment. But, he said, “we will not turn a blind eye, because no one is above the law.”
Brazilians cited crime as a top concern ahead of the election and insecurity featured prominently in the election cycle.

While Brazil's homicide rate last year fell to its lowest level since 2012, the country continues to face the expansion of criminal activities that use digital technology and online platforms, violence against vulnerable groups — including people of color, women and children — and the need to modernize security and justice institutions, according to this year’s annual report from the Brazilian Forum on Public Safety.

Drug-trafficking gangs have expanded their reach in recent years and are now present in large swathes of the country, including parts of the Amazon rainforest, while paramilitary-type militias have entrenched their power in Rio and other states.
Brazil’s Senate recently approved legislation that strengthens the government’s power to fight criminal gangs. Lula has touted the changes as key to tackling one of his nation’s biggest problems.
Navigating the rivalry between the U.S. and China will be key in Lula’s fourth term, said Ana Garcia, an international relations professor at the Rural Federal University of Rio de Janeiro.

Relations between Brazil and the U.S. fell to an all-time low during Lula’s third term, after the Trump administration imposed several rounds of tariffs. Meanwhile, ties with China deepened, displeasing the U.S., analysts say.

But Democrats' sweeping gains in the midterm election also reflected a repudiation of Trump’s tariffs, and pressure to reduce them — including those targeting Brazil — is likely to increase, Garcia said.

Garcia expects Flávio Bolsonaro and his brother Eduardo, who lives in Texas, to continue lobbying Trump administration allies against Lula’s government. But Democrats may increase scrutiny of Trump's policies abroad. In September, 31 Democratic members of Congress sent a letter to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio accusing the Trump administration of “an apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine” Brazil’s election.
“The midterms were a rude awakening for the Bolsonaros,” Garcia said.
Follow AP’s coverage of Latin America and the Caribbean at https://apnews.com/hub/latin-america

title: Russia fends off swarms of Ukrainian drones a day across its vast territory. But some get through
summary: The skies from the Black Sea to Moscow buzzed overnight with hundreds of Ukrainian drones, keeping Russia’s air defenses busy for hours
story: The skies from the Black Sea to Moscow buzzed overnight with hundreds of Ukrainian drones, keeping Russia’s air defenses busy for hours
The skies from the Black Sea to Moscow buzzed overnight with hundreds of Ukrainian drones, keeping Russia’s air defenses busy for hours.
By daybreak Monday, the military said it shot down 1,336 drones. That marked the largest number of them brought down since the start of the full-fledged invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The Russian military, in turn, ramped up its missile and drone attacks on Ukraine’s power grid, seeking to disrupt electricity and heat as winter sets in.
The surge in aerial attacks follows a week that saw little progress in the first U.S.-mediated talks in nine months.
Here's a look at Russia’s air defenses as it fends off challenges posed by Ukraine’s attacks:
Russia has more land than any other country in the world, and protecting that vast space is a major challenge despite its massive arsenal of defensive systems.

“Russia’s air defense system, like many air defense systems around the world, is not necessarily designed to protect the entirety of Russia’s territory and the air approaches to the country,” said Thomas Withington, an associate fellow with the Royal United Services Institute.
While Ukrainian drones cruise at about 150 kph (about 95 mph), they fly very low, making it harder for radar to spot them.

Their range allows them to strike deep inside Russia. In one recent attack, they hit an oil refinery in Omsk in eastern Siberia, about 2,500 kilometers (about 1,550 miles) from the border. While their payload of about 50 kilograms (110 pounds) is relatively small, their precision allows them to inflict massive damage to such facilities and other infrastructure.
Ukraine also has used long-range Flamingo cruise missiles, capable of reaching up to 950 kph (590 mph), carrying a much heavier payload. Kyiv has fewer of these missiles than drones.

Like in previous attacks, the number of Ukrainian drones reported downed by Russia early Monday couldn’t be independently verified, and official reports haven’t said how many actually got through air defenses to hit their targets.
Withington noted that as a general rule of thumb, 10% get through and hit their targets.
“It’s a game of averages," he said, so launching more drones means that more get through.

He said Russia's air defenses, like most integrated air-defense systems around the world, are designed to shoot down aircraft, air launched weapons and ballistic missiles, and thus could struggle to engage drones.

“Drones are a very different calculus, and because of it, the performance of those systems is never going to be as optimal as it would be against a conventional threat," he said, adding that while air defenses shoot down or jam most of them, some will always get through.
While Russian air defenses around key facilities such as refineries have been bolstered, Ukrainian drones have continued to set them ablaze.

The large size of the targets makes them more vulnerable, Withington said, adding that Ukraine has learned a lot about the operation of Russia's air defense systems, enabling the military to polish its tactics and find loopholes.

“All of Russia’s air defenses, all of the systems they deployed, by and large have given up their secrets” after years of fighting, he said. “The more of that information and data you are armed with, the easier it becomes to defeat Russian air defenses."

In June, a Ukrainian drone set ablaze an oil terminal in St. Petersburg and also hit a nearby naval base, casting a cloud over President Vladimir Putin’s showcase economic forum in his hometown. Putin acknowledged the damage from the attacks, saying Russia would strengthen its air defenses.

On Monday, a Ukrainian drone damaged the well-protected Kerch Bridge linking the mainland and the Crimean Peninsula that Moscow illegally annexed in 2014, temporarily disrupting car traffic. The bridge has been attacked repeatedly over the years.

“Our air defense systems keep operating very effectively,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said. “The system is working, but, unfortunately, no system in the world can provide 100% protection for various facilities against such massive strikes.”
From the early stages of the conflict, Russian authorities have prioritized protecting Moscow.

Media reports said additional air defense systems have been put on the outskirts of the capital, and some could be seen on top of some of the Moscow buildings, including the Defense Ministry’s headquarters facing the Gorky Park across the Moskva River.
While Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin repeatedly claimed that the bulk of the drones were downed, it's impossible to independently verify his claims.

Despite the dense protection around the capital, Ukrainian drones have managed to pierce the shield. Russia scaled down the annual May 9 Victory Day parade, fearing Ukrainian drone strikes. Days later, a massive drone attack on Moscow’s suburbs killed three people. Successive attacks repeatedly struck the oil refinery on the outskirts of the capital, disrupting its operation.

Another top priority has been to protect Putin’s residence in Valdai in northwestern Russia. In December 2025, Russian authorities reported a massive Ukrainian attack on the residence but claimed that none of the 91 drones hit the target.
Since Soviet times, Russia has developed a broad array of air defense systems, from portable ones to long-range weapons capable of shooting down ballistic missiles.
The S-400 Triumph is the main long-range air defense system capable of spotting and engaging aircraft and ballistic missiles at ranges of up to 400 kilometers (about 250 miles).

The even more potent S-500 Prometheus system that reaches as far as 600 kilometers (about 370 miles) also is available in small numbers. Russia also uses various models of S-300 air defense missile systems, an older but still very advanced and powerful long-range weapon.
For shorter ranges, the military has relied on the Pantsyr, the Tor and the Buk air defense systems.
While Buk and Tor use missiles to shoot down aerial targets, Pantsyr can use a combination of guns and missiles. A Pantsyr system sits atop the Defense Ministry building in Moscow.
Russia also has deployed teams armed with shoulder-fired Igla and Verba air defense missiles and machine guns for protection of key facilities. Helicopter gunships also are involved.
Withington said Ukraine and Russia could be expected to further ramp up the number of attacking drones to overwhelm air defenses.
“The long-term direction of travel, both for Ukraine and Russia, will be a continued exponential increase in the number of drones that can be launched at any given time," he said.

title: Some Afghan women quietly defy Taliban bans
summary: In the shadows of the Afghan capital’s bustling streets, many women live in a hidden world, secretly defying the laws imposed on them when the Taliban seized power in August 2021
story: In the shadows of the Afghan capital’s bustling streets, many women live in a hidden world, secretly defying the laws imposed on them when the Taliban seized power in August 2021

KABUL, Afghanistan -- In the shadows of the Afghan capital’s bustling streets lies a hidden world: the world of women, quietly defying the draconian bans imposed when the Taliban seized power after the withdrawal of U.S.-led troops in August 2021.

For women, schooling beyond primary grades is banned, except for Islamic religious education and language courses. Parks and gyms are off-limits, beauty salons are outlawed, and a strict head-to-toe dress code applies. Although women can obtain some business licenses, they’re barred from most jobs.
“Being a woman in Afghanistan is a crime,” said a former soccer player whose dreams were shattered by a sports ban.

Rules are enforced by the widely feared morality police from the Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice. They patrol the streets in doctor-like white coats and can detain women violating rules. Some have been beaten.

The ministry is “fully committed” to ensuring the rights of all under Islamic Sharia law, spokesman Mohammad Aslam Badriwal told The Associated Press in response to questions about restrictions on women.

“Our sisters may also conduct their social and commercial affairs, provided they strictly adhere to the principles of Islamic Sharia and the laws currently in force," he said, adding that the ministry's priority is ”to ensure that our sisters are completely safe within society and are able to enjoy all their Sharia-granted rights."
Some women have found ways to defy the bans, despite the risks.
Here is a look at the hidden lives of three such women in Kabul, all speaking on condition of anonymity for fear of arrest.
For years, the 40-year-old worked in one of Kabul’s beauty salons. When authorities banned them, she felt her life contract.

“You just feel a sense of hopelessness; you become completely despondent,” she said. “Right now, in Afghanistan, there’s nothing left to bring any joy or comfort. There’s no travel, no parks, no schools, there’s absolutely nothing.”
Work was all she had left.
“But now, they won’t even allow that," she said. "It’s as if, for women in Afghanistan, working has become a crime.”
Despite the salon ban, she decided to open her own. Demand was high, particularly for weddings, where women are expected to sport elaborate hairstyles and makeup.
She rented an apartment and bought equipment. Soon, she had about 30 clients. With her husband among the millions of Afghan men unable to find work, it was a lifeline.
But authorities found her secret salon. Their raid took all the equipment, nearly all the furniture.

“I felt completely hopeless,” she said. “If my work, the only thing that gave me any sense of purpose, is taken away, what am I left with? How am I supposed to feed my children? How am I supposed to cover household expenses? I reached a point of total despair and thought: ‘I’m just going to leave.’”

But clients kept calling, and she had bills to pay. Eventually, she decided to try again. She rented another apartment and reopened. Now she has seven employees – young women supporting their own families.
One recent October day, the salon was full of women getting wedding makeovers. They lay on cushions on the floor as beauticians brushed powder onto their cheeks.
The atmosphere was light, but with an undercurrent of fear.
“Every time there’s a knock on the door," the salon owner said, "I worry the Taliban might be on the other side.”

As a teenager, all her ambitions were tied up in soccer. And it looked as if her dreams were coming true: She was picked for the national team. But two years later, the ban on women’s sports crushed them.
Plunged into depression, she spent six months barely leaving her room.
Her family was worried, and she knew she had to find a way out. Eventually, she started playing again – not on pitches, but in the cramped confines of her home.
She also started boxing, turning a stack of old car tires into a rudimentary punching bag. It helped her work through her emotions, she said.

Her true love is still soccer. Unable to play properly herself, she's decided to pass on her knowledge and skills to a new generation. She coaches a small group of young boys in her home’s tiny walled courtyard.

“I saw in them the same dreams and the same passion I had held during my own childhood,” she said, tears welling in her eyes. “It feels really good for me to train with them. Sometimes, I see myself in them.”
Between boxing and coaching, she manages to get through the days. But her view of the future is bleak. She wants to leave and find refuge in another country.
“I see no hope for myself in Afghanistan,” she said.
“No doors are open to us.”
Students stagger arrivals to avoid raising suspicion. The door opens just enough to let them in.

Inside, the subjects are ordinary: history, science, geography, math, languages, Quranic studies. But it's no ordinary school. Set up inside a private home, its students are boys but also girls as old as 20. With teenage girls included, classes must be held in secret.
Teachers here — a 20-year-old with help from her teenage sister — aren’t professionally trained. They do the best they can to pass on what they learned before they were banned from school.
“The current situation in Afghanistan is far from ideal. I had been experiencing increasing levels of depression, so I decided to organize this class,” the 20-year-old said.
She started over a year ago, she said, hoping to help girls “by giving them a sense of hope and allowing them to continue their education." Now she has about 30 students.
A room in the house has been converted into a classroom, with students sitting on the floor at low plastic tables. Brightly colored drawings decorate the walls.
The education restrictions have been the most widely disliked of the Taliban's bans. Officials have repeatedly said they're working on a solution.

“Regarding the part (of education) that still has shortcomings, we are striving to resolve it comprehensively,” government spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said in August. But there's been no sign of progress.
The teenage teaching assistant said many girls have fallen behind, and “we wanted to create an environment where girls can study and strive to reach their goals.”
But with every class they hold, they risk arrest.

“We are very afraid of the Taliban," she said. "We fear that one day, they might come after us, accuse us of violating their rules, arrest us and take us away. We are absolutely terrified of that possibility.”

title: Warren Buffett says kindness 'compounds' as he gifts over $5B to family's foundations
summary: Warren Buffett upped his annual Thanksgiving donation as he advances plans to give away his entire wealth
story: Warren Buffett upped his annual Thanksgiving donation as he advances plans to give away his entire wealth
NEW YORK -- NEW YORK (AP) — Warren Buffett upped his annual Thanksgiving donation as he advances plans to give away his entire fortune.

The billionaire investor pledged Monday to donate about $5.5 billion worth of Berkshire Hathaway shares to his family's foundations — an estimated value more than four times as large as recent years' November stock gifts.

The goal, he reiterated Monday, is to grow the grants each year as he donates all his shares by 2034 to four charitable foundations associated with his three children. He emphasized his faith in his children Monday, writing that they “have given thoughtfully to worthy causes for decades” and that he trusts “their abilities and their fidelity.”

In brief comments, Buffett wrote that kindness “compounds” as he reflected on the “costless benefits” he and his longtime business partner received from their teachers. His good fortune, he said, “has come in the form of people who were kind to me and expected nothing in return.”
“This Thanksgiving, thank one of the selfless people in your own life,” Buffett wrote. “Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else.”

Buffett donated 9,225,000 Class B shares of Berkshire Hathaway stock to the foundations — 3,690,000 shares to The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation and 1,845,000 shares each to The Sherwood Foundation, The Howard G. Buffett Foundation and NoVo Foundation. Berkshire Hathaway Class B shares opened trading Monday at $594 a share.

The next generation of Buffetts tends to fly under the radar even as the children have grown poised to join the ranks of the country's largest donors. The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation, named after Warren Buffett’s first wife, has supported reproductive healthcare organizations in the U.S. and internationally.

The Sherwood Foundation, Susie Buffett's organization, has been a stalwart funder for early childhood education within the U.S. Much of Howard Buffett's grantmaking supports food security and conflict mitigation internationally — with a recent focus on Ukraine. Peter Buffett and his wife, Jennifer, have largely sought to empower women and girls around the world through the NoVo Foundation.

The Thanksgiving donations have, in recent years, come in addition to the main gifts made every summer by Warren Buffett. This year he cut off the Gates Foundation, the longtime beneficiary of the bulk of his charity, from all future gifts. He said the decision was driven more so by his belief in his three kids' readiness than Bill Gates' ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

This year's Thanksgiving stock gift is Buffett's first since stepping down as the chairman and CEO of the $1 trillion conglomerate he built. He wrote Monday that his confidence in Berkshire Hathaway is “as strong as ever.” The third quarter saw the company repurchase $9.6 billion worth of its own shares and a return to growth for its massive cash pile.
