title: Turkish authorities carry out a raid on another opposition TV station and appoint trustees
summary: Turkish authorities have raided the headquarters of one of the country's last major opposition-aligned television stations, Sozcu TV
story: Turkish authorities have raided the headquarters of one of the country's last major opposition-aligned television stations, Sozcu TV

ANKARA, Turkey -- ANKARA, Turkey (AP) — Turkish authorities raided the headquarters of one of the country's last major opposition-aligned television stations on Tuesday, detaining several executives and appointing trustees to manage operations in a move critics described as the latest step in a crackdown on independent media.

The predawn raid against Sozcu TV came just weeks after trustees similarly took control of another opposition-leaning news channel, Halk TV, in an alleged corruption investigation that critics said was politically motivated.

Press freedoms in Turkey have steadily eroded during the more than two decades that President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has been in power, and a majority of media outlets are either under government control or aligned with it. The country ranks 163rd out of 180 countries in the Reporters Without Borders’ world press freedom index.

A statement from the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s office said the move against Sozcu TV was part of an investigation into the channel’s alleged violation of Turkey’s anti-terror financing laws and suspected links to a network that was led by the late U.S.-based cleric Fethullah Gulen.

The cleric, who died in 2024, was accused by Turkey of orchestrating a failed military coup in 2016 and his network of supporters has been branded a terrorist organization. Gulen had denied the accusations.
The prosecutors' office cited suspicion that Sozcu TV and other media outlets linked to its owner, Burak Akbay, were being financed by overseas accounts.

Tuesday's raid follows a widening crackdown on the opposition, with dozens of mayors from the main opposition party arrested on corruption charges since 2024, including former Istanbul mayor Ekrem Imamoglu. The popular politician was widely regarded as a possible challenger to Erdogan.
The government denies any involvement in legal moves against the opposition, insisting that Turkey’s courts operate independently.

The action against Sozcu TV drew condemnation from opposition parties and media groups. Some critics linked the decision to impose a trusteeship to the channel devoting extensive coverage to an investment fund scandal that led to the resignation and subsequent arrest of a senior member of Erdogan’s ruling party.
Main opposition New Party leader Ozgur Ozel accused Erdogan’s government of intolerance toward “even the smallest criticism or a single inconvenient truth being heard.”
He vowed not to “surrender to these would-be dictators.”

Musavat Dervisoglu, the leader of the center-right opposition Good Party, described the move as “an overt assault on democracy, the rule of law, the sense of justice, and the public’s right to be informed.”
“Turkey will speak, and the voice of the truth cannot be silenced!” he wrote on X.
In a joint statement, Turkish journalism associations expressed solidarity with Sozcu TV journalists and called for the decision to appoint trustees to be reversed.
“Following Halk TV, the appointment of trustees to Sozcu shows that the media climate in Turkey has entered a dark winter,” the statement read.
On Tuesday, Sozcu TV’s regular early morning news program was replaced by a recorded discussion about longevity.
Other television stations, including HaberTurk and Tele1, have similarly been placed under trusteeship.

title: Federal Reserve's Cook refuses to participate in White House hearing
summary: Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook declined through her lawyers to appear next month before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome
story: Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook declined through her lawyers to appear next month before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome

WASHINGTON -- Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook declined through her lawyers to appear next month before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome.

The refusal extends the wrangling between the White House and Cook's lawyers regarding her appearance before the committee, which the administration initially demanded for Nov. 6. Trump administration officials have demanded that Cook appear before the committee to address allegations she committed mortgage fraud in 2021, before she joined the Fed's board of governors, a charge she denies.

President Donald Trump has sought to fire Cook since August 2025, and she has argued that the president's efforts to do so represent a threat to the Fed's independence and reflect Trump's desire to force the central bank to reduce borrowing costs.

“Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution’s unique status and independence,” Abbe David Lowell, Cook's lawyer, wrote in a letter released Tuesday to White House counsel William Scharf. The three-person panel set up by the White House to consider the allegations “appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook.”

In June, the Supreme Court blocked the Trump from removing Cook while litigation over the attempted firing continues, finding that "the fact of independence but also the appearance of independence is key to the Federal Reserve’s design.”

Trump officials have threatened to move ahead with the hearing even without Cook, and in a Nov. 3 letter said that the three-member committee “reserves the right to draw adverse inferences against you” for not participating.

The unusual “committee of inquiry” set up by the White House consists of Kevin Hassett, Trump’s top economic adviser; Andrea Lucas, whom Trump appointed to lead the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission; and Keith Sonderling, Trump’s pick for Labor Secretary.

The Supreme Court said in a footnote to its June ruling that Trump could try again to fire her if the administration provided her adequate notice and an opportunity to respond. The committee of inquiry is an effort to meet those conditions.

Under the law governing the Fed, the president can only fire a Fed governor “for cause,” but the Supreme Court didn’t address whether Cook’s actions met that standard. The committee will ultimately recommend whether there is cause to fire Cook, the White House has said.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh was asked at a press conference Oct. 28 if he or the Fed would be involved in the hearing against Cook, and he said, “not to my knowledge.”

title: Anthropic forges ahead with its IPO even as AI fears mount and markets wobble
summary: Anthropic is preparing to sell stock to the public in a shaky moment for artificial intelligence companies
story: Anthropic is preparing to sell stock to the public in a shaky moment for artificial intelligence companies
NEW YORK -- Investors fearing an AI bubble are getting jittery. Financing costs are rising. Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry.
It's not an ideal time for an artificial intelligence company to sell stock, but Anthropic is pressing ahead with its blockbuster initial public offering anyway.
No ordinary sale, the Claude chatbot maker's IPO could raise more than $60 billion on Thursday, a massive haul that, depending on the ultimate pricing and other issues, could rival SpaceX's in June.
But Anthropic is facing headwinds as it prepares for its coming-out party.
Tech stocks have done well so far this year, but the path higher has been rocky, especially for AI-related companies. That's not a reassuring setup for the IPO.

One particularly volatile AI stock, CoreWeave, plunged 15.5% on Oct. 14 over fears it wouldn't be able to borrow enough, cheaply enough to fund its growth. The stock then swung wildly. On Wednesday, the company, which buys chips and then rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, surged 25% after an encouraging earnings report, only to plunge 7% the next day.
Most stocks move no more than 2% on the average trading day.

Adding to the sector volatility recently has been the abrupt departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang over extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang, a high-profile AI booster, built Nvidia into a linchpin of the industry and a major financial backer of other AI companies. Stock in the AI chip designer dropped 4% Monday, dragging the broader S&P 500 down for a third day in a row.
Nvidia has agreed to buy an estimated $10 billion of Anthropic stock after the IPO. It also sells chips to Anthropic but the latter also buys from AMD and others.

As to whether the gyration in AI-tied stocks argues for an IPO delay, note that volatility can cut both ways: It might be signaling the much debated AI bubble could burst soon so it's better to sell stock now, fast. And history shows demand for IPOs can disappear quickly.
In 2021, nearly 400 companies went public in the U.S., but then investors got scared of a possible recession the next year and demand dried up with only 71 making market debuts.

Another reason to sell stock now is that the other way to raise money — borrowing — has gotten more expensive. That's partly due to inflation fears and partly due to the sector’s massive cash needs, which have drawn comparisons to the Gilded Age splurge on railroads. Lenders fear AI companies have taken on too much debt to expand while having no clear path to profitability.

Anthropic already has taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is “substantial." Adding to the strain, the company is unprofitable, at least under standard accounting rules, suggesting its resources are limited to pay interest and principal.

On the plus side, it has ample cash, although it will likely run through it quickly if it can't raise more soon given its outsized spending plans. The company said it has already signed leases and other deals requiring it to spend $900 billion in computing and infrastructure in the coming years, including $70 billion in the next 12 months.
Higher interest rates are not the only problem. Politics threatens to slow growth, too.

Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a national backlash against data centers, giving new impetus to a Congressional effort last year to enact a national moratorium on new ones.
And two big states offering incentives for data centers, Texas and Georgia, just elected Democrat governors vowing to stop new construction.
It wouldn't be unprecedented for Anthropic to postpone its IPO at the last minute.

After a bout of volatility following President Donald Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs in April 2025, several companies postponed their initial offerings, including the online ticket marketplace StubHub and Klarna, a buy now, pay later business. And an Australian data center company, Firmus, called off its IPO last month because of jitters in the market.
But newly elected Democrats don't take office until January. Anthropic could be betting that selling now is best before the feared crackdown begins in earnest.

If the company does go ahead as expected, it will beat rival OpenAI to the market. That's an important advantage should investors suddenly fear they have too much exposure to the sector and decide they don't want to buy stock in the next public AI company.
And despite the jitters, companies on public markets are still fetching top prices. One measure of investor enthusiasm shows they are paying nearly as much as ever to buy stocks.

The measure championed by the famed American economist Robert Shiller comparing share prices to corporate profits over the previous decade shows shares have been more expensive only once before — the 2000 dot-com crash — and are higher now than on the eve of the 2008-09 Financial Crisis.
Stocks currently trade at 40 times their long term earnings, according to Shiller's measure. That is a third higher — meaning more expensive — than the average going back before 1900.
That's good news for Anthropic, meaning it may be able to fetch top dollars for its shares this week, though maybe not so good for its IPO investors.

title: Should court filings related to the search of Ilhan Omar's home be released? A judge will decide
summary: It's been more than a month after federal agents searched the home of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar
story: It's been more than a month after federal agents searched the home of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar

WASHINGTON -- More than a month after federal agents searched the home of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, a federal judge heard arguments Tuesday on a request by media organizations to unseal court records related to the search — and to an immigration-fraud investigation that the Minnesota Democrat claims is politically motivated.

Over a dozen news organizations, including The Associated Press, maintain that the public has a First Amendment right to access the search warrant and other court filings that led to the Oct. 12 search of Omar's Washington, D.C., home by Department of Homeland Security agents.

During a hearing on the request, Chief Judge James Boasberg said he agrees with Justice Department attorneys that it's premature to unseal a search warrant affidavit containing sensitive details of the government's investigation. But the judge said he will privately review other sealed court filings for possible public release as soon as next week.

Omar, a naturalized U.S. citizen born in Somalia, has been a target of anti-immigrant rhetoric by President Donald Trump and many Republican allies. Omar, who has denied wrongdoing, said in a social media post that the search was an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”

Federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork and have issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives, a person briefed on the investigation told The AP last month on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation.

Agents conducted the court-authorized search less than a month before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Omar won her reelection bid. The Justice Department historically has avoided public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of an election.
Omar has said DHS agents seized 17 items, including phones, notebooks, a Somali-language children’s book and a vintage camera that her husband had received as a gift.

Boasberg gave the government until Friday to provide him with proposed redactions to sealed court filings that could shed light on some of the underlying legal arguments involved in the Omar investigation. The judge said redacted versions of those documents could be released as soon as next Monday.

The 67-page search warrant affidavit, which contains information about witnesses and other details of the investigation, will remain under wraps for now. In a court filing last month, the government argued that it would jeopardize the investigation to unseal the court records before a charging decision is made.

The news organizations' attorneys argue that the government's privacy concerns are outweighed by the “enormous public interest in and historic significance of a search warrant executed at the home of a sitting member of Congress.”
Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano said the government isn't trying to keep the affidavit under seal permanently.
“It's not our position. It's never been our position,” she told the judge.

Boasberg noted that Vice President JD Vance and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin already have publicly commented on the contours of the Omar investigation. Serano said she can't control what others in the Trump administration say about the case.
“It seems to be a common refrain,” Boasberg replied.

Boasberg, who was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Barack Obama, is himself a frequent target of Trump's ire. Trump called for Boasberg's impeachment last year after the judge blocked the president's administration from deporting planeloads of Venezuelan migrants to El Salvador under the Alien Enemies Act.
___ Associated Press writer Alanna Durkin Richer contributed to this report.

title: More drops for Nvidia and other AI stocks drag the US market lower
summary: More drops for AI stocks are dragging the U.S. market lower, led by Nvidia
story: More drops for AI stocks are dragging the U.S. market lower, led by Nvidia
NEW YORK -- NEW YORK (AP) — More drops for stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are dragging the U.S. market lower on Monday, led by Nvidia.

The S&P 500 fell 1.1% and was on track for a third straight loss. The weakness for tech stocks pulled the Nasdaq composite down a market-leading 1.6%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 289 points, or 0.6%, as of 11 a.m. Eastern time.

Nvidia sank 2.5% and was again the heaviest weight on Wall Street following its crisis of leadership. Nvidia is one of the most influential companies in the world not only because its chips are powering much of the world’s move into AI technology but also because its cash has helped companies across the industry to grow.

Now, following Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO last week, both the chip company and the broad industry are facing a more uncertain future without the leather-jacketed man who became one of AI’s biggest celebrities.

It’s the latest challenge for the AI industry, which had already been shaky because of criticism that stock prices in the industry shot too high and were in a bubble. The sweeping victories for Democrats in this month’s U.S. midterm elections also raised worries about possible restrictions on further construction of AI data centers.

“The market was already worried about this risk before what happened at Nvidia,” Zhiwei Zhang, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, said in a commentary. “Now the risk has become even more serious.”

Outside of Nvidia, other chip companies also fell. They had climbed in the earlier days of Nvidia’s fall on hopes that they could gain a competitive advantage. But Broadcom dropped 3.8% and was on track for a second straight loss on concerns about the broader industry. So was Advanced Micro Devices, which fell 4.5%.
CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and then rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, sank 5%. GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centers, fell 3.3%.

The next big milestone for the AI industry may arrive Tuesday after trading in the U.S. stock market ends for the day. That’s when Nvidia will report its latest quarterly results, and interim CEO Colette Kress is set to speak to Wall Street. Investors have become accustomed to Nvidia not only reporting stronger results than analysts expected for each quarter but also giving a forecast for upcoming revenue that’s well above expectations.

Elsewhere on Wall Street, L3Harris Technologies fell 2.5% after officials in President Donald Trump’s administration suggested the contractor for the Federal Aviation Administration may be at fault for a nationwide ground stop Friday. L3Harris said Saturday that it’s supporting the FAA in its investigation.

Summit Therapeutics sank 13.4% after the biopharmaceutical company said the U.S. Food and Drug Administration indicated it cannot approve its application for a therapy to treat certain patients with lung cancer.

Tyson Foods helped to limit the market’s losses and rose 7.5% after reporting a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The company behind the Jimmy Dean and Hillshire Farm brands, though, also reported weaker revenue than expected after selling less beef than it did a year earlier.

The recent swings for AI stocks have overshadowed what's been another strong earnings reporting season for U.S. companies. The big businesses in the S&P 500 index are on track to deliver earnings per share for the summer nearly 32% higher than a year earlier, according to FactSet.

It's the third straight quarter of growth above 25% for the index, which is important because corporate profits are one of the two big levers that set stock prices over the long term, along with interest rates.
In the bond market, Treasury yields eased back following last week's jump due to a worse-than-expected report on U.S. inflation.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 5.13% from 5.15% late Friday, though it remains well above a low of 4.80% reached earlier this month. Higher yields make borrowing money more expensive for everyone, and they’ve already hurt the housing industry through expensive mortgage rates.

Yields fell as oil prices sank, which took away some of the upward pressure on inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil fell 2.1% to $93.81. It’s been yo-yoing amid uncertainty about what will happen in the war with Iran.
In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia.

South Korea’s Kospi dropped 3.6%, and Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 2.4% for two of the world’s sharpest losses because of weakness for tech and AI-related stocks. A report also showed that Japan’s economy contracted in the latest quarter.
AP Business Writers Chan Ho-him and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.

title: Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail
summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry
story: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry

PHNOM PENH, Cambodia -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.

Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where Chinese auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions.”

Carney said Saturday in Manila, Philippines, that any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry. He said Monday that negotiations with the United States remain his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers.
Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in the U.S. negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.”

“If they’re not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said of Canada’s auto workers and manufacturing assets. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”

The Detroit Three — Ford, General Motors and Stellantis — operate factories across Canada, the United States and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the United States from Canada.

Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would require proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles.
“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”

Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.
Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs.

The deal drew criticism from Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the U.S. market.

Trump’s tariffs have disrupted Canada’s auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the automaker shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.

Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior U.S. officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.

title: Trump administration moves to block China from indirect access to American AI technology
summary: The Trump administration has issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers
story: The Trump administration has issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers

WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best artificial intelligence models.

Last week, Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following scrutiny of his ties to a Chinese executive who used to lead Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. The company provides computing power to Chinese companies using chips housed in Southeast Asian data centers, including facilities in Malaysia.

“The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries,” the Bureau of Industry and Security under the Commerce Department said in issuing the rule that took effect immediately.
The rule came on the same day President Donald Trump departed for a trip to Asia, where he expects to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the third time this year amid a fragile truce on trade.

Under the new rule, overseas data centers that serve companies in countries including China, Russia, Iran and Cuba are required to identify their end users. There also will be additional licensing requirements for sales of chips for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil — countries that “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" to unauthorized destinations, the rule says.

In Beijing, China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun accused Washington of arbitrarily interfering with China's trade and technological cooperation with other countries and suppressing the development of China's high-tech industries.

“This is a typical example of economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction, runs counter to the common understanding between the two sides,” he told reporter, adding that it infringes upon the rights of Chinese companies and disrupts the stability of global supply chains.
He said China would take necessary measures to safeguard its interests.

The U.S. bans sales of the country's most advanced AI chips to China, seeking to maintain an edge in its rivalry with China for predominance in artificial intelligence. However, many lawmakers and policymakers believe the country's export control rules are not tough enough and filled with loopholes such as cloud computing that allows China to rent processing power built on American technology.

Last year, U.S. Rep. Michael Lawler, a New York Republican, introduced a bill to broaden the U.S. export controls to include remote access. He told Congress “physical export controls” under current rules do not apply to remote access, allowing China to “access our tech through the cloud” and giving it “a real tool to sidestep” U.S. export restrictions. The bill has passed the House.

In the Senate, lawmakers also are seeking tougher legislation to prevent China from accessing advanced U.S. chip and AI technologies. Bills include proposals that would let Congress review licenses to sell advanced AI chips to China, ask the Department of Commerce to track AI chips to ensure they are not diverted to unauthorized regions, and compel U.S. allies such as the Netherlands and Japan to match U.S. restrictions on exports to Chinese chipmakers.
Last week, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick came under pressure when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Commerce Department was late to place restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed.

On Monday, Trump acknowledged tension between Treasury and Commerce on the matter. He suggested that Lutnick may have delayed placing the export restrictions to avoid a “blow up” in the fragile U.S.-China relationship.
“We’re having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, Trump said.

In a joint statement late Monday by the Commerce and Justice departments, it said Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed for potential export control violations in 2024, which was followed by requests to Nvidia for records in May 2025 related to sales to Megaspeed. The following month, it said, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list, and agents from the Commerce Department in conjunction with Singapore law enforcement conducted on-site checks of Megaspeed and interviewed Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang. The Justice Department then took the lead role in the criminal probe of Megaspeed, the statement said.

“The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” the statement said.

Last week, the Singapore government confirmed that it had investigated Megaspeed over “potential false declarations" involving servers that were exported through Singapore to Malaysia but might have “subsequently been routed from Malaysia to another destination, contrary to declaration made in Singapore.”
The Malaysian government also said last week that it was investigating if chips brought into Malaysia have been re-exported to other countries as permitted by its own law.

“Malaysia welcomes investment in data centers and technology, but will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls,” read the Friday statement by Malaysia's Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry.

title: A top Puerto Rico government official resigns as corruption allegations swirl
summary: Puerto Rico’s embattled secretary of the Department of Family has announced that she would resign by year’s end as she denies the corruption allegations swirling around her
story: Puerto Rico’s embattled secretary of the Department of Family has announced that she would resign by year’s end as she denies the corruption allegations swirling around her
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- Puerto Rico’s embattled secretary of the Department of Family announced Monday that she would resign by year’s end as she denied corruption allegations swirling around her.

Lawmakers in the U.S. territory had demanded for months that Suzanne Roig step down over the latest political scandal to hit the administration of Gov. Jenniffer González, which has seen several high-ranking officials resign or be fired in recent years.
Roig is under investigation by Puerto Rico’s Senate, the island’s Justice Department and its Office of the Inspector General.

In recent months, Blanca Medina Díaz, who was dismissed as head of the Administration for the Socioeconomic Development of the Family, which is within the department Roig oversees, publicly accused Roig of pressuring her to approve a nearly $40 million contract that Medina alleges was illegal and would have used federal funds from the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program. The alleged push came after Roig and other officials visited Louisiana.
Roig and NOLA Education LLC, a Louisiana-based education company, have said that no contract was signed.
Medina, who has met with U.S. federal authorities, also accused Roig of pressuring her to approve an unrelated contract worth more than $300,000.
Roig has been under fire, as has the governor, who has publicly supported her.
Roig testified before Puerto Rico’s Senate in recent weeks as certain lawmakers who are members of the governor’s pro-statehood party called for her to step down.
Puerto Rico Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz, also a member of the governor’s New Progressive Party, has said that ongoing legislative investigations would continue even if Roig resigned.
As Roig faced increasing scrutiny, she alleged in recent months that she was being stalked and persecuted as she denied all accusations.
In a statement Monday, Roig said that nobody asked her to resign as she thanked the governor for “the time and space that allowed me to defend my reputation against attacks full of falsehoods.”
Her decision to step down on Dec. 31 angered many.

“The resignation should have been immediate,” said Puerto Rico Sen. Juan Oscar Morales, majority whip and a member of the governor’s party. “The Department of the Family needs leadership focused on addressing the agency’s problems and ensuring services for those who depend on it.”

Roig’s announcement came nearly four months after the governor’s chief of staff and deputy chief of staff announced their resignations as they, too, denied corruption allegations. The governor stood by them as she has by Roig.

title: 1.5-hour-long system outage forces United Airlines to delay departing flights
summary: A system outage that lasted more than 90 minutes forced United Airlines to delay departing flights
story: A system outage that lasted more than 90 minutes forced United Airlines to delay departing flights

A system outage that lasted more than 90 minutes forced United Airlines to delay departing flights Monday, just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration's network prompted a nationwide ground stop.

Chicago-based United said in a statement that flights that were in the air and flights on its United Express regional network were not affected. The airline also said there was “no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.”
United apologized on social media to customers for the inconvenience. It resolved the issue about one hour and 40 minutes after pilots first began reporting problems to air traffic controllers.

United did not immediately provide details about which of its systems were affected, but pilots told air traffic controllers that the problem was related to a system that helps them determine a plane's final weight.

Before every departure, pilots use performance software, often on a cockpit tablet, to check that the aircraft can safely take off under current weather and runway conditions. The preflight calculations include the aircraft's weight along with information about the fuel, baggage, cargo and passengers the plane is carrying.
The information is also used to guide the autopilot system and the decisions pilots make, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said.

“It is extremely important to have all of these numbers accurate and precise,” said Arroyo, who flew for United. “Pilots use that information to establish guidance and performance for their flights from takeoff to landing.”
Arroyo said he has seen problems with the weight and balance system before in his career, but the airline did the right thing by delaying flights to ensure safety.

Years ago, pilots used to do all those weight calculations manually with a pencil and paper and then radio in the numbers, but today it is all calculated electronically and then loaded into the plane’s computers.

In August 2025, United grounded planes at major U.S. airports, delaying more than 1,000 flights because of an hourslong outage of a system called Unimatic, which houses flight information that is fed to other systems including those that calculate weight and balance and track flight times.
United said in response to a message from The Associated Press that it had no further information to provide about whether the same system was affected by Monday’s outage.

A recording posted Monday on the ATC app showed a United pilot in Houston asking the tower for permission to stay put at the gate until the system was working again. The app combines live air traffic control radio feeds with real-time visual aircraft tracking.
The flight-tracking website FlightAware showed United with about 600 delayed flights Monday evening, though it was unclear how many were directly related to the system outage.
The United computer problem is just the latest high-profile technology meltdown in recent days.
Earlier Monday, thousands of people reported being unable to access their online accounts at several major U.S. banks after JPMorgan Chase had a technical problem.
On Friday, the FAA ordered every flight grounded because a newly installed router malfunctioned, overwhelming the aging air traffic control system.
And one day earlier, Microsoft experienced a major disruption to its Outlook email service. Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored.

title: Xi and Carney call for deeper ties as Canada looks beyond US for trade
summary: The leaders of China and Canada have called for deeper ties as Ottawa navigates strained relations with the United States and seeks closer cooperation with Beijing
story: The leaders of China and Canada have called for deeper ties as Ottawa navigates strained relations with the United States and seeks closer cooperation with Beijing
SHENZHEN, China -- The leaders of China and Canada  called for deeper ties Tuesday as Ottawa navigates strained relations with the United States and seeks closer cooperation with Beijing.

Chinese President Xi Jinping and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ summit, and both praised the strategic partnership they agreed to pursue this year and pointed to improving economic ties.
The meeting came a day after Carney said Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to maintain an integrated North American auto industry.

“Improving and developing China-Canada relations serves the interests of the people of both countries and is also conducive to safeguarding world peace, stability, development and prosperity,” said Xi. “This is the right choice.”
Carney said that the exchanges between Canada and China have increased in the past months and praised that now there is “greater predictability and stability” in their relationship.
“The stabilization of our bilateral trade arrangement is indicative of how we can work together more broadly, pragmatically, to solve problems,” he said.
Xi and Carney reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.

title: Amazon vows to fight the company's first North American union contract at a Canadian warehouse
summary: Hundreds of Amazon workers at a warehouse in Delta, British Columbia, are now being covered by a union contract, marking the company’s first site in North America under a collective bargaining agreement
story: Hundreds of Amazon workers at a warehouse in Delta, British Columbia, are now being covered by a union contract, marking the company’s first site in North America under a collective bargaining agreement

NEW YORK -- Hundreds of Amazon workers at a warehouse in Delta, British Columbia, are now being covered by a union contract, marking the company's first site in North America under a collective bargaining agreement.

The terms of the contract, which is set to run until Nov. 13, 2029, were imposed by an independent arbitrator between Canadian union Unifor and Amazon. Amazon said the facility employs more than 700 workers.

In a statement on Friday, Unifor's National President Lana Payne praised the workers who "stood up to one of the most powerful companies on earth and won rights in writing that Amazon cannot take away.”

But the Seattle-based online giant argued that the arbitrator set the terms without giving its workers “the chance to ratify or vote on it." It also said that the terms were imposed despite a pending effort by some of Amazon's employees to decertify the union.
Amazon said in a blog posted late Friday that the agreement sets terms for wages, scheduling, layoffs, and benefits that are largely similar to what the workers had already.

Amazon said the contract requires every employee in the unit to join the union, whether they want to or not, and to have union dues of up to C$1,064 ($744.03 US) deducted from their pay in the first year. That means they could actually take home less money than they did before, Amazon said.
“We believe that this process was improper, unfair, and defies common sense,” J. Ofori Agboka, Amazon's vice president of people, wrote in the blog post.

Unifor and Amazon have been locked in a fight since 2024 when employees at the facility started an organizing drive. In July 2025, the British Labour Relations Board certified the worker union for the warehouse through a rare process called “remedial certification” after it found that Amazon committed unfair labor practices including what it described as an unnecessary hiring spree to stop the certification process. The regulatory board said in its decision that Amazon pursued a “lengthy and pervasive anti-union campaign." Amazon had filed an appeal.
Remedial certification is used when an employer pursues unfair labor practices during an organizing drive that makes a fair vote unlikely.

Amazon said that it has filed a request for judicial review in the British Columbia Supreme Court, asking to halt implementation of the collective agreement until its decertification application is resolved and to overturn the board’s order imposing a contract through arbitration.

“We think the best workplace is one where associates have direct input and we work together to make progress quickly, and where nobody should have to pay dues or go through a third party to be heard,” Amazon's Agboka said.

In 2022, Amazon workers in Staten Island, New York, voted to unionize, marking the first successful U.S. organizing effort in the retail giant’s history. The workers were represented by Amazon Labor Union, which affiliated with the International Brotherhood of Teamsters two years later.
But workers don't have a contract yet, with the National Labor Relations Board ordering Amazon to negotiate and Amazon continuing to fight the union certification in court.

title: As outages persist, Puerto Rico finds a way to help keep the lights on with 'virtual power plant'
summary: Hector Ríos is part of Puerto Rico's innovative “virtual power plant” system, which uses household batteries to support the island's electric grid
story: Hector Ríos is part of Puerto Rico's innovative “virtual power plant” system, which uses household batteries to support the island's electric grid

SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- On nearly 20 days in October, an electric utility took energy from a battery attached to Hector Ríos’ house in Cabo Rojo, on the southwest corner of Puerto Rico, and used it to support the power grid.
Ríos was happy to share.

With the U.S. territory's frequent power outages that disrupt daily life and restrain its economy, he likes the idea of helping prevent blackouts for other people. He's also compensated for the energy.
“It just seems like a good deal, to contribute to the community and make money at the same time,” Ríos said.

Ríos, 75, is part of what has become one of Puerto Rico's most effective tools for energy resilience amid nearly a decade of electricity woes: a “virtual power plant,” or VPP, that harnesses batteries from nearly 115,000 households to bolster the grid when its aging and fickle power plants can't meet demand.

Nine years after Puerto Rico's public power utility filed for bankruptcy and Hurricane Maria ravaged its already dilapidated energy grid, residents still face unpredictable blackouts and electricity rates higher than in almost any state. Few new utility-scale power sources have been built since Maria, and most of the federal dollars promised for grid recovery have not yet reached the territory.

But the VPP — the first of its kind in Latin America and the Caribbean, and the U.S.' second largest in terms of capacity — showed its potential this summer, preventing or mitigating outages more than 60 times since June 1, according to Luma Energy, its transmission and distribution utility.
“There’s nothing virtual about it,” said Javier Rúa Jovet, chief policy officer at the Solar and Energy Storage Association of Puerto Rico. “It’s real, and it’s better than a power plant.”

Dozens of states now operate similar networks of distributed energy sources like battery storage systems, electric vehicles and smart thermostats to help manage the grid. Experts expect their role to grow in the U.S. amid energy constraints, rising utility prices, and tech companies’ push to build power-hungry data centers.

As President Donald Trump’s administration promotes fossil fuel expansion and redirects dollars away from solar adoption in Puerto Rico, proponents of the territory's system say it highlights the value of distributed solar and storage, and shows how these systems can bolster resilience for other energy-vulnerable communities.

“There’s a way for this technology to benefit not just the individual buildings that they’re on,” but instead be “in service to the community all the time,” said Nathalie Jordi, community solar lead at Together New Orleans, a nonprofit that championed an upcoming $23 million city program to provide and network over 1,000 batteries on homes and businesses across New Orleans.

The opportunity to harness a vast network of residential batteries arose after Hurricane Maria in 2017, which left some communities without electricity for nearly a year. Experts linked the infrastructure failure to thousands of post-hurricane deaths.
“We had to procure resiliency in some other way,” said Rúa Jovet, “not a centralized system that will completely fail for a whole year.”

There are now over 207,000 rooftop solar systems on an archipelago of fewer than 3.2 million people, a 20-fold increase from before Maria that was propelled by households who could afford installations, philanthropy, and some federal dollars. Because of the territory's unique need for resiliency, nearly every installation includes at least one battery, a necessary add-on to keep the system running in a blackout.

“The mindset was, get yourself ready for everything,” recalled Ríos, who after Maria bought a diesel generator for his house, then installed panels and a Tesla Powerwall battery in 2023. The system also cut his utility bill in half, from about $400 to $200 in the summer.

Solar panels create an energy boon during the day, charging batteries and sending excess power to the grid. But when the sun sets and demand rises, Puerto Rico barely has enough power to meet the need. Any power plant malfunction can prompt an outage.

In late 2023, Luma launched a small pilot program that would leverage residential battery capacity to offset the shortages. Ríos was among the first to enroll; now over half of solar customers participate.

If Luma predicts an energy deficit, customers are digitally notified that a battery sharing event is coming. They can opt out via app, or adjust how much of their battery — enrollees typically offer 30% — they make available.

The experiment has faced challenges. In a 2026 survey of solar customers by the nonprofit Solar United Neighbors, some participants criticized the compensation structure, which varies by solar provider. Others expressed hesitation to enroll in the program because they did not understand it or feared losing backup power.
Ríos said he’s only had that problem once — when a storm knocked out power right after he shared his battery. He now skips battery sharing events if there's bad weather forecast.
He acknowledged the payment system is “a little vague.” He and his wife received $162 last year, which they happily redeemed as a Marshalls gift card.

Luma told The Associated Press that relying so often on battery sharing has contributed in part to recent rate increases. The utility pays solar providers three times the residential electricity price for the battery energy it takes, recovering the costs through rates.

Rúa Jovet says that expense doesn’t compare to the societywide economic losses of frequent power outages that spoil food, endanger health and shutter schools and businesses. The territory is also set to spend more than $1.7 billion this year importing fuel for most of its power generation.

Luma said each battery sharing event, typically about four hours, supports the equivalent of about 80,000 residential customers. Enrolling more households would enable supplemental power for more hours.
But experts believe Puerto Rico can think bigger.

“The VPP in Puerto Rico is like an emergency escape valve, but the batteries should be a grid asset,” said Jigar Shah, director of the Department of Energy’s Loan Programs Office under former President Joe Biden and comanaging director of the advisory firm Multiplier.

Instead of only being tapped in an emergency, Shah said, the batteries could dispatch power every day — offsetting the need to burn fossil fuels — and help absorb excess energy across the grid when solar panels are producing at their peak. Several states, including California and Texas, use solar and batteries this way.

VPPs “could potentially play a larger role in Puerto Rico’s energy future,” Alejandro Figueroa, Luma chief regulatory officer, told The Associated Press. But, he said, a program used daily would require a different design and compensation structure to be sustainable.

Providing daily power is a natural next step, Rúa Jovet said, and could help Puerto Rico meet its own legal mandate that the archipelago reach 100% renewable energy by 2050. But a virtual power plant alone cannot solve the territory’s energy crisis.
That will require deploying billions of unspent federal recovery dollars, continuing improvements to transmission and distribution infrastructure and building new large-scale generation and storage.
“You don’t want the situation to be a persistent emergency forever,” he said.

title: Taiwan may take a backseat when Xi and Trump meet for a third time at an APEC summit
summary: Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet at the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week
story: Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet at the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week

TAIPEI, Taiwan -- Taiwan is likely to be overshadowed as presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week, even as the threat from China evolves and grows stronger.

Leaders from China, the U.S. and some 21 other economies will gather at the APEC summit this week in Shenzhen, China. Recent events like the scandal that forced Nvidia's CEO to resign, export controls and the ongoing trade dispute have made the tech competition between Beijing and Washington all the more pressing.

Few expect major breakthroughs on Taiwan, a self-ruled island that is claimed by Beijing. While the U.S. does not formally recognize Taiwan, it is the island’s biggest informal ally and seller of arms.
“For the Trump administration, this isn’t a core issue between the U.S. and China,” said Arthur Zhin-Sheng Wang, an expert on cross-Straits relations at Taiwan’s Central Police University.
Experts largely say that cooperation with the U.S. remains strong below the level of rhetoric, despite Trump’s public ambivalence toward Taiwan.

One sign of this came from the summer, when the de facto United States embassy in Taiwan posted a photo showing joint patrols between the two coast guards, a rare occurrence, as the U.S. does not usually acknowledge it has direct cooperation with Taiwan in any defense capacity.

“This also is proof of the decades that Taiwan and U.S. have had of cooperation and training. I was also surprised,” said Kuo Yu-jen, a defense studies expert and director of the Institute for National Policy Research in Taiwan.

The U.S. is obligated by law to help Taiwan defend itself, which has manifested in the form of arms sales, while the government officially adopts a stance of ambiguity on whether it would intervene militarily in the case of a Chinese invasion.

The Taiwanese public is used to the continued uncertainties of the island’s relationship with the U.S. Research from the Institute of National Defense and Security Research in Taiwan, a government-funded think tank, showed that public attitudes toward the U.S. remain around the same. Polls conducted in the past five years show that about half of the public believes the U.S. will send soldiers to support Taiwan in the event of a Chinese invasion, and about half don’t.

“I do think they will take some actions, though it may not be sending soldiers,” said Allen Hsieh, a 28-year-old media professional in Taipei. “I think Taiwan’s importance to the U.S. is even more important than Ukraine.”
Since starting his second term, Trump called for Taiwan to spend more on its own defense and Taiwan responded that it would commit to 5% of its GDP on defense.

Arms sales are ongoing. While much media attention has focused on a $14 billion package that remains stalled, an earlier package of $11 billion approved at the end of last year is in progress. Some of the stalled arms packages have been delayed since before Trump came into office, experts have also said.

Those include fighter jets. Taiwan received the first two of long-delayed F-16V fighter jets from the U.S. in October, and three more jets earlier this month. The aircraft are a part of a long list of backlogged U.S. orders worth almost $30 billion, according to the Taiwan Security Monitor research project which tracks defense-related developments on the island at George Mason University.

But the delays are not necessarily because of political considerations with China, a concern that was raised when Trump said he discussed arms sales with Xi earlier this year. Instead, it may be more of an issue with manufacturing capacity, particularly for future sales.

Congress approved the sale of long-range precision strike systems to Taiwan in December 2025, but Taiwan faces competition because of limited supplies. Kuo noted that among the missiles approved for sale are the same ones being used by the U.S. military in the ongoing Iran war, such as the HIMARS rockets and supplies were low.
“I don’t think this is a political issue. They just can’t produce so many of these missiles in a short period,” he said.

Meanwhile, China has intensified its military and nonmilitary pressure on Taiwan. In 2025, the People’s Liberation Army flew about 5,448 fighter jet sorties toward the island during military exercises, according to Skyfaring, an open-source website that compiles public data from Taiwan’s Ministry of Defense. That marked a sharp increase from the years before 2023, when such flights were sporadic.

Beijing also recently held unannounced military drills in the Western Pacific, deploying more than 100 vessels in waters near Taiwan and Japan, Taiwan’s National Security Council chief Joseph Wu said in a Nov. 3 post on X.
The number of PLA flights recorded this year stood at 2,401 as of Nov. 12, below the full-year total for 2025.

“I think the threat is transforming ... for example, more of its exercises are now about blockading and sealing off” Taiwan, Wang said, rather than firing live missiles. He said Beijing was expanding its gray-zone tactics — aggressive actions that fall short of open warfare.

These include greater use of the coast guard to assert China’s claims, mirroring its approach elsewhere. In June, the Chinese coast guard began patrolling off Taiwan’s east coast, which faces the open Pacific, extending its activities beyond Taiwan’s outlying islands closer to China.

Wang compared the approach to Beijing’s tactics in the South China Sea, where Chinese coast guard vessels patrol waters disputed with the Philippines. China has also designated a shoal claimed by the Philippines as a nature reserve under Chinese protection.
“It’s telling the whole world it has sovereignty here.”
Wu reported from Bangkok.

title: Outage math at the airport: When a four-hour Uber beats waiting out a ground stop
summary: Flight delays are becoming more common, causing financial and emotional stress for travelers
story: Flight delays are becoming more common, causing financial and emotional stress for travelers
CHICAGO -- New airline tickets: $300. Hours waiting for luggage: four. And the topper: a four-hour Uber ride from Detroit to Chicago that cost $400.
Call it outage math, a hellish calculation spawned by ever-more-common flight delays. This one was part of Angelina and Kyle Phoenix's anniversary trip to Chicago.

On Friday, they flew from Jacksonville, Florida, into the maw of the Great Ground Stoppage of 2026 with as many as a million other travelers. Instantly, the financial and emotional toll of the four-hour flight outage radiated outward from the airports as everyone involved scrambled for costly workarounds to a crisis no one expected, can fully explain or wants to pay for.
Emergency child care. Outrageous taxi ride fees. Rebooked tickets, lost vacation rentals and little idea what expenses might be reimbursed.

But beyond finances, travelers told The Associated Press on Monday, perhaps the most consequential cost is also the most intimate: Stress and grief over time lost — a cumulative toll that is generally not, as customer service might say, eligible for reimbursement.

Kyle Phoenix got a whiff of it more than 12 hours and hundreds of dollars of unexpected expenses into the couple’s journey, as he watched chaos unfold in the baggage claim area of Detroit airport. Officials, he noticed, had stopped announcing which canceled flights would disgorge checked baggage onto which turnstiles.
Answers were hard to come by. That made decisions about what to do next increasingly difficult.
“A lot of confusion, a lot of scrambling from a lot of people,” Kyle recalls of the scene. “I think that was probably the roughest part, not knowing anything.”

When the couple finally retrieved their luggage at midnight, the $400 Uber ride began to look like the best option. They forfeited their rebooked flight — as well as a hotel room they would have stayed in for a few hours — and embarked on the four-hour ride to Chicago.
“We just took the loss,” Angelina Phoenix said.
Dread lingers around such events because they're getting more commonplace, with no end in sight.

Even as travelers spoke to the AP about Friday's ground stop, United Airlines suffered a malfunction and halted its flights for 90 minutes. Several top U.S. banks reported significant slowdowns. And that was after AI chaos and Microsoft’s global meltdown just a few days earlier. Ahead loomed the busy Thanksgiving travel week, when TSA agents typically screen more than 2 million passengers nationwide.
It was enough to make any thinking person ask: Could everything be broken? And it forced humanity to reckon once again with the fragility of the systems that anchor modern life.

Delays are accelerating faster than the increase of scheduled passenger flights since the COVID-19 pandemic, the International Air Transport Association reported in July. Between 2015 and 2025, delays affecting scheduled passenger flights generated about $10.9 billion in costs for airlines and travelers, with sharp increases in holdups starting in 2021.
The issues are costing travelers time, which even the Federal Aviation Administration agrees is worth money.

Federal guidance issued a decade ago valued airline passengers’ time at $47.10 an hour, expressed in 2015 dollars. That's about $66 an hour today. The figure accounted for travel time that would otherwise be available for work or leisure.

More recently, an economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond estimated that last year’s 43-day federal government shutdown caused roughly 1 million additional hours of passenger delays at six airports. Economist Russell Wong calculated the lost time’s value at $66 million, based on metro area wage data and the higher-than-average incomes of people who take flights. Wong excluded canceled flights.
Harder to measure is the loss absorbed by the population downstream from the airports, including hourly workers, freelancers and caregivers — in short, everyone affected by the ripples.
Another cost: Trust in government, which has been low for years.

The nationwide shutdown, the nation's longest in 25 years, could cost billions of dollars, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said over the weekend. He blamed a contractor and aging infrastructure. President Donald Trump testily pointed to Democrats, who in turn demanded answers about how the administration has spent billions it’s already been given and why its funding request has soared to $50 billion.
Downplaying the event as a glitch with a faulty router raised questions, if not suspicions, one communications expert says.

“It wasn’t simply a crisis, it was an actual emergency of impending disaster-level scale,” Shannon A. Bowen, a journalism and mass communications professor at the University of South Carolina told “The Conversation.”
Inside airports, travelers weren't easily accepting the official explanation.

“I’m super skeptical about what we’re being told as to why this event happened at all,” said Sonia Saini Simpson, 56, whose flight from Orlando, Florida, landed in Philadelphia after hours of uncertainty, during which she said she considered renting a car to drive the nearly 1,000 miles (1,587 kilometers). “I look forward to getting some answers that are believable.”
Days after the stoppage, questions arose among some travelers about delays that sound like routine maintenance issues.
Glenn Anthony Cooper, a disc jockey, said he was told his flight from Philadelphia to Toronto on Monday had been delayed nine hours for “a hole in the tire.”

“It’s like, what’s really going on, you know? Is there something behind it, or what are they doing?” he said in an interview at the Philadelphia airport. “It’s just a bummer to just have these types of situations happen and you can’t really control it.”

The most cursory scroll through social media reveals the nightmare of Friday's historic stoppage in all its dramatic detail, much of it posted live: The 10-hour drives, the epic Uber rides, the lost wages, the stunned faces.

There's advice, too: Buy travel insurance, advised some. Don't check luggage if it's avoidable. Be nice to airline and security workers. And skip, if you can, to the acceptance phase of grief — because there's a limit to what you can control.

For young father William Ware, 24, the peak of stress may have been the moment he realized the shutdown created overwhelming traffic outside LAX that was keeping his Uber from dropping him off in time to make his flight home to Chicago to care for his child.

Ware was rebooked for the next day and could only find a hotel in Long Beach more than 20 miles away — “scary, but that was the only hotel that was available.” That meant another two Uber rides round trip back to the airport.
Maybe, Ware thinks, he'll get a refund for the ticket. But there was another cost: his time.

“I actually had to get home to my kid and I couldn’t, so it was horrible for me,” he told the AP Monday, back in Chicago at last. “I got a great support system, so my family was able to watch my child.”
Kellman reported from London. AP writers Lisa Leff in London and Mingson Lau in Philadelphia contributed to this report.

title: Malaysia-France rare earths project to begin operations in early 2027, Macron says
summary: A joint rare earths mining and processing venture between Malaysia and France is expected to begin operations in early 2027
story: A joint rare earths mining and processing venture between Malaysia and France is expected to begin operations in early 2027

KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia -- A joint rare earths mining and processing venture between Malaysia and France is expected to begin operations in early 2027 as the two nations agreed to deepen cooperation and elevate ties to a strategic partnership, French President Emmanuel Macron said Tuesday.

The project, which involves French company Carester and Malaysian firm Malaco Mining Sendirian Berhad, would cover the extraction and processing of rare earths in Malaysia, with reserved volumes and the possibility of refining in France, Macron said.

“Operations are due to begin in early 2027,” he said at a joint news conference after talks with Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim. “This will allow us to proceed ... involving not only extraction, but also processing here, with reserved volumes and capacity, including the possibility of refining in France, which is crucial for our entire value chain.”

The arrangement reflects Malaysia’s move to build domestic processing capabilities, while France seeks to secure and diversify supplies of critical minerals used in a wide range of products from electric vehicles, electronics and renewable energy to defense industries.

The two leaders said that they agreed to elevate bilateral ties to a broader strategic partnership, focusing cooperation on defense, energy, semiconductors and digital connectivity, among other areas.

Anwar said that Malaysia has made an exception in its policy against exporting rare earth minerals in return for collaboration with France in developing its rare earths industry. He didn’t provide further details. He said that cooperation with France demonstrated how resource-rich countries could work with foreign partners while securing technology transfer, training and industrial expertise.
“We do not export raw materials, but with France we have done so, because you are committed to that processing and working with the Malaysians as a team,” Anwar said.
Macron said that the partnership reflected a shared commitment to national sovereignty and greater independence in a world increasingly shaped by competing major powers.

Plans for defense cooperation will include a new industrial road map, support for a regional center to counter hybrid threats and Malaysia's procurement of combat search-and-rescue helicopters from Airbus, he said. For semiconductors, Macron said that Malaysian firm SkyeChip and French company SiPearl will collaborate to develop a high-performance computing platform.
More than 300 French companies operate in Malaysia, making France its second-largest European investor, he said.

Macron's visit was the third by a French president since diplomatic relations were established in 1957. He earlier visited Cambodia to attend a summit of French-speaking nations, before arriving late Monday in Malaysia.

title: Shoppers slowed spending in October with high prices leading to caution
summary: Shoppers increased spending more slowly in October as economic uncertainty and high prices led more Americans to become cautious with their moneyRetail sales rose 0.2% in October, down from a revised 0.8% gain in September, according to the Commerce De...
story: Shoppers increased spending more slowly in October as economic uncertainty and high prices led more Americans to become cautious with their moneyRetail sales rose 0.2% in October, down from a revised 0.8% gain in September, according to the Commerce De...

NEW YORK -- Shoppers increased spending more slowly in October as economic uncertainty and high prices led more Americans to become cautious with their money ahead of the unofficial start to the holiday shopping season.
Retail sales rose 0.2% in October, down from a 0.8% gain in September, according to the Commerce Department's report released Tuesday.
Sales at gas stations rose 1.5% last month after spiking 30.3% in September, according to the Commerce Department. Excluding gas stations, retail sales rose just 0.1%.

Overall retail sales were pulled down by decline in sales at motor vehicle and parts dealers. Auto vehicles and parts dealers had a 1.6% drop in sales in October, reversing a 1.3% increase in September.

“There are hints of weakening consumer spending as prices rise," wrote Carl B. Weinberg, chief economist at High Frequency Economics. “Let’s call this report a mixed report card on the health of the consumer."
Spending was mixed across different sectors.

Business at furniture and home furnishings stores fell 2.3%, while clothing and accessories stores declined 0.7%. Sales at consumer electronics and appliance stores were unchanged. Sales at online retailers rose 1.2%.
The data offers only a snapshot of consumer spending and doesn’t include activities like travel and hotel stays. But the lone services category – restaurants registered a 0.2% increase.
The weaker sales data followed new evidence that inflation continued to weigh on Americans last month.

Higher energy prices are ricocheting into other parts of the economy, with airfares, public transportation and shipping all jumping in price. Grocery prices, for example, increased 0.4%, a painful uptick after years of increases, according to new Labor Department data.
Massive investments in artificial intelligence have exacerbated inflation by driving up computer chip prices and, in turn, prices for laptops, phones and other consumer electronics.

Retailers are preparing for a surge in business over the Thanksgiving weekend, the unofficial start of the holiday shopping period. Stores have heavily advertised deals to lure customers who increasingly buy when they think prices have dropped.
Companies like Kohl’s and Target and Walmart are trying to drive the affordability message home through marketing.

Target said it’s offering more than 8,000 new gifts for the winter holidays, with more than half exclusive to the retailer. Most of the new holiday items at Target are $20 or less, including thousands of items that are priced at $5 and under. Kohl’s has increased the number of gift sets across different types of merchandise.
Americans, despite the rising cost of credit, continue to rely on cards to finance spending, and credit experts say that defaults have been stable.
“More Americans are carrying credit cards than ever, and they’re handling them well,” said Charles Wise, head of global research and consulting at the credit reporting agency TransUnion.

Wise noted that outstanding credit card balances as of last month hit $1.17 trillion, up 5.1% from the year-ago period, based on data covering 178.5 million consumers who held an active credit card as of last month. Yet serious delinquency rates held steady, he said.
That signals that “consumers remain disciplined borrowers heading into the holidays,” he added.

title: India seeks to triple clean energy capacity to 900 gigawatts by 2035, but major hurdles remain
summary: India has set an ambitious goal to install enough clean energy to power over 1 billion homes by 2035
story: India has set an ambitious goal to install enough clean energy to power over 1 billion homes by 2035

BENGALURU, India -- With the United Nations climate talks underway, India has set an ambitious goal of installing enough clean power to supply more than 1 billion homes by 2035, and has approved nearly $20 billion in power grid upgrades to ease bottlenecks that prevent some solar and wind energy from reaching consumers.

The world's most populous country and one of the biggest carbon polluters is also among the fastest to expand clean power. Accelerating the shift away from fossil fuels is a key goal of this year’s climate talks, known as COP31, in Turkey.

India announced the 900-gigawatt goal in late September. It covers nonfossil power sources, including solar, wind, hydropower and nuclear energy. It is nearly twice India’s existing target of 500 gigawatts of clean power by 2030. India's current clean power capacity of just over 300 gigawatts ranks it third behind China and the United States.
Experts say meeting the target could lower electricity costs, curb coal construction and accelerate the transition to clean energy.

The push comes as India struggles to use all the renewable electricity it can generate because of inadequate transmission infrastructure. The new goal refers to installed generating capacity, rather than the amount of electricity actually produced.

“If the grid doesn’t catch up, then there is no way India can meet this target,” Nikit Abhyankar from the India Energy and Climate Center at the University of California, Berkeley, said. “A robust and innovative transmission grid is an absolute must.”
The government also approved nearly $20 billion in funding for transmission infrastructure and battery storage under its Green Energy Corridor plan.
Economist Ajay Shah of the Mumbai-based XKDR Forum described the transition as the emergence of an Indian “electrostate,” in which electricity increasingly replaces coal and petroleum products.
“So now in India you have two assets — not only do you have cheap labor, you also have cheap energy,” Shah said.

The shift mirrors a global trend toward cleaner power, even as fossil fuel energy remains a key energy source amid rising electricity demand. Brazil, which ranks close behind India in clean energy capacity, projects renewables will supply nearly 90% of its electricity in the next decade, even as it expands oil and gas production. In the United States, where President Donald Trump supports fossil fuels, electricity demand is expected to grow by 40%, with natural gas remaining a major source.

India’s clean energy expansion could help industries replace costly imported fossil fuels with domestically produced electricity. Abhyankar said solar and wind power, even when combined with battery storage, are increasingly cost-competitive with power from coal, oil and natural gas.
Lower generation costs could eventually translate into cheaper electricity for households, though utilities also factor in transmission costs and other expenses.

However, India’s continued dependence on coal presents a major challenge to its clean energy transition. Coal generated about 71% of the country’s electricity in 2025, according to energy think tank Ember.

India’s power planners remain concerned about meeting growing demand and maintaining reliable electricity when solar and wind output fluctuates. Ghanshyam Prasad, chair of the Central Electricity Authority, said earlier this month that India could need as much as 150 gigawatts of additional coal-fired generating capacity by 2035.
Ember energy analyst Neshwin Rodrigues said coal will remain important for years, particularly until large-scale batteries can store solar energy to reliably meet demand when the sun isn't shining.

Existing coal plants also pose operational challenges. Many cannot quickly reduce output when renewable electricity becomes available, making it difficult for the grid to accommodate growing solar and wind power.

Researchers at Berkeley estimate that beyond approximately 35 gigawatts of coal capacity already under construction, additional coal plants would not be economically necessary under the country's new clean energy goals. Berkeley's Abhyankar warned that newly built coal plants could become stranded assets if the government meets its renewable energy targets.
Meeting the 2035 target requires more than building more renewable power plants. Their electricity must be able to reach consumers.

India’s rapid clean energy expansion is already testing the grid's limits. Although clean power accounted for 55% of installed power capacity by September, it generated about a third of the country’s electricity in the preceding three months, according to government data.
Over the past 16 months, India curtailed enough solar generation to power about 10 million homes because the grid could not accommodate it, according to government data and Ember.

The Green Energy Corridor plan aims to help states accommodate up to 135 gigawatts of renewable energy by 2033 by adding thousands of kilometers (miles) of transmission lines. The plan also includes additional battery storage.
But analysts question whether that's enough. The Berkeley researchers estimate that India needs as much as 250 gigawatts of energy storage to integrate renewable electricity over the next decade.
“You either have more transmission to get the power out and transfer it. Or if you cannot get the power out, you store it and then transfer it during some other hours,” Ember's Rodrigues said.

Shah, the economist, said two types of government policy could discourage investment in renewable energy: requirements that businesses pay higher rates to subsidize other consumers, and restrictions on electricity producers selling directly to private buyers.

He said India needs to allow electricity prices to rise and fall based on supply and demand, and make it easier for foreign investors to fund power projects. Domestic financing alone would not be enough to meet the country’s growing energy needs, he said.
“Currently, the government is a man in the middle, trying to interfere in a transaction between a private generator and a private buyer,” which creates a “choke point,” Shah said.

Battery supply chains pose another challenge, particularly India’s dependence on imported battery cells, mainly from China. Abhyankar said expanding domestic battery manufacturing could help India capture more economic benefits from the transition.

Despite those challenges, Abhyankar said India has already overtaken the United States in annual renewable energy growth, and its experience in expanding clean energy could be a model for other developing countries.
“What India is doing can be replicated in many countries in the Global South and can help these countries make the energy transition in an economically affordable manner," he said.
Sibi Arasu can be followed on X at @sibi123. Reach him at sarasu@ap.org.
