title: Tens of thousands march in Portuguese cities against surging home prices
summary: Tens of thousands of people have marched in Portugal in the biggest protest yet against surging housing prices
story: Tens of thousands of people have marched in Portugal in the biggest protest yet against surging housing prices

LISBON, Portugal -- Tens of thousands of people marched through more than 30 cities and towns across Portugal on Saturday in the largest protest yet against soaring housing costs that many say have put buying or renting a home beyond their reach.

The housing crisis has fueled weeks of demonstrations. Some activists have camped in central squares in Lisbon and Porto, the country’s two largest cities. Riot police with dogs have dispersed some protests, drawing accusations of heavy-handed tactics.
The demonstrations took inspiration from protests that began in neighboring Spain last month over similar housing concerns. They come amid widespread social unrest across Europe this autumn.

Marching under the slogan “We won’t let them steal our right to housing,” participants ranged from teenagers to retirees. Drums, music and chants accompanied the Lisbon march as protesters carried large banners and flags.

Susana Pacheco, a 35-year-old data analyst who works part-time as an astrologer to help pay her mortgage, said she worried about whether her younger sister could afford to move out of their parents’ home.
“I’m really worried about young people,” Pacheco said. “I don’t know how they’re going to be able to pay” for their own home.
“Things have become intolerable,” said Ana Encarnação, 42, citing rising living costs and the widening gap between rich and poor.
Activists want ceilings placed on rent increases, greater legal protection for tenants against eviction, and more affordable housing.
House prices in Portugal have risen much faster than incomes, statistics show.

Between 2015 and 2025, Portugal posted the biggest jump in the European Union in the home price-to-income ratio, with an increase of 61%, followed by the Netherlands with 34%, the EU statistical office Eurostat said last week.

There is no indication that the rise in housing costs is slowing. Between the first quarter of last year and the first quarter of 2026, housing prices rose by almost 20%, the National Statistics Institute, a government agency, said last month.
Rental prices, too, have climbed significantly, recording a 68% increase since 2020, according to the government.

Foreign buyers and investment funds have fueled price rises by buying Portuguese real estate. The country’s mild climate and long coastline have helped it grow popular with digital nomads and other remote workers, as well as retirees. Tourism has also surged, with many city center apartments switched to short-term rentals.

The government has responded with measures such as lowering taxes on new construction, restricting short-term rentals and promising to build 145,000 new homes. But it acknowledges that the effects won’t be immediate.

Portuguese President António José Seguro, whose role is mostly ceremonial but who wields political influence, convened a Council of State, an advisory body, to discuss the protests earlier this month and met Friday with some of the protesters.
AP reporter Helena Alves in Lisbon contributed to this story.

title: Czechs gather in big numbers to reject government's plan to overhaul funding of public media
summary: Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague against the Czech government's plan to overhaul funding for public broadcasters
story: Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague against the Czech government's plan to overhaul funding for public broadcasters

PRAGUE -- Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague on Sunday against a plan by the government of Czech billionaire Andrej Babiš to overhaul funding for public broadcasters that many say will erode media independence and democracy.
The massive protest took place at the capital's Letná Park, where huge crowds gathered during the 1989 Velvet Revolution, which ended more than 40 years of communist rule in the country.

The rally, just two days before the anniversary of the 1989 protests, drew an estimated 350,000 people, said Mikuláš Minář, the lead organizer from the Million Moments for Democracy group. They demanded that the government withdraw its plan and expressed concern that Babiš and his coalition partners pose a threat to democracy.
“We do witness here something extraordinary today,” Minář said. “It's just a beginning.”

Under the plan, the country’s public radio and television broadcasters would be financed from the state budget, replacing the existing system of regular fees paid by individuals, households and businesses. The broadcasters would receive about 15% less money than they do now, which could lead to layoffs, limited production and program cancellations.

Critics say the overhaul would give the three-party coalition the means to take control of the media, similar to what populist governments did in Slovakia under Prime Minister Robert Fico and in Hungary, before former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán was ousted from power in April.
“We refuse the Slovak scenario,” one protest banner read. “Hands off the media,” said another.

One of the protesters, singer Šarka Dumišincová, said that for her “the media represent freedom. And the fact that someone here is trying to control that freedom is unacceptable to me. That’s why I’m here today.”

The ruling coalition unexpectedly moved ahead with the plan in the lower house of Parliament on Oct. 24. Its lawmakers limited the opposition's speaking time before voting at 4:36 a.m. to advance the bill through the first of three parliamentary readings.

Thousands took to the streets the following day to protest the rushed process, and public media employees went on strike on Nov. 3. The strike was backed by labor unions, universities, students, churches, artists, athletes and international media organizations, among others.
“We are here to stand up against the rule by force in the style of 4:36,” Minář said Sunday, referring to the time the bill cleared its first reading.

Media freedom and the rule of law in the Czech Republic were debated Wednesday in the European Parliament. EU Justice Commissioner Michael McGrath said national legislation must ensure that funding for public service iis based on transparent and objective criteria and guarantees "adequate, sustainable and predictable financial resources.”
Babiš vowed to press ahead with the plan despite the protests and denied that it would affect media freedom.

He returned to power in the Czech Republic after his ANO, or YES, movement, won the country’s election last year and formed a coalition with two small political groups — the anti-migrant and pro-Russian party Freedom and Direct Democracy, and the right-wing Motorists for Themselves.
Babiš has opposed some key European Union policies on environment and migration and rejected financial aid for Ukraine and guarantees for EU loans to help it fight the Russian invasion.

His government has been under fire from NATO allies for failing to spend enough on defense. Protesters also condemned its defense policy and demanded the resignation of the Freedom party leader, parliamentary Speaker Tomio Okamura, and Defense Minister Jaromír Zůna. The party is in charge of the ministry.

"While (Russia's President Vladimir) Putin threatens Europe, the pro-Russian (party) is systematically undermining the state’s defensive capability and endangering national security,” Minář, the main protest organizer, said.
Associated Press video journalist Stanislav Hodina contributed to this report.

title: Trump heads to Asia with hopes of shifting the momentum after midterm setbacks hurt him at home
summary: President Donald Trump heads to Asia this week and he's aiming to shift the momentum after Republican losses in the midterm elections
story: President Donald Trump heads to Asia this week and he's aiming to shift the momentum after Republican losses in the midterm elections

WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump heads to Asia this week, hoping to make some big attention-grabbing moves on the world stage after his party suffered deep losses in the midterm elections, diminishing his standing at home.

The Republican president is using the international trip to try to shift momentum, and he is poised to make a splash with a historic three-way meeting with Presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia to talk about their nuclear stockpiles. Trump has long boasted about leveraging his relationships with the leaders of two of America’s biggest global adversaries, though he has failed so far to achieve major breakthroughs with them.

He first heads to the Philippines to meet on Tuesday with Southeast Asian leaders who look to the United States for help countering Beijing's aggression in the region. Trump will then go to China on Wednesday for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. There, he will have his third face-to-face meeting this year with Xi and see Putin, too.

A year ago, Trump used a similar Asia trip to agree on a trade truce with China and secure investment pledges from Japan and South Korea. This time, Trump is going with his party no longer in control of Congress as of January and with attention beginning to turn to a crop of presidential hopefuls who aim to replace him in 2028.

“I think he, like other presidents, has figured out that in a moment where things are really hard domestically: Get on an airplane and go international,” said Kurt Campbell, a former deputy secretary of state in Democratic President Joe Biden's administration and chairman of The Asia Group, a consultancy.
It's a pattern followed by some of Trump's predecessors.

Democratic President Barack Obama flew to Beijing days after his party lost the Senate in 2014 to negotiate carbon emission targets with Xi. Republican President George W. Bush went to APEC in Vietnam after the GOP lost control of Congress in 2006, though the Iraq War hung over his travels.

The White House said Trump will sign a trade deal with Thailand in Manila as well as a host of commercial deals and will be the “guest of honor” at a leaders' dinner. In Shenzhen, he will focus on trade issues before the meeting with Xi and Putin.

Trump is leaving as airlines struggled to get passengers onto flights after a nationwide ground stop on Friday led to thousands of flight cancellations. Trump and his officials have blamed their predecessors, a contractor and Congress for the problems.
Trump is about to be bogged down at home in ways that may curb what he can do overseas.

His tariffs and war with Iran proved to be poisonous with voters. Going forward, Trump's ability to threaten import taxes or military assaults — two of his major foreign policy tools — will be limited by Democratic majorities on Capitol Hill in the new year.

Just last week, in a newfound vulnerability, his push to boost artificial intelligence was complicated when Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. Beijing has said it was not involved.
Huang had traveled with Trump on Air Force One during his May trip to China, and he and his wife were at the head table when Trump hosted Xi in Washington for a state dinner in September.

Trump has argued that America needs to preserve its leadership on AI and warned of dire consequences if China wins that competition. But Trump does not plan to confront Xi on the issue, said administration officials who insisted on anonymity as a condition for previewing the president’s plans on a call with reporters.

The officials said they do not think the Nvidia situation will loom over the trip. Even though the administration is discussing ways to close loopholes and further prevent Chinese businesses from using advanced chips made by Nvidia and other U.S. companies, the officials said they do not expect the restrictions to cause retaliation by Beijing.

Trump will be accompanied by Elon Musk, the head of SpaceX and Tesla, who is the world's wealthiest man and a frequent adviser to the president. Musk spent at least $445 million to try to help Republicans keep control of Congress, and Democrats are keen to investigate his ties to the administration.

Trump may find it easier to be in the company of foreign leaders than his own crumbling coalition at home. But his words and actions at the summits are now more likely to draw scrutiny in committee hearings when he returns to Washington.
“We’re going to have a very close eye on it," said Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
Meeks and other leading Democrats on the committee have already called on the administration to provide more information about its approval of advanced AI chip exports after the Nvidia disclosures.
Democrats also will be pushing for a much tougher approach to Putin and Xi, leaders they view as authoritarian strongmen.
“It seems as though when Xi or Putin comes to America, he rolls out the red carpet for them — but other American allies come, he has not rolled out the red carpet for them,” Meeks said.

Democrats want the administration to impose tougher sanctions on Russia over the war in Ukraine and have called for the administration to fulfill an arms agreement with Taiwan, which China has sought to block.

Trump has suggested he wants to talk to Xi and Putin about nuclear weapons, an area that China has been reluctant to engage on in the past. China has a much smaller stockpile than the U.S. and Russia, giving it less incentive to agree to restraints.

The visit comes as Trump is at a crossroads over the war with Iran, which is widely blamed for his political support cratering at home. It's also a source of economic instability in Asia as jet fuel and diesel costs have soared. Trump has tried to play down the chances he will order major strikes against Iran to be resumed, though he also has said he does not see the need for talks.
Democrats are likely to scrutinize whether the president confronts Xi and Putin over r eports that China and Russia have aided Tehran, something Trump has previously dismissed.

Trump recently has played up chances for a settlement to Russia’s war in Ukraine. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not been invited to the talks in China, drawing outrage from Democrats and some Russia hawks in his own party. Administration officials said Trump is not expected to talk about Ukraine with Putin at the meeting.

The sheer number of issues hanging over Trump threatens to overshadow some important issues for the other regional leaders he'll talk to — namely the strength of U.S. support for countering China's influence in the Asia Pacific. In Manila, Trump is expected to participate in talks with the leaders of the Quad, a group of nations including the U.S., Australia, India, and Japan. It will be the first meeting of the Quad leaders since Trump returned to the White House last year.
Associated Press writer Joey Cappelletti contributed to this report.

title: New Orleans port sues to get control of tanker that crashed into cruise ship on Mississippi River
summary: New Orleans port officials have sued the owner of a tanker that slammed into a cruise ship on the Mississippi River
story: New Orleans port officials have sued the owner of a tanker that slammed into a cruise ship on the Mississippi River

Just hours after a tanker in New Orleans lost its steering and slammed into a docked river cruise boat, the city’s port sued to make sure federal investigators can seize the vessel that is owned by a subsidiary of a Chinese company.
All 197 passengers and crew on the American Heritage cruise ship survived Friday as well as the crew on the tanker.

Officials said 32 people were brought to the hospital, including two police officers thrown into the Mississippi River when the boat rolled. But none of the injuries were critical and eight remained hospitalized Saturday.
The National Transportation Safety Board said the tanker’s voyage data recorder has been recovered. A 16-member team will spend a week in New Orleans investigating the incident.
NTSB member John DeLeeuw said the agency expects to release a preliminary report within 24 to 30 days, with the final investigation report expected in 18 to 24 months.

The lawsuit, filed by the Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans, said the Atlantic Asphalt tanker caused at least $1 million in damage to its terminal. A judge issued a warrant Friday giving federal officials control of the ship for now.

The tanker has been towed away from the site, but it could take weeks to move the cruise ship, which remains turned on its side against a terminal in the Mississippi River, Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham told reporters Saturday.
The first step is to make sure the 16,000 gallons (60,500 liters) of fuel on the boat are removed safely, she said.
Traffic has been limited on the Mississippi River, but Burnham said boats should be able to move both upstream and downstream soon.
The tanker appeared to lose steering, but the exact cause of the crash is not known, Burnham said. The National Transportation Safety Board was sending investigators to New Orleans.
The first warning people on board the American Heritage had was the tanker blasting its horn several times as it floated toward the cruise ship, passenger Joe Knab told WDSU-TV.

The hit was hard, and the ship immediately started leaning. The crew gathered everyone on the third deck to put on life vests and start getting them off the boat, but it suddenly rolled and sent Knab and about 100 other passengers and crew into the muddy Mississippi River, where the water was 66 degrees Fahrenheit (19 degrees Celsius).
Tugboat operators, other cruise ship captains, nearby workers, police and other rescuers rushed to help.

“It’s fine now, but it was a little scary there at the time. I thought I was drowning because I kept bobbing underneath — and the water doesn’t taste very good,” Knab told the television station, still in the jeans he was wearing on the boat, now covered in mud.
Knab said he thinks he was in the water about 15 minutes. He laughed and said his 20 years in the Navy likely helped him.
“They taught us not to drown,” Knab said.

Knab was wearing a shirt from a Hilton hotel where the passengers gathered. The rest of his belongings were in the river. Somehow his cellphone still worked. He hoped to get on a plane soon back to Wichita, Kansas, but he was not sure how Friday’s nationwide ground stop was going to throw another problem at him.

Putting the life vests on the passengers as they waited to get off the boat likely saved a number of lives when the boat suddenly turned into the water, New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said.

“Whether it’s 10 feet of water or 200 feet, having those vests, having that population put those vests on and kind of float upriver while we retrieve them — I think was the best factor of success,” Montroll said.
The American Heritage was finishing an eight-day cruise to several Mississippi River destinations.
The Atlantic Asphalt is a 520-foot-long (160-meter-long) vessel. It had a final destination in New Orleans, according to MarineTraffic, and was sailing under a flag for the Marshall Islands.

The ship is owned by a company called Nave Shipping SA, which is registered in Monrovia, Liberia, according to the International Maritime Organization and was one of the defendants in the lawsuit filed Friday.
Nave Shipping is a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation, a sprawling Chinese state-owned conglomerate, according to the live shipping tracker MarineTraffic.
China State Shipbuilding Corp. didn’t respond to an emailed request for comment.

The tanker involved in the crash specializes in carrying large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, a semi-solid substance that is often used for road construction and roofing, according to MarineTraffic.

title: 2 planes collide on the ground in Miami, only minor injuries reported
summary: Federal aviation safety officials are investigating a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at Miami International Airport
story: Federal aviation safety officials are investigating a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at Miami International Airport

MIAMI -- Federal aviation safety officials on Sunday were investigating a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at Miami International Airport, where one aircraft's wingtip struck the nose of another, authorities said. Two people reported minor injuries.

The accident happened at about 9 p.m. Saturday and involved a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 aircraft with 172 people aboard and a UPS Boeing 767 cargo plane, according to the National Transportation Safety Board and Copa Airlines. The wing of the Copa flight and the nose of the UPS plane collided, the NTSB said.
Photos taken at the scene show the UPS plane nose with a horizontal gash on one side and a larger hole in the middle.

On audio recorded by ATC.com, a pilot on the UPS plane told air traffic control that he went too far at the intersection and his plane was clipped by the Copa flight. Air traffic control told the UPS pilot that he was supposed to yield to the Copa aircraft.

The NTSB said Sunday that preliminary information showed the UPS plane was instructed to give way to the Copa Airlines flight but did not stop. The UPS aircraft had substantial damage, while an assessment of the Copa plane had not been completed, it said. The NTSB said it opened an investigation and expected a preliminary report to be released within 30 days.
The Copa plane had just arrived from Panama City and the UPS plane was headed to Bogota, Colombia, officials said.
In a statement on social media, Copa called the collision minor and said two of its passengers were treated at the scene for minor injuries.
UPS said it was working with authorities to determine what happened.

“We cannot speculate on the details of the incident,” UPS said in a statement. “The National Transportation Safety Board is responsible for investigating incidents like this and will control the flow of information.”
The mishap came two months after an Amazon cargo plane careened off a runway at Miami International and smashed into a van carrying workers for a company that cleans airplanes, killing five people.

title: Prada’s new Milan exhibition turns a century of fashion into fresh discoveries
summary: Prada has launched a new permanent exhibition in Milan called “Pradasphere,” showcasing over a century of fashion history
story: Prada has launched a new permanent exhibition in Milan called “Pradasphere,” showcasing over a century of fashion history

MILAN -- MILAN (AP) — Iconic A-line skirts twirl overhead, silver-covered handbags gleam in a secret underground passage and a spacesuit prototype brings more than a century of fashion history into the future at Prada’s new permanent exhibition in Milan, called “Pradasphere.”

The highly visual journey through the Italian luxury brand’s evolution is connecting Prada aficionados with the fashion house’s heritage in ways that go beyond nostalgia, and already is promising a commercial payoff.
“The exhibition is a multiplier,” said Lorenzo Bertelli, Prada Group's chief group marketing officer.

Prada projects that the Pradasphere exhibition anchoring the brand's expansion in the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele shopping arcade will add 100 million euros ($111 million) in annual revenues, and Bertelli said that target could be surpassed.

Pradasphere is fully booked into the new year and Bertelli said visitors have shown a tendency to spend more after immersing themselves in the brand’s history, sometimes going back to make an additional purchase after walking through the eight Pradasphere spaces.

“We see that the customers who go through the museum have a completely different perspective of the brand and also they browse the store with completely different minds,” said Bertelli, who has been identified as the future leader of the Prada Group. The 38-year-old, whose roles include executive chairman of Versace, is the son of creative director Miuccia Prada and Prada Group chairman Patrizio Bertelli.

Longtime Prada lovers will know that Mario and Martino Prada founded Fratelli Prada in 1913 in the historic Galleria. But they may never have seen in person the luxury bags and accessories, including a pleated evening bag with a devilish head-shaped clasp, its tongue sticking out, a detail that appeared on the Spring-Summer 2024 runway.
And it may be news that the brothers designed the brand’s signature inverted triangle logo.

Miuccia Prada’s third-generation entrance into the family business is announced with trademark nylon bags that she began designing in the 1970s, embodying the Prada high-low, industrial-luxury paradox, and a chocolate brown opera coat from her first runway collection presented in 1988.

The exhibition contains many runway hits, including the 2012 Flame heels and the Formica tile prints that gave birth to Prada’s “ugly chic” reputation, while also highlighting Miuccia Prada’s and the senior Bertelli’s reach into art, architecture, film and sport.

“Curiosity and having fun is what drives my parents,” the younger Bertelli said, adding that experimentation doesn't always bring immediate financial success, “but for sure it drives the enrichment of our story, and our culture and our knowledge.”

He cited as an example investments in sports and engineering made with the formation of the Luna Rossa America’s Cup sailing team in the 1990s, which helped develop the kind of materials expertise that led Prada to collaborate with Axiom Space on a space suit, a prototype of which is displayed at the end of the exhibition.

Prada helped design the suit’s outer layer, which is engineered to withstand extreme thermal conditions, as well as the high-performance inner layer, with a focus on thermal regulation and comfort. It is intended for astronauts walking on the moon on NASA’s Artemis IV mission, targeted for 2028.
Just 20 visitors are admitted to Pradasphere by appointment each hour to explore the compact eight rooms of the exhibition, which Bertelli promises will be in constant evolution.

Prada’s presence in the Galleria now spans eight floors, encompassing the existing Marchesi 1824 pastry shop and Osservatorio Fondazione Prada contemporary art space, alongside the new exhibition, private salon and apartment.
Most visitors end their journey in a secret underground passage connecting the menswear and womenswear boutiques, the latter occupying the original Fratelli Prada premises.
The passage contains “lesser-known” chapters from the brand’s history, including a chandelier dress created for Baz Luhrmann’s “The Great Gatsby.”

“It was a great experience,” said Luca Missio, an architect from the northeastern Italian city of Udine. “I recognized the stores I’ve visited around the world, in Tokyo and New York, in the models and displays. That was lovely.”

title: An iconic puzzle comes home as production of the Rubik's Cube returns to Hungary
summary: The Rubik's Cube, invented by Hungarian architect Ernő Rubik in 1974, has become one of the world's most beloved puzzles
story: The Rubik's Cube, invented by Hungarian architect Ernő Rubik in 1974, has become one of the world's most beloved puzzles

BUDAPEST, Hungary -- More than half a century ago, a Hungarian architect, sculptor and professor invented what would become one of the world's most popular and beloved puzzles whose appeal has spanned generations: the colorful, mind-bending, six-sided Rubik's Cube.

Now, after selling more than half a billion units and becoming a worldwide cultural touchstone, production of the cube is returning to Hungary, where its inventor, Ernő Rubik, first conceived of the iconic object that bears his name.
Hungary “is the home of the cube. The cube was born here,” Rubik, 82, said on Tuesday at the opening of a new, fully automated Rubik's Cube production line in the Hungarian city of Jászberény.

The journey of the Rubik's Cube began in 1974, when Rubik was teaching design at the Academy of Applied Arts and Design in Budapest. Seeking to create a three-dimensional object that was “infinite,” he said, he completed a prototype — then made of wood — of a cube that could rotate on multiple axes and was made up of 27 blocks.

Recognizing its consumer value, Rubik soon began producing more of the puzzles. Beginning in 1977, an initial 5,000 units of what was then called the “Magic Cube” were sold at specialty shops in the Hungarian capital.

The invention — or what Rubik prefers to describe as a “discovery” — gained popularity, and after having difficulties procuring materials for the cubes in then-socialist Hungary, he realized: “We were not prepared for that size of production ... We can’t fulfill the needs of the market worldwide.”

The cube was licensed to a British and then a U.S. toy company, and its production was moved abroad. By the early 1980s, its popularity had exploded in what Rubik called “the first big wave,” in which he said 200 million units were sold between 1980 and 1983.
While sales of the cube dipped after its initial success, it still attracts plenty of users eager to try their hand at solving the puzzle. Millions are sold every year.

At the new production line in Hungary, a series of robotic arms assembles the cubes and tests them for functionality and durability — a level of automation Rubik said was “very different” than in the early days when the cubes were assembled by hand.
The new line in Jászberény plans to produce 1 million cubes annually.

Steve Radewych, a senior vice president with Canadian toy company Spin Master, which owns the Rubik's Cube trademark, said at Tuesday's opening that the theme of the day was: “Back to its roots: The cube comes home.”
“Ernő, your discovery is more than a toy,” Radewych told Rubik. “It's a global social phenomenon.”
Radewych noted the “incredible staying power” of the Rubik's Cube, and the fact that the puzzle continues to hold the fascination of young people even today.
“The cube represents an intellectual journey, a symbol of intelligence, problem-solving and cognitive discipline,” he added, which “has brought joy — and frustration — to many generations.”
The cube has enjoyed another surge in popularity in recent years as global competitions have proliferated, measuring who can solve the puzzle the fastest.
The current record, set only last month in China by nine-year-old Xuanyi Geng, is 2.51 seconds, according to the World Cube Association, which organizes and certifies competitions across the world.

Rubik, who does not consider himself a speed competitor, said that for him, the cube represents a “transformable sculpture,” the place where art and engineering meet and users can manipulate and change the cube in nearly endless variations.
“If you are doing something, creating something, you have the chance to do something that is meaningful — that’s one part — and beautiful,” he said.

title: Ten-man Portugal wins with a goal from new No. 7 in Nations League and Norway stuns Denmark
summary: Portugal had a goal from its new No. 7 and the grit to hold on with 10 players in a 3-2 win against Wales in the Nations League
story: Portugal had a goal from its new No. 7 and the grit to hold on with 10 players in a 3-2 win against Wales in the Nations League

Portugal had a goal from its new No. 7 and the grit to hold on with 10 players in a 3-2 win against Wales in the Nations League on Tuesday, but it was another shaky display following Cristiano Ronaldo's retirement from the national team.

Erling Haaland scored a last-chance penalty winner as Norway stunned Denmark 3-2 for the last quarterfinal spot. That set off wild celebrations as the Manchester City striker tore off his shirt and rushed toward the fans.

Poor defending and discipline were issues for Portugal, but there were still far more positives than in Saturday's 4-1 loss to Denmark. Portugal finished its Nations League group with five wins from six games in a campaign overshadowed by the absence of Ronaldo.
Tribute banners were again on show among the Portugal fans in Cardiff, nearly two months after Ronaldo's last game for Portugal, a 1-0 win over Wales in September.

Ronaldo fell out with coach Jorge Jesus when he was an unused substitute for the following game against Norway, and then walked out on the squad. He declared his retirement from the national team Nov. 5.

Bruno Fernandes gave Portugal the lead when he curled the ball into the top corner but it lasted just two minutes before David Brooks leveled for Wales. When Sorba Thomas put Wales ahead on a rapid counter just before halftime, it was Portugal's turn for a quickfire equalizer from Pedro Neto.
Wearing the No. 7 shirt that was for so long Ronaldo's — with a line across the number to honor Ronaldo — Carlos Forbs scored the winner in the 70th with smart movement to set up a low shot.
The 22-year-old winger is a very different player to “CR7,” not least because he's still making his name in the Belgian league with Brugge and all his three Portugal games have been off the bench.
It looked like Portugal might give the lead away again after Chelsea winger Neto was sent off for two reckless tackles in as many minutes, but Wales struggled to create many chances after that.
Denmark needed a draw against Norway to keep hold of second place and a quarterfinal place, but Haaland had other plans.
Denmark raced into an early 2-0 lead, cut by Haaland to 2-1 just before halftime. Martin Odegaard leveled the score in the 84th to ensure a nervous finish.

There was more drama at the very end with a penalty for handball against Danish defender Joachim Andersen and a lengthy video review ended with Haaland sending the goalkeeper the wrong way from the spot in the 96th minute to push Norway into second above the Danes and into the quarterfinals.
It was his 68th goal in 61 games for Norway and his 25th in the Nations League, where he is by far the competition's highest-ever scorer.
Portugal tops the group and will be one of the four seeded teams in Friday's draw along with France, Germany and England. The non-seeded teams are Norway, Belgium, the Netherlands and Spain.
The quarterfinals are played over two legs in March, with the winners heading to a final four tournament in June.

title: No. 8 Houston uses balanced scoring to beat Rutgers 85-73 in 1st round of Players Era 8 tourney
summary: Dedan Thomas Jr. scored 21 points and No. 8 Houston defeated Rutgers 85-73 in the opening round of the Players Era 8 tournament
story: Dedan Thomas Jr. scored 21 points and No. 8 Houston defeated Rutgers 85-73 in the opening round of the Players Era 8 tournament
LAS VEGAS -- Dedan Thomas Jr. scored 21 points and No. 8 Houston defeated Rutgers 85-73 on Tuesday in the opening round of the Players Era 8 tournament.
Houston (4-0) dominated midway through the first half, taking a 45-30 lead into the break and cruised to its fourth straight win to open the season.
Mercy Miller added 15 points for the Cougars and Chase McCarty scored 12. Chendall Weaver and Delrecco Gillespie scored 11 apiece as Houston showcased its offensive balance.
Rutgers (3-1) was led by Lino Mark, who scored a game-high 22 points. Christian Gurdak finished with 20.

The Scarlet Knights committed a season-high 15 turnovers that Houston converted into 21 points. The Cougars’ defensive pressure disrupted Rutgers’ offensive rhythm and created additional scoring opportunities throughout the game.
Rutgers kept pace early, briefly leading 11-10 before Houston began asserting itself on both ends of the floor.
The Cougars responded with an 8-0 run, highlighted by a 3-pointer from Weaver and consecutive baskets from Weaver and Kordel Jefferson, to establish an 18-11 advantage.
The Cougars eventually stretched their advantage to 33-17, putting the Scarlet Knights in a difficult position well before halftime.
Rutgers tried to regain momentum late in the first half, but Houston maintained control and carried a 15-point cushion into the locker room.
The Scarlet Knights showed offensive improvement after halftime, scoring 43 second-half points, but couldn’t overcome the lead Houston built in the first half.
Houston’s ability to generate offense from multiple contributors, combined with its opportunistic defense, proved too much for Rutgers, which lost for the first time this season.
Rutgers: Will play the loser of Florida/Notre Dame in the consolation round Wednesday.
Houston: Will play the winner of Florida/Notre Dame in Wednesday’s semifinal.

title: Giannis vs. the Bucks awaits for the first time, with Milwaukee visiting Miami
summary: Giannis Antetokounmpo insists that facing the Milwaukee Bucks for the first time in his career will be just another game
story: Giannis Antetokounmpo insists that facing the Milwaukee Bucks for the first time in his career will be just another game
MIAMI -- Giannis Antetokounmpo insists that facing the Milwaukee Bucks for the first time in his career will be just another game.
It's unclear if he really believes that. History says he's wrong anyway.

The first Milwaukee vs. Miami meeting of the season is Wednesday night, meaning it'll be the first time that Antetokounmpo opposes the Bucks — the franchise that drafted him and had him for 13 seasons before he was traded to the Heat. He went to Milwaukee as a teenager and left as a champion, one who holds most of the significant team records and is generally considered the best player in Milwaukee history.
“Emotions are for movies,” Antetokounmpo said. “This is just basketball.”

An admirable stance, but those who have been in this spot before — and there aren't many who have walked the path that Antetokounmpo will walk on Wednesday — tell a different tale about the day they faced their former team for the first time.
He'll be the 11th player who spent at least 895 games with one team without interruption, then left that team and faced it as an opponent.

The previous 10: Karl Malone against Utah, Tony Parker against San Antonio, Hakeem Olajuwon against Houston, Robert Parish against Boston, Paul Pierce against Boston, Patrick Ewing against New York, Gary Payton against Seattle, Kevin Garnett against Minnesota, Michael Jordan against Chicago, and Dwyane Wade against Miami.

They combined for more than 261,000 points in their careers, averaging a combined 20.1 points per game. But in those first games against their former teams, they averaged a combined 11.6 points — well below their averages, though still going 9-1 in those 10 games.
And their reactions were largely the same: When those games were over, they were relieved.
— “One of the weirdest games I’ve ever played in,” Wade said.
— “Draining, mentally and emotionally,” Parker said.
— “Very strange to be on the other side,” Olajuwon said.

There are other subplots awaiting on Wednesday in Miami. The Heat will wear new uniforms and play on a new court, part of the team's collaboration involving Thursday's release of the “ Grand Theft Auto VI ” video game — perhaps the most anticipated game release ever.

And the Bucks are coming in with former Heat players Tyler Herro, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kel’el Ware and Kasparas Jakucionis, all former first-round draft picks by Miami. The Heat plan a video tribute to welcome them back, centered around Herro.

“Part of the business,” Heat coach Erik Spoelstra said. “We did pour into them. I hope the storylines aren’t about a bunch of other things, because we developed deep relationships with those guys. ... It’s hard not to root for them. I haven’t seen a ton of their games, but I've seen a little bit. And I root for the guys that were in this uniform."

The Bucks are 1-13, having lost 10 straight. The Heat are 8-6, going 8-2 in their last 10. Antetokounmpo wasn't talking about that on Monday, strictly insisting that his pregame routine — eat the same thing, kiss his kids and get ready to play — won't change. And he still speaks highly of Milwaukee, as would be expected.
“My kids were born there,” Antetokounmpo said. “I was pretty much raised there.”
Whether the emotions are there or not, Heat forward Bobby Portis Jr. — who came to Miami from Milwaukee with Antetokounmpo — said the task when the game starts is clear and simple.
“I don't have any bad blood, bro,” Portis said. “Our only job here is to win.”

title: In scathing rebuke of college sports, former Big 12 AD calls NIL system 'money laundering'
summary: Former Iowa State athletic director Jamie Pollard equates the system that generates NIL payments to college players as a money-laundering operation
story: Former Iowa State athletic director Jamie Pollard equates the system that generates NIL payments to college players as a money-laundering operation

Former Iowa State athletic director Jamie Pollard delivered a scorching appraisal of the world he recently left, predicting college sports could be triggering the country's next savings-and-loan crisis and equating the system that generates NIL payments to players as a money-laundering operation.

“Somehow we’re taking money that was supposed to come to our institution and find a way for it to be not given to our institution so we can launder it and create a manufactured NIL deal," Pollard said Wednesday at a seminar held by the college watchdog Knight Commission.

He was referring to the practice most Power Four schools use when they work with third parties to broker NIL deals for players, which is an allowable construct that lets the schools blow past the $21.5 million revenue-sharing cap set by the landmark House settlement that allows college athletes to be paid.

Since the onset of NIL, some sports-focused donations that would normally go to an athletic department have been diverted to businesses closely affiliated to the schools. They, in turn, have negotiated the so-called third-party NIL contracts.

Pollard, who spent 21 years as the Cyclones AD before stepping down this fall, decried this process as creating a lack of transparency that “is fueling emotional and irrational decisions” made by schools.

While schools must report player contracts to the newly created College Sports Commission and the commission gives a broad-brush overview of how much money is spent, there's still very little verified information about how much each school spends on rosters or how much individual athletes make.
Without that transparency, a handful of schools are reportedly spending $50 million on football rosters to stay competitive.
“Those decisions are multiplying like rabbits,” Pollard said. “We've created distrust within our industry, (among) our colleagues.”

Pollard, whose Big 12 program was a steady presence at both men’s and women’s March Madness in basketball but rarely broke through in football, cited other research that showed about 16% of public universities lost money in at least five fiscal years between 2014-23. He linked spiraling expenses in sports as part of the reason.
A report this year from the U.S. Government Accountability Office found that 94% of NCAA Division I athletic programs spent more money than they generated in athletics revenue in 2023-24.
“If we’re not careful, we’re sitting on the next savings and loans crisis in higher education,” Pollard said.
A combination of high interest rates and poor management led to the closure of more than 1,000 savings-and-loan institutions around the country in the late 1980s and early ’90s.

Other seminar speakers included Robin Harris, the executive director of the Ivy League, and Steve Eigenbrot, the athletic director at Towson, which plays in Division I's smaller-school Football Championship Subdivision.
Harris lauded the Ivy League's efforts to stay relevant despite not tapping into revenue sharing models that all but about four dozen of the 365 schools in Division I have signed onto.
“The Ivy League remains even more committed to our model in the face of these external pressures,” Harris said.

She said in light of the recent announcement of the College Football Playoff's recent expansion to 24 teams that “it is time for a meaningful examination of the CFP and FBS football’s financial relationship with the NCAA, given the many services the NCAA provides FBS.”
FBS is the Football Bowl Subdivision that includes the Power Four and Group of Six conferences — a total of 137 teams.
Eigenbrot questioned the legitimacy of the market college sports has established for its players.

He compared the $45,000 average salary of a player in the NBA's developmental G-League — considered an option for players who don't want to attend college — against the six and seven-figure payments that often go to college players.

“I'm not so sure that if we fast forward three, four, five years down the line, that we haven't done ourselves a disservice relative to the actual name, image and likeness value of an 18- to 22-year-old,” Eigenbrot said.

title: Several teams without a Super Bowl win are positioned for a title run, led by the Bills and Jaguars
summary: Several NFL teams that have never won a Super Bowl are in strong positions to change that this season
story: Several NFL teams that have never won a Super Bowl are in strong positions to change that this season
The Super Bowl title drought club might be shrinking come Valentine's Day.

Several NFL teams that have never lifted a Lombardi Trophy are positioned to make a run at their first Super Bowl title, much like the Milwaukee Brewers recently left the ranks of Major League Baseball teams that hadn't won a World Series championship — and celebrated by doing the Lambeau Leap at a Packers game.

The Brew Crew's dominance of Tampa Bay in five games left four MLB teams that have never won it all — the Rays, Padres, Rockies and Mariners, with Seattle being the only team that hasn't reached a World Series.
There are a dozen NFL teams that haven't won the Super Bowl, including four that have never reached the big game: Cleveland, Detroit, Houston and Jacksonville.

Three of those teams are off to good starts — the Jaguars (7-2), Lions (7-2) and Browns (6-4). So are the Buffalo Bills (8-1) — who famously lost four consecutive Super Bowls in the 1990s — and Cincinnati Bengals (7-2), two other teams that have never had a Super Bowl victory parade.

A snapshot of the NFC playoff picture shows the Lions atop the ultra-competitive NFC North and the Minnesota Vikings — losers of four early Super Bowls — in fifth place with the same 7-2 record. The Carolina Panthers lead the middling NFC South at 4-5.
The Super Bowl is on Feb. 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.

Although no teams have been officially eliminated from playoff contention yet, five teams all but certainly will have to wait for another year to break free from the Super Bowl wannabe's list: the Texans (3-6), Atlanta Falcons (3-7), Arizona Cardinals (3-7), Tennessee Titans (1-8) and Los Angeles Chargers (1-8).

The Bills' only loss was 29-26 to New England in Week 4. Josh Allen is having another MVP-type season and a defense that surrendered 30 or more points to four teams early on has allowed just 9.3 points per game since their early bye in Week 7.

After hosting the Dolphins next Sunday, the Bills face a tough five-game stretch featuring home games against the Chiefs and Bears and road games at Green Bay and Denver along with a trip to New England that appears a lot less daunting with Drake Maye injured.

Trevor Lawrence and the Jaguars have been on a heater since the bye week last year, which followed a humiliating 35-7 loss to the Rams in Week 7. Since then, they've gone 16-4, and their losses have been by seven and three points to Houston, seven points to Denver and three points to Buffalo in the playoffs.
The schedule favors the Jaguars, who face five teams with losing records at the moment, including their last four: Houston, Dallas, Washington, Indianapolis.
After back-to-back losses to Pittsburgh and Jacksonville, the Bengals have won five straight, bullying their way back into the playoff picture after an extended stay on the outside looking in.
They've averaged 36.2 points during their winning streak and their remaining schedule features just two teams — Cleveland and Kansas City — with winning records.
First-year head coach Todd Monken has led the Browns to their first 4-0 start at home since 1963. After a bye this weekend, they play three in a row at home, against the Raiders, Bengals and Falcons.
That means they'll have a 42-day stretch without a road game by the time they visit the Giants on Dec. 20, their only game left aside from Cincinnati twice against an opponent with a winning record.
The downer of Detroit's big win in Munich was star Aiden Hutchinson injuring his right knee while celebrating a sack of Drake Maye in the Lions' 35-10 rout of New England on Sunday.

The Lions have a brutal upcoming schedule with two games against Chicago and trips to Minnesota and Green Bay to go with a home game against the Giants. Only three of their remaining games are against teams with losing records.

The Vikings looked like frauds in a 23-6 loss to Buffalo with Carson Wentz under center two weeks ago. Enter Kirk Cousins via a trade with Las Vegas for a third-rounder and voila, Minnesota is magic again as evidenced by its 30-10 clobbering of Jordan Love and the Packers at Lambeau Field.

Now for the hard part: they play the 49ers in Mexico City on Sunday and only three of their remaining opponents have losing records. The good news: they get Carolina, Detroit and Chicago at home down the stretch.
Carolina's 4-5 record would be good for last place in three other divisions but fortunately for the Panthers they reside in the awful NFC South, where they're the cream of a bad crop.

Half of their eight remaining games are against winning teams and the opponents that aren't above .500 include banged-up Baltimore and all three of the Panthers' division foes. Win the division crown and they'll host a playoff game against a team with a better record, renewing another round of debate about seeding the playoffs.

title: WNBA Commissioner search underway with Cathy Engelbert to retire at year’s end
summary: The search for a successor to WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert is well underway with more than a dozen candidates in the mix so far
story: The search for a successor to WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert is well underway with more than a dozen candidates in the mix so far
NEW YORK -- The search for a successor to WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert is well underway with more than a dozen candidates in the mix so far.

Engelbert, who will retire at the end of the calendar year after serving in the position since 2019, said she hasn’t interviewed anyone yet, but most likely would start once the list is narrowed down.

Engelbert presided over her final board of governors meeting Monday with representatives from all 15 teams as well as the three expansion franchises that will join the league over the next four years — Cleveland, Detroit and Philadelphia. NBA Commissioner Adam Silver was also there.
That meeting came a few days after Engelbert met with coaches, general managers and team presidents last week at the WNBA offices for the annual competition committee meetings.

Engelbert told The Associated Press when she announced her retirement that she would stay on past Dec. 31 if no replacement was in place. If the league doesn't want that, there's also the option of going with NBA Deputy Commissioner Mark Tatum, who served as the interim WNBA Commissioner for nine months before Engelbert was hired following the departure of Lisa Borders in 2018.
The next commissioner of the league will inherit a host of issues, including officiating, the transgender debate, scheduling and improving a strained relationship with players.

The league thrived in many ways during Engelbert’s tenure. Under her leadership, the WNBA enjoyed record growth and popularity, and signed a record-breaking broadcasting deal. Players surpassed million-dollar annual salaries.

But despite her accomplishments, Engelbert’s relationship with players was cordial at best, confrontational at other times. New York Liberty star Breanna Stewart may have summed it up best when said players “respect” Engelbert.
Building a stronger relationship with players likely will be one of the first things on the new commissioner’s to-do list.

title: Fils beats Jodar for 1st win at ATP Finals. Zverev vs. Shelton next in rematch of US Open final
summary: Arthur Fils has claimed his first win at the ATP Finals by rallying past fellow debutant Rafael Jodar 4-6, 6-2, 6-2 in Turin
story: Arthur Fils has claimed his first win at the ATP Finals by rallying past fellow debutant Rafael Jodar 4-6, 6-2, 6-2 in Turin
TURIN, Italy -- TURIN, Italy (AP) — Arthur Fils claimed his first win at the ATP Finals by rallying past fellow debutant Rafael Jodar 4-6, 6-2, 6-2 on Tuesday.
Now Fils needs another solid result against top-ranked Alexander Zverev in his final group match to advance to the semifinals.

Jodar appeared to be struggling physically midway through the second set and was given medicine to mix into his water bottle during a medical timeout. He also downed a banana and then a gel and an energy bar during the next changeover.
Both players lost their opening matches and Jodar is on the verge of being eliminated with two defeats.
Later, Zverev plays Ben Shelton in a rematch of the U.S. Open final.
Zverev can advance if he beats Shelton in straight sets, while Shelton can secure a semifinal spot with a victory of any kind.
The 22-year-old Fils is the first Frenchman to compete at the Finals since Gael Monfils a decade ago.
The 20-year-old Jodar is the first man to qualify for the year-end finals in the same season in which he made his tour-level debut.

summary: Vinicius Jr. has scored a first-half hat trick to help Brazil thrash Singapore 7-0 in its final game of 2026
story: Vinicius Jr. has scored a first-half hat trick to help Brazil thrash Singapore 7-0 in its final game of 2026
SINGAPORE -- Vinicius Jr. scored a first-half hat trick on Tuesday as Brazil thrashed Singapore 7-0 in its final game of 2026.

Brazil coach Carlo Ancelotti watched the soccer friendly from the stands, after receiving a red card in Saturday’s 3-2 loss to Japan, as the five-time world champion ran riot at Singapore National Stadium.
Vinicius Jr. scored both goals in that defeat and the Real Madrid forward picked up where he left off with three goals in the first 21 minutes against Singapore, ranked 148th in the world.
Unlike his spectacular long-range strikes against Japan, all three came from inside the area.
After nine minutes, the 26-year-old forward side-footed home a pass from Bruno Guimaraes. He then did the same soon after from an Endrick assist.
In the 21st, Vinicius Jr. scored into an empty net from inside the six-yard box after good work from Estevao.
Endrick added a fourth before the break and Estevao made it 5-0 six minutes after the restart.
Rayan claimed the sixth goal in the 65th and Raoul Suhaimi’s own goal completed the rout in Brazil's first meeting with Singapore, giving Ancelotti his biggest win since taking the job in May 2025.

title: Bryson DeChambeau heads slew of former LIV players on European tour for 2027 season
summary: Bryson DeChambeau will play on the European tour for the 2027 season following the demise of LIV Golf
story: Bryson DeChambeau will play on the European tour for the 2027 season following the demise of LIV Golf

Bryson DeChambeau headlined an influx of former LIV players who will compete on the European tour in the 2027 season, marking a realignment of the golfing landscape following the demise of the breakaway circuit.

DeChambeau, a two-time major champion and social-media influencer with 3 million subscribers on his YouTube channel, will add heft to a circuit that has trailed in the wake of the PGA Tour but now has a sprinkling of new — or returning — talent to raise its profile.

Courtesy of his second U.S. Open title in 2024, the 33-year-old American has taken Category 1 status for the first time on the European tour, the highest priority ranking, which means he can play in whichever tournament he chooses.
DeChambeau was planning to play the Nedbank Golf Challenge in South Africa — an event co-sanctioned by the European tour — on Dec. 4-7.
He was a star name on LIV, which announced two weeks ago in bankruptcy court it planned to wind down operations instead of launching a new version after losing the financial support of Saudi Arabia.
A return to the PGA Tour, which typically has a one-year ban on players dating to their most recent LIV appearance, will have to wait.
On Monday, PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp said his board had “thoughtful discussions” about the future of players at LIV Golf, adding: "I hope to have more to say in the beginning of the new year.”
That meant departing LIV players instead were flocking to the DP World Tour — the title name of the European circuit — that is now golf's global tour.

Eighteen players competing on LIV in 2026 are now on the European tour and they include one-time stalwarts of the circuit like former Ryder Cup stars Lee Westwood, Sergio Garcia, Henrik Stenson and Ian Poulter, via a category related to career earnings.
Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton — winners of the last two events of the 2026 European tour season — already had announced they would be returning to the tour after the collapse of LIV.

The tour added that major champions Dustin Johnson and Cameron Smith were among nine players coming off LIV to have signed agreements to receive invites to a specific number of tournaments next season.
They would not be the high-profile, lucrative Rolex Series events, but smaller tournaments where the presence of these former LIV players would “add value,” the European tour said.
The other seven players on that nine-man list were Bubba Watson, Abraham Ancer, Lucas Herbert, Michael La Sasso, Joaquin Niemann, Carlos Ortiz and Thomas Pieters.
Guy Kinnings, CEO of the European tour, said the decision to offer these invites had to be “carefully managed” by the circuit “to ensure and preserve playing opportunities for existing members.”

“There has been significant change in the landscape of men’s professional golf over the past 12 months,” Kinnings said. “As golf’s global tour, we have taken a pragmatic approach to this unique and unprecedented situation as we go into next year, always with the best interests of our entire membership at the forefront of our minds.”
Kinnings said the 2027 season was set to be “one of the most keenly contested campaigns in our 55-year history.”
The season starts next week at the BMW Australian PGA Championship.

title: Fan convicted of racially insulting Mbappé at Spanish league game

story: Real Madrid says a fan has been convicted of racially insulting Kylian Mbappé during a Spanish league game last year
MADRID -- A fan has been convicted of racially insulting Kylian Mbappé during a Spanish league game last year, Real Madrid said Tuesday.

Madrid said the fan was convicted of a hate crime and given a suspended prison sentence of 11 months following the insults directed at Mbappé in a match against Oviedo at Carlos Tartiere stadium in August 2025.
The fan, who was not named in the club's statement, was also fined. The sentence was suspended on condition the fan stay away from soccer stadiums for two years.
Other fans have previously been convicted for racial insults against Madrid players, including forward Vinícius Júnior.

title: French soccer leader Diallo set to challenge Infantino for FIFA presidency
summary: French soccer leader Philippe Diallo wants to restore “broken” trust in the sport's governance and rid the game of the “poison of division” after having confirmed his intention to challenge Gianni Infantino for the FIFA presidency
story: French soccer leader Philippe Diallo wants to restore “broken” trust in the sport's governance and rid the game of the “poison of division” after having confirmed his intention to challenge Gianni Infantino for the FIFA presidency

PARIS -- French soccer leader Philippe Diallo wants to restore “broken” trust in the sport's governance and rid the game of the “poison of division” after confirming his intention on Tuesday to challenge Gianni Infantino for the FIFA presidency.
His candidacy was ratified following an executive committee meeting at the French soccer federation’s headquarters in Paris.

“A few days ago, my colleagues from the UEFA Executive Committee asked me if I could carry this voice in the world of football," Diallo, 63, said. “I wasn’t initially a candidate, but the insistence of my European colleagues led me to accept the offer to be the candidate for the FIFA presidency.”

UEFA is pursuing legal action in U.S. courts and seeks discovery of evidence for a possible criminal complaint against Infantino in his and FIFA’s home country Switzerland alleging financial mismanagement.
FIFA accused UEFA of a “smear campaign” against its president in a court filing in Colorado.

Concerns include Infantino seeming to act alone in creating a peace prize for U.S. President Donald Trump last year and, at the World Cup, letting United States forward Folarin Balogun avoid a mandatory ban for a red card after Trump intervened.

“Since a few months there have been a series of decisions taken inside FIFA: I think of the peace prize, I think of the distribution of revenue of television rights in the United States, the red card for Balogun, the length of the halftime break in the final and the private investors (sell-off plan),” Diallo said.
“All of these decisions shocked the world of football in a very big way, the fans, the clubs, the sponsors, the federations.”
Diallo said “there are a lot of questions” for Infantino and that the turmoil and fall-out has seriously damaged the game.
“It created a situation this summer whereby the trust placed in FIFA and it’s president was broken," he said. “They have damaged the image of football and have introduced the poison of division.”
UEFA, European soccer’s ruling body, proposed Diallo on Monday after a meeting of its 21-member executive committee that includes the French Football Federation president.

“It was important that another voice can carry another vision, more respectful toward what we love in football," Diallo added on Tuesday. “I could not shy away from the demands. I think I have the experience, the convictions and the values which offer a credible alternative.

“I think with my candidature comes hope of a change. It is support of my European colleagues and my executive committee which allows me to say this. Football deserves a credible change which I represent. I am candidate for the FIFA presidency. What happened in recent months was shocking.”
Diallo sat smiling alongside Zinedine Zidane when he was announced as France’s new national team coach in late July.

Diallo is a long-time soccer administrator with French clubs, and the league, who rose to interim president at the FFF in January 2023, before being fast-tracked in an election of UEFA member federations to join the European body’s executive committee.
Diallo has worked for world soccer's ruling body FIFA as a judge on its Dispute Resolution Chamber, handling contract disputes between players and clubs.

Until his emergence, speculation on a candidate focused on Qatari soccer and broadcast executive Nasser Al-Khelaïfi, the president of Champions League titleholder Paris Saint-Germain and a UEFA executive committee member. He said he would not run against Infantino, who has backing from Qatar.
Focus them shifted onto former Arsenal coach Arsène Wenger, hired by FIFA since 2019 as the global head of developing the game. He made it clear he would not stand.

When the World Cup ended on July 19, Infantino was set to be re-elected unopposed effectively by a coronation. FIFA said he had about 200 letters of support from the 211 member federations who will vote in March in Rabat, Morocco.
One of those letters was from France.

But Diallo formally withdrew the FFF in September, citing that trust in Infantino was broken by the World Cup sell-off plan secretly devised with Joshua Kushner, the younger brother of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.

“The last time I saw him (Infantino) was at the World Cup, he came to a few France games. I have known him for a long time," Diallo said. “I regret, as others did, that he did not share the ideas of his projects ... it was an unacceptable act of defiance."

Diallo said the 48-team men’s 2026 World Cup generated record profits of $15-16 million, vastly more than the 2022 edition of 32 teams in Qatar. Therefore the sell-off plan, which “no one really understands", was totally baffling.
“FIFA’s (cash) reserves are $5-6 million,” Diallo said. “We find it hard to understand ... the need to find private investors to bring further billions, when these billions are already here.”
Infantino has promised at least $25 million in development funds to each member federation through 2030.

“On the basis of (cash) reserves that had lay dormant for years and would still be dormant in FIFA accounts if we had not intervened,” Diallo said. “There are a lot of things that need answering, there is no clarity regarding this and there are curious strategies.”
Germany coach Jürgen Klopp said he’d welcome a new FIFA president and that Infantino has turned out worse than Blatter.

“To beat him I need 106 votes, the absolute majority,” said Diallo, who will announce his campaign team in Belfast in early December. “I will have a clear program of solidarity and excellence, and guarantee those who love soccer that these values will be respected.”
He can count on the support, too, of French President Emmanuel Macron.

“The President supports my candidature,” he said, adding that he has been “pleasantly surprised” by the number of people from the African and Asian soccer federations who have offered him their support since his candidacy became known.
