title: Trump administration moves to block China from indirect access to American AI technology
summary: The Trump administration has issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers
story: The Trump administration has issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers

WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best artificial intelligence models.

Last week, Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following scrutiny of his ties to a Chinese executive who used to lead Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. The company provides computing power to Chinese companies using chips housed in Southeast Asian data centers, including facilities in Malaysia.

“The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries,” the Bureau of Industry and Security under the Commerce Department said in issuing the rule that took effect immediately.
The rule came on the same day President Donald Trump departed for a trip to Asia, where he expects to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the third time this year amid a fragile truce on trade.

Under the new rule, overseas data centers that serve companies in countries including China, Russia, Iran and Cuba are required to identify their end users. There also will be additional licensing requirements for sales of chips for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil — countries that “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" to unauthorized destinations, the rule says.

In Beijing, China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun accused Washington of arbitrarily interfering with China's trade and technological cooperation with other countries and suppressing the development of China's high-tech industries.

“This is a typical example of economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction, runs counter to the common understanding between the two sides,” he told reporter, adding that it infringes upon the rights of Chinese companies and disrupts the stability of global supply chains.
He said China would take necessary measures to safeguard its interests.

The U.S. bans sales of the country's most advanced AI chips to China, seeking to maintain an edge in its rivalry with China for predominance in artificial intelligence. However, many lawmakers and policymakers believe the country's export control rules are not tough enough and filled with loopholes such as cloud computing that allows China to rent processing power built on American technology.

Last year, U.S. Rep. Michael Lawler, a New York Republican, introduced a bill to broaden the U.S. export controls to include remote access. He told Congress “physical export controls” under current rules do not apply to remote access, allowing China to “access our tech through the cloud” and giving it “a real tool to sidestep” U.S. export restrictions. The bill has passed the House.

In the Senate, lawmakers also are seeking tougher legislation to prevent China from accessing advanced U.S. chip and AI technologies. Bills include proposals that would let Congress review licenses to sell advanced AI chips to China, ask the Department of Commerce to track AI chips to ensure they are not diverted to unauthorized regions, and compel U.S. allies such as the Netherlands and Japan to match U.S. restrictions on exports to Chinese chipmakers.
Last week, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick came under pressure when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Commerce Department was late to place restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed.

On Monday, Trump acknowledged tension between Treasury and Commerce on the matter. He suggested that Lutnick may have delayed placing the export restrictions to avoid a “blow up” in the fragile U.S.-China relationship.
“We’re having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, Trump said.

In a joint statement late Monday by the Commerce and Justice departments, it said Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed for potential export control violations in 2024, which was followed by requests to Nvidia for records in May 2025 related to sales to Megaspeed. The following month, it said, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list, and agents from the Commerce Department in conjunction with Singapore law enforcement conducted on-site checks of Megaspeed and interviewed Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang. The Justice Department then took the lead role in the criminal probe of Megaspeed, the statement said.

“The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” the statement said.

Last week, the Singapore government confirmed that it had investigated Megaspeed over “potential false declarations" involving servers that were exported through Singapore to Malaysia but might have “subsequently been routed from Malaysia to another destination, contrary to declaration made in Singapore.”
The Malaysian government also said last week that it was investigating if chips brought into Malaysia have been re-exported to other countries as permitted by its own law.

“Malaysia welcomes investment in data centers and technology, but will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls,” read the Friday statement by Malaysia's Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry.

title: Apple joins a parade of technology hiccups in recent days
summary: A pair of technology failures at Apple and Marriott International follows several other recent major outages at the Federal Aviation Administration, United Airlines and Microsoft, highlighting the risks of relying on just a few major providers of essen...
story: A pair of technology failures at Apple and Marriott International follows several other recent major outages at the Federal Aviation Administration, United Airlines and Microsoft, highlighting the risks of relying on just a few major providers of essen...
An update gone awry Tuesday at Apple followed a rash of major outages in recent days, including problems affecting the Federal Aviation Administration, United Airlines and Microsoft.

Apple acknowledged on its system status page that its Apple Music, App Store and AppleCare services suffered full outages and that its iCloud sign-in interface was also having issues. The technology monitoring site Downdetector.com also showed a spike in user complaints about Apple Pay.

“Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,” the company said in an emailed statement. “We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.”

Marriott International, the largest U.S. hotel operator, also had technology issues affecting reservations and check-ins, among other problems, according to users posting on Reddit. Downdetector.com also reported that Marriott was experiencing an outage.
Marriott, which has 10,200 properties and more than 1.8 million rooms under its corporate umbrella, did not immediately respond to an email inquiry from The Associated Press.
The outages are the latest in a string of technology breakdowns.

On Monday, a system outage at United Airlines lasted more than 90 minutes, forcing the carrier to delay departing flights. The problem at United came just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s network prompted a nationwide ground stop that delayed hundreds of flights and stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers across the country.
Chicago-based United said there was no indication its outage was cybersecurity-related.

Also Monday, thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.
Chase said Monday the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack, and on Tuesday confirmed the bank's systems were operating normally.

Last week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business chatter and everyday services into disarray worldwide. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted.

The tech giant said there was “no indication” that malicious activity caused the disruptions, specifically noting on Friday that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.

title: Taiwan may take a backseat when Xi and Trump meet for a third time at an APEC summit
summary: Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet at the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week
story: Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet at the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week

TAIPEI, Taiwan -- Taiwan is likely to be overshadowed as presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week, even as the threat from China evolves and grows stronger.

Leaders from China, the U.S. and some 21 other economies will gather at the APEC summit this week in Shenzhen, China. Recent events like the scandal that forced Nvidia's CEO to resign, export controls and the ongoing trade dispute have made the tech competition between Beijing and Washington all the more pressing.

Few expect major breakthroughs on Taiwan, a self-ruled island that is claimed by Beijing. While the U.S. does not formally recognize Taiwan, it is the island’s biggest informal ally and seller of arms.
“For the Trump administration, this isn’t a core issue between the U.S. and China,” said Arthur Zhin-Sheng Wang, an expert on cross-Straits relations at Taiwan’s Central Police University.
Experts largely say that cooperation with the U.S. remains strong below the level of rhetoric, despite Trump’s public ambivalence toward Taiwan.

One sign of this came from the summer, when the de facto United States embassy in Taiwan posted a photo showing joint patrols between the two coast guards, a rare occurrence, as the U.S. does not usually acknowledge it has direct cooperation with Taiwan in any defense capacity.

“This also is proof of the decades that Taiwan and U.S. have had of cooperation and training. I was also surprised,” said Kuo Yu-jen, a defense studies expert and director of the Institute for National Policy Research in Taiwan.

The U.S. is obligated by law to help Taiwan defend itself, which has manifested in the form of arms sales, while the government officially adopts a stance of ambiguity on whether it would intervene militarily in the case of a Chinese invasion.

The Taiwanese public is used to the continued uncertainties of the island’s relationship with the U.S. Research from the Institute of National Defense and Security Research in Taiwan, a government-funded think tank, showed that public attitudes toward the U.S. remain around the same. Polls conducted in the past five years show that about half of the public believes the U.S. will send soldiers to support Taiwan in the event of a Chinese invasion, and about half don’t.

“I do think they will take some actions, though it may not be sending soldiers,” said Allen Hsieh, a 28-year-old media professional in Taipei. “I think Taiwan’s importance to the U.S. is even more important than Ukraine.”
Since starting his second term, Trump called for Taiwan to spend more on its own defense and Taiwan responded that it would commit to 5% of its GDP on defense.

Arms sales are ongoing. While much media attention has focused on a $14 billion package that remains stalled, an earlier package of $11 billion approved at the end of last year is in progress. Some of the stalled arms packages have been delayed since before Trump came into office, experts have also said.

Those include fighter jets. Taiwan received the first two of long-delayed F-16V fighter jets from the U.S. in October, and three more jets earlier this month. The aircraft are a part of a long list of backlogged U.S. orders worth almost $30 billion, according to the Taiwan Security Monitor research project which tracks defense-related developments on the island at George Mason University.

But the delays are not necessarily because of political considerations with China, a concern that was raised when Trump said he discussed arms sales with Xi earlier this year. Instead, it may be more of an issue with manufacturing capacity, particularly for future sales.

Congress approved the sale of long-range precision strike systems to Taiwan in December 2025, but Taiwan faces competition because of limited supplies. Kuo noted that among the missiles approved for sale are the same ones being used by the U.S. military in the ongoing Iran war, such as the HIMARS rockets and supplies were low.
“I don’t think this is a political issue. They just can’t produce so many of these missiles in a short period,” he said.

Meanwhile, China has intensified its military and nonmilitary pressure on Taiwan. In 2025, the People’s Liberation Army flew about 5,448 fighter jet sorties toward the island during military exercises, according to Skyfaring, an open-source website that compiles public data from Taiwan’s Ministry of Defense. That marked a sharp increase from the years before 2023, when such flights were sporadic.

Beijing also recently held unannounced military drills in the Western Pacific, deploying more than 100 vessels in waters near Taiwan and Japan, Taiwan’s National Security Council chief Joseph Wu said in a Nov. 3 post on X.
The number of PLA flights recorded this year stood at 2,401 as of Nov. 12, below the full-year total for 2025.

“I think the threat is transforming ... for example, more of its exercises are now about blockading and sealing off” Taiwan, Wang said, rather than firing live missiles. He said Beijing was expanding its gray-zone tactics — aggressive actions that fall short of open warfare.

These include greater use of the coast guard to assert China’s claims, mirroring its approach elsewhere. In June, the Chinese coast guard began patrolling off Taiwan’s east coast, which faces the open Pacific, extending its activities beyond Taiwan’s outlying islands closer to China.

Wang compared the approach to Beijing’s tactics in the South China Sea, where Chinese coast guard vessels patrol waters disputed with the Philippines. China has also designated a shoal claimed by the Philippines as a nature reserve under Chinese protection.
“It’s telling the whole world it has sovereignty here.”
Wu reported from Bangkok.

title: Glasses and shirt buttons will be examined to stop cheating in South Korea's college entrance exams
summary: Proctors in South Korea will inspect every test-taker’s glasses and seal their shirt buttons with stickers
story: Proctors in South Korea will inspect every test-taker’s glasses and seal their shirt buttons with stickers

SEOUL, South Korea -- Proctors will inspect every test-taker’s glasses and seal their shirt buttons with stickers, and authorities will deploy 8,400 additional supervisors at South Korea’s college entrance exams on Thursday.

The country will also send an emergency alert that will set nearly all mobile phones in the country buzzing for about 10 seconds that morning, using a tool typically reserved for major crises like large earthquakes or war to expose any devices hidden by test-takers.
The sweeping measures to fight cheating are in response to concerns that artificial intelligence and smart devices are making fraud harder to detect.

More than 550,000 people will participate in the exam at around 1,300 test sites in what’s a pivotal annual event for the country. South Korea is known for its intense academic competition, where job opportunities, social standing and even marriage prospects often hinge on which school a person attends.

Concerns about cheating grew after the top scorer on a national tax accountant exam admitted to using a hidden camera, a smartphone and generative AI tools to obtain answers, the latest in a string of AI-assisted cheating cases to affect exams in recent months.

In a televised briefing on Tuesday, Prime Minister Han Seongsook said that proctors will use metal detectors on test-takers who act suspiciously to search for hidden devices and that the exam ban for cheaters will be lengthened from the current one year to 10. College students retaking the exam to go to different universities will be expelled from their current schools if they are caught cheating, in addition to facing a 10-year ban on entering any school, Han said.

Test-takers will be prohibited from bringing electronic devices such as smartphones, smart glasses and smart watches, or any object with a camera, and failing to hand them over to proctors before the exam will be treated as cheating, regardless of whether they were used.

Those who wear glasses will be asked to place them on the desk for inspection before the exam, and supervisors will monitor for smart glasses throughout the hourslong test. Han advised test-takers to avoid clothing with buttons, and any buttons will be covered with stickers to guard against hidden cameras.

She said that global technology companies that operate AI chatbots have also agreed to cooperate with any post-exam investigations into suspected cheating, such as queries involving photographed test pages.

The “Suneung,” or the College Scholastic Ability Test, is a crucial annual event for which the education-obsessed country goes to extraordinary lengths to create an ideal testing environment. The start of work hours and stock trading are delayed to ease traffic for test-takers, and flights are halted during the English listening section. Police often use cars or motorcycles to escort test-takers who are running late, while the military sometimes suspends training near testing sites.

Growing public concerns about AI-assisted cheating have drastically raised the stakes for this year’s exam, with some experts and politicians even calling for the government to postpone the test until reliable anti-cheating measures are in place.

President Lee Jae Myung, who is in the Philippines for a regional summit, chaired an emergency meeting by video to review the government’s exam preparations and vowed a stern, “zero-tolerance” response toward anyone caught cheating. He also instructed officials to consider sending more text alerts at unpredictable times during the exam.
“Would even the boldest student risk getting dragged out during the test because their telecommunications device went off?” Lee said on his X account.

Vice Education Minister Choi Eun-ok said that “there could be critics who say our measures are excessive, but a failure to conduct Suneung in a strict and fair manner will bring a (major) disruption to our society that would really be worse than a disaster.”
“We believe we are in a situation where excessive measures are necessary,” Choi said.

Government officials scrambled to strengthen anti-cheating measures this week after a 34-year-old man who topped a national tax accountant exam confessed in a video posted on his lawyer’s YouTube channel Sunday that he had used a hidden microcamera and smartphone to obtain answers from AI.

Han Won-seok’s unusually high scores had drawn suspicion after he discussed them during recent media interviews. The case follows other incidents involving AI-assisted cheating in the past several months, including test-takers caught using AI-powered smart glasses on an English standardized test in June and on some university essay exams in October.
Han Won-seok told reporters he would cooperate with the criminal investigation into his actions as he arrived for questioning by Seoul police on Tuesday.

title: AI cheating fears spook South Korea ahead of high-stakes college entrance exam
summary: South Korean officials are scrambling to prevent cheating on a national college entrance exam using technology
story: South Korean officials are scrambling to prevent cheating on a national college entrance exam using technology

SEOUL, South Korea -- Days before South Korea comes to a standstill for its all-important college entrance exam, the nation is reeling after the top scorer on its tax accountant test was found to have cheated with a hidden camera and artificial intelligence.

The scandal has left authorities scrambling to prevent cheating on the exam, which will be taken Thursday by more than 500,000 students, as concerns grow that AI and smart devices are making fraud harder to detect.

Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin on Monday rejected calls by some lawmakers to postpone the exam until stronger anti-cheating measures are in place, telling a legislative hearing that a delay would cause “even a larger disruption” to students.

Choi said that he was confident that proctors could spot AI-powered smart glasses, which typically have thick, horn-rimmed frames. Education authorities are also offering guidance on detecting devices such as microcameras, Education Ministry officials said.

Worries about cheating deepened over the weekend after a 34-year-old man who scored the highest on a national tax accountant exam confessed to using a hidden microcamera and smartphone to get answers from AI.

Han Won-seok’s unusually high scores had drawn suspicion after he discussed them during recent media interviews. The case follows other incidents involving AI-assisted cheating in the past several months, including test-takers caught using AI-powered smart glasses on an English standardized test in June and on some university essay exams in October.

In a video posted Sunday on his lawyer’s YouTube channel, Han said that he used a concealed camera to capture the questions, fed the images to a generative AI tool and received answers on a smartphone. He said that he would cooperate with police, who are investigating the case.

Han had previously said that he scored 397.5 out of a possible 400 points on the first-stage, multiple-choice test in April, and 663 out of 800 on the second-stage essay exam in July, unusually high marks that one Korean newspaper likened to “running a 100-meter sprint in under five seconds.”

The national college entrance exam, known as “Suneung,” or the College Scholastic Ability Test, is a high-stakes annual event in a country notorious for intense academic competition, where prospects for jobs, social standing and even marriage can depend on which university a person attends.

South Korea goes to great lengths each year to create an ideal testing environment, effectively bringing the country to a standstill by delaying the start of the workday and stock market trading to ease traffic for test-takers and pausing flights during the English listening section of the exam. Police officers often use cars and motorcycles to escort test-takers who are running late, while the military sometimes suspends training in areas near testing sites.

But it’s difficult for authorities to come up with equally sweeping measures to prevent cheating with AI devices, which the Seoul-based Hankyoreh newspaper warned in an editorial Monday could threaten “the very foundations of the examination system.”

Education authorities had focused for months on preventing the use of AI-powered glasses, but Han’s case has raised doubts about whether they are prepared for cheating involving other, less conspicuous devices.

Education authorities will deploy at least one specially trained supervisor at each of the 1,300 test sites nationwide to identify such glasses. Officials also are considering requiring test takers to hand over their smart devices and shutting down public Wi-Fi connections at test sites, according to Prime Minister Han Seongsook's office.

Song Geun-hyeon, another senior Education Ministry official, said that the ministry has provided proctors with new guidance on detecting test-takers using hidden cameras and other devices, including watching for suspicious movements involving “their sleeves, collars or buttons, and certain gestures.”
The ministry was working with the Ministry of Science and Information and Communication Technology on anti-cheating measures for the college entrance exam, which are due to be announced on Tuesday.

Vice Education Minister Choi Eun-ok said that the discussions with the science ministry also include temporarily restricting telecommunications at test sites. It wasn't immediately clear whether that's feasible, considering laws prohibiting electronic signal jamming, or concerns that it could interfere with communication in surrounding areas.

Song said that metal detectors and radio detectors would be limited, while deploying thermal cameras would be highly unlikely because of privacy concerns. Supervisors can't search belongings without the consent of the test-takers.

“At the government-wide level, we would also need to give further consideration to measures that will make it easier to identify (AI) smart devices,” said Song, adding that officials are debating whether to require manufacturers to design the devices to emit “flashing lights or sounds” while in use.

title: Measles is surging in the US. Here’s how the Trump administration has responded
summary: International health experts have decided that the U.S. has lost its status as a country that eliminated the continuous spread of measles
story: International health experts have decided that the U.S. has lost its status as a country that eliminated the continuous spread of measles

WASHINGTON -- With the U.S. experiencing its worst year for measles in decades, international health experts have decided that the U.S. has lost its status as a country that eliminated the continuous spread of the disease.
The U.S. has racked up more measles cases than in any year since 1991, with confirmed cases surpassing 5,000 in 2026, according to the latest data. Pennsylvania alone has seen more than 1,500 cases.
The Pan American Health Organization 's decision underscores a significant public health setback for the United States as the Trump administration reshapes federal vaccine policy.

Experts say that while the Trump administration did not create the underlying vaccination problem — which predates President Donald Trump’s return to office — the Republican administration's policies and public messaging may have exacerbated it.

Asked about the administration's response to the outbreak, the Department of Health and Human Services referred to a statement by Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director Erica Schwartz, which said it would remain focused on stopping outbreaks, despite losing the measles designation.

Nationally, 92.4% of kindergartners received their required measles-mumps-rubella shots in the 2025-26 school year, down from 92.5% the previous year and 95.2% in 2019-20, according to data from the CDC. That is below the approximately 95% coverage needed to prevent measles outbreaks, and some communities have substantially lower vaccination rates.
Here's a look at how the Trump administration has handled the worst year for measles in more than three decades:

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has a long record of questioning vaccine safety, has repeatedly promoted claims that vaccines are associated with autism, despite extensive scientific evidence finding no causal relationship.

And he has delivered mixed messaging on measles specifically. He has occasionally endorsed the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine as “effective,” but also continues to raise unfounded safety concerns about the shots. In August, he told CNN: "I believe that the MMR vaccine prevents measles.” In that same interview he questioned the safety of the vaccine.

Trump reinforced those doubts at an event over the summer where he signed an executive order calling for splitting up the MMR vaccine. He said falsely that taken together the shot was “quite lethal.” Doctors say, and years of real-world evidence prove, that the combination MMR vaccine is both safe and effective at protecting children from illness.
Separate vaccines for measles, mumps and rubella are not available in the United States and producing them that way would be a logistical feat for drugmakers.

Josh Michaud, associate director of global and public health policy at healthcare research nonprofit KFF, said past administrations back to the 1990s, when confronted with measles outbreaks, were aggressive in telling the public how important vaccination is against the disease. That’s not happening now, he said.
"What we’re not seeing from the administration is strong communications about the need for vaccinations,” he said.

During the most recent measles outbreak, Kennedy promoted vitamin A as a possible treatment, which created concern among medical professionals that the administration was giving undue attention to alternatives rather than emphasizing vaccination.
Throughout the surge of measles cases, Kennedy has repeatedly challenged health officials’ accounts of deaths from the disease.
In August, Pennsylvania officials reported two measles-related deaths. The county coroner later said they involved infants too young to be vaccinated, with the virus itself causing one of the deaths.

After Gov. Josh Shapiro stressed that vaccinations could have averted the deaths, Kennedy said the deaths “may even have been altogether fabricated.” He later acknowledged that one of the deaths was due to measles.
The remark echoed similar statements he made after last year, when three measles-related deaths were recorded. Kennedy questioned whether one of the children who died was killed by measles.
Medical experts said the political quarreling over the deaths diverted focus from an exploding public health threat.

As health secretary, Kennedy has spearheaded an overhaul of the nation's vaccine policy. Last year, he fired all 17 members of a key vaccine advisory committee and hired vaccine critics among the replacements. In January, his department downsized the childhood immunization schedule. The moves were temporarily halted by a judge earlier this year.
Kennedy also acknowledged personally directing the CDC to update its website late last year to contradict its longtime guidance that vaccines don’t cause autism.
Critics say the overhaul and the administration's overt questioning of immunization safety have fueled skepticism about vaccines.

Surveys indicate growing public wavering over support for the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine. An August 2025 Annenberg survey found that 82% would be “very” or “somewhat” likely to recommend that an eligible child in their household get the MMR vaccine, compared to 90% in November 2024.

Kennedy has defended his upending of federal health policy by saying the changes will restore trust in America’s public health agencies. Doctors counter that the false and unverified information he promotes and the vaccine policy changes undermine confidence in vaccination and leave more people vulnerable to preventable disease.

Along with freezing and canceling billions in research under Kennedy’s leadership at the start of the Trump administration, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services laid off more than 10,000 workers and shut down entire offices and programs. Experts say those cuts may have impacted state and local health departments’ ability to adequately respond to outbreaks.

PAHO officials expect the U.S., along with Bolivia and Mexico which also lost their elimination status, to each submit a plan “in the coming weeks” for how they will go about trying to stop transmission for at least a year and regain measles elimination status, said Dr. Daniel Salas, PAHO’s executive manager for immunizations.
A decision to strip the U.S. of its measles elimination status will not change how federal health officials are addressing outbreaks, Schwartz said.
“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans,” she said. “Vaccination does.”

She said federal officials have invested $100 million to help state and local health departments to reach communities with measles outbreaks. “Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.”
Michaud said the designation change is “a marker for how we backtracked on public health, particularly related to measles prevention, and particularly related to vaccines.”
“It encapsulates this idea that the United States is more vulnerable than ever to infectious diseases," he said.

title: LeBron James sues makers of AI sports-betting app, saying they used his likeness
summary: NBA superstar LeBron James has sued the makers of an AI sports-betting app, saying they deliberately violated his publicity rights and trademarks by calling it “Bron” and using artificially generated images of him in their marketing
story: NBA superstar LeBron James has sued the makers of an AI sports-betting app, saying they deliberately violated his publicity rights and trademarks by calling it “Bron” and using artificially generated images of him in their marketing

NBA superstar LeBron James sued the makers of an AI sports-betting app Tuesday, saying they have deliberately violated his publicity rights and trademarks by calling it “Bron” and using artificially generated images of him in their marketing.
In a lawsuit filed in U.S. District Court in New York, James' attorneys called it “a willful, bad-faith tactic” to use the player's fame, likeness and nickname to promote “a new and unknown product.”

The complaint asks the court to block the makers from using the Philadelphia 76ers star's name, to give up any money they've already made, and to award damages — including fair market value for the use of his name as well as punitive damages.

“Defendants did not care that they had engaged in illegal conduct to gain notoriety for their previously unknown app,” the lawsuit states. “They intentionally created the false impression that Mr. James endorsed and was affiliated with their Bron App, in an effort to drive downloads and paid subscriptions."
Messages sent by The Associated Press through the app’s website and to email addresses for its founders seeking comment were not immediately returned Tuesday.

The app’s developer, PlayVision Inc., is based in California. It was launched by Chief Executive Anish Gupta and Chief Technology Officer Marc Zoghby in 2025, with backing from the startup accelerator Y Combinator, as a program that would use artificial intelligence to analyze game and practice footage for sports teams and fans.

This year, the company released its “Bron” app, which it says does not take direct wagers but charges a subscription fee for services like bet tracking and odds comparisons. It launched a marketing campaign this month that featured an image of a person resembling James — down to his tattoos, voice and number 23 jersey — sitting in a locker room and scrolling through the app.

James' lawyers sent a cease-and-desist letter, as previously reported by Front Office Sports. The company took the ad down, but not before it had been reposted and viewed about 1 million times, the lawsuit said.

Gupta responded to the attorneys' demand on social media by writing that the app would get a new name, but no new name had been adopted by the time the lawsuit was filed, leading James' legal team to suggest the company was milking the controversy for attention. Gupta wrote on social media this week that the new name will be announced Wednesday.

The lawsuit notes that James typically commands tens of millions of dollars for such endorsement deals, and that he already has an exclusive deal with the prediction market platform Polymarket. It alleges that the app's marketing was especially harmful in part because it showed the AI-generated James scrolling through bets involving NBA players.

“The integrity of NBA competition — and the public’s confidence that players are not betting on the games they play — is of paramount importance to the league, its players, and its fans,” the lawsuit said. “Any suggestion that an active NBA player is betting on NBA games is therefore far from a trivial matter, and it should not be used for clicks and views."

title: In closings, Chinese tech giant Huawei is cast by prosecutors as a villain as its lawyer disagrees
summary: The racketeering conspiracy trial of Huawei Technologies is drawing closer to an end after two days of closing arguments
story: The racketeering conspiracy trial of Huawei Technologies is drawing closer to an end after two days of closing arguments

NEW YORK -- The racketeering conspiracy trial of Huawei Technologies approached its end Tuesday after a prosecutor told jurors that the Chinese telecommunications giant helped Iran spy on its citizens and steal from U.S. companies and a defense lawyer accused the U.S. of embracing a false narrative.

Defense attorney Brian Heberlig said in a closing argument in Brooklyn federal court after a two-month-long trial that federal prosecutors “decided Huawei was a criminal enterprise” and built a case from that premise.
“They began with guilt and worked backwards,” Heberlig said. “When the evidence didn't fit, they moved the goalposts.”

He spoke a day after Assistant U.S. Attorney Meredith Arfa said the company for two decades encouraged a workforce of over 200,000 workers in 170 countries to lie, cheat and steal “for a competitive advantage to grow and protect its business.”
She said Huawei had committed crimes targeting American companies, the U.S. financial system and the American government while providing Iran with the equipment to spy on its citizens.

Huawei is the world’s largest supplier of gear for wireless telecom networks, but it is not allowed to sell equipment to U.S. carriers over fears it poses a security risk. It has also been blacklisted by other Western allies, including Canada and Britain.
Heberlig credited Huawei’s remarkable growth to its success in engineering, investment, innovation and competition.
He said prosecutors built their case in part by focusing on acts of wrongdoing by a few employees who were fired after their misdeeds were discovered.
Prosecutors sometimes blamed the company for gaining access to the intellectual property of competitors when the materials were already public, he said.
“You can't steal a secret that isn't secret,” Heberlig said.

Huawei makes phones and other consumer electronics, but it has been cut off from other lines of business. More recently, it has expanded into chipmaking as the boom in artificial intelligence fuels demand for microprocessors.

During President Donald Trump’s first term, his administration raised national security concerns about Huawei and began lobbying Western allies against including the company’s products in their next-generation high-speed wireless networks. The U.S. announced the criminal charges in early 2019 and has since expanded the allegations.
Chinese officials said the U.S. has engaged in “economic bullying” and improperly used national security as a pretext for “oppressing Chinese companies.”
The jury was expected to begin deliberations sometime on Wednesday.

title: Is it OK to have AI text your boyfriend? When using chatbots crosses a line
summary: As more people turn to chatbots to write emails or handle mundane tasks, it raises the question: Does using them for personal messages cross a line
story: As more people turn to chatbots to write emails or handle mundane tasks, it raises the question: Does using them for personal messages cross a line
A purple box set up on a folding table in San Francisco’s Alamo Square could have been mistaken for a tissue box. Instead, it held dozens of secrets.
Oliva Tai was nearby, watching as passersby puzzled over a sign that read, “Confession box: Everyone has an AI secret.”

Among confessions about farming out too much work or using artificial intelligence to suggest a first-date spot were several admissions about using it to write deeply personal messages: “I had AI write my breakup text.” “I had ChatGPT date my boyfriend. Every text.” “I used AI to write my girlfriend’s grandmother’s 80th birthday letter.”
“I used AI to win an argument. Lol, not proud, but I won.”

Tai, an artist who has repeated the project more than a dozen times in the Bay Area, New York and Denver, said calling it a “confession” suggested people were admitting that using AI made them feel at least a little guilty. But they used it anyway.

As more people turn to a chatbot to write emails or handle mundane tasks, it raises the question: Does using it for personal messages cross a line? Is it ever OK to use AI to write a holiday card or birthday message? What about a love letter or wedding vows?

As part of research for a Ph.D. in consumer behavior, Danielle Hass conducted vignette-based experiments to determine how people felt about using AI to write personal messages. She found that people who had used AI before felt just as guilty as those who hadn't.
“Everyone felt guilty,” said Hass, a professor at Kennesaw State University in Georgia. “The driver of this relationship was dishonesty, that people felt like they were manipulating.”
Even if people are honest about their AI use, others still view them negatively, said Scott Claessens, a senior researcher at the University of Bristol in the UK.
Claessens says his research suggests that people who use AI are perceived as lazier, less competent and less trustworthy.

He noted that people often already supplement social tasks, such as using pre-written birthday cards or poems in love notes. But something about the effortless way that AI works turns people off, he said.
“What we really want in our social relationships is for people to put effort in, because it shows that as a signal that you’re invested in the relationship,” he said.

Sarah Newman, who collaborated with Tai as director of art and education at Harvard University’s metaLAB, said AI adoption is happening so quickly that norms will likely emerge about when it’s appropriate and when it's not.
She suggested using conflicted feelings as a guide. If you imagine using AI to write your wedding vows, would you be comfortable telling your partner you used it? If not, then don’t.
“Personal messages don’t need to be perfect,” Newman said. “Part of what makes these messages authentic and endearing is that they are imperfect.”

Tai and Claessens said some situations could warrant using AI in personal situations, such as people in relationships who use it to communicate better with a partner who doesn’t share a native language. People with learning disabilities, such as dyslexia, could also use it for help.
Hass believes people are quickly accepting that AI can make them more efficient in some work contexts, but she said she’s glad people feel guilty using it for personal messages.
“Guilt’s purpose in this context is to show us our interpersonal wrongdoings,” Hass said. “It’s showing us, ‘hey, this is where you’re supposed to be human.’”
Albert Stumm writes about travel, food and wellness. Find his work at https://www.albertstumm.com

title: Microsoft says services fully restored after hourslong global outage
summary: Microsoft says services are fully restored after a massive, global outage that lasted for hours
story: Microsoft says services are fully restored after a massive, global outage that lasted for hours
Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored after a massive outage that lasted for hours.
“We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions,” the company said in an update on X.

Users reported that Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Downdetector, an online tracker, said it received outage reports from users in more than 70 countries and territories.

The outage affected governments, courts, healthcare services, businesses, airlines and banks in many places. Governments including those of Japan, Singapore and Australia reported that the hourslong episode had impacted some of their operations.
Over 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft said on its website. Problems started appearing around midday Thursday in the U.S.
The Redmond, Washington-based company apologized on Friday for the disruptions and said the outage was “not related to cyber” or artificial intelligence agents.
It said the incident “was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced” following a recent network change.

The disruptions offer the latest example of the cascading problems that can erupt when so many communications and technology platforms depend on the same provider. Some lawmakers outside the U.S. have also argued that the outage shows the consequences of overreliance on American tech.
“With no emails coming or going, many office workers feel like they are having a virtual snow day,” said Jeremy Singer, a professor at the University of Glasgow’s School of Computing Science.

Still, he added, “this problem serves to emphasize the dependence we have built on one company’s digital infrastructure, and may lead us to question whether we need more resilience in our IT ecosystem.”

The global reach of the outage was swift. After problems first emerged midday Thursday in the U.S., online tracker Downdetector said it received outage reports from 74 countries and territories within an hour.
The total number of people affected was not clear, but Microsoft said in January it had more than 450 million paid commercial subscriptions to its 365 services.

A series of posts by Microsoft 365 on X suggested its engineers struggled to get the problem under control for some time, drawing teasing from other companies and users alike. But the tech giant has said there is “no indication” that the disruptions were caused by malicious activity, specifically noting Friday that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.
Microsoft said a technical issue arose during an upgrade that followed “a recent network change.” The company added that it restored services gradually, which took longer.
As Microsoft addressed issues affecting its Exchange Online mailboxes, it earlier cited a failure that it said caused a number of its servers to be “unexpectedly unavailable” during automated checks.
For Outlook, many users said they couldn’t send or receive emails, or had trouble loading their inboxes altogether. Those problems piled up across much of the world into Friday.
In Britain, the outage brought a halt to a trial in Manchester. Judge Maurice Greene sent jurors home because of delays that he said illustrated the danger of the court’s reliance on technology.
The British government said it was “working closely” with Microsoft to assess any impact on public services but that “robust contingency plans” were in place to minimize disruption.

British police said they were unable to receive crime reports online and urged people to phone in urgent requests. The outage also affected some law enforcement in the U.S. The sheriff’s office in Colorado’s Arapahoe County, for example, noted that online bond payments were affected.

Also in Britain, the National Pharmacy Association warned customers of delays in getting medication. The outage affected the National Health Service and threatened to prevent doctors from emailing prescriptions to pharmacies.
“Please bear with your pharmacy teams today, where waits may be longer than normal and there may be delays to some prescriptions,” a spokesperson said.
Governments in Singapore, Japan, Greece and Norway said the outage affected some of their operations, including email communications for certain ministries or agencies.

And of course, businesses were wracked with disruptions. Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum company, said his business couldn’t receive updates from its U.S. customers through Outlook.
Some banks in Hong Kong, an Asian financial hub, also saw disruptions.

OpenAI and Anthropic reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies’ software.

title: Meta fined $887M in Italy over Android gallery photos, videos on Facebook
summary: Meta violated a European privacy directive incorporated into Italian law.
story: Meta violated a European privacy directive incorporated into Italian law.

ROME -- Italy announced an €805 million ($887 million) fine against Meta on Saturday for using photos and videos from Android users’ galleries on Facebook without specific consent or adequate disclosure.

The Italian Data Protection Authority said the feature, called “Get suggestions from gallery when browsing Facebook,” violated a European privacy directive incorporated into Italian law. The directive protects smartphones as part of a person’s private sphere and requires “free and informed consent” for such access, the authority said.
Investigators found that the feature was enabled by default and that Facebook requested gallery access through a single permission covering multiple app functions with different purposes.
The authority gave Meta 60 days to disable the feature and seek separate consent for its use. Italy has about 20 million Android users, the agency said.
Meta made no immediate comment.
The fine was imposed on Meta Platforms Ireland Limited, which challenged Italy’s jurisdiction, according to the statement.
The authority said Meta’s “lack of cooperation” with the investigation factored into the penalty, which amounts to approximately 0.47% of the group’s global turnover.

title: SpaceX’s Starship returns from orbit, caught by launch pad arms in dramatic first
summary: It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for.
story: CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. -- SpaceX’s Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.

It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for — the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space. But with the first-stage booster exploding shortly after Friday’s liftoff from Texas, the company fell short of its desired double catch, still the goal for accelerating moon and Mars travel.
Wreckage remained in the Gulf of Mexico, cordoned off by buoys, as the stainless steel, bullet-shaped spacecraft lowered itself upright at the launch pad.
The dramatic, sci-fi-like capture helped blot out the booster’s messy miss. Cameras panned the spacecraft up and down as it hung high above the ground, supported by the arms of the launch tower.
“Can you believe it?” SpaceX commentator Dan Huot shouted, dragging out each word. “Look at her! Baby, she’s back!”
Calling it an “epic day,” Musk later ascended the launch tower to take up-close video with his phone. He even hugged the spacecraft. “Looks great,” he reported via X.

SpaceX officials said Saturday’s catch demonstrates the full reusability of Starship, crucial for rapid and low-cost recycling. Although Friday’s booster recovery failed, the company had already made three previous booster catches, validating the technique.

NASA welcomed Saturday’s news. The space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. Musk’s ambitions are even grander: He wants to launch a fleet of Starships to build a city on Mars.
“It was almost magic,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said via X. “Making more believers by the day ... one step closer to (emojis of the moon and the U.S. flag)."

The world’s largest and most powerful rocket — a 407-foot (124-meter) behemoth — blasted off late Friday afternoon from SpaceX’s Starship base near the U.S.-Mexican border. Separating neatly from its booster before things went awry, the upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites.

Starship continued circling the world 165 miles (265 kilometers) up, with live views of itself and Earth streaming down via Starlink. The spacecraft completed 14 laps around Earth, outshining the previous mission’s one to two laps.
It was SpaceX’s 15th flight of a full-scale Starship since 2023 and its only second trip to orbit.
SpaceX reported that everything on the spacecraft, including its vital heat shield, appeared to work well.

As for the booster, SpaceX’s Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down. The booster’s guidance system sensed it wasn’t in the right position and automatically initiated the watery detour and self-destruction. Engineers are still investigating the cause.

SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida’s Kennedy Space Center within the next few months. That is the starting point for NASA’s next Artemis mission, which will skip the moon and remain in orbit around Earth for lunar lander practice.

Artemis III’s four astronauts will attempt to dock their capsule with not only Starship but Blue Origin’s Blue Moon. The two companies will take turns delivering crews to the lunar surface. NASA is targeting as soon as 2028 for Artemis IV, humanity’s first moon landing since the Apollo era more than half a century ago.

title: Fans cheer as popular online platform for spinoff stories nears full return after security incident
summary: The Archive of Our Own, a popular global fandom site, is making a limited return after a security incident led to a shutdown on Oct. 29
story: The Archive of Our Own, a popular global fandom site, is making a limited return after a security incident led to a shutdown on Oct. 29

In a comeback tale like one from Harry Potter battling back his nemesis or a “Heated Rivalry” hockey hero rebounding from injury, a top global fandom site that was sidelined by a security incident is now on the mend.

The activist group behind the popular Archive of Our Own, or AO3, platform, a collaborative online space which serves up fans’ spinoff narratives derived from well-known published stories, says it’s undergoing a limited return after a shutdown on Oct. 29.
“AO3 is now up!” said a status page for the Organization for Transformative Works, an activist group behind the platform, on Sunday.

The outage sent fans of the platform — readers and authors alike — into a desperate void for the past two weeks with a “Bad Gateway” message stirring frustration. The return drew many expressions of joy Sunday.

The organization, in a summary it posted on Instagram of its 2025 results, said nearly 2.6 million AO3 works were created, with nearly 40 billion page views. Nearly 2 million accounts have been created, it said.
AO3 hasn't been without its critics, who have warned about sexual content that could be available to minors and fandom racism through the platform.

The group said some features like user icons have been disabled and importing of external work isn’t available, while downloads are currently only possible in the web-language HTML format. It promised those features will ultimately return.

The team predicted that the security incident would take up to four weeks for AO3 to get back up, while floating the prospect of a partial revival “in a degraded state” — which appears to be what was taking place on Sunday.

The organization said contributors’ “works, bookmarks, kudos, etc., are still safe” and that no drafts were deleted during the outage — but it couldn’t rule out that the user database might have been compromised.
“We understand that the wait and uncertainty surrounding AO3’s return have been difficult, and we apologize for the inconvenience,” the status update said.

AO3 is a hub of content from fans who have produced content that riffs off fiction, art and other culture and entertainment: Imagine a repository of sequels, prequels and derivatives dreamt up by adoring aficionados of some of the world’s best-known titles.
The result is catchy products like “fanfic” — fiction from fans — and similar fanart, as well as “podfics,” readings of narratives shared in audio form.

A recent listing of “ship stats” — or the number of references to relationships of stars from literature — shows that pairings of characters featured in the Harry Potter, Heated Rivalry and anime fandoms were the most prominent this summer.
The reaction from fans of the fandom platform was swift and exuberant.
“So, we've all agreed we don't need to sleep tonight, now that AO3 is finally back, right? Right!?” quipped yet.another.loon on the Threads social media site.
User Verkielos gushed: “Just got email from AO3 about a fic update. The world is healing!”
Associated Press writer Stefanie Dazio in Berlin contributed to this report.

title: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025, company conducts probe over Nvidia fallout
summary: Singapore-based company has been at the center of the claims involving Nvidia.
story: Singapore-based company has been at the center of the claims involving Nvidia.

Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International said Sunday that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whose relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang sparked U.S. national security concerns, left the company last year.
Megaspeed, which is under scrutiny over alleged transfers of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies, also announced an internal investigation led by outside lawyers.

The company told The Associated Press that it runs a “legitimate and lawful business” and was aware of media reports containing claims about its business, supply chain and global operations “that are not supported by verifiable evidence.” It did not address specific allegations.
“The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation,” it said in an emailed statement.
Alice Huang “left Megaspeed effective Aug. 30, 2025, and currently has no role with the company,” the statement said. “Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang’s personal and private matters.”

A customer and cloud partner of Nvidia, Megaspeed has faced scrutiny in recent months, including from U.S. authorities, over allegations that it circumvented U.S. export restrictions to route large quantities of advanced chips to Chinese companies. Last December, it said there was “no evidence” of illicit chip transfers.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that “it doesn't matter to me” whether Alice Huang is a spy. He said his concern is “whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the U.S. export restrictions” or not.

“Jensen’s foibles are his foibles. Obviously, it’s a problem if in fact he was having relationships with subordinates,” Bessent said in an appearance on Fox News Channel's “Sunday Morning Futures.” “I want to keep coming back to: ‘What was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?’”
Bessent said the Nvidia board of directors should look outside the company for a new CEO because “they need a dramatic shake-up.”
Singapore’s government said Thursday that it initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in February 2025, including possible “false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers.”
Authorities also investigated Alice Huang, whom the government identified as Megaspeed’s then-CEO, chairperson and one of its key controllers.

Singapore authorities questioned her and withheld her passport last year. They later concluded there was insufficient evidence that she had committed a crime, despite suspecting she had provided “inaccurate” information to downplay her role at the company.
An earlier New York Times report suggested U.S. officials believed Alice Huang was a Chinese spy recruited to potentially influence Nvidia to make its advanced chips more available to China.
As scrutiny intensified and reports of her romantic relationship with Jensen Huang gained attention, Nvidia announced Thursday that he was stepping down as CEO.

U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said Thursday, however, that the Justice Department had not concluded whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Asked whether she was a spy, President Donald Trump said: “I don’t know if that’s been determined yet.”
Beijing rejected the allegations as unsubstantiated.
The Associated Press has been unable to reach Alice Huang for comment.

Megaspeed began as the overseas arm of a Chinese video game developer and was incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International. It adopted its current name in March 2023, when all its shares were transferred to Huang Le Limited, a British Virgin Islands company. Alice Huang is also known by her Chinese name, Huang Le.
By November 2023, she was no longer listed as a Megaspeed director, and all her shares had been transferred to an entity owned by Singaporean businessman Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan.

Despite those public records, short seller Culper Research cited a Megaspeed employee in a report released this May as saying Alice Huang was “actually still our boss” and remained involved in daily operations.
The company’s finances have also attracted attention. Singapore corporate records show its total assets rose roughly 90-fold from end-2023 to 2024, reaching almost $3 billion.
In a separate statement Thursday issued under James Tan’s name, Megaspeed said it takes its obligations under U.S. export control laws “extremely seriously.”
The company said it had cooperated with inspections by the U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security and was ready to cooperate fully with other relevant U.S. authorities.

title: Advocacy groups sue AI giants to freeze new models, warning of 'catastrophic' risks
summary: A coalition of online safety and consumer advocacy groups has sued five leading AI companies to halt further development
story: A coalition of online safety and consumer advocacy groups has sued five leading AI companies to halt further development

NEW YORK -- A coalition of online safety and consumer advocacy groups on Thursday sued five of the world’s leading artificial intelligence companies to halt further development, alleging the tech giants can’t prevent their own creations from causing “catastrophic” harm.

The lawsuit in San Francisco Superior Court follows a midterm election that could bring a moment of reckoning for the fast-moving AI industry, as Democrats who won back control of Congress stress the need to regulate the technology.

The filing, first reported on by The Associated Press, asks a judge to stop Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceXSI from developing or deploying new AI models, pointing to documented examples of cyberattacks and other harmful actions by AI systems and the companies’ own alarming acknowledgments that their technology has the potential to someday destroy humanity.

“No other industry is allowed to treat its own development of unsafe products — much less ones that could kill us all — as inevitable,” reads the complaint from the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative and the Alliance for Secure AI. “Plaintiffs bring this suit to stop Defendants from continuing their unlawful path to disaster.”

The AI industry has generated excitement and stock market gains, but also deep fears that the technology could go rogue and escape human control. Recent incidents of AI agents hacking government websites and companies — including when OpenAI's ChatGPT hacked into another AI company on its own in July — have accelerated those concerns.

President Donald Trump, a proponent of rapid AI development to keep the U.S. ahead of foreign competitors like China, has so far encouraged the companies to police themselves on matters of safety, though he has expressed openness to more guardrails. Congress also has stopped short of regulating the technology, but that may change with its Democratic takeover.

Some CEOs of major AI companies, meanwhile, have voiced support for slowing development of the technology to give safety measures a chance to catch up. They also haven't held back in recognizing the risks. Anthropic's Dario Amodei, for example, last year said he thinks there’s a 1 in 4 chance AI’s future goes “really, really badly,” compared with a 3 in 4 chance it goes well. Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, told Fox News in 2023 that AI could lead to “civilization destruction.”

The plaintiffs, all nonprofits, allege that the companies named in the lawsuit have violated a California unfair competition law by endangering public health and interfering with the use of property such as computer systems. They claim they’ve had to divert resources away from other planned work to address the acute harms threatened by each of the companies’ advancing AI models.

They also warn that the companies' goals of creating AI systems that are broadly as smart as humans and can increasingly manage tasks and learn things autonomously could result in a permanent loss of control of the technology and heighten existential risks to humanity.
The companies named in Thursday's lawsuit didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

title: How Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital affair could cause collateral damage in Washington
summary: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, is under scrutiny after revelations of an affair with a Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, who is suspected of spying
story: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, is under scrutiny after revelations of an affair with a Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, who is suspected of spying
WASHINGTON -- Extramarital affairs are usually private matters. Jensen Huang’s has global implications.

The 63-year-old is the leading face of the artificial intelligence revolution with his black leather jackets and fluff of grey hair. He runs the company Nvidia, which produces highly coveted computer chips. That's landed him on a late-night-phone-call basis with President Donald Trump, a promoter of the industry.

But Huang was also liaising with a Chinese businesswoman who has allegedly fed intelligence — as well as advanced chips — to China. The woman, Alice Huang, is a former executive at the Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed.

It's a saga of personal betrayal, corporate espionage and high-tech development, and the fallout is spreading across Washington. There are bipartisan calls for investigations on Capitol Hill. The U.S. Department of Justice has opened its own probe. Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, is conducting an internal review.

Some expect the technology to reshape human civilization by imbuing computers with the vast powers of creation and analysis, and Trump has repeated that “whoever wins AI, wins." Nvidia is the backbone of America's plans for dominating the field.
When asked about Huang's affair, Trump said this week that he had spoken to the tech executive as the scandal grew.
“I think he’ll be in good shape," Trump said, adding that "he said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”
As for when the president first learned about the concerns involving Alice Huang, Trump brushed off the question.
“They could have been mentioned," he said. "Certainly it didn’t make much of an impact on me.”
With the AI race between the U.S. and China often framed as a fierce and consequential rivalry, the Justice Department has persistently warned of the espionage threat posed by Beijing.
That includes efforts to cultivate well-placed relationships in government and private industry, as well as to acquire sensitive technology such as AI chips developed in the U.S.

Last year, Megaspeed faced scrutiny from the U.S. Commerce Department over its alleged skirting of U.S. export laws and routing of a large amount of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese users. The company denied those allegations. U.S. intelligence officials eventually concluded that Alice Huang had spied for China, according to The New York Times.

The Commerce Department's probe was handed off to the Justice Department, and its National Security Division is investigating whether Megaspeed violated export control laws in an inquiry that will also include scrutiny of Alice Huang, according to a person familiar with the matter who insisted on anonymity to discuss an ongoing law enforcement probe.
Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday, and The Associated Press was unable to reach Alice Huang.

Jensen Huang has apologized to his company about the affair, saying he hurt his wife and their children, but he didn’t address reports that Alice Huang was a suspected spy. Nvidia’s board said that it had “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, and that Huang would remain in charge while cooperating with the investigation.
Beijing has said the “Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated" and called it “nothing but smears.”
After their first dinner together at Mar-a-Lago in early 2025, Trump latched onto Huang as a tech titan positioned to deliver on the president’s own promises of an economic renaissance.

The computer chips produced by Nvidia would essentially turn data centers into factories that made raw intelligence, which could then be applied across the economy to produce cars, new pharmaceutical drugs, advanced weapons and seemingly unparalleled wealth.
Trump would regularly phone Huang to discuss this future.

“From the moment that I met him, the only thing that he’s ever talked to me about is creating more jobs, re-industrializing the United States, of protection, of national security,” Huang told AP in an interview this summer. "He knows that if America is wealthy, we have a lot of tax revenues. We can fund the military, we can fund our economy, we fund our communities, create more jobs.”

Trump saw his political fortunes — and that of the country — in Huang's Nvidia. Huang joined Trump on Air Force One for a state visit to Beijing earlier this year. Just last month, Trump awarded Huang with a National Medal of Science.
The president called him “a man whose determination laid the foundations for the explosion of super intelligence and put America at the front of the race, an amazing man, gotten to know him so well.”
Nvidia also donated $25 million to help fund the construction of Trump’s White House ballroom.
Multiple estimates suggest that more than half of the stock market gains during Trump's second term came from the growth of the AI industry and the construction of data centers.

Without that growth, consumer spending could slump, delivering another economic setback to a president who has already failed to deliver on his campaign promise of stopping inflation. Rising prices were among the reasons that voters delivered a harsh rebuke to Republicans in last week's midterm elections, returning control of Congress to the Democrats.

While Huang said his interests were in helping America succeed, he also expressed a strong view that Nvidia should be able to sell some of its less advanced chips such as the H200 to China. Nvidia long argued that the sales would help ensure that the broader AI ecosystem was tied to America, boxing out Chinese chipmakers that are developing semiconductors and systems to compete with his company.

Those arguments previously came under scrutiny, including from Massachusetts Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who wanted him to appear before the Senate Banking Committee to answer questions about his desire to loosen export restrictions.

Huang has so far refused to appear, and Democrats responded angrily when his infidelity came to light, raising concerns that a bulwark of American technology may have been compromised by the Chinese government.
Warren said in a statement Monday that Nvidia had reportedly gotten approvals to export “hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips to China, including to companies tied to China’s military.”
And Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, Warren continued, “raises important questions NVIDIA must answer about the extent to which these activities were related."

Chan reported from Hong Kong and Ng from Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. Associated Press journalists Wu Jia in Beijing, Didi Tang in Washington and Russ Bynum in Savannah, Georgia, contributed to this report.

title: SpaceX’s Starship soars into orbit after booster explosion prevents an unprecedented double catch
summary: SpaceX has lost out on its attempt to recover its entire Starship back at the Texas launch pad
story: SpaceX has lost out on its attempt to recover its entire Starship back at the Texas launch pad

SpaceX's attempt to recover its entire Starship back at the launch pad was thwarted when the booster fell into the Gulf of Mexico and exploded Friday, but the spacecraft still soared into orbit in its boldest test yet.

Instead of returning to its Texas pad following liftoff, the first-stage booster was diverted to a point offshore. Despite the setback, the spacecraft continued on its way. It will steer toward the pad Saturday, barring further trouble. The flight could last as long as 22 hours.

It’s the first time that Starship will try to return to the pad from orbit, to be plucked in midair by mechanical arms secured to the launch tower. The loss of the booster meant Elon Musk's company missed out on a double catch.

The original goal was to retrieve every single piece of the rocket for the purpose of future recycling, something yet to be achieved anywhere in the world. Musk sees this leading to the kind of fast and consistent launch rates necessary for building moon bases and sending people to Mars.

Shortly after reaching orbit, Starship dropped off 26 of the company’s most advanced Starlink satellites. The plan is for Starship to complete 15 laps around the world at an altitude of around 170 miles (275 kilometers) before heading back to the launch site for Saturday’s grand finale.
SpaceX had already made three booster grabs at the company’s sprawling Starbase near the U.S.-Mexico border. That made Friday's miss all the more surprising.

“Well, that certainly isn’t the news that we had hoped to hear for today,” observed SpaceX launch commentator Kate Tice, adding that it was in line with the many rigorous safety checks to protect the pad. No explanation was provided for what went wrong.

This was the first attempt to capture the upgraded version of the booster that stretches 236 feet (72 meters) — the production model for moon and Mars expeditions. It will also be the first time the company attempts to catch the spacecraft, which spans 171 feet (52 meters). Together, they form the world’s biggest and most powerful rocket — an astounding 407 feet (124 meters) in height.

The spacecraft portion of the 14 previous Starships ended up in the ocean, either by design at flight’s end or by accident in a stream of flaming wreckage. During the first full-scale test flight in 2023, multiple engines failed to ignite and the tumbling rocket’s self-destruct system was activated.
The last test, in September, was the first to reach orbit, but SpaceX did not try to recover any of the rocket stages.

SpaceX plans to start launching Starships from Florida within a few months and from Louisiana in a few years. Scaled-up infrastructure, combined with full rocket reusability, is “how you go from zero launches to 10 to 100 to 1,000 to 10,000 to 100,000,” SpaceX’s Kiko Dontchev, vice president of launch, said at a NASA tech summit last week at Florida’s Kennedy Space Center.

SpaceX’s smaller Falcon rockets will continue to fly from Cape Canaveral, carrying astronauts to the International Space Station for NASA and from California carrying Starlinks. Satellites also will keep hitching Falcon rides for now. Musk wants Starships to eventually replace Falcons.

Falcon rockets “are still not fully reusable. We still throw that second stage away every single flight. Starship, we’re going to catch both the first stage and second stage,” Dontchev said ahead of Friday's launch.

NASA is paying SpaceX billions of dollars to land Artemis astronauts on the moon with Starships. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin is the other major player. NASA expects to decide a year before the Artemis IV lunar landing — the first by astronauts in more than half a century — whether to get the moonwalkers to the surface with Musk’s Starship or Bezos’ Blue Moon.

During next summer’s Artemis III mission, astronauts will practice docking their capsule with a Blue Moon and then a Starship in orbit around Earth. That will set the stage for an Artemis moon touchdown as early as 2028.
“We are looking forward to some of that on-orbit Starlink capability on Artemis III,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said via X after Starship reached orbit.
