Kuwaiti air defenses are countering hostile drone attacks, the Kuwait Army said.
The General Staff of the Army said any explosions heard were the result of air defense systems intercepting hostile attacks.
US conducts airstrikes on Qeshm Island in response to IRGC attacks, US military official says
The U.S. conducted airstrikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island on Tuesday, targeting launchers in response to IRGC targeting of U.S. personnel and assets, according to a U.S. military official.
"U.S. Central Command remains highly vigilant and fully postured to protect Americans across the region," the official said.
Tanker transiting in Strait of Hormuz struck second time according to reports, UKMTO says
A tanker transiting in the Strait of Hormuz was reportedly struck for a second time, which caused a fire onboard, a maritime security agency reported to the UKMTO.
This comes after a third party reported an attack on the same vessel on Monday, which resulted in the vessel being disabled and resulted in an engine room fire, according to the UKMTO.
The crew are currently unaccounted for and a damage assessment is currently unknown, according to the UKMTO.
"Vessels are advised to transit with caution and report any suspicious activity to UKMTO, whilst authorities investigate," the UKMTO said in an update Tuesday.
CENTCOM says Iranian drone attack on Bahrain defeated 'without any damage'
U.S. Central Command said on Tuesday that air defenses defeated an Iranian drone attack that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said targeted an American radar facility in Bahrain.

"Multiple Iranian one-way attack drones launched by the IRGC today towards Bahrain were intercepted without any damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel. CENTCOM and partner forces remain highly vigilant," the command said in a post to X.

title: Trump picks LaNeve, Hegseth's former aide, as top Army officer
summary: LaNeve was tapped for the job after Hegseth fired his predecessor.
story: LaNeve was tapped for the job after Hegseth fired his predecessor.
President Donald Trump on Tuesday formally nominated Gen. Chris LaNeve to be Army chief of staff, the service's top officer.
The move comes after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth suddenly fired Gen. Randy George in April without explanation. George was a seasoned Army officer who had bipartisan popularity on Capitol Hill.
LaNeve has been serving as acting chief of staff of the Army since George's ousting.
The change also comes months after Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned from his role amid growing tension between him and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, according to a U.S. official.
Driscoll, who resigned in August, had a close working relationship with George and said at a congressional hearing that he did not know why George had been removed.

LaNeve previously served as a military aide to Hegseth. In less than two years, LaNeve rose from a senior command post in South Korea to serving as one of Hegseth's top military aides before becoming the Army’s vice chief of staff, its second-highest uniformed position.

His nomination comes as lawmakers, including Republicans, have voiced frustration with Hegseth's leadership of the Pentagon and his firing of many of the military’s most seasoned officers without explanation.

LaNeve, an infantry officer, was commissioned through the Reserve Officers’ Training Corps in 1990 from the University of Arizona. He previously served as commander of the famed 82nd Airborne Division based out of Ft. Bragg, North Carolina.

“For 36 years, I’ve served in the U.S. Army, currently as the Vice Chief of Staff," LaNeve said in a statement. "I’m deeply honored by the President’s trust and confidence for the nomination to serve as the Chief of Staff of the U.S. Army, and, if confirmed, I look forward to continuing to serve our Soldiers, their families, and our nation."
A confirmation hearing for LaNeve would likely come with scrutiny from lawmakers over the conditions that have led to George's firing and LaNeve effectively set to replace him.

title: The advice Biden got from Mitt Romney, and other takeaways from his memoir
summary: Biden's memoir "Promise Me, America," which drops Tuesday, recounts his 2020 run for the presidency, his years in the White House and his tumultuous 2024 run.
story: Biden's new book "Promise Me, America" releases on Tuesday.

Former President Joe Biden's new memoir "Promise Me, America," which releases Tuesday, recounts his run for the presidency in 2020, his four years in the White House and his tumultuous run for president in 2024 that ended with him stepping aside as the nominee.

The book comes as the former president attempts to reframe his legacy even as his successor, President Donald Trump, continues to undo many of his policies. It features some new details about Biden grappling with his age, about his strained relationships with figures such as former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and about how Trump acted both as Biden began and ended his presidency.
Here are some takeaways from Biden's memoir:
One major preoccupation of Biden's throughout the book: the January 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol and what he frames as Trump's complicity.

The book opens with a recounting of Biden giving remarks from Wilmington, Delaware, on Jan. 6 because he felt Trump was not able to live up to a presidential standard. He writes, "Throughout my campaign, I had often felt as if I had to simultaneously run for president and be the president -- to model responsible behavior, to speak of hope, to stay optimistic, to share empathy, to hold a nation together. So it was not much of a departure for me to tell my team that the American people needed to hear from their incoming president in a way that they had never heard from their outgoing one."

Biden also slams Trump for not addressing Americans about the riot for hours, writing, "America's president wasn't leading America, he was leading an insurrection. It was among the worst derelictions of duty by any president in our history." He later says that Trump's actions on Jan. 6 should "follow him to his grave."
Throughout the book, Biden seems convinced that he could have run for reelection and served another four years as president.
"I had asked the hard questions of myself," Biden says. "I answered that yes, physically I would be able to do the job. And that not only did I want to do it, I wanted to do it more than ever."
Still, Biden admits that he displayed several signs of advanced age, including a "tendency to misstate places and names" and a "halting gait."

In one anecdote, Biden describes receiving guidance from then-Sen. Mitt Romney on how to walk in a more youthful way. During a private White House tour that Biden arranged for Romney and his family, Romney pulled Biden aside and gave him some blunt advice.

"You're holding your hands stiffly by your side when you walk," Romney tells Biden. "Pump your arms and you'll look more energetic and confident." Biden called the incident a "memorable conversation" and said he tried to follow the advice.
Zelenskyy, Netanyahu relationships more strained than publicly seen

Even though Biden has stood by his administration's actions of supporting Ukraine and providing financial support to the country in its war with Russia, he says that Zelenskyy could be "moody" and "stubborn" during their private conversations, adding that he was not "as grateful as I would have expected."

Biden called his commitment to Israel "long-standing," and recounted his concerns with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's leadership, saying that after the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas terror attacks he "had a feeling that [Netanyahu's] response would be overwhelming -- to compensate for what was close to dereliction of duty on his part."
"Increasingly, since Netanyahu's return to power at the end of 2022, I felt that the work of protecting Israel meant protecting it both from its enemies and itself," Biden added.
He talked about sparring with Netanyahu and said while they could be “direct” with each other, “there wasn’t a ton of trust” between the two.

"I was also worried about Bibi's Trump-like tendencies. He could play fast and loose with the truth, and thought nothing of bending democratic institutions to serve his personal needs. Despite a thin electoral majority, he had quickly turned his victory into an attempt to weaken the Israeli Supreme Court, in order to prevent it from looking into his unsavory financial dealings."

In a section on his poor debate performance against Trump on June 27, 2024, Biden says he was tired and unwell leading up to the debate, and that he was preoccupied by his son Hunter Biden's worsening legal woes. He says the debate "didn't feel right from the start."

According to Biden, his infamous misstatement about healthcare policy -- "We finally beat Medicare" -- was meant to be "We finally beat Big Pharma," but came out jumbled. He calls his treatment in the media after the debate "one of the worst poundings ever delivered by the free press."

As pressure mounted on Biden to drop out of the race after the debate, he received a visit from Rep. Nancy Pelosi in the White House. Biden describes Pelosi as a "great friend," but says that she had already started working to undermine his candidacy.

"Publicly she was still saying it was my decision to make. But privately she was working furiously behind the scenes to get elected officials and Biden delegates to defect," Biden says. "She told me all the polling she had seen said I couldn't win, but I could be the George Washington of our time if I passed the torch."
Biden also recounts a conversation he had with Sen. Chuck Schumer about dropping out. Schumer told Biden he thought he had been a great president but was convinced he could no longer win re-election.

"I have to admit it was personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me," Biden says. "I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption (I may have said it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race. Loyalty matters to me."

The mood of Biden's meeting with Trump in the Oval Office after Trump won re-election in 2024 was unexpected, Biden says. Trump surprised Biden "by adopting a tone so friendly that I thought he might be putting me on. It bordered on fawning."
According to Biden, Trump said that Biden's record on job creation had been "extraordinary," and that if it weren't for politics, the two would be "good friends."

A conversation the two had about a range of foreign policy issues was also idiosyncratic, Biden says. He describes Trump as being "focused on the personalities of the leaders, as if we were sharing gossip about people at a dinner party, not discussing issues of global significance."

title: Duffy asked for $50B for air traffic control after ground stop, a marked increase
summary: The nationwide ground stop thrust funding for the FAA into the spotlight as Transportation Secretary Duffy and President Trump call for more money to fix a broken system.
story: The FAA administrator said earlier this year an additional $10B was needed.

The nationwide ground stop last week thrust funding for the Federal Aviation Administration into the spotlight as Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and President Donald Trump call for more money to fix a system they say is broken.
The number has ballooned over the course of a year, from the $12.5 billion that was appropriated by Congress to an additional $50 billion that Duffy asked for in the wake of the ground stop.
Their calls come as a lame-duck Congress looks to wrap up its work for the year.
Here's a look at where things stand:

When the Department of Transportation announced its plan in 2025 to build a new air traffic control system, the agency said it would need $20 billion in addition to $12.5 billion appropriated last year by Congress under Trump's so-called "One Big Beautiful Bill" to complete air traffic control modernization efforts -- digitizing its communications and technological capabilities -- by 2028.
Despite that initial estimate, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford testified in September 2026 that the agency would only need about an additional $10 billion to modernize the air traffic control system.

Still, later that month, Duffy increased his initial ask and requested $30 billion from Congress to complete the nationwide air traffic control overhaul. Duffy said at the time that the $12.5 billion was a down payment and additional funding was always needed to complete it.

On Friday, when the nationwide ground stop occurred, Duffy increased that prior funding request significantly, saying in a Friday night press conference that he is now asking Congress to give the DOT $50 billion.

"I did make a request for $30 billion. I've talked about $30 billion, and what I'm trying to do is get a number that I think the Congress will give me that gets a massive portion of the needs of the airspace completed," Duffy said in a Saturday press conference about the ground stop. "It's not a cheap proposition, and so let's make the investment and let's do it now. So I'm going to put in that full request. I'll detail it and send it over to the Hill in conjunction with the president."

Duffy has not released a breakdown of the costs for the $50 billion in funds he's now requesting, but only $10 billion of the DOT's previous $30 billion request was slated to "complete reliable digital architecture," according to a DOT press release.

Duffy's latest request was also for funds to create a more reliable digital architecture, overhaul outdated airport infrastructure, build world-class airports and to continue upgrades needed to build a brand-new air traffic control system.
The secretary's funding request garnered support from United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby who released a statement Sunday on the nationwide ground stop saying, "this moment must be a call to action."

"It is critical for safety, our passengers, and our economy that we fix our nation's Air Traffic Control system now. The FAA has incredible people who work hard, keep the skies safe, and take pride in what they do. They need to get to 100% staffing and to have the funds to modernize the technology. And they need and deserve 100% support from all of us," Kirby said in a post on LinkedIn.
Duffy's justification for his growing request was met with a mix of skepticism -- even by members of his own party.

"Well, of course they should use that money," Sen. John Hoeven, R-South Dakota, told reporters on Capitol Hill. "What Secretary Duffy said that you've probably seen is he's saying, 'well, that's for certain technology,' but then there's other -- some of the communications technology that they need to upgrade too -- wasn't included in that $12.5 because that $12.5 was laid out for certain things, which it should be."
Hoeven emphasized that he has a seat on the Senate Appropriations Committee.
"We have to have accountability too," he said.

Duffy will come to Congress hat in hand on Tuesday when he joins Senate Republicans for lunch in the Capitol. But the group of Republicans he'll be addressing is the same group that already gave the FAA a sizable amount of money for air traffic control last year.

Republicans allocated $12.5 billion for air traffic control as part of the so-called "One Big Beautiful Bill" -- later rebranded as the Working Families Tax Cuts Act, which passed out of Congress with almost exclusively Republican support in July 2025. Within that pot is $4.75 billion specifically allocated for "telecommunications infrastructure modernization and systems upgrades."
Duffy spoke with top House leaders on Monday, multiple sources told ABC News.

The secretary talked by phone with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, according to a person familiar with the conversation. Duffy also spoke by phone with House Speaker Mike Johnson, according to a source familiar with the conversation.

Johnson said over the weekend that Congress would consider Duffy’s call for up to $50 billion to modernize air traffic control and airport infrastructure. The speaker’s office did not immediately respond to ABC News’ request for comment on how Congress would address the funding during the lame-duck session.
Friday's ground stop happened because of a telecommunications issue, both Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said.

According to a breakdown of spending recently released by DOT, much of that $12.5 billion remains unspent. The money that has been spent has been used on things such as making foundational upgrades, copper fiber replacement and radar and surveillance, according to DOT.

On Sunday, Duffy argued that the full amount Republicans gave to DOT through the One Big Beautiful Bill has not been spent because Congress has restricted how the department could spend it. The agency contends that the legislation does not give them "the legal flexibility" to use the money beyond parameters set by Congress.

"Congress placed parameters on the [OBBB] funding outlining exactly how much of the total package could be spent on specific categories of work. The Department does not have the legal flexibility to move funds from one workstream to another," DOT says.

"They gave me money for tower, for radios, money for radar, money for systems. But I don't have any money in that $12.5 billion for a new architecture for telecom. I don't have any money given by Congress to build a new software system to manage the airspace. They're very specific on how we spend the $12.5 [billion], and none of the money goes to this telecom that I have to build," Duffy said on CBS' "Face the Nation." "We're building at an amazing speed that's happening safely, but $12.5 billion is not nearly enough to fix a system that has been neglected for decades."
The bill passed through both chambers of Congress in July 2025 and was signed by Trump -- something the GOP achieved almost entirely without Democratic buy-in.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune on Monday rebuffed Duffy's assertion that Congress didn't properly allocate money to fund upgrades, pointing out that some of the funding hasn't yet been spent.

"There's some explanations that have to be given as to why that number is where it is. But I think we have attempted to do what we can to ensure that the concerns they have about modernization are being met," Thune said.
The One Big Beautiful Bill is not the only source of funding for the FAA that Congress has approved in the last several years.

President Joe Biden signed the FAA Reauthorization Act in 2024 -- a four-year, $105.5 billion bill. A provision in the package called for technology partnerships with stakeholders that identified software, systems, services and technologies that could improve aviation safety and the operations and management of the air traffic control system.

Congress also passed the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act under Biden in 2021. That bill allocated $25 billion for the FAA. Though $5 billion of that was specifically for air traffic control, much of it was to update towers at airports and other FAA facilities.
Democrats contend that the Trump administration has blocked or stalled billions in funding that passed in the bipartisan infrastructure bill since taking office.

"Instead of laying out the facts, Secretary Duffy commanded the public's attention to demand a $50 billion ransom without a real plan to deliver," Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the incoming chair of the House Appropriations Committee noted Sunday. "Secretary Duffy and the Federal Aviation Administration have received historical and monumental investments over the last two years, over $12.5 billion of which was provided without meaningful guardrails or accountability requirements and largely remains unspent. No federal leader should be free to do their work without Congressional oversight. Congress has shown its willingness to modernize the FAA's systems and support its workforce as part of annual bipartisan legislation, but we need a competent partner at the Department of Transportation to carry this out in a sustainable, transparent manner. Right now, it is clear that we lack such a partner."
The short answer: no.

In Trump's FY2027 budget request sent to Congress last spring, the administration requested $481 million more than the previous year for FAA operations and capital. But that budget request encompassed a number of FAA-related priorities -- not just funding to upgrade the air traffic control systems.

That same budget also included a $4 billion request for "facilities and equipment" -- explaining that when "paired with the $12.5 billion" in the One Big Beautiful Bill, the latest request for an influx of money "would allow the FAA to continue to build a Brand New Air Traffic Control System."

White House budgets are generally viewed as a wish list presented by the administration ahead of the congressional budget and appropriations seasons. Though the 2027 fiscal year began in October, Congress has not yet passed any funding bills into law. The government is currently operating on a short-term extension of fiscal year 2026's appropriations levels.
Congress, meanwhile, is working with limited time and limited ability to approve additional funding for the agency -- given that the 119th session will end on Jan. 3.

The government is set to run out of funding on Dec. 12 -- and while lawmakers could include additional funding for the FAA in a short-term funding bill or try to pass a stand-alone funding bill for the FAA. Negotiations over funding this close to a new Congress convening could create massive headaches and risk government shutdowns.z

With Democrats growing increasingly frustrated with a lack of clarity around Duffy's funding requests, Speaker Mike Johnson said over the weekend that Congress would take up the administration's verbalized request for up to $50 billion to modernize air traffic control and airport infrastructure. ABC News has asked the speaker's office for clarification on how Congress would address the funding.

"We're working on an aggressive legislative package to finish out the year strong, run through the tape ... and this will be added to that," Johnson said on Fox News on Saturday. "We don't really need any investigation to understand we need further investmen. ... some of this equipment dates back to the '80s, so it's got to be updated, and that's our responsibility. We're going to work to get it done."
Staff members from the DOT will provide a virtual briefing to staff members of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on Tuesday.

title: 'Everybody's shell-shocked': GOP operatives face 2028 prospects after midterm defeats
summary: GOP sources told ABC News the party leaned on culture wars over costs and lost key Latino voters. Some doubt JD Vance is still the presumptive 2028 nominee.
story: Some argued JD Vance may no longer be the presumptive 2028 nominee.
On Election Day, many Republicans were bracing for a tough outcome, but not what has been described as a blue tsunami.

"I thought that we were going to keep the Senate," former Republican National Committee Chair Ronna McDaniel told ABC News. "I didn't think that Democrats could make inroads in states like South Carolina and Kansas and even Texas."

Democrats did more than make inroads. They flipped eight GOP-held Senate seats and as of Monday, Democrats hold 256 House seats to the GOP's 170. There are still some outstanding races as of Monday: nine House races and one Senate race.

Over a dozen Republican donors and operatives told ABC News that the Republican Party is still in shock after the sweeping midterm losses. They pointed to a message that focused on culture wars and failed to reach voters squeezed by costs tied to the war in Iran and a Latino coalition that slipped away. Some argued Vice President JD Vance may no longer be the presumptive 2028 nominee. Vance, who has not formally announced he is launching a presidential bid for 2028, has acknowledged "there's a chance" he won't run in 2028.
The president’s record-low approval ratings were also difficult to ignore, some said.

"The losses are all about Trump," said one Republican consultant who worked on races out West and spoke to ABC News on the condition of anonymity. "This was a total rebuke of Donald Trump, both him personally and his politics."

RNC National Press Secretary Natalie Baldassarre said in a statement that Republicans will "continue to put America first,” highlighting that the RNC raised $130 million, sending more than $60 million directly to Republican campaigns.
When reached for comment, the White House emphasized Trump’s signature tax legislation and said that Trump will continue to work for the American people.

"Under President Trump’s leadership, this administration has signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, secured the border, cut the cost of prescription drugs, added more than one million private-sector jobs, and locked in nearly 20 trade deals. President Trump will never stop delivering results for the American people and he will undoubtedly go down as the most successful and consequential president in American history," White House spokesman Davis Ingle told ABC News in a statement.
Vance's office, when asked for comment, deferred to the White House.
The donors and operatives who spoke to ABC News agreed Republicans lacked a clear message on affordability -- a key issue for voters.
"We need to talk about pocketbook issues. We didn’t do that,” said Sarah Chamberlain, president and CEO of the Republican Main Street Partnership, a group that fundraises for moderate Republicans.

T.W. Arrighi, a Republican strategist who worked on Republican Darline Graham’s Senate race, said Democrats were talking about affordability "in a more tangible way than we were … We have conservative solutions to these issues, we just didn’t deliver."

A GOP strategist involved in many 2026 races said the party's turnout operation will likely take much of the blame. ABC News' analysis of early voting in Texas and Georgia a week before Election Day showed greater Democratic enthusiasm.
"We just weren't hitting the numbers we needed to hit of just sheer Republicans voting. A lot of them stayed home, and we knew that was happening," the strategist said.
The Republican consultant who worked on races out West added that Republicans had "no choice" but to run on culture war issues because of the high costs brought on by the Iran war.
"You can't tell people to ignore your lying eyes,” the source said. "[Republicans] had no choice but to go down the culture-war road because we couldn't talk about the economy."

Trump said in a phone interview with Fox News on election night that he was "a little bit surprised" by the midterm results and added that part of the reason was the Iran war, directly linking it to gas prices.
In a social media post after the election, Trump wrote that Republicans would have been more successful had he been on the ballot.
Reversal among Latino voters
According to the ABC News Voter Poll, in 2026, Latino voters nationally supported Democratic House candidates by a 30-point margin. In 2024, it was a 13-point margin.
Trump acknowledged his mass-deportation policies may have been "too tough" in an interview with CBS News' "60 Minutes" after the midterms.
Mike Madrid, a GOP consultant who studies Latino voting behavior, said "there is no question that the ICE stuff and deportations played a role."
"There’s also no question that the economy was the No. 1 factor. But in some districts, like south Texas, they're one and the same. Immigration is the economy there," Madrid said.
Democrats swept every congressional district along the southern border, flipping several Republican-held seats in Texas.
Billionaire donor John Catsimatidis told ABC News that the losses came down to the war in Iran and "ICE being too tough on waiters and busboys."

Immigration enforcement under the Trump administration has reached local businesses and restaurants. ABC News reported last May that in D.C., federal law enforcement officials visited dozens of restaurants, carry-out spots and bars across several neighborhoods.
RNC Co-Chair KC Crosbie announced on Nov. 5 that she's challenging RNC Chair Joe Gruters, saying the party should "be willing to confront where we fell short."
A source close to Gruters confirmed to ABC News that he is running for reelection.
While Trump has since reaffirmed his support for Gruters, some Republicans questioned Gruters' competence.
“Joe Gruters failed the Republican Party, and I find it puzzling that he believes he deserves to be reelected,” said an RNC member.

Florida GOP Chairman Evan Power said in a statement, however, that "Gruters was a key partner in our fight to keep the Free State of Florida red, and he’s the leader I trust to keep our party on offense and ready to win in 2028."
McDaniel said "the committee should support whoever the president wants to be the RNC chair."
She added that donors who may be discouraged from giving in the future need an autopsy from the party over what went wrong.

"People are still wondering what happened, and the sooner that a plan is put forward, and they get in the field and they get data … That's going to be what’s going to bring donors back. But right now, I think everybody's shell-shocked."
While Vance hasn't ruled out a run in 2028, some donors told ABC News that his proximity to Trump may be a liability.
But a Vance ally who spoke to ABC News cautioned against writing off Vance, comparing it to the 2016 and 2024 election cycles, when different parts of the Republican Party wrote Trump off.

And although Vance is still undecided about a 2028 presidential run, many of Vance's allies expect that he will run for president in 2028, sources confirmed to ABC News Chief Washington Correspondent Jonathan Karl.
Vance's allies say he will decide whether to pursue a White House bid on his own timeline.
But some Republicans see an opening for Secretary of State Marco Rubio to run for president in 2028 following the midterm elections.
Rubio has said he has no plans to run for president in 2028, adding that he would support Vance if he mounted a presidential run.
Catsimatidis said his family has been supporters of Vance, but he has known Rubio for 15 years and considers the nomination "still open."
A Texas-based GOP donor said the next nominee must appeal to "most all Republicans, a majority of independents and a reasonable group of conservative Democrats."
"We're in like stage two with a five-stage model of grief or something. We're not at the writing-checks-for-new-people yet stage," said one donor. "America doesn't want more MAGA."

title: Trump says he 'would not mind' if Jensen Huang is reinstated as Nvidia CEO
summary: President Donald Trump said Monday morning that he "would not mind" if Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO of Nvidia.
story: Trump also said, "I don't know" if Alice Huang is a Chinese spy.

President Donald Trump said Monday morning that he "would not mind" if Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO of Nvidia and claimed that he doesn't know whether Alice Huang, the woman Huang allegedly had an affair with, is an intelligence asset for China.

Before departing from the White House for a high-stakes trip to Asia, including meetings with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China, Trump addressed the scandal that prompted Huang to resign from the company he co-founded in 1993 and turned into an artificial intelligence giant.

Asked specifically by ABC News senior political correspondent Rachel Scott if he trusted U.S. intelligence reports that Alice Huang was a suspected intelligence asset for China, Trump responded, "I don't know that she is a spy."

"Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country, that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy. I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't know," Trump said.

Trump had been briefed twice over the past year on Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang by intelligence officials and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a U.S. official and sources briefed on the matter told ABC News. The president did not take any action at the time, the sources said.
Trump was first briefed on U.S. intelligence that Jensen Huang was having an affair with a woman believed to be working for Chinese intelligence in the fall of 2025, the sources told ABC News.

On May 12, 2026, Secretary of State Marco Rubio shared intelligence with Trump on Air Force One showing Huang was in a relationship with a woman believed to be an intelligence asset for China, the U.S. official and sources said. Trump was briefed by Rubio shortly before Huang was set to join Trump on the trip to China, the U.S. official and sources said.

Jensen Huang's stunning resignation was announced on Nov. 8 along with his admission to having an extramarital affair. Huang, however, did not admit to an affair with Alice Hung, just that he had been "unfaithful to my wife."
The Nvidia Board appointed Colette Kress, the company's CFO, to take over as interim CEO while a search for a permanent replacement is launched.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun denied reports that Alice Huang, a one-time executive at Megaspeed International, was an intelligence agent. He told reporters, "The claim regarding a so-called Chinese spy is completely groundless and pure slander."
The Singaporean cloud-computing company released a statement saying Alice Huang "left Megaspeed effective Aug. 30, 2025, and currently has no role with the company."
"Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang’s personal and private matters," the company's statement said.
The company, which is under scrutiny over alleged transfers of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies, also announced an internal investigation led by outside lawyers.

Megaspeed told The Associated Press that it runs a "legitimate and lawful business" and was aware of media reports containing claims about its business, supply chain and global operations "that are not supported by verifiable evidence.” The company did not address specific allegations.

Jensen Huang, 63, has become a trusted ally of Trump and an adviser to the president on AI technology, visiting the White House for events more than a half-dozen times between January 2025 and October 2026, according to ABC News' reporting. This year, he has traveled with Trump on a state visit to China and joined the president during a state visit to Great Britain.

When asked Monday if Jensen Huang should be reinstated at Nvidia, Trump said, "I think having Jensen go back, a lot of people are asking Jensen... They think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn't a bad idea."

Trump's comments on Monday came as ABC News has learned that Jensen Huang will likely testify before Congress during the first week of December, sources with knowledge of the negotiations to get Huang to testify told ABC News.
Jensen Huang and House lawmakers are continuing to negotiate a joint, behind-closed-doors testimony with multiple House committees.

Sources with knowledge of the negotiations told ABC News that Jensen Huang is expected to appear voluntarily and House lawmakers are not expected to subpoena him, although sources have made it clear they maintain the option.

The Senate Banking Committee has also requested that both Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify before the panel. Both have expressed willingness to testify before the panel, but they have not yet settled on dates.
A third committee, the House Intelligence Committee, has also asked Lutnick to testify. It's unclear where those talks stand.
Lawmakers have raised concerns about national security implications of Jensen Huang's reported extramarital relationship given that he ran the world's largest computer chip manufacturer.
"Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Commerce Department spokesperson Kristen Eichamer said last week.
On Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the Commerce Department for dragging its feet on blacklisting Megaspeed as an alleged national security threat.
"Many other departments were pushing for this and Commerce had the pen," Bessent told Fox News.
Bessent said the real question is whether Nvidia’s chips were illegally being diverted to China.

"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings,” said Bessent, adding that he would like to see Nvidia’s next CEO come from outside the company.
Meanwhile, Trump isn't the only one open to Jensen Huang making a comeback at Nvidia, whose stock has lost more than 30% of its value since early October.

The Financial Times reported over the weekend that one of Jensen Huang's allies, whose name was not disclosed, is building a war room to lobby Nvidia's Board of Directors and the White House to reinstall Huang as Nvidia CEO.

More than 177,000 supporters of Jensen Huang, including Elon Musk and nearly 93,000 Nvidia shareholders and more than 8,800 current Nvidia employees, have signed a letter addressed to Nvidia's Board of Directors demanding that Huang be reinstated as the company's CEO.
"Bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts, unless and until you can provide compelling evidence that his removal is in NVIDIA's best interest," the letter says.
The letter goes on to raise concerns that Jensen Huang was removed "without meaningful due process."

"We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the center of this controversy was a spy," the letter says. "Suspicion or association alone is not a sufficient basis for ending Jensen's leadership. The inquiry must establish the facts, not merely justify an outcome already imposed."
Organizers of the letter are encouraging Nvidia investors to dial in to Nvidia's earnings call on Tuesday, the first without Jensen Huang, to voice support for the demands in the letter.
ABC News' Rachel Scott, Lauren Peller and Jay O'Brien contributed to this report.

title: Supreme Court rebuffs Trump administration appeal over DEI funding cuts
summary: The Supreme Court has rejected a Trump administration appeal on DEI funding cuts to academic research
story: The Supreme Court has rejected a Trump administration appeal on DEI funding cuts to academic research

WASHINGTON -- The Supreme Court on Monday rejected a Trump administration appeal on DEI funding cuts to academic research even as some conservative justices raised questions about implicit bias training in a separate case.

The justices’ first decision left in place lower court rulings that the Trump administration likely ran afoul of the First Amendment when it terminated millions of dollars in grants to University of California researchers.

The cuts came after an executive order issued in January 2025 telling the government to end programs linked to DEI, which stands for diversity, equity and inclusion. The Trump administration argued that the government is not obligated to continue funding research that no longer fits its priorities.
The lawsuit, which involves only a portion of the Trump administration’s research funding cuts, will continue to play out.
No justices publicly dissented from the brief order declining to hear the case.

The Supreme Court also declined Monday to hear a challenge to California’s requirement for continuing medical education courses to include discussion of how unconscious bias can affect healthcare outcomes.

In that case, though, three conservative justices voiced an interest in the claims. Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito dissented, saying the requirement raises questions about state regulation of private speech.
Justice Neil Gorsuch also noted briefly that he would have heard the case.

title: Mullin defends use of government plane to go to college football game after ground stop
summary: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defends using a government plane to attend a college football game after a nationwide ground stop caused travel chaos
story: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defends using a government plane to attend a college football game after a nationwide ground stop caused travel chaos

WASHINGTON -- Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Tuesday defended his use of a government plane to fly to a college football game the day after a nationwide ground stop which caused massive travel disruptions and left people stranded across the country.
Mullin, speaking on CNBC, acknowledged earlier reporting in the New York Post that he flew to the LSU-Texas college football game a day after all planes were grounded.
Asked whether he is required to fly on government planes and whether he paid for the trip personally, Mullin said yes.
“We would have never went if the airways weren’t completely open,” he said on CNBC. “They’d been completely open for 21 hours.”
He added: “We would have never taken airspace if airspace wasn't open. And we still gotta live our lives at the same time.”
The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the flight.
The day before his flight, Mullin was at the White House alongside Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy giving updates on the ground stop.
The longest flight stoppage in 25 years lasted more than four hours and ended around 8:15 p.m. ET Friday, allowing some domestic flights to take off from U.S. airports.

President Donald Trump's administration has said last week’s air traffic snarls were caused by a router issue in the aging air traffic control system. Trump on Monday got defensive during a lengthy — sometimes testy — exchange with reporters as he left the White House for his trip to Asia.
He faulted old technology and Democrats for the incident that caused upheaval at the country’s airports — especially his predecessor, President Joe Biden.
“I don’t take any responsibility” for Friday’s ground stop, Trump said,
“What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack,” the president said. He later noted: “Incredibly, everybody was safe. Nobody was hurt. No crashes, no nothing.”
Trump was silent on the chaos until Sunday, when he posted on social media blasting his Democratic predecessor and asking Congress for more money to cover the cost of system improvements.

title: What to know about flights after the US nationwide ground stop
summary: The Federal Aviation Administration has lifted a nationwide ground stop, allowing some domestic flights to depart from U.S. airports
story: The Federal Aviation Administration has lifted a nationwide ground stop, allowing some domestic flights to depart from U.S. airports
A nationwide ground stop ended around 8:15 p.m. ET, and some domestic flights have now departed from U.S. airports.
However, normalizing air traffic after the longest flight stoppage in 25 years will be slow, authorities warned.
Officials say the system is likely to be operating normally in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.
Here’s what to know.
The Federal Aviation Administration said airplane departures could late Friday evening Eastern time. Passengers should contact their airlines for information about their flights, the FAA said.
The ripple effect from the stoppage could be felt for days, however.
More than 2,500 flights were canceled in the U.S. on Saturday and hundreds more were delayed, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned Americans traveling that getting air traffic back to normal won't be quick.
International flights are being handled on a case-by-case basis, according to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.
San Francisco airport said that flights headed across the Pacific Ocean were cleared to leave the airport from Friday evening. That included flights destined for Hawaii and Asia.
Europe’s aviation agency suspended U.S.-bound departures at the request of the FAA from 5 p.m. Eastern on Friday until midnight.
Airlines are obligated to offer free rebooking on another flight for travelers who want to continue their journey, or a refund if their flight was canceled and they decide not to take the trip.
New technology being hooked up to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment, Trump administration officials said.
That caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the flight shutdown of more than four hours, according to officials.
Duffy suggested more disruptions might occur.
“We didn’t think we would have this kind of outage. We did,” he said.
The air traffic control modernization began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
Microsoft said it had no indication that the ground stop was related to the service disruption that took Outlook and other services offline Thursday, a spokesperson for the company said.
Mullin said there is no indication the failure was related to a cyberattack, either.
“There was never any lives at risk,” Mullin added. “There was no flights at risk. FAA was able to handle it. We did it."
The ground stop was enacted “out of an abundance of caution,” he said.

title: What to know about flights after the US nationwide ground stop
summary: U.S. air travel operations are still recovering after the nationwide ground stop
story: U.S. air travel operations are still recovering after the nationwide ground stop
Officials said they expect airline schedules to fully recover by the end of the day Sunday after a nationwide ground stop that was initiated out of caution caused massive travel disruptions.
The longest flight stoppage in 25 years lasted more than four hours and ended around 8:15 p.m. ET Friday, allowing some domestic flights to take off from U.S. airports.

Of the 41,000 flights scheduled Saturday, more than 6,600 were canceled, according to FlightAware. Just over 1,300 of the more than 26,000 flights scheduled for Sunday were canceled, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics firm. That amounts to about 5.2% of scheduled flights. Prior to Friday, the average cancellation rate for U.S. departures was 3.4%.
But officials said the U.S. airspace was safe and operational and would recover well ahead of the Thanksgiving travel rush.
Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication the failure was related to a cyberattack and no lives were at risk.
Here’s what to know:

Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford said the system was stable Saturday. Several thousand flights were able to fly after the ground stop, but ultimately, some 12,000 scheduled flights were unable to take off Friday, he said.
Officials acknowledged the disruption but said safety was paramount.

Bedford offered an apology for stranded travelers and thanked air traffic controllers, pilots and flight attendants for managing the fallout. He said officials were confident the system is operating safely or else they would keep airplanes on the ground.

American Airlines said in a statement Saturday night that some individual flights might still be canceled as it continued working to fully restore its operations. It urged travelers to check their flight statuses.
Airlines are obligated to offer free rebooking on another flight or a full refund if a flight is canceled.
Bedford said the administration was working closely with airlines and said they were waiving all terms and conditions.
Some airlines were allowing passengers to rebook if they had travel scheduled Friday or Saturday. Others extended the offer to people with reservations for Sunday or even Monday.
Bedford advised passengers to contact their airlines.

A contractor was replacing a section of the system’s old and discontinued copper wire with new fiber wire in a remote location Friday afternoon, Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said Saturday. That kind of work has been happening across the country and across industries for decades, he said.

But on Friday, the router in that location started overloading the air traffic control system and causing intermittent disruptions to communications and radar feeds. When officials couldn’t quickly locate the cause of the overload, they grounded flights nationwide.
“We did that out of an abundance of caution,” Bedford said. “I’m sorry that we put you through this, but we did it for the right reasons.”

Officials stressed that the ground stop was not the result of a system outage or nefarious activity by a foreign actor. Duffy said officials were investigating whether contractor error or a faulty router was the cause.

The air traffic control modernization began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work. About 70% of copper wire has been switched to fiber already, officials said Saturday.

Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored after its own massive outage. There was no indication the FAA ground stop was related to the service disruption that took Microsoft services offline Thursday, according to federal officials and a company spokesperson.
Over 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft said on its website. Users reported Microsoft 365 services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were interrupted.

title: Trump administration blames ‘overloaded’ systems for ground stop after FAA lets flights resume
summary: The Federal Aviation Administration says airplane departures can resume after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop caused by communications problems
story: The Federal Aviation Administration says airplane departures can resume after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop caused by communications problems

WASHINGTON -- Trump administration officials said Friday that new technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated parts of it and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years.
It was lifted in the evening after a five-hour stretch when most flights were not allowed to take off from airports in the U.S.

Thousands of flights and potentially over a million travelers were affected. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that no one was in any danger as more than 3,000 flights were safely landed. But Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said he could not guarantee it wouldn’t happen again.
Mullin said the FAA was installing “new equipment, new technology” and “it was overwhelming the older system.” There appeared to be no indication of a cyberattack, he said.

A limited number of domestic flights began departing late Friday after the ground stop was lifted, but it will likely take days for airlines to fully recover because so many planes and crews were out of position. Officials said they think the system will be back to normal in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.

The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when another key FAA computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

Asked whether he could rule out a cyberattack or rogue artificial intelligence incident, Mullin said there are no “footprints” showing an attack and that the problem appears to be “mechanically driven.” He said officials were still looking for the cause.

At least 827 flights had been diverted. By 7:05 p.m. EST, 670 flights were sent back to the airport from where they originally took off, while 157 were redirected to a different airport, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company.

Duffy was defensive, blaming Congress for failing to approve more funding for new technology, while downplaying the fact that trying to implement new fixes overtaxed the system. He implored lawmakers to act.
“By doing nothing, you inject way more risk into the system,” he said.

Duffy said he expected flights around the country to be “back up and operational as we come into the heat of travel” next weekend ahead of Thanksgiving, but he also suggested more disruptions might occur.
“We didn’t think we would have this kind of outage. We did,” he said, while also noting, “We were able to review what went wrong, and then reboot the system and go. But, you will have more of these.”
Duffy said the problems were not linked to the FAA’s new AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky because that isn’t connected to what failed on Friday.
“This is all the old legacy equipment. All of the new equipment that’s been deployed did not go down,” Duffy said.

The FAA has already replaced thousands of old copper wires with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
Many flights ended up being diverted to places including Washington Dulles International Airport, Los Angeles International Airport and Nashville International Airport.
Some 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers had been scheduled to take off from airports in the U.S. after 4 p.m. EST.
At the time of the ground stoppage, more than 3,500 airplanes were in the sky, Duffy said.

At Chicago O’Hare Airport on Friday, travelers passing through security learned about the ground stop when they looked up at screens that showed flight delays across the board. Some called friends or family members, debating whether to stay the night in Chicago or find another way to their destinations.
Amber McQuilkin, 27, sat on a bench, disappointed that she might miss a trip with friends to New York for the League of Legends world finals.

“There’s not really any information being passed to me,” said the Seattle software engineer. “I contemplated just abandoning the flight and driving, but then the more I thought about it, the more I’m like, that would be miserable.”

Ruth Coles was still stuck on her plane five hours after it landed at the Los Angeles International Airport from Newark even after the ground stop was lifted. She said they were told they were waiting for a gate to open up.
“The pilot keeps saying they are telling him we are next in line,” Coles said, but that was several hours ago.

NBA, NHL and college teams were left stranded as they tried to reach their destinations. Meanwhile, NFL teams were left to wonder whether the issue would be resolved in time to travel to their games this weekend.
Duffy said NCAA teams will be prioritized ahead of football games on Saturday.
“I would encourage those football teams to reach out to the FAA, to schedule their flight times and make sure they can move” to make their kickoff, he said.
Cargo flights were also delayed by the ground stop.
FedEx, the world’s largest cargo airline, said it was prepared to activate contingency plans to keep any possible disruptions at a minimum.

U.S. airlines move about 61,000 tons (55,340 metric tonnes) of goods — from letters to packages — to and from more than 220 countries daily, according to the industry trade group Airlines for America.

The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, although that disruption was linked to a construction crew cutting a fiber optic line. Aging equipment was also blamed for the brief radar outages last year that disrupted Newark airport.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the difference this time is that it happened on a nationwide scale that left controllers unable to reliably talk to pilots.

“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground and not put them in the air, where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them,” said Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot.

Friday’s ground stop was also different than the one after 9/11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said.

Funk reported from Omaha, Nebraska. AP writers Mead Gruver in Fort Collins, Colorado; Ali Swenson in Chicago; Alex Veiga and Jaimie Ding in Los Angeles; Seung Min Kim and Aamer Madhani in Washington; Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City; and Hallie Golden in Seattle contributed to this report.
This story has been corrected to show the Sept. 11 attacks were in 2001.

title: Questions around FAA's new SMART AI system, officials say no link to ground stop
summary: The airline ground stop that has wreaked havoc on travel since Friday was not related to the FAA’s new, $875 million AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky
story: The airline ground stop that has wreaked havoc on travel since Friday was not related to the FAA’s new, $875 million AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky

The airline ground stop that wreaked havoc on travel since Friday was not related to the FAA's new, $875 million AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky, according to government officials and the artificial intelligence company behind the technology.

But the timing of the ground stop, so close to the national rollout of the Federal Aviation Administration's SMART system, has raised questions about what the system does, its benefits and risks compared with the existing human system and what guardrails there are to address potential problems.

The SMART system is based in a single location near Washington where a team of experts analyzes flight schedules, weather forecasts and hundreds of other streams of data. Then that office sends recommendations to the FAA’s command center, which relays them to air traffic controllers across the country for consideration.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday there’s no indication the communications issues that caused the ground stop are linked to the new computer system, and the top officials at the Transportation Department and FAA reiterated that Saturday.
The startup that designed the system, Air Space Intelligence, or ASI, said the ground stop wasn’t caused by “the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.”

But lawmakers and outside groups raised questions about the SMART system before Friday's ground stop. Last month, House Democrats sent a letter to the U.S. Government Accountability Office requesting an audit of the new software, raising concerns about safety and guardrails.

“Concerningly, the nation’s front line aviation safety workforce apparently had little to no input into SMART’s development and have received limited training and information during the current deployment process,” the Oct. 13 letter said. “The use of artificial intelligence within SMART has rightfully raised serious questions about its reliability and safety benefits, particularly on its potential to interfere with decision-making by experienced air traffic controllers or to hallucinate safety-critical information.”
SMART, however, is not — at least not yet — set up for AI to be in charge of flight control. Rather, it is making recommendations to humans who do so.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford unveiled the system in September, calling it a “cutting-edge tool that centralizes 200 data streams — including weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow, and controller staffing metrics — into one platform.” SMART stands for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories.

The system's AI-supported engine synthesizes the data systems and shows a “comprehensive visualization” of where planes are going, how much traffic the system can handle and where congestion or weather could cause problems, according to the announcement. The idea is for specialists to then use the platform to fix problems before they arise.

The FAA says that during the initial test of the system in the Washington area this fall, the system helped reroute 180 flights and saved an average of 10 minutes and 80 gallons of fuel per flight by diverting around weather or other issues. The agency said that one flight cut 42 minutes off its trip from Tampa, Florida, to Dallas thanks to the system's recommendations.
So SMART was expanded for use nationwide on Nov. 10 for the airspace of all 22 air traffic control centers. That was three days before the ground stop.

According to a government fact sheet on the tool, SMART can predict where air traffic is headed and identify other routes before an area becomes too congested. The system can also help reopen restricted airspace faster and better manage airport arrivals.
SMART is also supposed to help with weather-related issues faster.

Currently, the FAA blocks off portions of airspace affected by weather as “large, rectangular boxes,” according to the fact sheet, which doesn't reflect how weather actually looks, with quick-moving thunderstorms and storm systems that are “often irregular in shape, with narrow gaps or corridors that aircraft could safely fly through.”

To help with this, SMART gives the FAA and airspace operators a “clearer picture of how weather will affect air traffic over time,” allowing air traffic controllers to plan around storms and use available airspace instead of unnecessarily shutting down large areas.

No other country has a working AI air traffic tool like the SMART system, according to Michael McCormick, a former FAA airspace manager and an associate professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. Eurocontrol, the European air traffic authority, has a system in testing and several manufacturers are prototyping similar tools.

While government officials and ASI, the company behind SMART, have stressed that its AI system is designed to assist humans and not run flight control, its deployment has raised concerns about relying on artificial intelligence when human lives are at stake, given that even the most advanced models are prone to hallucinations — when models fabricate false information and present it as fact.

Mike O’Donnell, a former top FAA official who worked for the agency for 17 years and now does aviation safety consulting work, said the agency “has got to make sure that this is just a tool in the toolbox and not the actual machine that’s doing the work.”
The FAA, he said, “cannot afford to be wrong on this.”

“It’s good to use it with the proper guardrails and backstops to ensure that they’re not giving wrong information to controllers based on what (AI) has come up with,” O’Donnell said. “There’s got to be a way to verify and validate what it’s doing to make sure that it’s not the wrong information.”
He cautioned against putting too much trust in AI “until we know for sure that it's proven itself time and time again. And that's going to take a while.”

The AI system's launch comes amid a longstanding shortage of air traffic controllers around the country. The National Air Traffic Controllers Association has been raising concerns about this for more than a decade, telling Congress in 2015 that the shortage was at a crisis level. It said then that the FAA had missed its hiring targets for five years in a row. The union represents about 14,000 controllers, roughly 3,000 of them trainees. That said, experts say no AI system can replace the human air traffic controllers who spend years training for this highly demanding and stressful job.
In an October interview with NPR, ASI co-founder and CEO Phillip Buckendorf said the SMART tool is designed for traffic managers who manage the entire U.S. airspace.

“The AI does the math, the AI does the computation,” Buckendorf told NPR, but it’s ultimately up to the human operator whether to take the system’s recommendation. “They make the decision, they are the decider, they are the judge.”

title: Fewer students are traveling from abroad to study at US universities, report shows
summary: Fewer international students are coming to U.S. universities to study as the Trump administration cracks down on immigration and reshapes higher education
story: Fewer international students are coming to U.S. universities to study as the Trump administration cracks down on immigration and reshapes higher education
Fewer international students are studying at U.S. universities as the Trump administration cracks down on immigration and reshapes higher education, data released Monday shows.

Overall, U.S. campuses saw a 9% decrease in international enrollment this fall compared with last year, according to a survey from the Institute of International Education. And the number of new students entering the United States for the first time fell by 15%.

“No one aspires to send their kids to get educated in the U.S.,” said Veena Dubal, general counsel for the American Association of University Professors, whose father traveled from India to attend Tuskegee University, then the Tuskegee Institute, in the late 1960s on a student visa.
“It feels like an unsafe place. That’s the message that the Trump administration has been sending to families all over the world and they’re listening.”

Last year, the enrollment decreases were partially offset by large numbers of students who stayed in the U.S. for temporary work after graduating. But after months of speculation, the Department of Homeland Security proposed requiring schools to pay a $70,000 fee for every student who participates in the optional practice training program.
Although the rule hasn't been finalized, participation in the program, known as OPT for short, dropped 6% this fall, according to the survey.

The proposed rule, which is expected to face legal challenges, is part of wider DHS efforts that include terminating the legal status of thousands of international students, along with detaining and deporting many of them.

And this summer, the administration finalized a rule that will prevent international students from staying in the U.S. for more than four years without approval from the federal government, although a judge has temporarily blocked it.
DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said the changes were intended to crack down on loopholes that international students were exploiting by extending their studies.
Although the U.S. remains the top destination for international students globally, the changes are having an effect, college leaders told the IIE.

Among more than 800 U.S. colleges and universities surveyed this fall, 88% blamed the visa application process and 70% blamed travel restrictions for the enrollment drops. And if OPT options are limited, 95% of schools predicted that international students would likely look to another country, according to the survey, which offers an early look at trends before full data is released next year.

Politics aren't the only reason students are looking elsewhere, said Mirka Martel, head of research, evaluation and learning for the institute. Its survey found more global competition for international students and the rising cost of a U.S. degree also contributed.

Fanta Aw, the executive director and CEO of NAFSA, an association that represents international education, said students also are worried about research funding. Last year, the Trump administration began dismantling the federal grant-giving process and attempting to exert more political influence over what projects get funded.

“They’re saying to themselves, ‘Too much uncertainty in the United States. It’s too difficult, and you know, more importantly, we have many more choices today than we did 10 years ago. Why subject ourselves to this?’” Aw said, noting that students are going to places like China.

NAFSA, in partnership with the international education technology company JB International, found that amid the enrollment decline, international students’ contributions to the U.S. economy dropped by $2.4 billion this fall.
American colleges and universities heavily recruit students from overseas as a source of tuition revenue. So the drops have punched big holes in tuition revenue at some schools.

At Cleveland State University, international enrollment has dropped by 46% in two years, from 1,542 in fall 2025 to 828 this fall. And fewer than 50 new international students started this fall, said Provost Nigamanth Sridhar, who estimated that the budgetary impact ranges from $2 million to $4 million.
Decades ago, he arrived in the U.S. on an F1 student visa and participated in OPT. Eventually, he went through the process to become a naturalized citizen.

“I am here in this position, in this job, because I had the opportunity to come to the United States as an international graduate student and then decided to stay here and build a career,” said Sridhar, who is from India. “So international education is personal to me.”

The biggest drops were at the graduate level. This fall's data shows a 15% drop in international graduate enrollment, compared to a 3% decrease at the undergraduate level. The report also found declines in international students from India, which sends more students to the U.S. to study than any other country.

Sarah Spreitzer, vice president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents, said substantial immigration bills are unlikely while Trump remains president. But she said congressional oversight might halt new policies targeted at international students.
“Those types of things could provide more certainty for our international students that there’s not just going to be these sudden or unexplainable changes,” Spreitzer said.
