title: Supreme Court rebuffs Trump administration appeal over DEI funding cuts
summary: The Supreme Court has rejected a Trump administration appeal on DEI funding cuts to academic research
story: The Supreme Court has rejected a Trump administration appeal on DEI funding cuts to academic research

WASHINGTON -- The Supreme Court on Monday rejected a Trump administration appeal on DEI funding cuts to academic research even as some conservative justices raised questions about implicit bias training in a separate case.

The justices’ first decision left in place lower court rulings that the Trump administration likely ran afoul of the First Amendment when it terminated millions of dollars in grants to University of California researchers.

The cuts came after an executive order issued in January 2025 telling the government to end programs linked to DEI, which stands for diversity, equity and inclusion. The Trump administration argued that the government is not obligated to continue funding research that no longer fits its priorities.
The lawsuit, which involves only a portion of the Trump administration’s research funding cuts, will continue to play out.
No justices publicly dissented from the brief order declining to hear the case.

The Supreme Court also declined Monday to hear a challenge to California’s requirement for continuing medical education courses to include discussion of how unconscious bias can affect healthcare outcomes.

In that case, though, three conservative justices voiced an interest in the claims. Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito dissented, saying the requirement raises questions about state regulation of private speech.
Justice Neil Gorsuch also noted briefly that he would have heard the case.

title: Federal review faults leadership failures in Grand Canyon fire that destroyed lodge
summary: Leadership failures along with a lack of preparedness and poor communication were the driving factors of a wildfire that destroyed a historic lodge and dozens of structures at Grand Canyon National Park
story: Leadership failures along with a lack of preparedness and poor communication were the driving factors of a wildfire that destroyed a historic lodge and dozens of structures at Grand Canyon National Park

Leadership failures along with a lack of preparedness and poor communication were the driving factors of a wildfire that destroyed a historic lodge and dozens of structures along the North Rim of Grand Canyon National Park.

A federal review of the Dragon Bravo Fire recently made public noted that while drought conditions and extreme fire behavior contributed, systemic weaknesses in the National Park Service related to authority and qualifications hindered decision-making at critical moments.
The 2025 fire should be considered a warning, according to the multiagency team of experts that reviewed the handling of the fire.

“The findings indicated many of the challenges observed during the fire were foreseeable, preventable, and reflective of broader institutional issues that extend beyond a single park, region, or agency,” the report stated.

The Dragon Bravo Fire was sparked by lightning in July 2025. The park service allowed it to burn for days before it exploded into a fast-moving conflagration that forced evacuations and consumed the Grand Canyon Lodge, historic cabins, employee housing and other critical infrastructure. Suppression costs topped $141 million over three months.
The park service initially defended its handling of the fire, saying a sudden and extreme shift in the wind far exceeded forecasts.

Grand Canyon officials referred questions about the findings to the U.S. Interior Department, which oversees the park service. The Interior Department did not immediately answer emails sent by The Associated Press.

The review, ordered by the Interior Department's deputy secretary, provides a timeline that starts with the day the fire ignited. It details weather conditions and includes photos of the towering plume that could be seen from the South Rim, the lodge awash in flames and the charred remains of the historic building.

The review noted that it was known by park officials that the region was experiencing persistent drought and had dense fuels in close proximity to nationally significant historic structures. Fire planning and policy documents existed, but the review stated those plans “were not fully translated into effective preseason preparedness actions or operational readiness.”

The recommendations include requiring agency administrators to undergo the needed training to handle complex incidents and ensuring that communication flows through proper channels so that decision-makers get firsthand, accurate and timely information.

The review highlighted a breakdown in communication that resulted in a multiday delay in fire retardant being used as the flames intensified. The decision to use retardant came only after several structures, including the lodge, already had been lost, according to the findings.

The review also stated that the park service's continued authorization of the confine and contain strategy did not reflect awareness of changing conditions or escalating risk. The recommendations also call for fire leadership to reevaluate their strategies regularly and to reconsider weather conditions, fire behavior and the availability of resources.
The review team described the Dragon Bravo Fire as a defining event for Grand Canyon National Park and a consequential case study for the Interior Department and the U.S. Wildland Fire Service.

The experts stated in the review that the resulting loss of historic structures, the displacement of employees, the risks to firefighters and the significant suppression costs underscore the stakes associated with managing wildfires in complex landscapes.

“What began as a small, naturally ignited fire rapidly evolved into a high-consequence, cross-boundary incident that tested leadership, governance, preparedness, decision quality, and execution across multiple programs and agencies,” the team stated.
Montoya Bryan reported from Albuquerque, New Mexico.

title: Divided appeals court blocks Pentagon from expelling several transgender troops from US military
summary: A federal appeals court has blocked the Pentagon from forcing several transgender troops out of the military, after finding President Donald Trump’s ban was unlawfully imposed
story: A federal appeals court has blocked the Pentagon from forcing several transgender troops out of the military, after finding President Donald Trump’s ban was unlawfully imposed

WASHINGTON -- A federal appeals court on Tuesday blocked the Pentagon from forcing more than two dozen transgender troops out of the military, several months after it found that President Donald Trump’s administration unlawfully imposed the ban.

The decision — implementing an earlier ruling by the same appeals court panel — could set the stage for the issue to return to the Supreme Court, which previously allowed the ban to go forward for now in a different case.

Trump's administration had asked the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit to delay the June 1 ruling's implementation while it petitions the Supreme Court to take up the case. A three-judge panel voted 2-1 on Tuesday to reject the administration's request for a stay of the circuit's decision.
The Supreme Court had ruled in the administration’s favor last year, allowing the Pentagon to start enforcing the ban while the litigation proceeded.

Circuit Judge Robert Wilkins, partially joined by Judge Judith Rogers, ruled in June that the Pentagon's policy was designed to exclude people from the military based on their gender identity. Their majority decision would bar the military from kicking out current service members named in the lawsuit, but it wouldn't allow new transgender recruits to join.

Plaintiffs’ attorneys challenging the Pentagon ban say 27 service members are covered by Tuesday’s order. Shannon Minter, legal director of the National Center for LGBTQ Rights, said the plaintiffs are all “decorated troops who have met every standard the military sets.”

“The Trump administration asked the court to let it keep pushing these service members toward the door while it tries to get a different answer from the Supreme Court. Today, the D.C. Circuit said no,” Minter said in a statement.

On Tuesday, Wilkins said the administration hasn’t shown how retaining the plaintiffs currently serving in the military would cause any irreparable harm to the government or endanger national security. Wilkins also noted that the scope of the June 1 majority opinion was narrower than the injunction that the Supreme Court stayed last year.
“To the extent the government suggests that any injunction against the Executive Branch imposes irreparable harm, I am also unpersuaded,” Wilkins wrote.

The panel's June 1 majority opinion partially upheld a March 2025 ruling by U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes, who concluded that Trump’s executive order to exclude transgender troops from military service likely violates their constitutional rights.

In January 2025, Trump signed an executive order that claims the sexual identity of transgender service members “conflicts with a soldier’s commitment to an honorable, truthful, and disciplined lifestyle, even in one’s personal life” and is harmful to military readiness.

In response, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued a policy that presumptively disqualifies people with gender dysphoria from military service. Gender dysphoria is the distress that a person feels because their assigned gender and gender identity don’t match. The medical condition has been linked to depression and suicidal thoughts.
Wilkins was nominated to the court by Democratic President Barack Obama. Rogers was nominated by President Bill Clinton, also a Democrat.

Circuit Judge Justin Walker, who was nominated by Trump, a Republican, wrote a dissenting opinion in June that said judges lack the power to second-guess the decision to exclude transgender troops. Walker also voted to grant the government's request to suspend the decision.

title: Trump administration signals plan for seawall work at Washington golf course as legal fight drags on
summary: The Interior Department intends to seek bids for a contractor to work on the seawall at a Washington, D.C., park where President Donald Trump plans to redevelop a historic public golf course into a world-class venue
story: The Interior Department intends to seek bids for a contractor to work on the seawall at a Washington, D.C., park where President Donald Trump plans to redevelop a historic public golf course into a world-class venue

WASHINGTON -- The Interior Department has issued a notice that it intends to seek bids for a contractor to begin work on the seawall at a Washington park where President Donald Trump plans to redevelop a historic public golf course into a world-class venue.

Those plans were put on hold by a judge over the weekend. The Interior Department's notice, announced Friday before the judge's action, said the formal solicitation will go out on Nov. 30. The notice said it was not a solicitation but “pre-notice of an upcoming solicitation ONLY.”

The seawall has recently become a central reason in the Trump administration’s argument over why East Potomac Park, which includes the East Potomac Golf Links, is in need of a renovation. Trump, a Republican, has targeted the golf course as one of his projects to remake the District of Columbia in his image.
The Trump administration sought to close the park, citing safety factors including the seawall, which it argued was in precarious condition.
U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes rejected that argument during a hearing on Friday in a lawsuit challenging Trump’s plans to renovate the historic public course.
Reyes issued a temporary restraining order the following day to stop work related to the construction of the golf course.
Reyes was nominated by President Joe Biden, a Democrat, in 2023.

title: Los Angeles homelessness agency reaches settlement with feds in dispute over spending
summary: A Los Angeles government agency that oversaw hundreds of millions of dollars in homelessness spending has reached a settlement with federal housing authorities in a dispute over claims that the agency misused funding
story: A Los Angeles government agency that oversaw hundreds of millions of dollars in homelessness spending has reached a settlement with federal housing authorities in a dispute over claims that the agency misused funding

LOS ANGELES -- A Los Angeles government agency that oversaw hundreds of millions of dollars in homelessness spending has reached a settlement with federal housing authorities in a dispute over claims that the local agency misused funding.

Under the deal announced Tuesday, the LA Homeless Services Authority will return $150 million and be “permanently severed” from federal funding by the end of 2027, according to a statement by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development.

California accounts for nearly a third of the homeless population in the United States. A 2025 survey found that more than 72,000 people were homeless on any given night across Los Angeles County, a slight decrease from the year before.

Last year, HUD moved to cut off the money going to LAHSA after audits found reckless spending and a lack of transparency at the authority, which was responsible for doling out money to provide shelter and services for homeless residents. LAHSA sued to overturn the suspension.
The settlement stipulates that Los Angeles County will take over LAHSA's portfolio of projects and responsibilities for homeless services, subject to oversight by HUD.

“From the outset, we have maintained that LAHSA did not engage in wrongdoing and that HUD’s suspension lacked a legal foundation," Gita O’Neill, LAHSA's interim CEO, said in a statement. “Our focus now is on working closely with our local partners to ensure continuity of services, support an orderly transition, and remain true to our mission of connecting our unhoused neighbors with the services, resources, and pathways to housing they need.”

LAHSA, which was jointly funded by the city and county, was formed in 1993 as a result of a lawsuit settlement. It coordinated and managed money for shelter, food programs and a wide range of services, but it had long been dogged by accusations of misspending.

In April 2025, the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors voted to shift more than $300 million in annual taxpayer money out of LAHSA to create a new department on homelessness. The city of Los Angeles also began exploring how it could sidestep LAHSA and directly contract with homeless service providers.

The region’s homelessness crisis is especially visible in downtown Los Angeles, where hundreds of people live in makeshift shanties that line entire blocks in the notorious neighborhood known as Skid Row. Encampments are increasingly found in suburban areas under freeway overpasses.

title: Trump administration moves to block China from indirect access to American AI technology
summary: The Trump administration has issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers
story: The Trump administration has issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers

WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best artificial intelligence models.

Last week, Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following scrutiny of his ties to a Chinese executive who used to lead Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. The company provides computing power to Chinese companies using chips housed in Southeast Asian data centers, including facilities in Malaysia.

“The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries,” the Bureau of Industry and Security under the Commerce Department said in issuing the rule that took effect immediately.
The rule came on the same day President Donald Trump departed for a trip to Asia, where he expects to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the third time this year amid a fragile truce on trade.

Under the new rule, overseas data centers that serve companies in countries including China, Russia, Iran and Cuba are required to identify their end users. There also will be additional licensing requirements for sales of chips for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil — countries that “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" to unauthorized destinations, the rule says.

In Beijing, China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun accused Washington of arbitrarily interfering with China's trade and technological cooperation with other countries and suppressing the development of China's high-tech industries.

“This is a typical example of economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction, runs counter to the common understanding between the two sides,” he told reporter, adding that it infringes upon the rights of Chinese companies and disrupts the stability of global supply chains.
He said China would take necessary measures to safeguard its interests.

The U.S. bans sales of the country's most advanced AI chips to China, seeking to maintain an edge in its rivalry with China for predominance in artificial intelligence. However, many lawmakers and policymakers believe the country's export control rules are not tough enough and filled with loopholes such as cloud computing that allows China to rent processing power built on American technology.

Last year, U.S. Rep. Michael Lawler, a New York Republican, introduced a bill to broaden the U.S. export controls to include remote access. He told Congress “physical export controls” under current rules do not apply to remote access, allowing China to “access our tech through the cloud” and giving it “a real tool to sidestep” U.S. export restrictions. The bill has passed the House.

In the Senate, lawmakers also are seeking tougher legislation to prevent China from accessing advanced U.S. chip and AI technologies. Bills include proposals that would let Congress review licenses to sell advanced AI chips to China, ask the Department of Commerce to track AI chips to ensure they are not diverted to unauthorized regions, and compel U.S. allies such as the Netherlands and Japan to match U.S. restrictions on exports to Chinese chipmakers.
Last week, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick came under pressure when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Commerce Department was late to place restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed.

On Monday, Trump acknowledged tension between Treasury and Commerce on the matter. He suggested that Lutnick may have delayed placing the export restrictions to avoid a “blow up” in the fragile U.S.-China relationship.
“We’re having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, Trump said.

In a joint statement late Monday by the Commerce and Justice departments, it said Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed for potential export control violations in 2024, which was followed by requests to Nvidia for records in May 2025 related to sales to Megaspeed. The following month, it said, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list, and agents from the Commerce Department in conjunction with Singapore law enforcement conducted on-site checks of Megaspeed and interviewed Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang. The Justice Department then took the lead role in the criminal probe of Megaspeed, the statement said.

“The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” the statement said.

Last week, the Singapore government confirmed that it had investigated Megaspeed over “potential false declarations" involving servers that were exported through Singapore to Malaysia but might have “subsequently been routed from Malaysia to another destination, contrary to declaration made in Singapore.”
The Malaysian government also said last week that it was investigating if chips brought into Malaysia have been re-exported to other countries as permitted by its own law.

“Malaysia welcomes investment in data centers and technology, but will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls,” read the Friday statement by Malaysia's Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry.

title: US Catholic bishops meet after Democrats' big wins help reshape abortion debates
summary: U.S. Catholic bishops are meeting in Baltimore this week following the Democrats’ midterm victories
story: U.S. Catholic bishops are meeting in Baltimore this week following the Democrats’ midterm victories

U.S. Catholic bishops are holding their annual fall meeting in Baltimore this week. The gathering comes just after Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories reset the political dynamics around some of the bishops’ priorities, including immigration, abortion and artificial intelligence.
The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops is now facing a divided government as it seeks to influence both the faithful and public policy.

“Midterm elections are the opportunity for people to assess where we are as a country and where we hope to go,” said Bishop Michael Burbidge of Arlington, Virginia. “I think what the citizens are asking — and we’re certainly praying for — is that those who are elected will be devoted to doing all that is right and just and true and somehow find a way to begin working together and addressing the issues that impact individuals and families.”

Catholics overall are politically mixed. Catholic voters split roughly evenly between Republican and Democratic candidates for the U.S. House, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters.

There was a split between white Catholics and Latino Catholics: Just over half of white Catholics supported the Republican House candidate in their area, while about two-thirds of Latino Catholics supported the Democratic House candidate in their area.

Nationally, just over half of Catholics said the Trump administration’s actions on immigration enforcement had “gone too far,” according to The AP Voter Poll. A similar share disapproved of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement was doing its job.

During the first half of Republican President Donald Trump’s second term, Catholic leaders emerged as strong critics of the administration’s immigration crackdown. Last fall, U.S. bishops issued a rare “special message” on immigration, decrying “the vilification of immigrants” and “indiscriminate mass deportation.”

Bishops are expected to hear updates Wednesday from their committees that deal with migration and abortion. They will also hear from a new task force on “preserving human dignity in the age of artificial intelligence.”

Catholic theology does not fit neatly into American political categories. While Catholic leaders have criticized current Republican immigration policies, they have also taken Democratic leaders to task over support for abortion rights. Targets of criticism included former Democratic President Joe Biden, who is Catholic.

“I think we're still trying to wrap our minds around what actually just happened,” said Bishop Robert Boxie III, an auxiliary bishop of the Archdiocese of Washington, while speaking about the midterms at a Georgetown University forum. He added the elections showed the power of “collective action” over money, including in “communities that had been sort of written off.”
Ahead of the midterms, U.S. bishops led a campaign urging Catholics to exercise their right to vote while putting faith before politics.

“The Church’s contribution to the public life of a nation is not a political or partisan program; rather, it reflects our commitment to the dignity of every person, who is created in the image and likeness of God,” Archbishop Paul Coakley, the conference's president, said in a statement.

That message became muddled in late October, when the White House released images and a video of a group of Catholic bishops praying over Trump in the Oval Office. At least two bishops expressed regret during the ensuing backlash.

“I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purpose,” Bishop William Joensen of Des Moines, Iowa, wrote in a statement. “I pray I am more prudent and wise going forward, even as I remain resolute in my openness to engaging and praying for political leaders at all levels.”

title: As outages persist, Puerto Rico finds a way to help keep the lights on
summary: Hector Ríos is part of Puerto Rico's innovative “virtual power plant” system, which uses household batteries to support the island's electric grid
story: Hector Ríos is part of Puerto Rico's innovative “virtual power plant” system, which uses household batteries to support the island's electric grid

SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- On nearly 20 days in October, an electric utility took energy from a battery attached to Hector Ríos’ house in Cabo Rojo, on the southwest corner of Puerto Rico, and used it to support the power grid.
Ríos was happy to share.

With the U.S. territory's frequent power outages that disrupt daily life and restrain its economy, he likes the idea of helping prevent blackouts for other people. He's also compensated for the energy.
“It just seems like a good deal, to contribute to the community and make money at the same time,” Ríos said.

Ríos, 75, is part of what has become one of Puerto Rico's most effective tools for energy resilience amid nearly a decade of electricity woes: a “virtual power plant,” or VPP, that harnesses batteries from nearly 115,000 households to bolster the grid when its aging and fickle power plants can't meet demand.

Nine years after Puerto Rico's public power utility filed for bankruptcy and Hurricane Maria ravaged its already dilapidated energy grid, residents still face unpredictable blackouts and electricity rates higher than in almost any state. Few new utility-scale power sources have been built since Maria, and most of the federal dollars promised for grid recovery have not yet reached the territory.

But the VPP — the first of its kind in Latin America and the Caribbean, and the U.S.' second largest in terms of capacity — showed its potential this summer, preventing or mitigating outages more than 60 times since June 1, according to Luma Energy, its transmission and distribution utility.
“There’s nothing virtual about it,” said Javier Rúa Jovet, chief policy officer at the Solar and Energy Storage Association of Puerto Rico. “It’s real, and it’s better than a power plant.”

Dozens of states now operate similar networks of distributed energy sources like battery storage systems, electric vehicles and smart thermostats to help manage the grid. Experts expect their role to grow in the U.S. amid energy constraints, rising utility prices, and tech companies’ push to build power-hungry data centers.

As President Donald Trump’s administration promotes fossil fuel expansion and redirects dollars away from solar adoption in Puerto Rico, proponents of the territory's system say it highlights the value of distributed solar and storage, and shows how these systems can bolster resilience for other energy-vulnerable communities.

“There’s a way for this technology to benefit not just the individual buildings that they’re on,” but instead be “in service to the community all the time,” said Nathalie Jordi, community solar lead at Together New Orleans, a nonprofit that championed an upcoming $23 million city program to provide and network over 1,000 batteries on homes and businesses across New Orleans.

The opportunity to harness a vast network of residential batteries arose after Hurricane Maria in 2017, which left some communities without electricity for nearly a year. Experts linked the infrastructure failure to thousands of post-hurricane deaths.
“We had to procure resiliency in some other way,” said Rúa Jovet, “not a centralized system that will completely fail for a whole year.”

There are now over 207,000 rooftop solar systems on an archipelago of fewer than 3.2 million people, a 20-fold increase from before Maria that was propelled by households who could afford installations, philanthropy, and some federal dollars. Because of the territory's unique need for resiliency, nearly every installation includes at least one battery, a necessary add-on to keep the system running in a blackout.

“The mindset was, get yourself ready for everything,” recalled Ríos, who after Maria bought a diesel generator for his house, then installed panels and a Tesla Powerwall battery in 2023. The system also cut his utility bill in half, from about $400 to $200 in the summer.

Solar panels create an energy boon during the day, charging batteries and sending excess power to the grid. But when the sun sets and demand rises, Puerto Rico barely has enough power to meet the need. Any power plant malfunction can prompt an outage.

In late 2023, Luma launched a small pilot program that would leverage residential battery capacity to offset the shortages. Ríos was among the first to enroll; now over half of solar customers participate.

If Luma predicts an energy deficit, customers are digitally notified that a battery sharing event is coming. They can opt out via app, or adjust how much of their battery — enrollees typically offer 30% — they make available.

The experiment has faced challenges. In a 2026 survey of solar customers by the nonprofit Solar United Neighbors, some participants criticized the compensation structure, which varies by solar provider. Others expressed hesitation to enroll in the program because they did not understand it or feared losing backup power.
Ríos said he’s only had that problem once — when a storm knocked out power right after he shared his battery. He now skips battery sharing events if there's bad weather forecast.
He acknowledged the payment system is “a little vague.” He and his wife received $162 last year, which they happily redeemed as a Marshalls gift card.

Luma told The Associated Press that relying so often on battery sharing has contributed in part to recent rate increases. The utility pays solar providers three times the residential electricity price for the battery energy it takes, recovering the costs through rates.

Rúa Jovet says that expense doesn’t compare to the societywide economic losses of frequent power outages that spoil food, endanger health and shutter schools and businesses. The territory is also set to spend more than $1.7 billion this year importing fuel for most of its power generation.

Luma said each battery sharing event, typically about four hours, supports the equivalent of about 80,000 residential customers. Enrolling more households would enable supplemental power for more hours.
But experts believe Puerto Rico can think bigger.

“The VPP in Puerto Rico is like an emergency escape valve, but the batteries should be a grid asset,” said Jigar Shah, director of the Department of Energy’s Loan Programs Office under former President Joe Biden and comanaging director of the advisory firm Multiplier.

Instead of only being tapped in an emergency, Shah said, the batteries could dispatch power every day — offsetting the need to burn fossil fuels — and help absorb excess energy across the grid when solar panels are producing at their peak. Several states, including California and Texas, use solar and batteries this way.

VPPs “could potentially play a larger role in Puerto Rico’s energy future,” Alejandro Figueroa, Luma chief regulatory officer, told The Associated Press. But, he said, a program used daily would require a different design and compensation structure to be sustainable.

Providing daily power is a natural next step, Rúa Jovet said, and could help Puerto Rico meet its own legal mandate that the archipelago reach 100% renewable energy by 2050. But a virtual power plant alone cannot solve the territory’s energy crisis.
That will require deploying billions of unspent federal recovery dollars, continuing improvements to transmission and distribution infrastructure and building new large-scale generation and storage.
“You don’t want the situation to be a persistent emergency forever,” he said.

title: Miami embraces its Vice City alter ego, seizing buzz around ‘GTA VI’ release
summary: The Grand Theft Auto video game franchise is returning to Miami-inspired Vice City
story: The Grand Theft Auto video game franchise is returning to Miami-inspired Vice City

MIAMI -- As gamers worldwide prepare to race stolen supercars, pull off heists and eliminate enemies in a Miami-inspired Vice City, this week’s “Grand Theft Auto VI” release will feel especially personal to Florida residents.

Felix Jarquin is among those who can barely wait to install the massive 200-plus gigabyte game file. “GTA VI” is scheduled to hit PlayStation and Xbox on Thursday, with a PC release expected next year.

“I’ve seen the trailers, the story looks phenomenal,” Jarquin said. “I’m waiting to see how they incorporate that to the environments that we have here in Miami. I want to see, did they do their homework?”
“I already have a group of friends that we’re going to be playing through together, trying to see if we can get to each other’s houses,” the lifelong resident added.
The action-adventure shooter game comes more than 13 years after the franchise’s previous installment, and developer Rockstar Games has promised its largest, most detailed open-world experience yet.
Rockstar’s designers immersed themselves in South Florida, driving around Miami, the Keys and surrounding towns and flying over the Everglades to capture the region’s feel.
They also researched Miami’s history and architecture and interviewed people, including former police officers and gang members, developer Aaron Garbut said.
Their efforts show in the short trailers and a 25-minute preview released in August, said Julie Fornary, a Miami Design Preservation League tour guide.

“I loved the way they got the color, the light, the mix of high and low here in Miami,” Fornary said. “We have the glitz but also the grunge. The chrome and the glass and also half-built, crumbling, unfinished construction. That’s the Miami all of us that live here know.”

Many of the locations featured in “GTA VI” are almost perfectly replicated, Fornary said. As with previous GTA installments set in Liberty City (New York City) and Los Santos (Los Angeles), game designers tend to distort geography a bit, so places might not be exactly where they are in real life.
But Fornary insists no compromises were made when it came to the neon lights and Art Deco architecture of Miami Beach’s iconic Ocean Drive, featured in films from “Bad Boys” to “The Birdcage.”

Among the changes are names — Miami becomes Vice City, with fictional monikers for streets, buildings, neighborhoods and businesses. One of Fornary’s favorites was changing Hotel Victor to Hotel Dixon — a nod to architect Lawrence Murray Dixon, who designed the real building in the 1930s, along with many other historic structures in the city.
Fornary hopes the new game brings attention to South Florida that helps protect its history.

Tour groups still ask about “Miami Vice” — the “cocaine-cowboy” TV crime drama that celebrated its 40th anniversary in 2024 — and “Scarface,” the 1983 film starring Al Pacino that was loosely inspired by the city's infamous gangster resident, Al Capone.
She said she anticipates similar questions after “GTA VI” is released.

“I have no qualms or no issues with anybody who wants to shine a light on the unique architecture and culture that we have here,” Fornary said. “Video games, television shows, feature films, we’ll take it all.”
Many Miami area businesses and government officials embraced the Vice City connection despite the name's negative connotation.

Miami-Dade County struck a $3.9 million deal with Rockstar that includes a giant “Welcome to Vice City” rooftop display at the Miami Heat's Kaseya Center. The team will wear black and pink “Vice City” jerseys Wednesday, the eve of the video game's release.

Meanwhile, the cities of Miami and Miami Beach made their own deals to promote the video game on public transportation, the beach and elsewhere. Rockstar also commissioned a series of murals, many in the Wynwood neighborhood, known worldwide for its street art.
The 24-hour club E11EVEN Miami transformed itself into NINE1NINE, its Vice City counterpart, and will host a launch party for the game on Friday.
Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz and others opposed using public resources to promote a game that rewards crime, including violence against law enforcement.
Miami Beach Commissioner David Suarez said the city has spent millions of dollars cracking down on the chaos around Spring Break in South Beach.

“As a city commissioner that is elected by the people, I can’t in good conscience associate our brand with something that we’ve been trying so desperately hard to move away from for the last couple of years,” Suarez said.
Fellow commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas thinks those concerns are overblown, though, explaining that people playing the game will understand they can’t go on a real-life crime spree.

“I do think that the city of Miami Beach can lean into this promotional material that’s only six weeks long without actually condoning the video game itself and the actions that happen,” Matteo-Salinas said.
The franchise previously used 1980s-era South Florida as a setting, including in 2002’s “Grand Theft Auto: Vice City” and 2006’s “Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories.”

Ren Veloz said he and his friends at ROK Gaming Lounge in Miami hope the game embraces the more modern “Florida Man” meme, which mocks the state’s reputation for bizarre incidents involving brawls, drinking, gunfire and even alligator wrangling.
“Everybody knows GTA for its cartoonish violence, because everyone says, ‘I may not be able to do this in real life, but I can definitely do it in GTA,’” Veloz said.

title: Gunman found dead after 2 public safety officers are shot at New York City apartment complex
summary: Two public safety officers have been shot at a New York City apartment complex
story: Two public safety officers have been shot at a New York City apartment complex
NEW YORK -- Two public safety officers were shot Monday at a New York City apartment complex, police said. Their injuries were not believed to be life-threatening.
The suspected gunman was found dead of a self-inflicted gunshot wound after barricading himself in an apartment at the massive Co-op City complex in the Bronx, police said.

The New York Police Department confirmed that the two victims were officers with the Co-op City Department of Public Safety, a private security force for the complex. They were taken to a hospital for treatment.
Police revised the number of victims after initially saying three people has been wounded.
Co-op City, built as middle-income housing in the 1960s and ’70s, has more than 15,300 cooperative apartments in high-rises and townhomes, 50,000 residents and its own ZIP code.
The complex’s emergency dispatchers said they had no information. A message was left for the property’s management.

title: Man charged in killing of a Black woman found hanging from a Mississippi tree is due in court
summary: One of three men charged in the death of a Black woman whose body was found hanging from a tree in Mississippi is due in court
story: One of three men charged in the death of a Black woman whose body was found hanging from a tree in Mississippi is due in court
JACKSON, Miss. -- One of three men charged in the death of a Black woman whose body was found hanging from a Jackson, Mississippi, tree last summer is due in court on Tuesday.
Earnest Lloyd Jr., 25, is expected to appear for the preliminary hearing on a charge of murder.

The positioning of Tasia Fortune’s body when it was found on Aug. 3 stoked fears that the 29-year-old was targeted because of her race and conjured memories of the state’s long and painful history of lynching. However, all three suspects in Fortune's death are Black. Authorities say that the three staged the scene after a drug dispute.
Some officials had called for a federal civil rights investigation, but Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney said that props were left at the scene “as part of the staging” of Fortune’s death.

Over the past two years, about a half-dozen Black women and men have been found hanged across the South. None of the deaths has been found to be criminal, though in some cases critics said that law enforcement appeared to move quickly to label them suicides before having sufficient evidence to rule out foul play.
Like Lloyd, 45-year-old Eric Clark and 51-year-old Jarques Ratliff are being held on murder charges. Police have said that Ratliff had an “association” with Fortune.
Judge Jeffery Reynolds, who set bond at $5 million for Clark following his arrest in late September, called Fortune's killing “heinous.”
“People justifiably didn’t know if we had a killer on the loose who might hang people for racial reasons,” Reynolds said.
Brackney said that the fear that the image of Fortune's hanging body evoked has damaged the community.

“We know we have a very sordid history around lynchings and racial terror across this nation and particularly around the South. That is still a very current narrative. It is still a very raw narrative,” she said.

Prior to any of the arrests, Fortune’s mother, Christy Spivey, told The Associated Press that she didn’t believe race had anything to do with her daughter’s death. Spivey is white. She said that Fortune’s father is Black.
“I think this is something very personal, very personal,” Spivey said, insisting that someone who was acquainted with Fortune was involved.
Spivey said that following a hearing for Ratliff earlier in September, Clark hugged her at the courthouse.
“He never said he did it, but he said he was there to turn himself in for murder,” Spivey told reporters following Clark’s own hearing later that month.

title: Large plume of gas billows out of California landfill
summary: A large plume of gas billowed high into the air after crews drilling at a landfill in Los Angeles County caused a rush of gas to escape along with decomposing garbage
story: A large plume of gas billowed high into the air after crews drilling at a landfill in Los Angeles County caused a rush of gas to escape along with decomposing garbage
CASTAIC, Calif. -- A large plume of gas billowed high into the air Monday after crews drilling at a landfill in Los Angeles County caused a rush of gas to escape along with decomposing garbage.
Six people were taken to the hospital with minor injuries, said Jonathan Torres, a spokesperson for the county’s fire department. He did not provide details on who those people were.

The crews were conducting routine drilling about 150 feet (46 meters) below ground at the Chiquita Canyon Landfill in Castaic, said Capt. Aaron Katon, a spokesperson with the fire department. They ran into gas that occurs naturally in landfills due to decomposing garbage.
“As that gas escaped through that hole, it carried with it small pieces of decomposing garbage, which made the appearance of a large cloud that went into the air," he said.
Officials monitored the air after the release and found that it poses no hazard to anyone in the community, Katon said.
By Monday night, the plume had diminished significantly, he said.
Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office said in a statement that it is monitoring the situation.
The city of Santa Clarita warned the public to avoid the area around the landfill and told some nearby residents that they should be prepared to evacuate.
The facility is a 639-acre (259-hectare) solid waste landfill, according to California's Department of Toxic Substances Control.

title: Bellagio's annual holiday flower show opens with tens of thousands of blooms
summary: More than 100 people worked around the clock over a six-day span to bring to life the latest display at the Bellagio's Conservatory and Botanical Gardens
story: More than 100 people worked around the clock over a six-day span to bring to life the latest display at the Bellagio's Conservatory and Botanical Gardens

LAS VEGAS -- As giant, silver snowflakes were hoisted toward the high glass ceiling at the Bellagio's Conservatory and Botanical Gardens, tourists snapped photos of the tens of thousands of flowers arranged underneath in one of Las Vegas’ most popular holiday displays.

Visitors over the weekend got a first look at “Postcards From Christmas,” which will be up until Jan. 2 and features holiday snapshots reminiscent of childhood. Trays of poinsettias and chrysanthemums and rows of winter evergreens filled the room with scents of pine and cinnamon.

Every year since the hotel's opening in 1998, the Bellagio showcases five different displays. “Postcards From Christmas” includes snapshots of classic holiday vignettes, from a giant, cozy chair sitting next to a fireplace decked with stockings, to a teddy bear dressed as a drummer boy.

“This feels like a childhood Christmas for me,” said Ed Libby, creative director and conservatory designer for the Bellagio. “But it also feels like a Christmas that I would want to come to as a guest and take as a journey.”

Installing the display was no small feat, with over 100 people working around the clock over a six-day span. More than 25,000 visitors are expected to stroll among the elaborate floral arrangements each day — a peaceful reprieve from the bustling casino floor.

Libby, who has been the brains behind the displays since 2016, said he travels constantly and attends fashion shows to find inspiration. He plans the full experience, from what guests smell and hear to how they should feel as they turn a corner.

The living room scene, where a dog sleeps curled up in front of the hearth, is meant to represent hospitality, Libby said. And a red and green train in the back of the gardens represents the journey to the Bellagio, he said.

In the middle of the room stands a white fir Christmas tree at 45 feet (13.72 meters) tall. The tree is adorned with red and gold ornaments and is surrounded by intricate designs of red preserved roses, hydrangeas and reindeer moss.

This year, guests can pose for holiday photos in a space cut into the garden bed. Libby sees the space as a postcard from the Bellagio to guests and as an opportunity for visitors to create their own postcards.
It is project manager Lea Jonic’s job to make Libby’s visions a reality, and it takes months of planning.

Roughly 20,000 plants from up to 150 different varieties are used in each display, sourced from growers around the world, Jonic said. Growers are contacted about a year in advance so they can get to work in growing many of the plants.
“They were born to be here,” she said.
The Bellagio's holiday exhibit showcases plants grown mostly in California.

The 42 fresh-cut Christmas trees in the display come from Mount Shasta in California. Jonic said the Bellagio works with a company that plants two trees for every one it harvests. The poinsettias are raised indoors in California, Jonic said.
Jonic's goal is to use as much plant material as possible throughout the 14,000-square-foot (1,300-square-meter) display.

Once the designs are approved, Jonic contacts between five and 10 artists and sculptors from around the country to build the structures and decor, which sometimes need to be hand-carved or hand-painted, she said.
After months of planning, a team of gardeners, electricians, carpenters, sculptors and artists spends two days taking down the old exhibit, and four days building the new one, Jonic said.
“It is an enormous effort from so many people,” she said.

In about a month, the display will make way for one celebrating the Lunar New Year. Nine gardeners work full-time to water the plants by hand and keep them fresh, Jonic said. If a plant doesn't look its best, an extra will be swapped in from a small nursery onsite.

When it’s time to dismantle, the plants that are nearing the end of their lives are taken to a composting facility. They’ll also have a plant sale for hotel employees, and that money is donated to the hotel’s foundation, Jonic said.

title: French soccer federation confirms Philippe Diallo as candidate for FIFA presidency
summary: French soccer federation confirms Philippe Diallo as candidate for FIFA presidency
story: French soccer federation confirms Philippe Diallo as candidate for FIFA presidency
PARIS -- French soccer federation confirms Philippe Diallo as candidate for FIFA presidency.
THIS IS AN APNewsAlert. Check back for updates. AP's earlier story is below.
French soccer leader Philippe Diallo is expected to confirm his intention to challenge Gianni Infantino for the FIFA presidency later on Tuesday.
His candidacy is due to be ratified following a meeting at the French soccer federation's headquarters in Paris.
UEFA, European soccer's ruling body, proposed Diallo on Monday after a meeting of its 21-member executive committee that includes the 63-year-old French Football Federation president.
He is set to join Japanese official Kohzo Tashima as official entries in the March 18 election by a FIFA-set deadline of midnight Swiss time (2300 GMT) on Wednesday.

Candidates must have letters of support from five of the 211 members of world soccer's ruling body. They then must pass eligibility and integrity checks by a FIFA-appointed panel to be confirmed by Feb. 18.
Should he win, Diallo would become the 10th elected FIFA president since 1904, the third from France and the first full-time president who is Black.
FIFA had a Black interim president for a few months before Infantino was first elected in February 2016, when Issa Hayatou of Cameroon took over from the suspended Sepp Blatter.

Infantino is seeking a fourth presidential term amid the biggest crisis of his near 11-year presidency, sparked by his divisive plan in July to sell stakes in future World Cup profits for $4.2 billion to private investors led by Joshua Kushner.
FIFA earned huge revenue from the 48-team men’s 2026 World Cup and has promised at least $25 million in development funds to each member federation through 2030.
See AP’s full soccer coverage here

title: Rare North Atlantic right whale population drops, alarming scientists
summary: The population of one of the world’s rarest whales has fallen after trending upward in recent years
story: The population of one of the world’s rarest whales has fallen after trending upward in recent years
PORTLAND, Maine -- The population of one of the world's rarest whales has fallen after trending upward in recent years, worrying scientists who fear the animal could still be at risk of extinction.

The North Atlantic right whale now numbers 382 animals, according to a consortium of scientists that released its annual population estimate for the animals on Monday. That represents about a 2% decline from last year's estimate, which showed a recent slow but steady climb in the whales' population continuing.

The whales were decimated by centuries of commercial whaling that mostly ended in the 1930s. The enormous animals have been slow to recover, and today they are threatened by entanglement in fishing gear and collisions with ships.

Those threats, combined with a warming ocean, have conspired to hold the population down, said Heather Pettis, chair of the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium. Pettis said the warming of the ocean has caused the whales' food — tiny organisms called copepods — to move, and the whales have followed them into areas of ocean not protected from ship strikes and entanglements.

“We know that this population can and will move around to find food and if we aren't protecting them throughout their range, we may see another situation where we have this tremendous decline again,” Pettis said.

The whales' population fell about 25% from 2010 to 2020 during a time when years of poor reproduction coincided with high mortality. Recent years have been slightly more encouraging, but scientists and conservationists have warned that the whales need years of high birth counts coupled with new protections to have a chance to rebuild.

The loss in population last year underscores the need to spare the whales from entanglements and ship strikes, said Nora Ives, a marine scientist on the environmental group Oceana’s right whale campaign.

Oceana was one of several environmental groups that opposed a proposal in Congress to delay new right whale protections until 2035. The proposal, which has passed the U.S. House of Representatives, is intended to protect commercial fishing interests from regulations that members of the industry describe as burdensome.

“The latest numbers are disappointing and make the road to recovery longer for critically endangered North Atlantic right whales. This iconic whale will not escape extinction if its population cannot grow,” Ives said.

The right whales, which can weigh 150,000 pounds (68,039 kilograms), give birth off the Carolinas, Florida and Georgia in the winter and venture north to feeding grounds off New England and Canada. Large groups of the animals that sometimes include a fifth of the entire population are sometimes seen off Massachusetts in spring. Last year was one of the most successful calving seasons on record with more than 20 babies born.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has said the last nine years have also been a time of unusually high numbers of injuries and deaths for the whales. The population is down to just 73 reproductive females, which makes replenishing the stock difficult.

They were hunted heavily because they tend to live fairly close to shore and floated when killed, and they yielded a high volume of oil. Some sources say they got their common name from the perception that they were the “right” whale to hunt.

title: Handwritten draft of MLK's 'I Have a Dream' speech on display before sold at auction
summary: A handwritten draft of Martin Luther King Jr.'s “I Have a Dream” speech is going on display before being auctioned in January
story: A handwritten draft of Martin Luther King Jr.'s “I Have a Dream” speech is going on display before being auctioned in January
ATLANTA -- Words scrawled in blue pen — and others scratched out — give an intimate peek into the writing of what would become the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr.'s most famous speech.

Delivered Aug. 28, 1963, from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, the “I Have a Dream” speech reflects on the shameful legacy of slavery, segregation and discrimination and looks forward with hope to future equality for the country's Black citizens. A handwritten draft of that speech goes on display in King's hometown Monday before it is sold to the highest bidder at auction in January.

“It shows a genius at work, that these words didn't just spill out perfectly,” said Jill Savitt, president and CEO of the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta, where the draft is on display through Sunday.

The words that became most famous do not appear in the draft. The “I have a dream” refrain was added by King as he stood before a crowd of tens of thousands of people gathered on the National Mall for the March on Washington. Watching footage from the speech that day, it is “almost like an electric charge goes through him and he is overcome and he goes on the riff about ‘I have a dream’ — that was ad-libbed from the stage,” Savitt said.

Other key parts of the speech, titled “Normalcy — Never Again,” are there in the civil rights icon's own handwriting, including the opening lines and the powerful finish invoking an African American spiritual.

The seven pages from a pad of yellow, lined paper are displayed in two cases in the Atlanta museum’s gallery devoted to the March on Washington. Video of King delivering the speech is projected on the wall behind them.

King completed the handwritten draft in his hotel room in the wee hours of the morning, less than 12 hours before it was delivered, according to Christie's, which will handle the sale of the manuscript. It was then given to assistants to be typed and sent to the media.

Peter Klarnet, a specialist in books and manuscripts at Christie's, said he was “just blown away” when he first saw the draft, which is so close to the final typed version that it must be the final handwritten draft, he said.
“It’s such an important piece of American history and it’s a part of world history,” Klarnet said. “This is a speech that inspired all of us to do better.”

Speechwriter Edward Clayton was among the multiple advisers who helped King hash out the content of the speech. His wife, Xernona Clayton, who worked alongside him in the civil rights movement, discovered the draft in the late 1990s, three decades after her husband's death. It was in a drawer of his desk, tucked inside an envelope labeled “speech.”

“The two of them gelled with writing and words,” Xernona Clayton said in a Christie's news release. “They would go back and forth and there was such respect. Dr. King, who was a great thinker, said Ed was so good at getting his words on paper and putting them in the right place at the right time.”
Clayton knew the document was important but didn't realize it was the only remaining handwritten draft and stuck it back in the drawer, finding it there again just two years ago.

Clayton, who established the Still Marching Irrevocable Charitable Unitrust to advance causes important to her, decided after consultation with trusted advisers to sell the draft to support charities that advance her own legacy and that of King. Christie's expects the draft to fetch more than $10 million. The organizations that will benefit include the Xernona Clayton Foundation and the King Center in Atlanta.
“I am so grateful for the opportunity to give this amazing speech new life, and to give new life to people who are in need,” Clayton said. “And we cannot wait to give that first gift.”

King's two remaining living children, the Rev. Bernice King and Martin Luther King III, said in the Christie's release that they are grateful the sale will support the legacy of the movement their father helped build.

“It is poetic that the past will protect the future,” Martin Luther King III said. “We are grateful that this treasure was preserved over decades by the Clayton family. It is a remarkable piece of history that shines a light on our father’s process as he prepared to make a speech that so profoundly affected the course of the Civil Rights movement and our nation. Now, for the first time, the public will have the opportunity to be inspired by this document.”

The draft is being publicly displayed for the first time at the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta from Monday through Sunday. It will be shown at Christie's in New York from Jan. 15, King's birthday, through Jan. 21 before being offered for auction on Jan. 22. Klarnet said they are also trying to arrange additional showings of the draft before the sale.

title: Ethanol plant trainee charged in connection with bomb at Illinois facility
summary: An Illinois man who worked as a trainee at a Peoria ethanol plant has been charged by a federal grand jury with two felonies related to a bomb that was found at the facility, resulting in a mass evacuation
story: An Illinois man who worked as a trainee at a Peoria ethanol plant has been charged by a federal grand jury with two felonies related to a bomb that was found at the facility, resulting in a mass evacuation

An Illinois man who worked as a trainee at a Peoria ethanol plant was charged Tuesday by a federal grand jury with two felonies related to a bomb that was found at the facility, resulting in a mass evacuation.

Police said they found a bomb on Friday at the BioUrja facility and “rendered it safe” before allowing residents who had been evacuated to return on Saturday. Hundreds of people who live within a 1-mile radius of the industrial site were evacuated.

Andrew Kozak, 41, of Chillicothe, Illinois, was charged by the grand jury in federal court with making threats involving explosives, a felony punishable by 10 to 25 years in prison. He was also charged with making that threat to BioUrja Renewables over email, a felony punishable by five to 10 years in prison.
Kozak has been a trainee at the facility for 10 months, according to his LinkedIn page.
“Learning how to operate an ethanol plant,” Kozak wrote under his job description.
Police said the suspect was arrested at the BioUrja facility on Monday morning. They did not name Kozak at the time of his arrest.
No attorney was listed for Kozak on the federal court website. He was scheduled to make his initial appearance in federal court in Peoria on Tuesday afternoon.
The criminal complaint detailing the charges against Kozak was sealed. The U.S. attorney's office in Peoria did not immediately return a message seeking comment.

Kozak has a criminal record in Nebraska, where prison records show he served two years in prison on burglary charges in three counties. He was released in 2008. Kozak went back to prison in 2013 on a burglary charge in a fourth county and was released in 2014, records show.
The BioUrja plant contains ethanol and “other highly combustible types of chemicals,” Peoria Mayor Rita Ali told WMBD-TV on Friday.

It is not unusual for law enforcement to receive bomb threats and suspicious package calls, but they often don’t result in a credible threat even though such calls are taken seriously by officials who must assess and investigate the claims.
Peoria, with a population of around 110,000, is located about 150 miles (about 240 kilometers) southwest of Chicago. Kozak lives about 15 miles north of Peoria.

title: Trump faces criticism as allies press the White House for answers on tech problems
summary: President Donald Trump faces criticism over service outages affecting travel, banking, and communications
story: President Donald Trump faces criticism over service outages affecting travel, banking, and communications

President Donald Trump faced a groundswell of criticism Tuesday as friends and foes alike said the White House must answer for a cascade of service outages that snarled travel, cut off work, limited bank access and disrupted classified communications.

Even staunch Trump allies accused the administration of lying to Americans or hiding information about the true cause of the disruptions. In recent days, Microsoft, Chase Bank, air traffic control and the National Security Agency have all been affected.

Each outage has been blamed on internal technical problems, with the companies and government agencies involved denying that they were the result of cyberattacks or rogue artificial intelligence systems. Trump was nonchalant after arriving in Asia on Tuesday, declaring that “things like that happen," a response that did little to calm the country.
Karoline Leavitt, Trump’s former press secretary, offered advice for her old colleagues in the administration.

“What I would say to the White House is transparency is key,” Leavitt said on Fox News. She said the president or someone else at the White House should explain what they know after Trump returns from Asia “to really calm the temperature.”

She later praised the White House for having Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton address the outages in an interview on Fox Business Network. “Looking very diligently across the landscape, we are not seeing this as a cyber attack incident,” Clayton said in a clip that Leavitt shared on X. He said the U.S. government believes the incidents are caused by organizations making security upgrades that are taking longer than planned and encountering unexpected hiccups.
Tricia McLaughlin, a former spokesperson for Trump’s Department of Homeland Security, was skeptical about the lack of information coming out of the federal government.
“Americans aren’t stupid," she posted on social media. "We want and deserve to know what’s really going on.”
Meghan McCain, who is sometimes at odds with Trump and his allies, had similar advice.
“Someone high in the administration needs to get on tv and tell the American people NOW what is going on,” McCain wrote on X. “No one who lived through Covid is believing this is all a coincidence.”
The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
Some prominent figures in Trump’s Make America Great Again movement expressed alarm.

“Our leaders are lying to us. This is very clearly a coordinated cyber attack,” Laura Loomer wrote on social media. “President Trump should come back to the United States.” She did not present any evidence of an attack.

The series of outages began on Thursday, when Microsoft's email and other tools went down, paralyzing millions of workers who rely on them. Microsoft traced the issue to “an earlier network capacity upgrade.”
Flights across the country were grounded the next day in the longest so-called ground stop since 9/11. The Federal Aviation Administration blamed a router upgrade.

By Monday, the banks were in the spotlight, as customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major financial institutions and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system. Chase said it was caused by “a software bug” and was “not cyber-related.”
The same day, United Airlines said that it had resolved an internal system outage that delayed departing flights.
And on Tuesday, an internal network that the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline after what the agency described as “routine maintenance.”
Trump was dismissive when asked whether he was concerned about the Chase outage.
“It's life. When you're big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It's fine,” Trump said in Manila, Philippines, where he began a three-day Asian trip on Tuesday.

Trump's nonchalance was not shared by those already distrustful of the government and big institutions. And for Americans across the political spectrum, the drip-drip-drip of alarming and frustrating outages is an unsettling reminder of perils posed by interconnected tech networks.

“Where is the transparency? Where is the accountability?” conservative commentator Kylie Jane Kremer wrote on X. “And why does it feel like we’re being told everything is fine while the very systems our country depends on are experiencing serious failures?”

title: Mullin defends use of government plane to go to college football game after ground stop
summary: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defends using a government plane to attend a college football game after a nationwide ground stop caused travel chaos
story: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defends using a government plane to attend a college football game after a nationwide ground stop caused travel chaos

WASHINGTON -- Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Tuesday defended his use of a government plane to fly to a college football game the day after a nationwide ground stop which caused massive travel disruptions and left people stranded across the country.
Mullin, speaking on CNBC, acknowledged earlier reporting in the New York Post that he flew to the LSU-Texas college football game a day after all planes were grounded.
Asked whether he is required to fly on government planes and whether he paid for the trip personally, Mullin said yes.
“We would have never went if the airways weren’t completely open,” he said on CNBC. “They’d been completely open for 21 hours.”
He added: “We would have never taken airspace if airspace wasn't open. And we still gotta live our lives at the same time.”
The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the flight.
The day before his flight, Mullin was at the White House alongside Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy giving updates on the ground stop.
The longest flight stoppage in 25 years lasted more than four hours and ended around 8:15 p.m. ET Friday, allowing some domestic flights to take off from U.S. airports.

President Donald Trump's administration has said last week’s air traffic snarls were caused by a router issue in the aging air traffic control system. Trump on Monday got defensive during a lengthy — sometimes testy — exchange with reporters as he left the White House for his trip to Asia.
He faulted old technology and Democrats for the incident that caused upheaval at the country’s airports — especially his predecessor, President Joe Biden.
“I don’t take any responsibility” for Friday’s ground stop, Trump said,
“What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack,” the president said. He later noted: “Incredibly, everybody was safe. Nobody was hurt. No crashes, no nothing.”
Trump was silent on the chaos until Sunday, when he posted on social media blasting his Democratic predecessor and asking Congress for more money to cover the cost of system improvements.

title: Do school phone bans help students learn? So far, gains are 'modest'
summary: Phone bans have now become common at U.S. schools
story: Phone bans have now become common at U.S. schools
The argument for school cellphone bans is simple: Phones offer endless distraction. Take them away and students can focus on classwork, engage with peers and, ultimately, learn more.
But the reality is more complicated, as emerging research shows. Schools can lock phones away in pouches or banish them to backpacks, but they can’t shut out the digital world.

In the past few years, more than 40 U.S. states have passed laws that restrict cellphones at schools, according to the Phone Free Schools State Report Card, which tracks state phone legislation. But those laws vary widely and often let schools design their own policies, resulting in a patchwork of rules and enforcement across the country.

A large-scale study published Tuesday found strict cellphone restrictions — ones that require students to put phones in locked pouches for the entire school day — result in small academic gains. But, the researchers said, the gains can add up if schools continue banning phones.

The study, led by Harvard’s Center for Education Policy Research, found the schools with strict phone restrictions saw “modest” improvements in academic growth, compared with students in similar schools without those restrictions. The study, which analyzed test scores of 3.3 million students at 4,600 schools nationally, estimates the academic gains were equivalent to about an additional week or two of learning over a school year.

Student achievement has been falling globally since 2013, which is roughly when social media-enabled smartphones took off. The researchers sought to determine if the decline is being reversed now that schools have started taking phones away, said Harvard professor Thomas Kane, one of the study’s authors.

“Our answer is yes, phone bans do have a positive effect on growth. But it’s not a panacea,” Kane said. Learning loss was gradual over a decade, he notes, and it’s not surprising that gains would also be gradual. The study used math and reading test data for grades four through 10 from the past five academic years.

“While schools should not expect large boosts in achievement immediately, storing students' phones seems to be a cost-effective way to add 1-2 weeks of instruction each year, which could add up over time, just as the initial declines did,” the study says.
The boost is equal to about half the annual decline in test scores since smartphones became mainstream, the study said.
Still, the connection between phones and learning is not clear-cut.
A different study published in May concluded strict school phone bans had “close to zero” effect on test scores. It compared schools with bans with tens of thousands of other schools.

The National Bureau of Economic Research study looked at a different set of standardized test scores than Harvard’s study, as well as GPS phone activity, teacher surveys and data from Yondr, the leading provider of lockable phone pouches, at 4,600 schools that use the pouches.

The study had found “modest positive effects” in high school test scores over three years, particularly in math. But the report’s authors, researchers at Stanford, the University of Michigan, Duke and the University of Pennsylvania, were hesitant to conclude overall learning benefits from the bans.

Both studies point to a similar conclusion, said Stanford education economist Thomas Dee, an author of the NBER study. “The early results from school phone bans are largely disappointing and raise unresolved questions,” Dee said.

Noting that the Harvard study showed learning gains may accumulate over time, Dee said: "I hope they're right. However, I’m not comfortable making that extrapolation from estimates that are small, sensitive and based on just a few years of phone bans.”

The reasons, Dee said, could be that students are still distracted on other devices at school. Or, he said, "it may be that we see these disappointing results because out-of-school phone use is harming child development.”

Just because schools or states have phone bans does not mean they’re being enforced, said Jean Twenge, a psychologist at San Diego State University and author of “10 Rules for Raising Kids in a High-Tech World.”

Ask any teacher — or teenager — and they’ll tell you that some phone bans are largely cosmetic. Teens come up with creative workarounds, including stowing burner phones or even phone-shaped rocks in their locked pouches. At schools that rely on students to keep phones in backpacks, adherence to the ban can be spotty.
“It happens pretty often that there’s a policy of no phones during the school day, bell-to-bell, and you go into the school and phones are everywhere,” Twenge said.
Even without phones, "Do they have laptops at school? Are they just doing social media on laptops instead?” Twenge said.
Phone use outside of school affects academics too, Twenge said. “If they have that phone available when they’re studying, how much are they really taking in?”

Kane, of the Harvard study, agrees the effect of cellphone use outside of school is “the big question.” But researchers have not been able to investigate parents and educators’ suspicions that late-night binges on YouTube and other platforms are costly for students.

“I find it astonishing that social media companies know how much time kids spend on their platforms, but that data has never been linked to student outcomes,” Kane said. “We can’t provide answers until the social media companies share data.”
