title: Microsoft says it "restored service" after major worldwide outage
summary: A Microsoft outage involving services like Outlook and Teams impacted many users, companies and government services.
story: Microsoft said early Saturday it had restored its services after a worldwide outage which involved services like Outlook and Teams impacted users, companies and government operations around the world.
In a post on X, the company said: "We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions."

The disruption, which lasted over 24 hours, affected a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services. Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down.
Microsoft said the outage was linked to a technical issue, not malicious or cyber activity, and apologised for the incident.

"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," the company said Friday on X. "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."

The outage affected Microsoft's suite of business products, as well as those tailored for personal use by individuals, students and families. Users in more than 70 countries and territories experienced disruptions, according to Downdetector, a website that tracks technology outages.

"Microsoft in a Friday the 13th moment as global outage [causes] a very bad day in Redmond," Yorkville Ives and Co. tech analyst Dan Ives said in an X post Friday. "There will be major questions for MSFT in this global outage."

Charles Lamanna, executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform at Microsoft, said in a social media post Friday that "technical challenges and failure modes" made the recovery process "more difficult than normal."

"I'm working closely with the engineering team to complete the full post-mortem," Lamanna said in the post. "We will publish the post-mortem shortly covering the step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future."
Widespread impact
Microsoft first flagged technical issues just before 1 p.m. ET Thursday. The company updated users about its recovery progress through a series of posts on its Microsoft 365 Status X account.
More than 130,000 users reported issues with Microsoft on Thursday, Downdetector's website shows. However, those reports started to wane by Friday morning as Microsoft worked to restore its services.
The outage disrupted email for hours, hampering work activity for some employees.
"It's just challenging sending reports or things that needed to be approved," one woman told CBS News Los Angeles.
However, some took delight in the slowdown, with social media users posting videos celebrating the freedom of not having access to email.
It's unclear how many people were impacted. More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, according to Microsoft's website.
Companies worldwide report issues

OpenAI and Anthropic each reported problems connecting to Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects of outages as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies' software.
U.S.-based industrial technology company Workhorse Group Inc. delayed a conference call on its quarterly earnings because of the outage.
In Australia, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Friday that Microsoft had likened the widespread outage to the CrowdStrike outage in 2024.
Burke said he had spoken to Microsoft's top executive in Australia and the government's national cybersecurity coordinator about the global disruption.

"They (Microsoft) don't believe they are dealing with a cyberattack. They believe that they are dealing in some ways (with something) similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry," Burke told reporters in Sydney.

Texas-based cybersecurity company CrowdStrike blamed a bug in an update that allowed its systems to push bad data out to millions of customer computers, setting off a global tech outage in July 2024 that grounded flights, took TV broadcasts off the air and disrupted banks, hospitals and retailers.

Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum firm, said his company's Outlook accounts couldn't receive updates from its U.S. customers due to the outage. If the situation dragged on further, it could "impact the production timeline," he said.

Air India said its flight operations were unaffected by the Microsoft outage. However, it temporarily rerouted its email services to ensure customer queries continued to reach the airline without interruption, the company said in a statement.

IndiGo, another Indian airline company, said it also reported disruptions to its email support services, which affected its ability to receive customer queries. The airline in a statement on X said its other support channels remained operational and its flight operations were unaffected.
Singapore's Government Technology Agency said government email services were down and that it is working with Microsoft to resolve the issue.
The Philippines' Supreme Court said in a statement on social media that the ongoing Microsoft 365 service outage had affected some of its operations, including email responses.
In Japan, Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said the outage impacted the government's IT infrastructure and that officials were "keeping a close eye on the developments."

title: Lutnick agrees to testify as Bessent blames him for chip sales
summary: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10, according to a U.S. official.
story: Washington — Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10, according to a U.S. official, amid intensifying scrutiny of the Commerce Department's oversight of the export of powerful AI chips following the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

A growing number of Republicans are calling on Lutnick to answer questions about the Commerce Department's apparent delay in adding Singapore-based company Megaspeed International to the U.S. government's Entity List, which would have restricted the company's ability to get access to advanced AI chips.

Megaspeed was previously led by Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy who had an affair with Jensen Huang. The U.S. government suspects Megaspeed of directing advanced Nvidia chips to China, circumventing a U.S. export ban.

GOP Sen. Jim Banks of Indiana, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, told Fox News on Thursday that "we know that the Department of Commerce, Secretary Lutnick, it appears, used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur even though President Trump has directed his administration and the Department of Commerce not to allow that to happen."

On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent repeatedly emphasized that the Treasury Department and other parts of the executive branch had pushed for restrictions on Megaspeed, laying the blame for the delay at the feet of the Commerce Department.

"Treasury, War, [the U.S. Trade Representative] and State, they were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the Entity List for months, but Commerce has the pen," Bessent told CNBC. "And you will have to ask them about their internal processes."
Bessent declined to comment on reported tensions between himself and Lutnick. The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.

title: Never bought Nvidia stock? Its slide could still hit your 401(k).
summary: Millions of Americans are exposed to Nvidia shares through their retirement plans. That's not as bad as it sounds (really!).
story: Even if you never bought a single share of Nvidia, the embattled chipmaker's steep slide this week could still ding your retirement savings.

Nvidia is a component of the S&P 500 and many other indexes, including the Nasdaq 100 and Dow Jones Industrial Average, all popular with retirement savers through funds offered by millions of employer retirement plans. About 97% of retirement plans now offer index funds, up from 79% in 2006, according to March research from the Investment Company Institute and ISS Market Intelligence.

That means even if you haven't directly bought Nvidia stock, your 401(k) is likely exposed to the chipmaker through an index fund, such as the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust or Vanguard's S&P 500 ETF (which trade under the tickers SPY and VOO, respectively).
Overall, Nvidia represents about 6% of the S&P 500 index, making it the second-largest component after Apple, according to Yahoo Finance.

Nvidia's shares started falling on Monday amid revelations that cofounder Jensen Huang had an extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Huang resigned from his role as CEO on Thursday, causing a further drop in the stock.

Since Nov. 6, the company's value has declined by more than $550 billion — a decline of about 13% in one week. While that will certainly hurt investors who directly own Nvidia shares, it may also impact people with indirect investments through funds that hold the chipmaker.

Nvidia's woes underline the risks inherent in many big tech companies widely held by U.S. investors, Shiva Rajgopal, a Columbia Business School professor who studies corporate governance, told CBS News.

The "Magnificent Seven" tech stocks account for about one-third of the S&P 500. As with Nvidia, several of those companies are closely associated with CEOs whom investors see as central to their success, such as Elon Musk at Tesla, Rajgopal noted. And as Nvidia's selloff showed this week, trouble for a charismatic CEO can quickly spill over into the company's stock.

"They are amazing wealth creators for shareholders," Rajgopal said. "But hopefully, shareholders know what they are doing when they buy the stock of these companies, because the exact same structure also has a lot of fragility built into it."
A drag on the S&P 500

The AI industry's influence on Wall Street was evident this week, as turmoil at Nvidia triggered a broader slump in technology stocks. Yet more companies within the S&P 500 rose rather than fell this week, boosting the index by 2.9% for the week through Thursday's close. Excluding Nvidia, the index would have gained an estimated 3.8%.

"If you check your account today, tomorrow, you're going to see some sort of fluctuation, especially if you own shares of Nvidia," Sabrina Escobar, a reporter at Barron's, told CBS News. "The decline we saw over the past couple of days will certainly have some implications in your daily or weekly stock movements."

For investors, Huang's sudden downfall and Nvidia's wobbly stock highlight the importance of properly diversifying their portfolios, Mercer Advisors chief investment officer Donald Calcagni said in a blog post.

"Events like this — where the outcome hinges on one company's leadership — are a risk we try to minimize through diversification," he wrote. "This is the core principle behind portfolio diversification strategies: spread your risk broadly enough that no single company's troubles can derail your long-term plan."

Of course, that's the idea behind holding a broad-based index fund like the S&P 500 — rather than concentrating your money in a handful of individual stocks, you're spreading your bets across hundreds of types of companies. And the fact that the S&P 500 is on track to post a weekly gain despite Nvidia's turmoil points to how that strategy can pay off.
Timing is not on your side

Investors may be tempted to sell when the market, a stock or a fund tumbles, but research has repeatedly shown that trying to determine the right time to buy or sell an investment usually results in losses.

Meanwhile, tech experts noted that Nvidia's chips remain essential to the artificial intelligence sector, a key competitive edge unlikely to change in the near term even with Huang's abrupt departure. In other words, holding Nvidia shares may be a way to bet on the broader AI industry, rather than on its executive roster.

"When a single company's stock drops on unexpected news, the best response is usually the simplest one: pause, keep the news in perspective and let your diversified portfolio do what it was designed to do," Calcagni said.

title: Family Dollar to pay $63M after FTC says it overcharged customers
summary: The discount retailer failed to honor prices displayed on store shelves, on price tags and in ads, the FTC and multiple states alleged.
story: Family Dollar has agreed to pay $63 million to settle allegations that it routinely overcharged customers by millions of dollars.
The Federal Trade Commission and 17 U.S. states accused the budget retailer of failing to honor prices displayed on store shelves, on price tags and in advertisements.

A proposed order bans Family Dollar from misleading customers on prices and requires the company to adopt what the FTC described as a "pricing accuracy program" that is independently assessed and certified annually.

"Today's order will ensure Family Dollar stops deceiving consumers about its prices and returns money to consumers harmed by these practices," Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement on Thursday.
Family Dollar operates more than 7,000 stores across 48 U.S. states and Washington, D.C. The Chesapeake, Virginia-based company did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the settlement.

The FTC and the states' complaint alleged that pricing inaccuracies are widespread at Family Dollar stores and that the retailer failed to correct errors. Customers regularly reported being charged higher prices at the register than those displayed on goods' price tags, in stores, on the retailer's website and in its mobile app, according to the complaint.
The states include Alabama, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Iowa, Illinois, Kansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Nebraska, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Utah and Wisconsin.
In October, the FTC and 20 states sued another discount retailer, Dollar General, over allegations of similar deceptive pricing practices. The litigation is ongoing.
Customer refunds and discounts
The proposed order requires Family Dollar to establish a $40 million fund to compensate eligible customers.

The retailer will notify customers of their eligibility for reimbursement through in-store notices and online. Eligible customers include anyone who made a purchase at a Family Dollar store from Jan. 1, 2023, to Oct. 1, 2026.

The order also establishes a separate $20 million discount program for customers. Under the program, Family Dollar must offer customers 15% off a range of goods for two days. State plaintiffs will receive $3 million to be divided among them.
The retailer must create a pricing accuracy program to ensure that it regularly monitors and verifies prices and trains employees to identify and correct pricing discrepancies.

title: Inflation isn't going away. Here's what that means for interest rates.
summary: As inflation seeps deeper into the U.S. economy, the Federal Reserve may have to step up the pace of rate hikes, according to Wall Street analysts.
story: The Federal Reserve is likely to accelerate the pace of interest rate hikes to rein in stubbornly high inflation, according to a growing number of Wall Street analysts.

Aditya Bhave, a U.S. economist with BofA Global Research, expects monetary policymakers to raise the Fed's benchmark rate by 0.25 percentage points at each of the central bank's next three meetings in December, January and March. Analysts at TD Securities also predict three straight quarter-point hikes, up from their previous forecast of two, because hotter inflation signals that price pressures across the U.S. are broadening.
The latest Consumer Price Index showed that inflation rose more than expected in October, climbing 0.4%.

"Inflation is not trending in the right direction," TD Securities said Friday in a note to investors. "The October report not only surprised our own forecast, it was also not driven by a particular factor or two as had been the case in recent reports. Price pressures appear to be broadening."

Hotter inflation in October was the third straight month that prices have risen faster than expected amid supply constraints and ample economic demand, according to EY-Parthenon chief economist Gregory Daco, who is penciling in rate hikes for December and January.

"For any borrower, this will mean a high cost of borrowing for any type of consumer loan people take out," Daco told CBS News. "A higher federal funds rate trajectory will generally mean higher long-term interest rates and increase the cost of borrowing for consumers across the country."

Interest rate traders put the odds of a quarter-point hike at the Fed's next meeting on Dec. 8-9 at nearly 90%, and also see a better-than-even chance of another such hike at the Jan. 26-27 gathering, according to CME FedWatch.

Some Fed officials themselves have said tightening may need to be more aggressive to bring inflation in line with their 2% annual target. At a conference in London on Tuesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said policymakers should consider a 0.50 percentage-point increase in December, adding that a smaller hike "would put our credibility at risk."
High energy prices continue to drive inflation, along with robust corporate spending on data centers and other equipment for powering AI.
"Together, these forces could keep inflation elevated into 2027 and weigh further on household purchasing power," Daco said in a report.

title: Major AI developers can't control their own tech, lawsuit alleges
summary: Companies including Anthropic, Meta and OpenAI are knowingly building technology that poses catastrophic risks to humanity, nonprofit groups claim in a lawsuit.
story: A coalition of nonprofit groups sued five major artificial intelligence developers on Thursday in a bid to block their development of AI models, alleging the companies knowingly created technology that poses catastrophic risks to humanity.

The lawsuit — filed in San Francisco Superior Court by the Alliance for Secure AI, alongside advocacy groups Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen and the Heat Initiative — named Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceXSI (SpaceX Super Intelligence).
"For years, the executives building these systems have warned us that their own frontier models pose catastrophic risks," Brendan Steinhauser, CEO of The Alliance for Secure AI, said in a statement.
"Yet they keep racing to develop and market increasingly powerful AI that they admit they cannot reliably control, and are now handing over AI research and development to AI itself," he added.
A Meta spokesperson for Meta declined to comment. The other tech companies targeted in the suit did not respond to a request for comment.
The litigation comes amid broader concerns about AI safety, sparked by several publicly reported incidents in which AI agents went rogue and carried out unauthorized actions.

The nonprofit groups contend that AI companies are developing technology they have admitted they can't control. The risk could grow as the companies rely more on their own AI models to develop future platforms without human intervention, a concept known as "recursive self-improvement," according to the suit.

"Defendants know these systems do not consistently act in accordance with their intentions," the lawsuit states. "And Defendants know there is no reliable method to control their AI systems and prevent them from causing harm."

The nonprofits also point to past comments by AI company executives acknowledging the potential harm from their technology. In 2015, for example, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said AI will "probably most likely lead to the end of the world." In 2025, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei suggested there was a 25% chance that the development of AI could lead to disastrous outcomes.

As scrutiny of their tech's safety grows, tech leaders have underlined their safety commitments. AI company leaders, including Altman, Amodei and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, in October voiced support for an industrywide slowdown in AI development after an Anthropic employee said there's a 10% chance AI "could kill all humans."

title: Trump FDA nominee Heidi Overton struggling to win GOP support
summary: Heidi Overton, Trump's pick to be FDA commissioner, is having trouble finding enough Republican support to advance her nomination, which could be pulled if she falls short.
story: Dr. Heidi Overton, President Trump's pick to be FDA commissioner, is struggling to shore up enough support in the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee as it prepares to vote on her nomination Wednesday.

Sources tell CBS News that she's having trouble finding enough Republicans on the committee to vote to advance her nomination, which could be pulled if she can't muster the support. None of the Democrats on the committee are expected to back her.

The White House knows it has a problem, one source said, and has already begun looking for a new candidate. A second source confirmed that the White House has been talking to potential candidates, including some who could serve in an acting capacity and thus forgo Senate confirmation.
CBS News has reached out to the White House for comment.

Overton's nomination has run aground over her testimony regarding the FDA-approved chemical abortion drug mifepristone and her execution of President Trump's pro-vaping policies while she served on the domestic policy council.

Missouri Republican Sen. Josh Hawley has emerged as one of the skeptics. Overton sidestepped questions on how she would handle a safety study long promised by the Trump administration into mifepristone, which Hawley has pressed for as well. The anti-abortion group Susan B. Anthony urged the Senate to delay her confirmation, and wants the FDA to commit to banning mail orders of mifepristone.

And two pro-abortion-access Republicans on the committee — Sens. Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska — have also not said whether they'll vote to advance her nomination. During Overton's confirmation hearing, Murkowski asked her whether she would restrict mifepristone, which is used in more than half of abortions in the U.S.

The administration has spoken with candidates about taking the FDA commissioner role in an acting capacity. That's one route to avoiding the Senate confirmation process during the narrow three-week legislative window ahead. The FDA oversees products that account for roughly 20% of consumer spending.
Two sources indicated Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas, a doctor, is making a play for the FDA post. He lost his reelection bid to Democrat Adam Hamilton earlier this month.
Overton is arguably the Trump nominee with the highest profile who is struggling to shore up sufficient support in the closing weeks of GOP congressional control.

On Tuesday, Hung Cao, Trump's pick to serve as secretary of the Navy, faced a bipartisan grilling over his management of wartime operations and the Pentagon's decision to block Democrats from some classified military briefings. And retiring North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis said Tuesday he opposes the nomination of Eric Ueland, currently the deputy director of the Office of Management and Budget, to lead the Government Accountability Office, because of the involvement of Ueland and OMB in implementing DOGE cuts.

The FDA has been helmed by Acting Commissioner Kyle Diamantas since the last Senate-confirmed chief, Marty Makary, was forced out by the White House last spring. Multiple sources familiar with his ouster told CBS News that ongoing White House pressure over flavored vapes caused significant friction.

Dr. Makary told CBS News in a statement on Nov. 8, that "big tobacco exploited their connections to administration and HHS officials to put repeated pressure on me to approve fruit-flavored vapes that appeal to children – I wouldn't do it."
Mr. Trump campaigned in 2024 on a promise to save vaping, a smoking alternative that can help with breaking the smoking habit, but also has been found to have serious health side effects.

CBS News' "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" asked outgoing HELP Chairman Sen. Bill Cassidy, Republican of Louisiana, about whether Republicans would be able to install a Senate-confirmed FDA commissioner in these last weeks that they control the Senate. He raised the concern that the alternative would mean installing acting commissioners.

"Do we want a series of short-term administrators who probably will have more influence from the secretary, as opposed to someone who may be not, you know, the perfect candidate in somebody's mind, but at least would be a permanent one and have the ability to establish some independence. And that's part of the thought process there. That weighs on one side, and of course other things weigh on the other," Cassidy said Sunday.

Asked by "Face the Nation" about his own past remarks that Overton's association with Mr. Trump's efforts around reducing childhood vaccine uptake was "almost disqualifying," Cassidy acknowledged he was still working the phones and uncertain about whether Overton's nomination would be advanced by the HELP Committee he chairs, and he also did not say which way he would vote.

Overton stood beside Mr. Trump in the Oval Office as he signed an executive order on vaccines this summer — and the president twice erroneously referred to the measles or MMR vaccine as "lethal." None of the health officials present corrected Mr. Trump.

Recently resigned MAHA leader Calley Means, a former top adviser to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., has also urged his followers to help block Overton's confirmation. He told "Face the Nation," "Heidi Overton was the biggest block to MAHA policies I encountered in the government."

Defenders of Overton dismissed criticism of her compliance with Trump's policies, and point to her medical background and her endorsement by two former FDA commissioners as a sign that she will be a professional.
At this hour, the vote to confirm Overton and a handful of other health officials is still scheduled to take place Wednesday morning.

title: Man convicted in Iran-backed plot to kill Trump is sentenced
summary: A man who was convicted of attempted terrorism and murder-for-hire plots, with potential targets including President Trump and former President Joe Biden, was sentenced to 27 1/2 years in federal prison.
story: A Pakistani man who was convicted of attempted terrorism and orchestrating a murder-for-hire plot at the direction of Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps, with potential targets including President Trump and former President Joe Biden, was sentenced to 27 1/2 years in federal prison on Tuesday.

Asif Merchant was convicted in March — shortly after the start of the Iran war — on terrorism and murder-for-hire charges and faced up to life in prison. Merchant shuffled into court with a serious expression and shackled ankles, peering around the room. He had wavy gray hair and wore a tan prison outfit. He pressed a headphone to his ear, for an Urdu translation of the proceedings, watching the judge intently and bobbing in his chair as he learned his fate.

"This was an exceptionally severe crime, an extreme instance of terroristic violence," said Brooklyn-based U.S. District Judge Eric R. Komitee, a Trump appointee. "No crimes are more serious than the targeted killing of a U.S. president or other U.S. officials."

Komitee called the "overlay of foreign influence" from Iran an aggravating factor, noting that Iran is the largest state sponsor of terrorism in the world. "The conduct we see here is not an isolated episode for that foreign actor," he said.

Merchant was accused of traveling to the United States to recruit criminal associates and hire hit men to carry out his scheme. The plot involved the assassination of a politician, stealing documents from a target's home and arranging a protest as a distraction after the murder occurred, according to court documents.
He was charged with one count of attempting to commit an act of terrorism transcending national boundaries and one count of murder for hire.

He testified in his own defense during the trial, and admitted that he had been recruited by a member of the Revolutionary Guard Corps, Iran's elite military branch that answers to the supreme leader. In addition to Mr. Trump and Biden, he testified that former U.N. Ambassador Nikki Haley was also a potential target of the plot.

To carry out the plot, Merchant reached out to a contact in the U.S. for assistance, but that person turned out to be a confidential source working with law enforcement. That confidential source, known by the pseudonym Nadeem Ali, ultimately connected Merchant with two alleged hit men who were actually undercover FBI agents. He paid them $5,000 each as down payments for the assassinations.

On the stand, Merchant claimed that he carried out the plot under duress, out of fear his wife and child in Iran would be harmed if he didn't comply. Merchant also has a wife and children in Pakistan. Prosecutors disputed his claim, saying there was no evidence that he had "fear for relatives." Iran has denied plotting to kill Mr. Trump or other high-ranking U.S. officials.

During sentencing, Komitee said the evidence was clear that Merchant was "highly motivated himself to do harm to this country." He said it was possible Merchant had some concern for his family's well-being in Iran, but did not accept the defense's characterization that was the sole motivation behind his actions.
The government pointed to Merchant's own social media posts as evidence, including a post of Mr. Trump's severed head with the words "coming soon" and "severe revenge."
According to trial exhibits, Merchant had searched for Trump campaign rally locations in 2024 and searched the address of at least one rally on Google Maps.

As a front for the plot, Merchant set up a garment business, and used terms related to articles of clothing as code words to communicate about the plan. He instructed the confidential source, who he thought was his associate, that "T-shirt" meant protest, "flannel shirt" meant stealing and "fleece jacket" was to "commit the act of the game," indicating murder.

Merchant's lawyer Christopher Neff disputed that the garment business was a front during sentencing, calling it a real business. The prosecution pointed to a video of Merchant, played at trial, in which he told Ali that "the goal is not to make a profit, the goal is to launder money for the IRGC murder plot."

Neff told the judge that Merchant's plot was "never particularly likely to succeed," since the IRGC sent him to "kill a politician with Secret Service protection and extraordinarily tight security yet gave him almost no resources to carry it out."
"Mr. Merchant is simply not the monster that the government would like you to believe," said Neff. "He is an ordinary guy."
The government countered that the plot was "not farfetched … it was straight out of the IRGC playbook."
Merchant was arrested on July 12, 2024, the day before the attempted assassination of Mr. Trump in Butler, Pennsylvania.
When Merchant was told about the Butler assassination attempt, he responded that what occurred at the rally was "the same thing he was sent here to do."

As the sentencing ended, Komitee wished Merchant the best, telling him: "No matter how serious the crimes of conviction, no human is to be judged entirely by the biggest mistakes they've made in their lives."

Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement after Merchant's sentencing: "The Department of Justice will not tolerate foreign terrorist plots against our leaders and will not stop until those responsible are held accountable."

Neff told reporters after court, "While we're upset with the verdict and will appeal and are disappointed with the length of the sentence, we are grateful that Judge Komitee did not impose the draconian sentence that was requested by the government."

When asked what he thought of a Trump-appointed judge not giving Merchant a life sentence for a plot potentially targeting the president, Neff replied, "I think what it shows is that our judiciary remains independent, thankfully."

title: Student accused of taking photos of planes for China to be detained
summary: A student accused of working with a Chinese Communist Party representative to take photos of airplanes in Chicago — and lying about it to U.S. investigators — will be detained pending trial, a judge ruled.
story: A college student accused of working with a Chinese Communist Party representative to take photos of American airplanes and logistic hubs in Chicago — and lying about it to U.S. investigators — will be detained pending trial, a federal judge ruled Tuesday.

Detroit-based federal Magistrate Judge Kimberly Altman denied a request from lawyers for Weiheng Zeng, a Chinese citizen who is currently an undergraduate at the University of Waterloo in Ontario, to remain free and return to Canada as his case proceeds.

According to the Justice Department, Zeng's legal team said in a court hearing Tuesday that his family would "pay any bond amount this court could impose" to keep their client out of detention, and suggested the family could even buy an apartment in the United States for Zeng to be bonded to.

Zeng was indicted earlier this month on one count of making false statements to a government agency. Prosecutors allege he sneaked into a FedEx property at Chicago's O'Hare International Airport and took photos of the facility, then later lied about the purpose of his trip to the United States to customs officials, calling it "hobby photography."
Zeng pleaded not guilty earlier this month. He hasn't explicitly been charged with taking photos of planes, but instead was charged with lying to investigators.

A criminal complaint filed in the Eastern District of Michigan alleges that in April, Zeng took photographs of the FedEx facility, climbed on a parked forklift and attempted to open locked trailers. The Justice Department says surveillance footage shows Zeng attempting to open a shipping container and using the forklift to take photos at a higher vantage point.

After leaving the country, Zeng attempted to reenter the U.S. on Aug. 23 through Detroit's Ambassador Bridge, which links Canada and Michigan, and was flagged for additional screening based on the April incident. He was then interviewed three subsequent times by Customs and Border Protection agents.

In his third interview, Zeng stated that a Chinese contact assigned him specific planes and tail numbers to photograph and that he would be paid between $20 and $30 per photo, according to the criminal complaint. Zeng said that he talked to the contact using SIM cards that were sent to him by mail, and after talking, he would destroy the SIM cards, delete the conversations and delete the photos that he had taken.

He allegedly told customs officers that the contact approached him on an "aviation spotter website" and said he believed the person was connected to the Chinese Communist Party, and was told that the photos were going to be used for "research."

Zeng was then interviewed by the FBI, the complaint says. He allegedly told law enforcement the contact was interested in getting photographs of rare airplanes, and believed the contact worked for the Chinese government because "when he started making more requests, the language he used was very organized and managed, not language typically used between friends." The photos, Zeng said, were also of "American United" aircraft at O'Hare.

Federal investigators said it was only after further questioning from the FBI that Zeng admitted that he had messaged with the contact for three months and said he wanted to help the contact because "he thought it was 'cool' and wanted 'to have the opportunity to work with someone like [agents] at the FBI.'"

He told the FBI that the contact wanted him to find out more about transportation and logistics in the United States, and wanted him to travel to Orlando, Las Vegas and Los Angeles to "obtain photographs of specific locations surrounding airports."
Zeng said he denied those tasks.
His lawyers did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the detention order.

title: Duffy pitches Senate GOP on $50 billion for FAA after ground stop
summary: Senate Republicans appeared skeptical after Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy made the case for tens of billions of more dollars for the Federal Aviation Administration.
story: Washington — Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Tuesday after Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy made the case for tens of billions of more dollars for the Federal Aviation Administration following a telecommunication outage that prompted a rare nationwide ground stop last week.
Overloaded routers prompted the FAA to issue the ground stop on Friday, resulting in thousands of canceled flights and stranded travelers.

Duffy is seeking $50 billion to overhaul the FAA's systems, some of which still rely on technology that is decades old. There was widespread concern among lawmakers about the problem, but GOP senators questioned the funding figure — and how the money could get approved.

Speaking at a news conference following a closed-door lunch meeting with Duffy, Senate Majority Leader John Thune said the secretary "fielded a lot of questions" about the funding and how it would be utilized.
"How we deal with that issue remains to be seen," Thune said. "There are ways in which we could do it with Republicans only, there are also ways in which we could do it with Democrats."

Senate Republicans have been considering pursuing another reconciliation bill, which would allow them to move forward without help from across the aisle. But the legislative maneuver is complicated and time-consuming. Thune said Republicans are continuing to have conversations, which will stretch into Wednesday, but he acknowledged that "the clock is ticking" down to the end of the current Congress.

Congress allocated $12.5 billion for the FAA in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act just last year. Duffy said the bulk of that money has been set aside for various projects, and Thune pointed to the funds on Tuesday, acknowledging that "we needed air traffic modernization."
"We did that then — there's more that's required," Thune said. "How that gets done is still an open question."

Thune suggested some senators have concerns about the $50 billion figure. He said the total the administration initially sought before the ground stop — $30 billion — reflected "not just the immediate needs," but also "a number of other things that they want to do." He said some of those projects should be funded through the normal government funding process, not reconciliation.
When asked about the $20 billion difference, Duffy told CBS News that he "decided to put everything on the table."
"There's been a historic underinvestment in aviation," Duffy said. "I hope we get the full investment."
GOP Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana told reporters he was "furious when they went from $30 billion to $50 billion."
"I mean, I'm not Bambi's baby brother," Kennedy said.
Sen. Rick Scott of Florida thanked Duffy in a post on X, while expressing support for a smaller investment.

"We absolutely need to update our air traffic control system, which would cost about $10 billion," Scott wrote, while stressing that "the airlines need to put up money and have skin in this game too."

But other Senate Republicans were entirely supportive of the transportation secretary's pitch. Sen. Eric Schmitt of Missouri, who's been working with the administration on proposed aviation infrastructure funding, told reporters that "the needs are pretty broad and pretty deep" for tech upgrades.
"So my position is: Let's go fix this on behalf of the American people," he said. "They saw what happened. I think they would want us to be responsive to that."
Schmitt advocated for approving the funds through reconciliation. He said he doesn't want to "make this partisan," but "some of my Democrat colleagues, I think, are taking a different tack."

"I was advocating for this before Friday, and then what we saw Friday, I just think this is something that we should do," Schmitt said. "I can't think of anything more important than the safety of the millions of Americans that fly."

Speaking after the meeting, Duffy said the engagement from Republicans was "fantastic." He said the GOP plans to "work through what they think is the right approach, the right funding levels, to make sure we have the resources to address the needs of the American airspace."

Duffy outlined his new request to Congress, saying the U.S. needs a new network that is "resilient," and an investment in infrastructure, like air traffic control towers, new runways and for airports more broadly. Asked about a piecemeal approach, Duffy said he'll take what he can get. But he said if the status quo continues, "I will replace every single tower in America in 300 years."
"So we have to do something different," Duffy said.

Caitlin  Huey-Burns
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: Professional misconduct complaints against DOJ officials are rising
summary: The number of professional misconduct complaints filed against Justice Department officials has increased by more than 50% over a two-year period, according to the department's inspector general.
story: The number of professional misconduct complaints filed against Justice Department officials has increased by more than 50% over a two-year period, which could strain DOJ's already limited resources to investigate the claims, the agency's internal watchdog said Tuesday.

In a new report, Justice Department Inspector General Don Berthiaume said that ensuring the fairness and integrity of the department's investigations and prosecutions is among the top six management challenges for senior leadership.

"The lawful and effective exercise of these authorities is indispensable to public safety and the rule of law. It also creates a corresponding management responsibility to ensure that Department investigations and prosecutions are conducted with integrity, objectivity, consistency, and fairness," he wrote in his report.

His report cited new statistics from the Office of Professional Responsibility, which is tasked with investigating attorney misconduct. During the 2026 fiscal year, which ended on Oct. 1, the office, which operates with a full-time staff of just 18 people, received 2,081 professional misconduct complaints.

By contrast, it received 1,666 in the same time frame in 2025. In fiscal year 2024, there were 1,346 complaints and 1,085 in the same time frame in 2023 — "an increase of approximately 54 percent in 2 years," the report says.

In the last fiscal year, the Office of Professional Responsibility opened 33 professional-misconduct inquiries and closed 35, and it completed nine out of 10 full investigations opened that same year.
In those nine cases, OPR determined there had been professional misconduct by attorneys, the report said.
During that same time period, OPR also received 50 new FBI whistleblower retaliation complaints and closed 41 matters.

"These results demonstrate that OPR has continued to resolve substantial workloads despite its limited size," the inspector general wrote. "However, the Department faces risk in its oversight capacity if OPR's staffing levels are insufficient to manage the workload generated by the Department's thousands of employees."

The uptick in professional misconduct allegations comes at a time when the Justice Department has faced intense scrutiny over investigations it has pursued against President Trump's political enemies, including some that Mr. Trump openly encouraged. The report does not describe the complaints, so it is not known if any of them stem from these investigations.
Former FBI Director James Comey, for example, has faced at least three separate criminal probes since last year.

Although an indictment accusing him of lying to Congress was dismissed, he is still facing charges in North Carolina over an Instagram post showing seashells on a beach arranged to read "86 47" — a message that prosecutors allege was intended as a threat against Mr. Trump.

Most recently, prosecutors filed a criminal information against Comey in order to pause the statute of limitations while they try to secure an indictment against him for allegedly leaking classified information.
Comey has denied wrongdoing in all three cases.

Earlier this year, a federal judge in the Middle District of Tennessee ruled that the Justice Department's prosecution of Kilmar Abrego Garcia was vindictive, citing in part extrajudicial statements that now-Attorney General Todd Blanche had made about the case.

Others who have been targeted with criminal investigations or prosecutions include Democratic election lawyer Marc Elias, Federal Reserve Board Governor Lisa Cook, former Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell, Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar, New York Attorney General Letitia James, Democratic Sen. Adam Schiff, several former FBI counterintelligence officials, former CNN anchor Don Lemon, and the Southern Poverty Law Center, a progressive civil rights nonprofit that has been critical of the Trump administration.
Although the department's inspector general has broad authority to investigate waste, fraud and abuse, it is more limited when it comes to allegations of misconduct involving DOJ lawyers.
That role typically falls to OPR, which is a smaller office that has less independence than the inspector general. Last year, the head of OPR was removed by senior Justice Department leadership.

Recently, the inspector general declined to open an investigation into the prosecutors who falsely accused Olympian David Hearn of vandalizing the Reflecting Pool, saying that the matter fell squarely in OPR's jurisdiction.

The Justice Department, in responding to the inspector general's report, said that it "emphasizes integrity, fairness, and accountability in its investigative and prosecutorial work, with the Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) serving as a central guardian of ethical standards."
"Despite resource constraints, OPR fulfilled its mission through disciplined case management, dedicated staff, and effective use of technology," the department said.

title: NSA's classified internal network goes down, sources say
summary: Two U.S. officials tell CBS News that so far there is no evidence of a cyberattack.
story: Washington — The National Security Agency's internal network used to store and share classified information went offline Tuesday, according to multiple U.S. officials familiar with the situation, prompting the agency to stagger arrival times for some personnel at its headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland.
The network, dubbed "NSA Net," is used for classified communications and information sharing within the nation's largest intelligence agency.

An NSA spokesperson said in a statement that the agency experienced a "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance." The statement continued that "while some internal systems were affected, mission/critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend National Security continues."
The spokesperson said that the agency's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.

Two U.S. officials told CBS News that, at this point, there is no evidence the disruption was caused by a cyberattack. Two sources familiar with the situation said the outage resulted from routine system patching, though the precise circumstances surrounding the disruption remain unclear.
The NSA has also implemented staggered arrival times for non-emergency personnel at Fort Meade, according to two sources familiar with the measure.
The news was first reported by CNN.

Multiple sources told CBS News that the agency was seeking to avoid having large numbers of employees log on to their computers simultaneously while the network was experiencing problems, which is why they decided to stagger arrivals. Sources referred to this as "Code Gray," part of a modified reporting schedule.

Sources familiar with Fort Meade's operations said the installation remains under normal operating conditions, with gates and campus-wide services unaffected. The sources explained that the NSA operates within its own secured campus and can establish unique reporting requirements for its personnel, independent of the larger installation.
In the meantime, some activities are being redirected to other NSA facilities around the country, according to sources familiar with the situation.
It was not immediately clear how long the network had been offline or when full service might be restored.

The NSA, home to one of the largest workforces in the U.S. intelligence community, is responsible for collecting and analyzing foreign signals intelligence, identifying and countering cyber threats, and protecting U.S. government communications.
CBS News has reached out to the White House, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the Pentagon for comment.

title: Cruz announces deal on stalled airline safety bill
summary: The measure would require all planes in busy airspace to be broadcasting their location, according to GOP Sen. Ted Cruz.
story: GOP Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas announced the Republican-controlled House and Senate have reached an agreement in principle to require planes in crowded airspace to be equipped with technology that enables them to see other aircraft in their area and to transmit their location. Cruz said it would be landmark legislation for aviation safety.

The equipment, known as ADS-B In, shows nearby air traffic with visual and audible alerts, and has been recommended as a required safety feature by the National Transportation Safety Board since 2008, but the Federal Aviation Administration has not adopted it.

After an American Airlines passenger jet collided with an Army Black Hawk helicopter on approach at Ronald Reagan National Airport in January 2025, killing 67 people, Cruz and other members of Congress argued that ADS-B In could help keep aircraft safer.

Cruz made the announcement during a press conference on Tuesday in front of the Capitol with the families of the DCA plane crash victims, who have been advocating for the technology since the deadly collision.

"We still have a couple of details to negotiate with the House Armed Services Committee, but with this agreement in principle, I believe we're going to get this bill done," Sen. Cruz said. "And my objective is to get it done this year, with this Congress, before we leave for the new year."

Proponents of the technology argue it could have prevented the fatal DCA crash and alerted the American Airlines pilots to the approach of the Army Black Hawk helicopter, which was conducting a training mission in the plane's vicinity directly in the path of their flight.

In December 2025, the Senate passed the ROTOR Act, which would have mandated ADS-B In for all commercial and military flights in busy airspace. It passed the Senate unanimously but failed in the House by one vote, a devastating blow to the victims' families after the Pentagon withdrew its support for the bill because of the requirements it would impose on military aircraft.

Since then, the House passed its own legislation, called the ALERT Act. It would close the "military loophole," requiring military flight crews to broadcast their location during non-sensitive missions.
Cruz and Democratic Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington opposed that legislation, arguing it lacks the critical improvements the aviation system needs.

"We must have strong military accountability in the national airspace. The military must be a willing partner with the Department of Transportation and the FAA to make sure that what happened that January never, ever happens again," Sen. Cruz said during Tuesday's press conference.

title: Fed's Lisa Cook rebuffs White House hearing without changes
summary: A lawyer for Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook said she has "no legal obligation" to appear at a White House hearing about mortgage fraud allegations.
story: Washington — Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook will not participate in an upcoming White House hearing to examine allegations she made false statements on mortgage documents unless concerns about the process are first addressed, her lawyer said in a letter to the White House obtained by CBS News.

Abbe Lowell, Cook's lawyer, told White House counsel Will Scharf that Cook has "no legal obligation" to appear at what he said is an "unfair" hearing before a three-member committee of Trump administration officials that is set for next month. He warned participating in the proceeding would undermine the Fed's "unique status" and independence.

"Consequently, this Committee process appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook or to unreasonably manufacture a supposed 'adverse inference' if she does not participate in a process that does not comport with the requirements of a fair hearing," Lowell wrote.

His letter to Scharf revealed that the two sides have exchanged numerous communications in the weeks since President Trump announced that he had created a "committee of inquiry" to look into the claims that Cook made misrepresentations on mortgage forms related to two properties before joining the Fed's Board of Governors in 2022.

The committee is made up of Kevin Hassett, assistant to the president for economic policy; Andrea Lucas, chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission; and Keith Sonderling, director of the Office of Government Ethics.
Cook has repeatedly denied wrongdoing and said Mr. Trump is attempting to remove her from the Fed because he disagrees with her decisions on interest rates.

"It is unfortunate that your latest correspondence fails to address the concerns Governor Cook has previously raised — making clear that you are uninterested in convening the 'substantive and fair hearing' you have claimed. Instead, you seek only to manufacture 'cause' for a predetermined removal outcome," Lowell wrote.

Cook had raised concerns in earlier letters to the White House about Hassett's membership on the committee because of comments he has made about the Fed governor, which Lowell said "demonstrate that he has prejudged the issue."
"Mr. Hassett's continued presence on the Committee remains unacceptable," Lowell said.

He also took issue with the White House's proposed process to exchange documents. Lowell said it is "fundamentally unfair" because it would require Cook to hand over documents immediately, while she would not gain access to information that the White House has until seven days before the hearing.

Lowell had also pressed the White House on the specific legal standard the committee would apply to determine what constitutes "cause" to remove a Fed governor and the participation of Justice Department personnel in the hearing, he said.

"Your and the Committee's failure to address these legitimate issues, over multiple weeks of back-and-forth correspondence, reinforces my prior observation: President Trump's decision to fire Governor Cook has already been made," Lowell wrote.

Mr. Trump first tried to fire Cook in August 2025 after Bill Pulte, the head of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, accused her of making false statements on mortgage applications. Cook filed a lawsuit claiming that her removal was in violation of federal law, which allows the president to remove a member of the Fed's board only "for cause."

The Supreme Court in June allowed Cook to remain in her job while her case continued and found that Mr. Trump failed to provide Cook with the procedural protections she was entitled to under the law, namely notice of the allegations against her and the opportunity to respond before she was fired.

Weeks after the Supreme Court's 5-4 decision, Mr. Trump again moved to oust Cook. The White House said in a letter to Cook in August that the president was considering terminating her because of the mortgage fraud accusations and gave her a chance to respond — seemingly an attempt to remedy the issues raised by the Supreme Court.
The president then announced last month that he had established the committee to look into the claims against Cook and determine whether he has cause to remove her.
The hearing at the White House was initially set to take place Nov. 5, with committee members set to consider evidence and allegations against Cook.

In his latest letter to Scharf, Lowell said the White House had attempted to schedule a hearing on dates that conflicted with the Fed's official business. He said that Scharf claimed in an Oct. 19 letter that if Cook didn't show up on the date selected by the White House, the hearing would proceed without her and the committee could "draw an adverse inference" from her failure to appear because of official obligations.

"To be clear, if the White House establishes an unbiased panel and implements fair procedures that do not prejudge the outcome — such as providing the evidence it claims to have gathered with sufficient time for review and response — Governor Cook would be prepared to appear," Lowell wrote. "But the ultimatums in your November 2, 2026 letter do not provide a productive path forward to enabling that participation."

title: Groups raise concerns over DOJ's new Civil Rights Division chief
summary: Eighteen civil rights organizations asked President Trump to withdraw his appointment of Craig Trainor as the new acting head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division.
story: Washington — Eighteen civil rights organizations asked President Trump on Tuesday to withdraw his appointment of Craig Trainor as the new acting assistant attorney general for the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, saying he has a track record of undermining the laws he is tasked with enforcing.
Trainor was appointed last week to replace Harmeet Dhillon, who resigned from her post shortly after the midterm elections.

Trainor most recently served as assistant secretary for fair housing and equal opportunity at the Department of Housing and Urban Development. Prior to that, he held several senior roles at the Department of Education.

He also previously served as a senior special counsel to GOP Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio on the House Judiciary Committee as well as the Select Subcommittee on the Weaponization of the Federal Government.

Tuesday's statement opposing his appointment was signed by a variety of organizations, including the National Center for Youth Law, the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights, National Council of Jewish Women, Human Rights Campaign, the Sikh Coalition and Stop Sexual Assault in Schools, among others.
"In the midterm elections, the American people rejected an agenda to divide, discriminate against, and diminish our communities," the groups said.

"Instead of rebuilding a Civil Rights Division decimated under Harmeet Dhillon, the Administration has chosen to elevate the official behind a court-blocked classroom censorship agenda who seeks to undermine the rights of survivors and equal opportunity in our schools and communities," they added.
CBS News has reached out to the Justice Department for comment.
The civil rights groups said that Trainor took action in his prior roles at the Department of Education and HUD that scaled back civil liberties.

After a court struck down a Department of Education rule that broadened the definition of what constitutes sexual harassment under Title IX of the Civil Rights Act, Trainor issued a directive to schools in February 2025 that ordered them to revert to less-stringent standards that were adopted in 2020.
Many civil rights groups have long criticized the 2020 standards and referred to them as "anti-survivor" rules because the definition of what constitutes sexual harassment is narrower.
The 2020 rules also only require schools to investigate allegations of sexual assault or harassment under Title IX that occur on school grounds, excluding conduct that may occur abroad or off campus.

The groups also pointed to threats that Trainor directed toward schools in a Feb. 14, 2025, letter, in which he threatened to withhold federal funding if they had diversity, equity and inclusion programs.
Several federal courts later enjoined the Department of Education from following through on its threats to withhold the funds.
After he left and went to HUD, Trainor also shuttered many discrimination investigations under the Fair Housing Act, the groups said.
In announcing his appointment, Attorney General Todd Blanche praised his actions at HUD, saying he helped to "cut the Biden-era Fair Housing case backlog in half."
Trainor is taking over the helm of a Civil Rights Division that was largely gutted under Dhillon's leadership, as more than 75% of its staff left since January 2025.
Although Dhillon later hired more attorneys, the staffing level is still not what it once was.

Dhillon reoriented the division away from its historical mission of protecting some of society's most vulnerable and marginalized groups. She shifted its focus to other priorities that included protecting gun owners' rights, curbing the use of equity, diversity and inclusion policies at universities, and adopting legal positions that oppose civil rights protections for transgender people.

title: Trump in Asia for Putin, Xi summit; possible Kim meeting
summary: The president arrived in Manila for the start of a multi-day swing in Asia, where he's scheduled to meet with Russia's Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping in a highly anticipated summit.
story: President Trump arrived Tuesday in the Philippines to start a multiday swing in Asia, where he's scheduled to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping for a highly anticipated summit later this week.

After landing in Manila, Mr. Trump met with the leaders of the Quad nations that have sought to counter China's influence in the Asia Pacific region, a relationship Mr. Trump described as "very special." Those nations are Australia, India and Japan, as well as the United States.
Mr. Trump announced an $85 million investment in artificial intelligence software, describing it as the "greatest opportunity for economic growth since the Industrial Revolution."

There were protests in Manila ahead of Mr. Trump's trip, with demonstrators holding signs reading "Trump Out," drawings of him as a clown or devil, and signs calling on the public to reject an AI hub named Pax Silica.
Mr. Trump acknowledged that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have "two lines of thought" on how to handle China, adding that "they handled that very well."

Ahead of his departure from Washington Monday, Mr. Trump called it a "big trip" and said he may also meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China. After arriving, he said Kim "would like to" come, but "we'll see what happens."

The meeting between Mr. Trump, Xi and Putin, which marks the first among the three leaders, is expected to center on decreasing the proliferation of nuclear weapons, the White House said, and comes as the wars in Iran and Ukraine remain in focus.

Mr. Trump said Monday they would discuss denuclearization, which he called a "tough subject," as well as Iran and Ukraine, although an official said over the weekend that Ukraine was not expected to be discussed.

In Manila, the president will attend the annual Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. He will meet with leaders of Japan, India and Australia on security in the Indo-Pacific on Tuesday. He's also scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand and attend a dinner with leaders of the Southeast Asian nations and other regional leaders, the White House said.

On Wednesday, the president is set to hold a state visit and lunch banquet with Philippine President Bongbong Marcos at the presidential palace, before departing for Shenzhen, China. There, he'll meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with APEC leaders, and on Thursday, hold the meeting with Putin and Xi. Mr. Trump said Tuesday that he would be open to a one-on-one meeting with Putin, but he didn't know if it had been scheduled.
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk is expected to join the president on the trip, according to a senior White House official, but will not be part of the meeting with Putin and Xi.

Mr. Trump's trip to Asia comes after he visited China in May for a summit with Xi, where he touted making "fantastic trade deals" and acknowledged a shared desire to end the U.S.-Iran conflict. Xi also visited the U.S. in September, marking his first visit to the White House in over a decade, as the two countries extended a tariff truce.

"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.
It will be Mr. Trump's third face-to-face meeting with Xi this year.

As for Putin, Mr. Trump and the Russian president last met in Alaska in August 2025 for a high-stakes summit on ending the war in Ukraine. But the talks failed to yield a ceasefire that the U.S. was seeking.

Mr. Trump's trip to Asia also coincides with issues back at home, including the recent revelations regarding an affair between Jensen Huang, the former CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, and a suspected Chinese spy. Beijing has said it was not involved.

Huang, who has a relationship with Mr. Trump, traveled on Air Force One during his May trip to China, and he and his wife were at the head table when Mr. Trump hosted Xi in Washington for a state dinner in September. White House officials said they do not think the Nvidia situation will loom over the trip.

"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," an official said.

When asked Monday if Secretary of State Marco Rubio had told him that the woman with whom Huang was having an affair, Alice Huang, was suspected of being a spy, Mr. Trump said he didn't know if she was, saying, "I haven't heard that." Mr. Trump also said it "isn't a bad idea" for Jensen Huang to be reinstated at Nvidia, but he also added that he recommended Apple's Tim Cook for the job.
Both Bessent and Lutnick are traveling with the president. Bessent last week accused Lutnick of failing to prevent China from getting some of Nvidia's most advanced chips.
Mr. Trump told reporters before he left that he was not considering replacing Lutnick.

The Nvidia Board of Directors announced Tuesday morning that it would be creating a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. Mr. Trump said on Tuesday that he believed that is a "good idea."

title: Hawley, Durbin introduce Roblox safety bill ahead of hearing
summary: The legislation would allow families of individuals harmed by tech products to take their claims to court even if they agreed to the company's terms of service for private arbitration.
story: Missouri Republican Josh Hawley and Illinois Democrat Dick Durbin are introducing new legislation targeting sexual abuse on Roblox and online gaming platforms, CBS News has learned.

The legislation, titled the No Forced Arbitration for Child Sexual Exploitation and Cyber Injuries Act, would allow families of individuals harmed by tech products to take their claims to court even if they agreed to the company's terms of service for private arbitration. Roblox is being sued by dozens of families and state attorneys general who claim online predators have been able to groom, extort and exploit kids they meet on the platform.

The measure is being rolled out ahead of an inaugural congressional hearing Tuesday into the popular gaming portal. The hearing, chaired by Hawley, will feature witness testimony from two abuse survivors and a pair of experts.

"I am investigating allegations that Roblox, a popular online gaming platform for kids, has become a breeding ground for sexual predators," Hawley said in a statement. "This week, as my Subcommittee holds the first-ever congressional hearing on Roblox's practices, Senator Durbin and I will introduce new bipartisan legislation to give survivors justice. We must hold these platforms accountable and ensure no child is left vulnerable to exploitation online."

The bill would close loopholes to ensure a child's rights aren't limited in click-through agreements, allow class-action lawsuits and let survivors and families choose whether to bring a claim in public court or through confidential arbitration.

"In the digital age, predators can target our kids from anywhere—including online gaming platforms like Roblox. And sadly, the numbers show that they have," said Durbin. "Therefore, an 'agreement' buried in the terms of service shouldn't limit a child's or family's rights to bring their claim before a judge or jury. I'm proud to partner with Senator Hawley on this bipartisan issue, and I won't stop until this bill—and other key measures to protect children online—are signed into law."
CEO Dave Baszucki was invited to testify at Tuesday's hearing but has declined to appear.

"The claims being made about Roblox are fundamentally misleading and ignore the rigorous safeguards we have in place to help protect users," a Roblox spokesperson said in a statement to CBS News. "Roblox's mandatory age checks for chat, age-based content, prohibition on sharing photos or videos via chat, and continuous monitoring and filtering of chat, help set the standard for youth protection online."
In August, Hawley and Durbin launched a joint investigation by the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism into child safety on Roblox.

"Roblox appears to prioritize revenue and engagement metrics over the safety and well-being of our children, and the alleged criminal activity on Roblox warrants congressional scrutiny," the Senators wrote in a letter to the company at the time.

Roblox has 138 million daily active users, ranging in age from five to over 25, according to its latest shareholder letter released at the end of October. The company currently faces nearly 200 lawsuits in federal court and has reached settlements with at least six states over online child safety issues.

This month, Roblox chief safety officer Matt Kaufman wrote that the company continues to partner with law enforcement and "aggressively look for bad behavior and report it through the appropriate channels."

Last year, the company announced it would strengthen its age verification protections for minors. Roblox CEO David Baszucki described the guardrails in an interview with "CBS Mornings" as "what we believe will become the gold standard for safety and civility on the internet."
This story published first on CBS News at 1:58 p.m. on Nov. 16, 2026.

title: Ex-Nvidia CEO agrees to testify to Congress amid affair probe
summary: The former Nvidia chief will appear for closed-door testimony on Dec. 1 after Republicans threatened to subpoena him.
story: Washington — Jensen Huang, who resigned last week as the CEO of Nvidia, agreed to answer questions from House lawmakers on Dec. 1 under the threat of a subpoena amid an investigation into his affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.

"The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia's role in allowing dangerous [People's Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal," House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, a Florida Republican, said in a joint statement announcing the date of the hearing. Mast issued the statement with GOP Rep. John Moolenaar of Michigan, the chair of the House China Committee, and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rep. Rick Crawford of Arkansas.
Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter voluntarily agreed to appear before the committees on Dec. 2, the lawmakers said.
"We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security," the lawmakers added.
A representative for Huang declined to comment.

The chairmen had given Huang until 8 p.m. Nov. 13 to respond to their request for a closed-door, transcribed interview after Thanksgiving. Negotiations for the interview continued past the deadline into this week.

In a Nov. 12 letter, the lawmakers warned that "failure to cooperate with this request will result in the House Foreign Affairs Committee issuing a subpoena to compel your testimony in a format of the committee's choosing."
"Other committees also reserve the right to separately issue subpoenas to compel your testimony," they wrote.
Moolenaar and Crawford signed the letter with Mast.

In an initial letter to Huang on Nov. 4, the lawmakers sought a briefing on Nvidia's security protocols against espionage from foreign adversaries and on his relationship with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who is not related to him.

The Singapore-based data center company gained access to Nvidia's highly prized chips that are banned from export to China under U.S. law. Megaspeed is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China — allegations Megaspeed has denied.
"It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk," the lawmakers wrote in their initial letter to Jensen Huang.
