title: Microsoft data center brings "a kind of boom" amid AI pushback
summary: Microsoft outlines the pledges it makes to data center communities as industry tries to sway public opinion on AI.
story: Opposition to data centers helped propel Democratic candidates who pledged to stall new construction to victory in last week's midterm elections. More than half of voters said artificial intelligence and data centers were a significant factor in their votes, according to a CBS News exit poll.
But one town says it has benefited from data centers, despite the pushback growing across the nation.
For 20 years, Microsoft has operated its Columbia Data Center in Quincy, Washington, where Mayor Paul Worley told CBS News its presence has created "a kind of boom" for the area.
Additional tax revenue from the project has funded a new high school and hospital, and helped improve other critical services, he said.
Microsoft president Brad Smith told CBS News about the pledge it makes to the communities where it builds and operates data centers.

"Basically, we will put the community first," he said. "We will not do anything that will increase the electricity rates of our neighbors. We'll ensure that we replenish more water, we put more water back into the community than we use."
He also highlighted the role data centers play in powering every action we take on our phones and other connected devices.
"Every time we tap on our phone, it's connecting through an app, it's pulling data from something like this," he said.
The industry, he said, needs to better inform opponents of data centers about the essential services the facilities enable.
"They're part of daily life, just like electricity is," Smith said.
Why Quincy?
The nearby Columbia River provides hydropower that has led seven additional companies to choose Quincy for their data centers.
It hasn't been entirely smooth. To accommodate the roughly two dozen data centers that have entered the area over the past two decades, some residents have been asked to vacate their homes.
Electricity rates per kilowatt-hour have risen by roughly 55% over the past 20 years, according to the Grant County public utility.

While that marks a steep increase, it's still lower than the average increases in national and state electricity rates over the same period. In Washington, electricity rates rose 107% over the same time period. Nationwide, they rose 66%.
Smith said he believes it is the company's "fundamental responsibility" to manage the industry's growth and the impact on residents' rising utility costs.
"You can't make the challenges go away, but you can be broad-minded, you can [be] committed, and you can take steps to manage growth well," he said.

For example, Microsoft pledges to replenish or give communities back more water than it uses. It also commits to paying for its own electricity and ensuring that its usage doesn't increase neighbors' utility rates, Smith said. He added that the facilities create local jobs, too, though many are temporary construction positions.
According to Microsoft, the company employs roughly 700 people, or almost 9% of Quincy's roughly 8,000 residents.
Questions to ask
Yale professor of environmental and energy economics Kenneth Gillingham outlined the questions communities should ask data center developers before they come to town.
They include:
What type of technology is it using for cooling?How large will it be?How is it going to generate its electricity?
What type of technology is it using for cooling?
How large will it be?
How is it going to generate its electricity?
Meanwhile, Microsoft's Smith has a clear message for Americans who say they don't want data centers in their backyards.

"Give us a chance to talk through what we want to do, and give us a chance to prove that we can do this in a way that will put the community first," he said. "We have to persuade you. But the people that you've elected, they're the ones who are gonna make a decision, not us."

title: Nvidia sees strong growth in first earnings report without Huang
summary: Nvidia's latest earnings are the first time the chipmaker has reported financial results without founder and former CEO Jensen Huang at the helm.
story: Nvidia reported robust growth on Tuesday, as interim CEO Colette Kress hosted her first earnings call since the company's founder and former chief executive, Jensen Huang, resigned last week after revelations of multiple extramarital affairs.

The chipmaker reported fiscal third-quarter profits of $65.3 billion, topping analyst forecasts and up 105% from earnings of $31.9 billion in the year-ago period. Nvidia's revenue rose to $115.8 billion, compared with $57 billion a year ago.

Nvidia expects revenue of $130 billion for its fiscal fourth quarter, with projected growth driven by strong demand for AI infrastructure, Kress said on a call with analysts discussing the latest results.
Wall Street analysts had expected third-quarter revenue of nearly $109 billion, according to financial research firm FactSet.
The financial results represent the first time Nvidia has reported earnings without Huang at the helm of the chip company he cofounded in 1993.
Strong beats

Nvidia's results for the period featured "beats on the top and bottom lines in Colette Kress' first print as interim CEO, five days after the board removed Jensen Huang, and the quarter answers the first question the market had about Nvidia without its founder: demand did not leave with him," analysts with investment adviser Yorkville Ives said in a report.
The chip firm reported third-quarter data center revenue of $107.6 billion, up 110% from one year ago, marking a record.

"Our momentum is real. Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people," Kress, who also serves as Nvidia's chief financial officer, said in a statement.

During the earnings call, Kress and new Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones declined to answer questions about the company's progress in finding a permanent chief executive. But Jones said that the company "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

The company's search for a new chief is underway, Jones added, noting the company is considering both internal and external candidates to replace Huang. In the meantime, the board has "every confidence" in Kress' ability to lead the company, Jones said.
Nvidia shares rose nearly 4%, to $161.57, in after-hours trading.
Confidence boost
Adam Crisafulli, a Wall Street analyst with Vital Knowledge, said Nvidia's stronger-than-expected results should boost investor confidence.

"The headline numbers for [the fiscal third quarter] are strong, and the FQ4 guide is solid, too. Given how depressed sentiment is, this should be enough to spur a rebound," he said in a note to investors.

Huang resigned last week after admitting he had an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence has identified as a Chinese spy. Beyond spurring his shock exit from the company, the scandal has raised questions over whether the company's advanced chips were being used in China in violation of export controls.

The U.S. government is moving to close any loopholes in those rules. The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security on Monday issued an interim rule limiting other countries' access to advanced chips that power artificial intelligence.

Kress addressed the new export controls in Tuesday's call, saying that "with demand far exceeding supply, we expect our performance to remain strong." The company will study the new export controls, she added.
On Tuesday, Nvidia's board also said it formed a new committee to ensure that the company's policies comply with U.S. export controls.

Nvidia employees, investors and prominent tech industry leaders have rallied around Huang since his departure from Nvidia and called for his reinstatement as CEO. But the company's board is against reinstating the tech entrepreneur in his post, a source directly familiar with its thinking told CBS News.
Nvidia faces longer-term risks related to finding a new leader, stricter U.S. export controls and international sales, according to Brian Colello, senior equity analyst at Morningstar.

"We're at a point of peak uncertainty because investors still don't know what Nvidia's long-term leadership will look like," he told CBS News. "Jensen Huang's departure could create some near-term disruption, but a credible succession plan should go a long way toward steadying the ship. The next CEO will have big shoes to fill, but Nvidia's long-term opportunity does not hinge on one person."

title: Apple restores services after internal update caused outages
summary: The company's system status shows that all Apple services, including iCloud sign-in, have been restored after experiencing issues earlier Tuesday.
story: Apple said it has restored all services after users reported issues with Apple Pay, Apple Support, iCloud and other products on Tuesday.
A spokesperson for the company told CBS News in an email that its services are "green across the board," referring to the System Status page on Apple's website, as of approximately 5:46 p.m. ET.

Thousands of people reported issues with Apple services on Tuesday, according to the tracking site Downdetector.com. The reports started to spike before noon ET and lasted several hours before tapering off in the afternoon, the site shows.

By 4:45 p.m. ET, Apple's system status page showed problems with iCloud sign-in and "AppleCare on device" had been resolved. However, some services, including Apple Business and Apple School Manager, were still experiencing issues, according to the tech giant.
The issues were not the result of a cyberattack, according to the spokesperson.

Apple is the latest company to experience service disruptions following a string of outages that affected everything from air travel to Microsoft email. On Monday, customers at JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and other major financial institutions also reported service issues affecting bank deposits and Zelle transfers.

Users also reported issues accessing Gmail on Tuesday. In a statement shared on X, Google said it isn't "currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption" and encouraged users to check its workplace status dashboard for updates.

title: Man with ax destroys $60M U.S. military plane, prosecutors say
summary: Daithi O'Corrain, 48, is charged in the U.S. with destruction of U.S. government property in connection with the April incident at Shannon Airport.
story: An ax-wielding man breached a security perimeter and destroyed an American military plane while it was parked overnight at an Irish airport, cutting hydraulic lines, smashing cockpit gauges and pouring ball bearings into fuel tanks, U.S. prosecutors said. The man's supporters attributed the attack to his anger at the United States' involvement in Middle East conflicts.

An indictment unsealed Tuesday in Manhattan charges Daithi O'Corrain, 48, with destruction of U.S. government property in connection with the April incident at Shannon Airport, an international gateway in the west of Ireland that serves as a hub for American troops and military equipment.

O'Corrain isn't in U.S. custody and his arraignment on the new charge hasn't been scheduled. If convicted, he faces up to 10 years in prison. Online court records do not list an attorney who might speak on his behalf.

The plane, a $60 million U.S. Air National Guard C-130 Hercules that had been en route to a military assignment in another country, was rendered inoperable and won't fly again, U.S. prosecutors said. The attack jeopardized critical military operations, the FBI said.

O'Corrain, described by supporters as an independent peace activist, was arrested immediately after the attack by Ireland's police force, An Garda Síochána. He was charged there with causing criminal damage and trespassing. The Limerick Post reported he is from Cork, about 60 miles southeast of Shannon.
Manhattan U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said the indictment sends "a clear and powerful message that attacks on U.S. military assets — and thus our national security — will not be tolerated."

An online fundraiser organized by people describing themselves as O'Corrain's friends and comrades said he disarmed the C-130 in protest of the U.S.'s war with Iran and support for Israel's war in Gaza — a flashpoint in Ireland, where many people have expressed solidarity with Palestinians.

"An inspiring act of direct action was carried out at Shannon Airport to resist the unwanted presence of the US Military in Ireland in the face of their illegal war & support of Israel's genocide," organizer Tracey Ryan wrote.

O'Corrain plotted the attack for months, U.S. prosecutors said. He searched online for information about the construction of the C-130, a quad-engine turboprop mainly used for transporting equipment and personnel, and looked up coordinates for sneaking onto the airport's grounds, prosecutors said.

He subscribed to a cellphone app that provided live flight tracking, including for military aircraft, and ordered capsules of gallium, a chemical that can corrode steel and break down aluminum, the primary material used to build the C-130, prosecutors said.
He even tried to get in touch with someone who had been involved in a prior breach at Shannon Airport, prosecutors said.
"This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism," James Barnacle, the head of the FBI's New York office, said in a statement.

O'Corrain attacked on April 11, breaching the airport's perimeter at around 4:40 a.m. and breaking into the C-130 as it was parked on a taxiway by destroying a locking mechanism on the rear crew door, his indictment said.

He used the crew's hammocks to cover the plane's windows but left the cockpit windshield exposed, the indictment said. He then barricaded himself inside the aircraft, securing the doors with straps, brackets and screws, and putting ball bearings mixed with epoxy in door tracks to prevent doors from being opened or closed, the indictment said.

O'Corrain laid waste to the plane over the next few hours, pulling, snipping and otherwise disabling its key components, the indictment said. He sliced wire bundles, crimped a liquid oxygen line, punctured air ducts and shattered every gauge in the cockpit, the indictment said.
Had O'Corrain cut the oxygen line instead, he would've risked blowing up the plane, prosecutors said.
Returning to the airport after resting elsewhere, the C-130 crew spotted O'Corrain through the uncovered cockpit at around 9:40 a.m. and alerted security, the indictment said.

Crew members then saw him emerging through a roof hatch and swinging an ax at the plane's exterior, according to the indictment, which included images taken from a video recording that show a man standing on the roof of the plane. O'Corrain then poured substances and objects into the fuel tanks, including ball bearings, before being arrested.

Shannon Airport, which was used by President Trump and Air Force One during his visit to Ireland in September, has had several security breaches in the last 18 months, including three people who were accused of spray-painting a U.S. military plane and three others who drove to a restricted area where a U.S. military jet was parked.

title: Jensen Huang says he "would be honored" to return as Nvidia CEO
summary: Huang addressed a petition, signed by 190,000 people, including thousands of Nvidia employees, calling for his reinstatement.
story: Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang broke his silence after resigning from the company following revelations of multiple affairs, saying he'd be willing to return as its CEO.

"I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life," Huang said in a statement Tuesday morning. "I created problems for the board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the board's independent investigation."

He added, "If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO."

Late Tuesday, however, Nvidia Chair Harvey Jones said the company's board doesn't intend to rehire Huang as chief executive. The company's search for a new chief is underway, he added, while noting that the board has "every confidence" in Kress' ability to lead the company. Jones said the company is considering both internal and external candidates to replace Huang.
Support for Huang's return

Huang has gained support from more than 190,000 people, including several thousand Nvidia employees, who signed a petition to reinstate him. On Monday, President Trump suggested to reporters that he would support Huang returning to Nvidia.
"I would not mind seeing that," Mr. Trump said. Later, the president said he recommended former Apple CEO Tim Cook as Nvidia's next leader.

In his Tuesday statement, Huang thanked his allies for their support since his departure last week, saying that in addition to the public calls for him to return to the company, many "continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive and geopolitical dynamics."

Nvidia's board said on Tuesday that it has formed a committee to oversee its national security policies and ensure compliance with U.S. export controls. The former CEO has also agreed to appear before House lawmakers on Dec. 1 to address questions about a potential breach of national security amid an investigation into his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
The former CEO's return to Nvidia is unlikely, said Yorkville Ives & Co. technology analyst Dan Ives.

"In our view the sequencing is the tell: Jensen has conditioned his return on a board decision, and the board's first public act this week was to build a compliance structure around the issue that forced him out, which is not what a board preparing to reverse itself does," he said in a Tuesday research note.
Shares of Nvidia declined $2.63, or 1.7%, to $153.51. The stock has lost 16% of its value since Huang's extramarital relationships became public.

title: Anthropic's IPO set for blastoff this week in key test for AI boom
summary: Anthropic's stock is poised to start trading on Nasdaq Thursday in one of the largest IPOs of all time. The AI world is watching.
story: Anthropic's blockbuster initial public offering is set to launch on Thursday, a milestone that will test investor enthusiasm for the company behind the popular Claude chatbot and the burgeoning artificial intelligence sector.

"This is a case where the deal is so large and important, so central to the AI thesis, that it's going to be a turning point for the AI sector," Matthew Kennedy, a senior market strategist at investment bank Renaissance Capital, told CBS News. "Even non-AI companies are going to feel the ripple effects, especially in the IPO market."
Anthropic shares are scheduled to start trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol "ANT" after markets open Thursday at 9:30 a.m. EST.
What the stock price will tell us

In its most recent regulatory filing, San Francisco-based Anthropic said it will offer 825 million shares priced at between $70 and $78, which is expected to raise up to $64.3 billion. The company also plans to raise an additional $26 billion from a slate of other companies, including chipmaker AMD, chip infrastructure provider Broadcom, Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, all of which have a stake in the AI race.
Anthropic is expected to formally set its stock price on Wednesday night.

"A price above the initial range would point to stronger-than-anticipated demand, while a price cut would signal that the company struggled to find buyers at the level it hoped for," analysts at Renaissance Capital, which tracks IPOs, said in a research note.

The market debut is expected to value Anthropic at up to $1.4 trillion, short of the $2 trillion valuation that some IPO experts projected earlier this year. Still, the AI developer — which launched only in 2021 — is on track to stage what could become the second-largest IPO ever. Elon Musk's SpaceX, which raised $75 billion and was valued at roughly $1.7 trillion when it went public in June, currently holds that mark for the largest IPO.

Kennedy thinks Anthropic shares will price at the high end, at around $78, and reach $100 by the end of their first day of trading, an increase that would represent a "solid pop," he said. If the stock rises closer to $140, "that would tell me that AI enthusiasm has come roaring back," he added.
Great expectations
Although many investors appear eager to own a piece of Anthropic, the IPO comes amid growing concerns about whether the torrid spending on AI will deliver the expected productivity and profit boom.

AI-related stocks have fluctuated in recent weeks following subpar earnings and the mountainous debt companies are taking on to finance data center construction. Jensen Huang's shock exit from Nvidia last week has also rattled investors, with the chipmaker's stock now down more than 35% from its October all-time high.

"The whole AI sector has sold off from its July peak. Investor enthusiasm was greatest then," Jay Ritter, an IPO expert and professor at the University of Florida's Warrington College of Business, told CBS News.

Although Anthropic has yet to turn a profit, the company has shown explosive revenue growth over its short time in business. Anthropic raked in nearly $17 billion in the third quarter this year, up 45% from the second quarter, a recent regulatory filing shows. Given that heady rate of expansion, Ritter expects Anthropic to reach profitability quickly.

To justify its projected trillion-dollar valuation, however, the company will need to sustain that momentum while operating under Wall Street's unsparing gaze. Compounding the challenge is how quickly the AI landscape itself is changing. For instance, Anthropic could struggle to maintain its growth rate as consumers shift from pricier AI models like Claude and ChatGPT to cheaper open-source models, Ritter noted.

Anthropic also will have to spend heavily to keep developing its AI models and stay ahead of rivals, from OpenAI, Alphabet and Meta to Chinese platforms. Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is "substantial." Meanwhile, the company has committed to spending nearly a trillion dollars on chips and AI infrastructure through 2045, according to a securities filing.

Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a national backlash against data centers, giving new impetus to a Congressional effort last year to enact a national moratorium on new ones.
"The company is likely to be very successful, but the market is pricing in very lofty expectations," Ritter said. "It could be hard for management to execute."
Wall Street analysts said Anthropic's share offering has broader ramifications for the AI sector, with the IPO's pricing setting a benchmark for other tech companies planning to go public.
Even if Anthropic's stock soars on the first day of trading, it won't necessarily create a swarm of IPO activity, Kennedy said. Still, it could reinvigorate markets, he added.

Meanwhile, by going public, Anthropic is effectively asking investors to discount the threats that Anthropic founder Dario Amodei himself has identified as posed by AI. In September, he called for an industrywide slowdown in AI development after a former Anthropic researcher warned of the existential threat AI poses to humanity.

title: Duffy pitches Senate GOP on $50 billion for FAA after ground stop
summary: Senate Republicans appeared skeptical after Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy made the case for tens of billions of more dollars for the Federal Aviation Administration.
story: Washington — Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Tuesday after Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy made the case for tens of billions of more dollars for the Federal Aviation Administration following a telecommunication outage that prompted a rare nationwide ground stop last week.
Overloaded routers prompted the FAA to issue the ground stop on Friday, resulting in thousands of canceled flights and stranded travelers.

Duffy is seeking $50 billion to overhaul the FAA's systems, some of which still rely on technology that is decades old. There was widespread concern among lawmakers about the problem, but GOP senators questioned the funding figure — and how the money could get approved.

Speaking at a news conference following a closed-door lunch meeting with Duffy, Senate Majority Leader John Thune said the secretary "fielded a lot of questions" about the funding and how it would be utilized.
"How we deal with that issue remains to be seen," Thune said. "There are ways in which we could do it with Republicans only, there are also ways in which we could do it with Democrats."

Senate Republicans have been considering pursuing another reconciliation bill, which would allow them to move forward without help from across the aisle. But the legislative maneuver is complicated and time-consuming. Thune said Republicans are continuing to have conversations, which will stretch into Wednesday, but he acknowledged that "the clock is ticking" down to the end of the current Congress.

Congress allocated $12.5 billion for the FAA in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act just last year. Duffy said the bulk of that money has been set aside for various projects, and Thune pointed to the funds on Tuesday, acknowledging that "we needed air traffic modernization."
"We did that then — there's more that's required," Thune said. "How that gets done is still an open question."

Thune suggested some senators have concerns about the $50 billion figure. He said the total the administration initially sought before the ground stop — $30 billion — reflected "not just the immediate needs," but also "a number of other things that they want to do." He said some of those projects should be funded through the normal government funding process, not reconciliation.
When asked about the $20 billion difference, Duffy told CBS News that he "decided to put everything on the table."
"There's been a historic underinvestment in aviation," Duffy said. "I hope we get the full investment."
GOP Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana told reporters he was "furious when they went from $30 billion to $50 billion."
"I mean, I'm not Bambi's baby brother," Kennedy said.
Sen. Rick Scott of Florida thanked Duffy in a post on X, while expressing support for a smaller investment.

"We absolutely need to update our air traffic control system, which would cost about $10 billion," Scott wrote, while stressing that "the airlines need to put up money and have skin in this game too."

But other Senate Republicans were entirely supportive of the transportation secretary's pitch. Sen. Eric Schmitt of Missouri, who's been working with the administration on proposed aviation infrastructure funding, told reporters that "the needs are pretty broad and pretty deep" for tech upgrades.
"So my position is: Let's go fix this on behalf of the American people," he said. "They saw what happened. I think they would want us to be responsive to that."
Schmitt advocated for approving the funds through reconciliation. He said he doesn't want to "make this partisan," but "some of my Democrat colleagues, I think, are taking a different tack."

"I was advocating for this before Friday, and then what we saw Friday, I just think this is something that we should do," Schmitt said. "I can't think of anything more important than the safety of the millions of Americans that fly."

Speaking after the meeting, Duffy said the engagement from Republicans was "fantastic." He said the GOP plans to "work through what they think is the right approach, the right funding levels, to make sure we have the resources to address the needs of the American airspace."

Duffy outlined his new request to Congress, saying the U.S. needs a new network that is "resilient," and an investment in infrastructure, like air traffic control towers, new runways and for airports more broadly. Asked about a piecemeal approach, Duffy said he'll take what he can get. But he said if the status quo continues, "I will replace every single tower in America in 300 years."
"So we have to do something different," Duffy said.

Caitlin  Huey-Burns
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: U.S. officially loses measles elimination status: "What a tragedy"
summary: The United States has lost its official measles elimination status for the first time in 26 years. Here's what to know.
story: The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, global health officials announced Tuesday.

The decision from the Pan American Health Organization came after the U.S. recorded over 5,400 measles cases so far this year — more than double last year's total. The Pan American Health Organization is a regional office for the World Health Organization, covering North and South America. Researchers with knowledge of the decision had previously confirmed it to CBS News partner KFF Health News on Saturday.
A country is considered as having eliminated the measles if there are "no locally transmitted measles infections or outbreaks lasting 12 months or longer," according to the World Health Organization.

The United States did not meet that standard for the first time since 2000. According to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about a third of this year's measles cases are linked to outbreaks that began in 2025 and continued to spread.

After a 30-year record of 2,242 cases last year, the CDC has tallied 5,412 cases to date in 2026, resulting in more than 590 hospitalizations and at least six measles-related deaths, with some states reporting additional fatalities.

"It's profoundly sad and disappointing," Dr. William Schaffner, a professor of preventive medicine and infectious diseases at the Vanderbilt University Medical Center, told CBS News. "What a tragedy. We have had children die of measles this past year. That should never have happened. Those deaths and all those cases, 5,000-plus, were completely preventable."

The biggest outbreak has been in Pennsylvania, where state health officials have reported more than 1,500 cases and seven deaths associated with the disease this year. Wisconsin reports two children have died and New York had its first measles death in more than 30 years.
Measles cases have been confirmed so far this year in 45 states and Washington, D.C.

"The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does," CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said in a statement. "We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities." She said the CDC remains focused on stopping outbreaks.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said Tuesday on social media, "We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles."
Kennedy pointed to "COVID-era disruptions" in childhood vaccinations and cited other countries, including Canada, Mexico, Spain and the United Kingdom, that have also lost measles elimination status.

"We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust," he said. "We will answer families' questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment.  We will support Americans who become ill, regardless of vaccination status, and for the first time equip health care providers with guidance to diagnose and treat measles and its complications."

Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Republican from Louisiana who is also a doctor, said health officials, including Kennedy, should be doing more to promote the importance of vaccination to protect against measles.

"Speaking as a physician, you may decide not to be vaccinated because it's your free will, but the child who's too young to be vaccinated is vulnerable if you come into that child's presence, and we're seeing children die from measles who are too young to be vaccinated," Cassidy said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
"So if you've not been vaccinated, you could be the person that brings death to another. That's something to remember."
What does it mean to lose measles elimination status?

A country or region loses its measles elimination status once its population immunity lowers enough that there is sustained spread of the disease, CBS News medical correspondent Dr. Céline Gounder explained. When a country has measles elimination status and a high rate of vaccination, a case of measles or small outbreak will soon fizzle out. But when there are this many gaps in the population's immunity, there can be "ongoing chains of transmission," Gounder said.

"It means that we're at risk of being exposed to measles and getting measles if we're not vaccinated," Gounder said. "It means ERs and pediatricians need to consider measles in anyone with a fever and rash, whether they've traveled overseas or not. And we may now become an exporter of measles to other countries."
Dr. Omer Awan, a trained epidemiologist and senior public health contributor for Forbes, said that the loss of measles elimination status is a setback to the nation's public health infrastructure.

"It's frustrating and heartbreaking ... because we have the tools to fight this. The tool is the MMR vaccine, which we know is 97% effective at preventing the onset of measles," Awan said. "It'd be one thing if we didn't have the tools to fight this, but the tools are at our disposal, we just aren't using the tools that can help us mitigate the spread and beat measles."
How can the U.S. regain measles elimination status?
A country earns measles elimination status by ensuring there is no local spread of the disease or outbreaks that last for more than a year.

PAHO says that the best way to maintain the elimination of measles is maintaining a vaccination rate of 95% or higher. Countries should also have sensitive surveillance systems to detect cases quickly, laboratory capacity and a guaranteed rapid response to outbreaks. Data about these trends must be submitted to and verified by the organization.

For the U.S. to curb outbreaks and regain measles elimination status, it needs to return to higher rates of vaccination, Awan said. He said battling misinformation and ramping up vaccination campaigns would be key to that effort.
Data shows childhood vaccination rates have declined in many communities around the U.S. in recent years, often below the threshold needed to help ward off measles outbreaks.
Gounder also noted that lawmakers can create policies that lead to increased vaccination rates.

"States set the school vaccine rules. Nine states made opting out of vaccination easier in 2025. States ending nonmedical exemptions saw kindergarten vaccination rise 2 to 4 points," Gounder said. "Most legislatures reconvene in January. Your state lawmakers will write next year's exemption rules."
Measles in the U.S.

The United States started collecting national data on measles in 1912, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. About 6,000 measles-related deaths were reported each year in the first decade of that data collection.

In the decade between 1953 and 1963, nearly all children in the U.S. caught measles before they turned 15, with an estimated 3 to 4 million people infected each year and tens of thousands hospitalized, according to the CDC. In those years, 400 to 500 people, mostly children, died of measles annually.
Then in 1963, the measles vaccine first became widely available. The numbers began a sharp decline and several generations of Americans grew up without ever encountering measles.
By 1981, reported measles cases had dropped by 80% compared to the previous year, the CDC said. The country was officially declared as having eliminated measles in 2000.

The U.S. maintained its elimination status for over 25 years. That didn't mean there were no cases at all — in 2015, an outbreak that spread among unvaccinated people was traced back to overseas visitors at Disneyland in Southern California, and a 2018-19 outbreak in New York was eventually contained by public health measures including curtailing vaccine exemptions. But those spikes were just a fraction of the spread now being seen in the U.S.

The nation recorded 2,242 measles cases in 2025, according to CDC data, linked to 48 separate outbreaks. The CDC reported 245 hospitalizations, mostly in children, and three measles deaths last year. Infections were confirmed in at least 44 states. It was the most cases the country had seen in over three decades.
That record was shattered in 2026, when the U.S. recorded more than double that number of cases by October — a total that topped 5,000 earlier this month.
Almost all of the cases have been in people who were not vaccinated. Measles-related deaths have been reported in Pennsylvania, New York and Wisconsin.

The CDC said 43 new outbreaks — defined as three or more related cases — have been reported so far in 2026, while about a third of the cases reported this year are tied to outbreaks that have been ongoing since 2025.
Who is at risk from measles?

Measles is one of the most contagious infectious diseases. Those who are unvaccinated for the disease are most at risk of getting it. CDC data shows that 96% of people infected with measles in 2026 had not been vaccinated for measles or were unsure of their vaccination status; only 2% of cases were in people who'd been fully vaccinated.
Medical research has shown that two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is extremely safe and effective at protecting against measles.
But some people — including babies, pregnant women or people with weakened immune systems — cannot get vaccinated and must rely on population immunity to keep the disease from spreading.
"They will be the ones that are most vulnerable to getting infected and experiencing the complications," such as pneumonia or encephalitis, Awan said.
Many of the recent cases have been occurring in tight-knit and largely unvaccinated Amish or Mennonite communities.

"It really shows you who's vulnerable because these are totally unvaccinated communities," said Dr. Deborah Birx, a longtime public health official who was a leader of the White House Coronavirus Task Force during the pandemic. "You can see it in who's hospitalized. The largest percentage are children under 4 and adults over 50."

"I hope this is a wake-up call to every parent," Birx told CBS News. "If you had decided to not vaccinate your children, you've been relatively protected by all of us and all of our grandchildren and other children who got vaccinated. But that protection and that shield is going away" as vaccination rates slip. "And so your child is now vulnerable at a level they never were vulnerable before."

Measles is known for causing a rash, but Schaffner said that's the least of it. "What's bothersome is children, even with uncomplicated measles, are miserable for a week or a week and a half with red eyes, runny nose, cough, and just debilitating fever and diarrhea. And then you have the complications of dehydration, pneumonia, and on occasion, encephalitis."

There can be other lingering health consequences, Birx warned. Measles patients "can end up with what we call immune suppression, so that they're more susceptible to all other diseases after they've had measles."
While many people recover, measles can cause severe infections in the lungs and brain that can lead to cognitive issues, deafness or death.
"Measles is a nasty, nasty virus," Schaffner said. "In contrast, the vaccine is wonderfully effective."

title: Professional misconduct complaints against DOJ officials are rising
summary: The number of professional misconduct complaints filed against Justice Department officials has increased by more than 50% over a two-year period, according to the department's inspector general.
story: The number of professional misconduct complaints filed against Justice Department officials has increased by more than 50% over a two-year period, which could strain DOJ's already limited resources to investigate the claims, the agency's internal watchdog said Tuesday.

In a new report, Justice Department Inspector General Don Berthiaume said that ensuring the fairness and integrity of the department's investigations and prosecutions is among the top six management challenges for senior leadership.

"The lawful and effective exercise of these authorities is indispensable to public safety and the rule of law. It also creates a corresponding management responsibility to ensure that Department investigations and prosecutions are conducted with integrity, objectivity, consistency, and fairness," he wrote in his report.

His report cited new statistics from the Office of Professional Responsibility, which is tasked with investigating attorney misconduct. During the 2026 fiscal year, which ended on Oct. 1, the office, which operates with a full-time staff of just 18 people, received 2,081 professional misconduct complaints.

By contrast, it received 1,666 in the same time frame in 2025. In fiscal year 2024, there were 1,346 complaints and 1,085 in the same time frame in 2023 — "an increase of approximately 54 percent in 2 years," the report says.

In the last fiscal year, the Office of Professional Responsibility opened 33 professional-misconduct inquiries and closed 35, and it completed nine out of 10 full investigations opened that same year.
In those nine cases, OPR determined there had been professional misconduct by attorneys, the report said.
During that same time period, OPR also received 50 new FBI whistleblower retaliation complaints and closed 41 matters.

"These results demonstrate that OPR has continued to resolve substantial workloads despite its limited size," the inspector general wrote. "However, the Department faces risk in its oversight capacity if OPR's staffing levels are insufficient to manage the workload generated by the Department's thousands of employees."

The uptick in professional misconduct allegations comes at a time when the Justice Department has faced intense scrutiny over investigations it has pursued against President Trump's political enemies, including some that Mr. Trump openly encouraged. The report does not describe the complaints, so it is not known if any of them stem from these investigations.
Former FBI Director James Comey, for example, has faced at least three separate criminal probes since last year.

Although an indictment accusing him of lying to Congress was dismissed, he is still facing charges in North Carolina over an Instagram post showing seashells on a beach arranged to read "86 47" — a message that prosecutors allege was intended as a threat against Mr. Trump.

Most recently, prosecutors filed a criminal information against Comey in order to pause the statute of limitations while they try to secure an indictment against him for allegedly leaking classified information.
Comey has denied wrongdoing in all three cases.

Earlier this year, a federal judge in the Middle District of Tennessee ruled that the Justice Department's prosecution of Kilmar Abrego Garcia was vindictive, citing in part extrajudicial statements that now-Attorney General Todd Blanche had made about the case.

Others who have been targeted with criminal investigations or prosecutions include Democratic election lawyer Marc Elias, Federal Reserve Board Governor Lisa Cook, former Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell, Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar, New York Attorney General Letitia James, Democratic Sen. Adam Schiff, several former FBI counterintelligence officials, former CNN anchor Don Lemon, and the Southern Poverty Law Center, a progressive civil rights nonprofit that has been critical of the Trump administration.
Although the department's inspector general has broad authority to investigate waste, fraud and abuse, it is more limited when it comes to allegations of misconduct involving DOJ lawyers.
That role typically falls to OPR, which is a smaller office that has less independence than the inspector general. Last year, the head of OPR was removed by senior Justice Department leadership.

Recently, the inspector general declined to open an investigation into the prosecutors who falsely accused Olympian David Hearn of vandalizing the Reflecting Pool, saying that the matter fell squarely in OPR's jurisdiction.

The Justice Department, in responding to the inspector general's report, said that it "emphasizes integrity, fairness, and accountability in its investigative and prosecutorial work, with the Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) serving as a central guardian of ethical standards."
"Despite resource constraints, OPR fulfilled its mission through disciplined case management, dedicated staff, and effective use of technology," the department said.

title: Kalshi pauses Trump "mention markets" in response to CFTC order
summary: Kalshi said it is complying with an order the Commodity Futures Trading Commission issued on Friday.
story: Kalshi is pausing markets that allow users to bet on what President Trump will say in response to a federal agency's request, a spokesperson for the prediction market confirmed.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission requested that Kalshi halt the so-called "mention markets" tied to the president on Friday.

Mention markets allow traders to bet on specific words or phrases a person will utter during public events, such as speeches or earnings calls. Users often spend hours researching a person's speech patterns to make an informed guess about what they might say.

"We are complying with the order," the Kalshi spokesperson said in an email. The company will still allow some mention markets related to the Trump administration, according to The Wall Street Journal, which earlier reported the pause.
Reached for comment, a CFTC spokesperson said the decision was consistent with a September order that stayed the certification of certain mention markets by Kalshi.

"These contract types present a heightened risk of manipulation because their settlement turns on the discrete conduct of a person that may be neither independently generated nor externally verifiable," the agency said at the time.

The CFTC's order follows a July incident in which a White House teleprompter operator made more than $100,000 on Kalshi bets tied to public speeches by President Trump. The trading activity by an administration employee fueled concerns about insider trading on prediction market platforms, an issue that has attracted lawmakers' attention.
Kalshi said it updated its rules in March to better detect insider trading and prevent market manipulation.

Kalshi has removed other markets at the CFTC's behest in the past. In August, the company removed all sports-related mention markets, which previously generated $90 million in monthly trading volume, according to a person familiar with the matter.

title: NSA's classified internal network goes down, sources say
summary: Two U.S. officials tell CBS News that so far there is no evidence of a cyberattack.
story: Washington — The National Security Agency's internal network used to store and share classified information went offline Tuesday, according to multiple U.S. officials familiar with the situation, prompting the agency to stagger arrival times for some personnel at its headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland.
The network, dubbed "NSA Net," is used for classified communications and information sharing within the nation's largest intelligence agency.

An NSA spokesperson said in a statement that the agency experienced a "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance." The statement continued that "while some internal systems were affected, mission/critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend National Security continues."
The spokesperson said that the agency's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.

Two U.S. officials told CBS News that, at this point, there is no evidence the disruption was caused by a cyberattack. Two sources familiar with the situation said the outage resulted from routine system patching, though the precise circumstances surrounding the disruption remain unclear.
The NSA has also implemented staggered arrival times for non-emergency personnel at Fort Meade, according to two sources familiar with the measure.
The news was first reported by CNN.

Multiple sources told CBS News that the agency was seeking to avoid having large numbers of employees log on to their computers simultaneously while the network was experiencing problems, which is why they decided to stagger arrivals. Sources referred to this as "Code Gray," part of a modified reporting schedule.

Sources familiar with Fort Meade's operations said the installation remains under normal operating conditions, with gates and campus-wide services unaffected. The sources explained that the NSA operates within its own secured campus and can establish unique reporting requirements for its personnel, independent of the larger installation.
In the meantime, some activities are being redirected to other NSA facilities around the country, according to sources familiar with the situation.
It was not immediately clear how long the network had been offline or when full service might be restored.

The NSA, home to one of the largest workforces in the U.S. intelligence community, is responsible for collecting and analyzing foreign signals intelligence, identifying and countering cyber threats, and protecting U.S. government communications.
CBS News has reached out to the White House, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the Pentagon for comment.

title: American soldier accused of spying in U.S. custody after U.K. arrest
summary: Federal Bureau of Investigation director Kash Patel said that the soldier was "a potential threat to national security."
story: A United States Army soldier arrested in the United Kingdom on suspicion that he engaged in espionage linked to Russia has been taken into the custody of the U.S. military, British and American officials said Tuesday.

A U.S. official previously identified the suspect as Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, a senior human resources officer based at Imjin Barracks, home to the headquarters of NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. Tyner, 41, joined the Army in 2008 and has been deployed to Afghanistan, Qatar and Iraq.
Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said in a news release that U.S. authorities will continue the investigation. The suspect is expected to be charged soon.

"These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," Taylor said.

The soldier is suspected of violating the U.K.'s National Security Act of 2023 to obtain or disclose protected information and to assist a foreign intelligence service. The London Metropolitan Police said the suspected activity relates to Russia. Federal Bureau of Investigation director Kash Patel said that the soldier was "a potential threat to national security."

He was arrested by the the London Metropolitan Police during a sting operation in Gloucester, about 100 miles west of London, on November 10. The operation involved the Met Police's Counter Terrorism Policing Unit, the U.S. military and the FBI.
"This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement on Tuesday.
Officials have carried out further searches in Gloucestershire, the county where Gloucester is located, related to the investigation, the Metropolitan Police Department said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow last week that Russia had "nothing to do with" the soldier's detention.

U.K. police said the arrest is not related to "any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations." The unit is investigating a recent suspected plot at RAF Fairford, a British Royal Air Force base where U.S. troops and aircraft are stationed. The U.S. military removed its bombers from that base after the security incident.

Five British men and one U.K.-Iranian national were arrested in late September. Last week, the U.S. Justice Department announced that three people it accuses of being Iran-backed operatives were charged with plotting a terrorist attack at the site. One suspect is in custody in New York, and the other two are not in custody, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

title: Cruz announces deal on stalled airline safety bill
summary: The measure would require all planes in busy airspace to be broadcasting their location, according to GOP Sen. Ted Cruz.
story: GOP Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas announced the Republican-controlled House and Senate have reached an agreement in principle to require planes in crowded airspace to be equipped with technology that enables them to see other aircraft in their area and to transmit their location. Cruz said it would be landmark legislation for aviation safety.

The equipment, known as ADS-B In, shows nearby air traffic with visual and audible alerts, and has been recommended as a required safety feature by the National Transportation Safety Board since 2008, but the Federal Aviation Administration has not adopted it.

After an American Airlines passenger jet collided with an Army Black Hawk helicopter on approach at Ronald Reagan National Airport in January 2025, killing 67 people, Cruz and other members of Congress argued that ADS-B In could help keep aircraft safer.

Cruz made the announcement during a press conference on Tuesday in front of the Capitol with the families of the DCA plane crash victims, who have been advocating for the technology since the deadly collision.

"We still have a couple of details to negotiate with the House Armed Services Committee, but with this agreement in principle, I believe we're going to get this bill done," Sen. Cruz said. "And my objective is to get it done this year, with this Congress, before we leave for the new year."

Proponents of the technology argue it could have prevented the fatal DCA crash and alerted the American Airlines pilots to the approach of the Army Black Hawk helicopter, which was conducting a training mission in the plane's vicinity directly in the path of their flight.

In December 2025, the Senate passed the ROTOR Act, which would have mandated ADS-B In for all commercial and military flights in busy airspace. It passed the Senate unanimously but failed in the House by one vote, a devastating blow to the victims' families after the Pentagon withdrew its support for the bill because of the requirements it would impose on military aircraft.

Since then, the House passed its own legislation, called the ALERT Act. It would close the "military loophole," requiring military flight crews to broadcast their location during non-sensitive missions.
Cruz and Democratic Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington opposed that legislation, arguing it lacks the critical improvements the aviation system needs.

"We must have strong military accountability in the national airspace. The military must be a willing partner with the Department of Transportation and the FAA to make sure that what happened that January never, ever happens again," Sen. Cruz said during Tuesday's press conference.

title: Fed's Lisa Cook rebuffs White House hearing without changes
summary: A lawyer for Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook said she has "no legal obligation" to appear at a White House hearing about mortgage fraud allegations.
story: Washington — Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook will not participate in an upcoming White House hearing to examine allegations she made false statements on mortgage documents unless concerns about the process are first addressed, her lawyer said in a letter to the White House obtained by CBS News.

Abbe Lowell, Cook's lawyer, told White House counsel Will Scharf that Cook has "no legal obligation" to appear at what he said is an "unfair" hearing before a three-member committee of Trump administration officials that is set for next month. He warned participating in the proceeding would undermine the Fed's "unique status" and independence.

"Consequently, this Committee process appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook or to unreasonably manufacture a supposed 'adverse inference' if she does not participate in a process that does not comport with the requirements of a fair hearing," Lowell wrote.

His letter to Scharf revealed that the two sides have exchanged numerous communications in the weeks since President Trump announced that he had created a "committee of inquiry" to look into the claims that Cook made misrepresentations on mortgage forms related to two properties before joining the Fed's Board of Governors in 2022.

The committee is made up of Kevin Hassett, assistant to the president for economic policy; Andrea Lucas, chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission; and Keith Sonderling, director of the Office of Government Ethics.
Cook has repeatedly denied wrongdoing and said Mr. Trump is attempting to remove her from the Fed because he disagrees with her decisions on interest rates.

"It is unfortunate that your latest correspondence fails to address the concerns Governor Cook has previously raised — making clear that you are uninterested in convening the 'substantive and fair hearing' you have claimed. Instead, you seek only to manufacture 'cause' for a predetermined removal outcome," Lowell wrote.

Cook had raised concerns in earlier letters to the White House about Hassett's membership on the committee because of comments he has made about the Fed governor, which Lowell said "demonstrate that he has prejudged the issue."
"Mr. Hassett's continued presence on the Committee remains unacceptable," Lowell said.

He also took issue with the White House's proposed process to exchange documents. Lowell said it is "fundamentally unfair" because it would require Cook to hand over documents immediately, while she would not gain access to information that the White House has until seven days before the hearing.

Lowell had also pressed the White House on the specific legal standard the committee would apply to determine what constitutes "cause" to remove a Fed governor and the participation of Justice Department personnel in the hearing, he said.

"Your and the Committee's failure to address these legitimate issues, over multiple weeks of back-and-forth correspondence, reinforces my prior observation: President Trump's decision to fire Governor Cook has already been made," Lowell wrote.

Mr. Trump first tried to fire Cook in August 2025 after Bill Pulte, the head of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, accused her of making false statements on mortgage applications. Cook filed a lawsuit claiming that her removal was in violation of federal law, which allows the president to remove a member of the Fed's board only "for cause."

The Supreme Court in June allowed Cook to remain in her job while her case continued and found that Mr. Trump failed to provide Cook with the procedural protections she was entitled to under the law, namely notice of the allegations against her and the opportunity to respond before she was fired.

Weeks after the Supreme Court's 5-4 decision, Mr. Trump again moved to oust Cook. The White House said in a letter to Cook in August that the president was considering terminating her because of the mortgage fraud accusations and gave her a chance to respond — seemingly an attempt to remedy the issues raised by the Supreme Court.
The president then announced last month that he had established the committee to look into the claims against Cook and determine whether he has cause to remove her.
The hearing at the White House was initially set to take place Nov. 5, with committee members set to consider evidence and allegations against Cook.

In his latest letter to Scharf, Lowell said the White House had attempted to schedule a hearing on dates that conflicted with the Fed's official business. He said that Scharf claimed in an Oct. 19 letter that if Cook didn't show up on the date selected by the White House, the hearing would proceed without her and the committee could "draw an adverse inference" from her failure to appear because of official obligations.

"To be clear, if the White House establishes an unbiased panel and implements fair procedures that do not prejudge the outcome — such as providing the evidence it claims to have gathered with sufficient time for review and response — Governor Cook would be prepared to appear," Lowell wrote. "But the ultimatums in your November 2, 2026 letter do not provide a productive path forward to enabling that participation."

title: Nvidia forms export control panel amid concerns over China sales
summary: Chipmaker creates new committee amid growing concerns that it has allowed restricted products to reach China.
story: Nvidia on Tuesday said its board has formed a committee to oversee its national security policies and compliance with U.S. export controls, a step that comes amid heightened scrutiny of the chipmaker's sales practices to some Southeast Asian companies.

The move comes days after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO over revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, as well as a subordinate at the company. The woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, Alice Huang (no relation), had worked for a Singapore-based data center company, Megaspeed, which had bought billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia chips.

Nvidia also faces mounting pressure in Washington, D.C., with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and lawmakers on both sides of the aisle expressing concern that China is gaining access to the company's advanced chips, which are critical to developing AI models. The U.S. has barred sales of Nvidia's highest-end chips to China due to national security and competitive concerns.
On Monday, the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim rule limiting other countries' access to advanced chips that power artificial intelligence.
Congressional pressure grows

Jensen Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter have agreed to appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the House Intelligence Committee, according to a statement on Tuesday from the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

"The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia's role in allowing dangerous [People's Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal," the committee chairs, Reps. Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, said in the statement.
Nvidia said its existing National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team will report directly to the new committee and its interim CEO, Colette Kress.

"Nvidia recognizes that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security," Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board of directors, said in a statement.
The company added that the decision to create the committee reflects the board's commitment "to demonstrate the highest standards of governance and oversight."

Nvidia shares have dropped 16% following news of Huang's extramarital relationships and his departure from the company, which has shed more than $700 billion in value in the wake of the scandal. Nvidia's business could also take a hit if new U.S. restrictions on sales of semiconductors and chipmaking equipment affect its sales to China, according to Wall Street analysts.

"Any new leadership will be very wary of drawing the ire of either the U.S. Congress or the U.S. Treasury and will consequently err on the side of caution when it comes to authorizing any non-U.S. sales," Louis-Vincent Gave, CEO of investment adviser Gavekal, said in a report.

The spotlight on Nvidia also comes at a delicate time for U.S.-China relations, especially as the countries compete in AI. President Trump arrived Tuesday in the Philippines to start a multiday swing in Asia, where he's scheduled to meet with China's President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin later this week.
Chinese government officials warned the U.S. last week against imposing additional guardrails on chip exports, which China said would disrupt global supply chains.

title: Anthropic files for IPO as it competes for AI dominance
summary: Anthropic, which developed the Claude chatbot, is barreling ahead with its public offering despite mounting concerns about AI going rogue.
story: Anthropic filed for an initial public offering on Monday, bringing the maker of artificial intelligence platform Claude a step closer to its highly anticipated public market debut and providing a key test for the rapidly emerging AI sector.
In the filing, Anthropic outlined its vision for a future profoundly shaped by AI, touting the technology's potential to transform the global economy and improve lives worldwide.

"We believe the diffusion of AI through the global economy represents one of the largest opportunities in history to improve how humans live and work, and it is just beginning," the company said in its S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The filing highlights Anthropic's rapid growth, with the company generating $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year. That staggering rate of expansion is likely to slow, with Anthropic noting that its revenue growth is expected to decline over time.

The company has yet to turn a profit. Anthropic reported a net loss of $80.7 billion for the first half of the year, more than six times the net loss of nearly $13 billion for the first two quarters in 2025.
Anthropic's founders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, pitched the IPO to investors in part as an opportunity to be part of a history-defining moment.

"We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms," the company's seven co-founders said in a letter included in the S-1. "We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater. The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history."
Referendum on AI

The IPO, which market analysts expect as early as November, could instantly rank Anthropic among the world's largest publicly traded companies. The offering could raise as much as $100 billion, according to reports. That would slingshot it past Elon Musk-owned SpaceX, which raised a record-breaking $86 billion when it went public in June.
Anthropic, which was valued at $965 billion in May, could see its value rise to $1.5 trillion or possibly $2 trillion, although its final valuation has not been established.
Anthropic shares will list on the Nasdaq stock exchange, according to the company's filing. The AI company will trade under the ticker symbol "ANT."

More broadly, the transaction will gauge the strength of investor demand not only for Anthropic shares, but also for the widening constellation of data center builders, chipmakers and other companies involved in developing the critical infrastructure powering AI services.

"This IPO is a referendum on the entire AI trade," Nigel Green, CEO of investment firm deVere Group, said in an email. "If it soars, expect a queue of AI listings and even more capital piling into the theme. If it stumbles, valuations across tech could reset fast."

The torrent of capital flowing into AI has helped propel the stock market to record highs. The question is whether AI can maintain its momentum amid signs that investors are fretting over when — and if — their money will eventually pay off and deliver the returns they are banking on.

Anthropic's prospectus shows that the company has funneled massive amounts of money toward building the computing resources necessary to power its AI models. The company spent $8.9 billion in the first half of the year on chips and other infrastructure to run its platform, compared to $2.3 billion over the same period last year.

"Anthropic could become the most valuable company in the world. It could also end up in bankruptcy," analysts with Lightshed, an investment advisory firm, said in a research note ahead of the IPO filing.
Potential obstacles to growth

Anthropic's IPO filing also outlines various risks that could hamper its growth or cause it to fall behind competitors. Much of the company's future growth hinges on whether it has access to sufficient capital, including debt financing, which more companies are using to finance the AI buildout.

To maintain its competitive edge, Anthropic also said it will need to use its existing AI models to design and train next-generation platforms, a process known as "recursive self-improvement," or RSI.

"If we fail to direct sufficient compute and research efforts to AI-assisted development, or if our competitors more effectively leverage AI to enhance their own innovation cycles, we risk falling progressively further behind. …" Anthropic said in the filing.

AI experts warn that using AI to build ever more powerful frontier models raises the risk of people losing control of the technology, potentially leading to disasters such as deadly pandemics or cyberattacks that cut off internet, electricity or water.
Barreling ahead despite safety concerns

Anthropic filed a confidential IPO with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, beating out rival OpenAI, which filed just over a week later. Both companies are barreling ahead with plans to go public despite concerns about the potential threats AI poses to humanity.

Reports of AI agents going rogue continue to pile up, stoking concern that the technology could escape human control and carry out cyberattacks. In September, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development after one of his company's former researchers said that there's a 10% chance the technology could wipe out humanity in the next decade.
In an interview with CBS News, Amodei said the pace of technological growth should serve as a warning sign, while making a case for continued development of AI.

title: U.S. identifies remains of 6 soldiers killed in Korean War, including teens
summary: The identifications are part of an ongoing effort to locate and identify the remains of U.S. soldiers killed in the Korean War.
story: Six soldiers who died in the Korean War, including two teenagers, have been accounted for decades after their deaths, the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency announced Monday.

The identifications are part of an ongoing effort to locate and identify the remains of those killed in the Korean War. When a soldier is marked as accounted for, they receive a burial with full military honors.

U.S. Army Cpl. Jackie Lee Thurman was a member of Battery B, 99th Field Artillery Battalion, 1st Cavalry Division. Thurman, 18, was a forward observer near Waegwan, South Korea, when his post came under heavy attack, according to the agency, and was last seen trying to evacuate a shell-shocked officer from the area while under heavy enemy fire.
Afterward, Thurman was reported missing in action. A presumptive finding of death was issued on Dec. 31, 1953. His remains were declared unrecoverable two years later, in January 1956.

The agency said that a set of remains, designated X-5814 Tanggok, was recovered by the Quartermaster Graves Registration Company near Kumhwa-dong, South Korea, in October 1952. The remains were interred as unknowns at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific in Honolulu, Hawaii. In November 2022, the agency disinterred the remains. Analysis allowed the agency's scientists to identify the remains as Thurman's. He was marked as accounted for by the agency on May 18, 2026.

U.S. Army 1st Lt. Raymond Banker Gilbert was a member of B Battery, 503rd Field Artillery Battalion, 2nd Infantry Division, who was reported missing during the battle of the Ch'ongch'on River in North Korea, according to the agency. Witness statements allowed the Army to determine that Gilbert, 23, had been taken as a prisoner of war by the Chinese People's Volunteer Army and died from battlefield wounds in a POW camp on Jan. 31, 1951.

After the war, a recovered set of remains was returned to U.S. custody as part of a 1954 exchange known as Operation Glory, the agency said. The remains could not be identified at the time and were buried as an unknown at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. They were disinterred on July 1, 2024, and sent to the agency's laboratory. Analysis, circumstantial and historical evidence allowed the agency to identify the remains as Gilbert's. His remains were marked as accounted for on June 4, 2026.

U.S. Army Cpl. William R. Laughlin Jr. was a member of Company D, 1st Battalion, 32nd Infantry Regiment, 7th Infantry Division, attached to the 31st Regimental Combat Team, according to the agency. Laughlin, 21, was among the U.S. soldiers ambushed by the Chinese People's Volunteer Army at the Chosin Reservoir in North Korea.

The ambush sparked a 17-day battle in frigid weather. Each side took thousands of casualties. U.S. and United Nations forces eventually retreated south toward the supply base of Hagaru-ri. Laughlin could not be located after the battle and was reported missing in action on Dec. 2, 1950. A presumptive finding of death was issued on Dec. 31, 1953.

A pair of remains returned during Operation Glory were connected to an isolated burial east of the Chosin Reservoir. They could not be identified and were interred as unknowns at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. The agency disinterred the remains in July 2022 and used modern forensic techniques at its laboratory to identify them as Laughlin's. He was marked as accounted for by the agency on Sept. 28, 2026.

U.S. Army Sgt. Joseph A. Platzkoester, a member of Company H, 2nd Battalion, 38th Infantry Regiment, 2nd Infantry Division, was last seen during an ambush near Inje in South Korea. Platzkoester, 28, was part of a convoy doing counteroffensive clearing operations at the time, the agency said. The convoy encountered an enemy roadblock. While his battalion pushed through, Platzkoester could not be found after the fight and was reported missing in action.
The area was searched, but Platzkoester's remains were not found. A presumptive finding of death was issued on Dec. 31, 1953, and his remains were declared nonrecoverable in January 1956.

In 1951, the 148th Quartermaster Graves Registration Company found a set of remains that could not be identified. They were interred as an unknown at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. In November 2023, the set of remains was disinterred and sent to the agency's laboratory, where analysis identified them as Platzkoester's. He was marked as accounted for by the agency on May 29, 2026. A photo of Platzkoester was not available.

U.S. Army Cpl. Andrew R. Tischler, 21, was assigned to Company F, 2nd Battalion, 15th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division, and was reported missing in action during a road march near Taewol Village in South Korea, according to the agency. The agency said it was able to account for him on May 5, 2026. Information about how his remains were found and identified was not available. A photo was not shared by the agency.

The other teen soldier, U.S. Army Cpl. Richard N. Lennox, 18, was accounted for on Aug. 7, 2025, the agency said. He was a member of Company C, 1st Battalion, 7th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division reported missing in action after his unit was attacked by enemy forces near Sachang-ni, North Korea, on Nov. 28, 1950. He was captured and marched to a prisoner-of-war camp in Changsong, where he died in October 1951.

Lennox's remains were among those handed over during Operation Glory, the agency said. They could not be identified at the time and were buried as an unknown at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. The remains were disinterred on June 13, 2016. The agency analyzed the remains and said that Lennox had been accounted for on Aug. 7, 2025. A photo of Lennox was not available.

Each missing soldier's name was engraved on the Walls of the Missing at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. Now that they have been accounted for, rosettes will be placed alongside their names.

More information about each soldier, including how they were identified, may be shared after their families are briefed by the agency. The agency told CBS News in 2024 that history, diplomacy and science all come into each investigation. First, researchers start with archival records. Investigators then search for surviving witnesses and clues. Once the potential location of a set of remains is identified, a recovery mission is sent to bring those remains to the agency's laboratory.

At the lab, scientists use dental evidence and other records to study the remains. For soldiers who disappeared during the Korean War, experts can use tuberculosis skin test results taken before someone shipped out. The remains also undergo X-rays, DNA analysis and isotope analysis. Finally, a reference sample of DNA from a family member is compared to the remains. The process can take decades, the agency told CBS News.

About 7,500 Americans are still unaccounted for from the Korean War, the agency says. Efforts to bring home fallen soldiers from the conflict are complicated by relations with North Korea: While the agency operates in 46 countries, North Korea is an outlier. Sometimes, war dead are recovered during exchanges like Operation Glory.
