title: U.S. gave Singapore scant help with Alice Huang probe, source says
summary: Singapore held Alice Huang's passport for 8 months and asked the U.S. to help investigate her firm's suspected Nvidia chip sales, but received little help, sources say.
story: Singaporean authorities seized the passport of then-Megaspeed chief executive Alice Huang in June 2025 and held it for eight months, preventing her departure while trying to engage the U.S. government to support their investigation into advanced Nvidia chips possibly being shipped to China.

One source with knowledge of the matter told CBS News on Friday the Singaporean government received no meaningful help from Washington during the time she was in the Asian city-state. This source said officials in Washington were "not forthcoming" in response to Singapore's requests for help, and no substantive assistance has been provided to date.
Singapore's government confirmed in a statement this week that it reached out to both the U.S. Department of Justice and the FBI for assistance with its investigation.
Alice Huang is the suspected Chinese spy at the center of the extramarital affair scandal that toppled Nvidia founder Jensen Huang from the helm of the global tech giant he built over three decades.

Since February 2025, Singaporean authorities have been investigating whether Alice Huang and Megaspeed worked with California-based Supermicro to ship the Silicon Valley firm's computer servers — equipped with advanced Nvidia chips — to China, the source told CBS News.
Alice Huang flew into Singapore in June 2025 for a voluntary interview with Singapore-based investigators from the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security, according to the source.

The agency sits within the U.S. Department of Commerce and regulates the export of sensitive products on national security and economic grounds. The American authorities requested the interview, according to a Thursday statement by Singapore's Home Affairs Ministry, as part of a post-shipment verification check, a process used to determine whether imported products have reached their declared recipient.
Singaporean police also interviewed Huang on the same day as the U.S. officials, and made the decision to impound her passport.
The source said it was not known where Huang, a Chinese national, arrived in Singapore from in June 2025.

By February 2026, however, the Singapore Police Force had not charged Huang with any crime and had no option but to return her passport, the source told CBS News. She was barred from ever returning to Singapore, as authorities assessed that she had given "inaccurate information" to downplay her role at Megaspeed, as noted in the statement from the home ministry.
That statement was released four days after Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with a woman who sources confirmed to CBS News was Alice Huang.

Singapore's investigation has focused on whether the then-Megaspeed CEO may have broken domestic law by lying about the details of purchases of computer servers from Supermicro, a San Jose-based technology company. The company's servers use Nvidia's advanced chips to run artificial intelligence software, data centers and cloud computing.

"The suspected domestic offenses pertained to potential false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers and other related offenses," Singapore's Home Affairs Ministry said in its statement this week.
Singaporean investigators have tried to determine the true ultimate destination of the Supermicro servers ordered by Megaspeed.

A second source familiar with the investigation told CBS News it is believed they may have been sent to Malaysia, but Singaporean investigators suspect "some or all" of them may then have been shipped onward to China. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.
Singapore's home ministry attempted to contact Supermicro, but the U.S. company only "provided limited cooperation," according to the home ministry statement.

A spokesperson for the California firm told CBS News that Megaspeed "is not, and has never been, a Supermicro customer,"  adding that the company had "been responsive to inquiries and has fully cooperated with U.S. and Taiwanese officials, while also voluntarily providing information and engaging with all requests from Singapore authorities to date."

The New York Times reported Wednesday that Malaysia kept Nvidia's chips and installed them in its own data centers, but then rented use of those centers to China, rather than physically shipping any chips to China.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Friday that there was "no indication" any chips linked to the Nvidia-Megaspeed issue had been re-exported out of the country.

Beijing has dismissed the claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China." Asked Thursday about a Bloomberg report that she had returned to China, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters: "I do not have information on what you mentioned."
Since 2022, the U.S. has restricted the export of Nvidia's most powerful chips to China over national security concerns as the world's two biggest economies race for dominance in the AI sector.

The Singapore police first raised the issue with U.S. authorities in July 2025 to try to secure Supermicro's cooperation in revealing where its servers were ultimately ending up, repeating requests "on several occasions to the U.S. Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation," according to the Home Affairs Ministry's Thursday statement.

The second source confirmed to CBS News that Washington did not meaningfully engage with the requests for help on the investigation and said it "would be useful to know" what Supermicro declared about its exports to fulfill orders by Megaspeed, whether those products were registered as being bound for Malaysia, and whether some or all of those products were actually "bound for somewhere else," such as China.

The Singapore home ministry said in its statement that six other individuals linked to Megaspeed, in addition to Alice Huang, are wanted for questioning, but none have been in the country since the government launched its investigation in February 2025.
"One is a Singaporean citizen and the rest are foreigners," said the first person familiar with the case.

Singapore has charged five other people in a wider fraud conspiracy case related to the suspected transfer of Nvidia chips, including one Chinese man charged on Friday. The case was launched at the same time as the probe into Alice Huang and Megaspeed, the first source told CBS News, but it is separate.

"Singapore is committed to upholding our reputation as a trusted and reliable business hub. We will not allow companies or individuals to misuse Singapore's business environment to engage in fraud or dishonest practices," the home ministry said in its statement, adding that it would "conduct its own investigations independently, in accordance with our laws and based on the evidence available. We will cooperate with foreign authorities where appropriate, and take firm enforcement action wherever the evidence warrants it."
This story published first on CBS News at 12:16 p.m. on Nov. 13, 2026.

title: Ukraine and Russia trade major strikes as Trump set to meet Putin
summary: Ukraine has struck the Kerch Bridge, which connects Russian-occupied Crimea and Russia, twice, taking it out of service, as Moscow attacks bridges in Kyiv.
story: Ukraine struck a major bridge connecting Russian-occupied Crimea and the Russian mainland Tuesday for the second night in a row, while Russia hit two major bridges in the Ukrainian capital Kyiv.

Traffic was halted for hours across the Kerch Bridge, which carries both automobile and rail traffic, after it was hit shortly after midnight on Tuesday. The bridge has been a target of previous Ukrainian attacks and holds symbolic value as it was built following Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014.
There was no official comment on the damage, but unverified social media images appeared to show a section of the road bridge completely collapsed and in the water.

Russian military blogger Alexander Kots called the damage "significant" and said cars would not be able to cross it for a month. Kots also said the train service that runs across the bridge had been suspended, citing Russia's Ministry of Transport, but added the railway's tracks were intact.

Meanwhile, Russia's defense ministry said it shot down 1,441 Ukrainian drones during a major overnight barrage — the second-highest one-day figure this year. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin reported that more than 800 had been headed to the capital itself, while officials reported attacks across 19 regions of the country.
In Kyiv, Russian ballistic missiles hit the Northern and Southern bridges — two major arteries that cross the Dnipro River.
Traffic was suspended, causing gridlock early on Tuesday morning. Russia's army confirmed it had hit both bridges in a "massive attack" on Ukraine's infrastructure.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned of a major Russian attack in the days leading up to a meeting in China on Thursday of Presidents Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the meeting would "only encourage Putin to continue this war."
The White House had earlier signaled that the Ukraine war would not be addressed by the leaders, but Mr. Trump said Monday as he prepared to fly to Asia that it would be among the topics discussed.
"We'll talk about my favorite subject, Ukraine," he told reporters.
China has said only that "safeguarding world peace" and "promoting strategic stability in major power relations" will be on the agenda for the trilateral summit.

title: U.K. mulls changing sexual consent laws after Russell Brand case
summary: Britain's government will consider adopting staggered ages for sexual consent in the wake of "appalling" stories of "abuse of power by powerful men."
story: London —  Britain's government is considering changing the U.K.'s laws on the legal age of sexual consent as a woman who claims she was raped by convicted sex offender Russell Brand campaigns to criminalize sex between adults and 16- or 17-year-olds.

British Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said over the weekend that "appalling" stories of "abuse of power by powerful men" had emerged last week, warranting consideration of a new law that would set out different ages of consent depending on the ages of the individuals involved.

Already practiced by several other nations, the merits of this staggered age of consent approach have "been raised and will be discussed" by the government, McFadden said, adding that he "can't tell you what the conclusion of that would be, but the last week has certainly put that up in lights."

A day after Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for rape and sexual assault, fellow British television personality and author David Walliams was named as the subject of multiple allegations of grooming young girls and harassing female colleagues.

Under current U.K. law, an adult of any age can have sex with a consenting person 16 years old or older. If a staggered system were imposed, it could make it illegal for anyone 18 or older, for instance, to have sex with individuals aged between 16 and 18, regardless of whether they gave verbal consent.

There is plenty of precedent: In eight U.S. states —   Idaho, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, North Dakota and Florida, where Brand was living before he was jailed — the age of consent varies depending on the age gap between the two people.

In Idaho, for example, if one person is under 16 and the other is 18 or older, or if the victim is 16 or 17 years old and the perpetrator is at least three years older, it is classed as rape. "Lewd contact with a child" younger than 16 is a crime regardless of the perpetrator's age.
In most U.S. states, the age of consent has a "close-in-age" exception for people under 18 who engage in mutually consentual sexual acts.

In Canada, where the age of consent is 16, the staggered-age system includes more detailed, age-dependent exemptions. For people aged 12-13, the partner must be less than two years older; age 14-15, the partner must be less than five years older, and between 16-17, people are generally seen as able to give consent, unless their sexual partner is in a position of trust or authority toward them.
Austria, Belgium, France, Ireland and South Africa also have close-in-age exemptions.
Mia Latter, now 37, has accused Brand of raping her when she was 16 and he was 30, and she is now campaigning for a staggered age of consent to be introduced in Britain.

Latter, whose allegations were not part of the case that saw Brand convicted last week of raping and sexually assaulting other women, abandoned her anonymity as an accuser of the celebrity in an interview published over the weekend by The Sunday Times. She told the newspaper she was speaking out to help "protect teenagers from being groomed by older men or women."

"I don't want to criminalize teenagers having sex with each other," she said. "If you're between the ages of 16 and 18, it seems reasonable that you can have relationships with each other, and [teenagers] are always going to. But … if you're in your thirties, forties and fifties and you're trying to have a relationship with someone under the age of 18, it [should be] a criminal offense."
Brand protested his innocence from jail on Sunday in a statement read out by his wife Laura.

The prime minister's office said Monday that the comments were under investigation, as "prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances."

title: Drawing China close, is Kim Jong Un bracing to confront the U.S.?
summary: As North Korea and China draw closer together, is Kim Jong Un ramping up for a confrontation with the U.S.?
story: Dandong, China — With a pair of binoculars and a camera hanging around his neck, retired Chinese government official Mr. Yang leaned against a fence on a boardwalk that meanders through the city of Dandong, peering across the wide Yalu River that separates China from North Korea.

He came to visit from Dalian, about 200 miles away, despite the temperature hovering just above freezing, to catch a glimpse of life inside China's heavily sanctioned, nuclear armed neighbor nation. But the main attraction he came to see is the massive new bridge towering over Dandong, which now links the two countries.
"The bridge is good, but it's only for trucks and cars, not for the trains," he complained. "But this is good for trade, and I do hope this means relations improve with North Korea."

At almost two miles long and four lanes across, the new Yalu River Bridge is a feat of engineering. The Chinese side was finished 12 years ago, but North Korea only recently completed its section, with leader Kim Jong Un making a surprise appearance for the official opening on Oct. 24.

As CBS News visited the new river crossing, a large group of tourists arrived from Fujian province, more than 1,000 miles to the south, to pose for photos in front of the impressive piece of infrastructure.

"This will enhance the friendship between China and North Korea for sure, but we hope that North Korea will open up to the West," tour group leader Mr. Sun told CBS News. "North Korea was an isolated country, and this shows they're trying to join the world."
That may be a message China's government is keen to encourage, but the recent actions and rhetoric from the Kim regime in Pyongyang suggests otherwise.
Kim Jong Un ramping up for a confrontation?
Since the beginning of October alone, North Korea has test-fired more than a dozen missiles — the most concentrated series of such launches by Pyongyang since 2023.
Kim has personally observed some of the launches, accompanied by his teenage daughter Kim Ju Ae, widely viewed as his potential successor.

Former U.S. State Department official Robert Carlin, who has half of a century of experience as a North Korea analyst, believes Kim could be preparing to take steps that will inevitably end in confrontation with the U.S.

"It's part of a pattern of preparations to get ready for what he (Kim) thinks he wants to do. So he's testing new systems, and there's been a flurry of them. They can test in private — they do it all the time —   so they want to make these visible for some reason," Carlin told CBS News. "When you put that together with the pretty aggressive probing along the demarcation line, the high-level statements with warnings and threats … we have to take seriously the possibility that KJU [Kim] is preparing something, putting himself into position for the moment he thinks the winds are at his back, the situation is ripe for him to make some sort of move against U.S. assets in the region and against South Korea."

President Trump has been pushing for a new meeting with Kim for months, citing what he considers his good personal rapport with the North Korean leader, and there has been speculation the two leaders could meet while Mr. Trump is in China this week to attend the APEC summit.

He fueled that speculation himself Monday as he departed for Asia, saying it would be up to the Chinese hosts of the summit, but telling reporters when asked about a possible meeting: "Yes, we might have Kim Jong Un."

Mr. Trump met three times with Kim during his first term, including two historic summits aimed at getting the North Korean leader to agree to steps toward his nuclear-armed country denuclearizing, but the discussions went nowhere.

Since then, Kim has only expanded his nuclear arsenal. South Korean intelligence agencies believe Pyongyang could now have as many as 120 nuclear warheads. Kim has made it clear, meanwhile, that he will only agree to a new round of negotiations if the U.S. first and formally recognizes North Korea as a nuclear state.
Burgeoning ties with Russia and China

While longstanding international sanctions against his country over its nuclear weapons program remain in place, since the failed talks with Mr. Trump, Kim has projected a sense of being emboldened — of no longer leading a nation ubiquitously dismissed as an international pariah.
The relationship with China, while at times strained, has been a constant, and it has helped Kim push the image of North Korea as a global player, rather than a "hermit kingdom."

Since Vladimir Putin ordered the ongoing, full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four years ago, Pyongyang has also proven a dependable ally to Russia. North Korea has sent a constant stream of munitions to replenish Moscow's depleted stocks, as well as thousands of soldiers to fight on the front lines. In return, Moscow has sent financial and technological assistance, helping North Korea further develop its nuclear weapons program.

The city of Dandong is a symbol of the China-North Korea bond. Hundreds of thousands of Chinese troops marched across the original Yalu River bridge to fight alongside North Korean soldiers in the Korean War. Almost 3 million Chinese soldiers were deployed to fight in that conflict between 1950 and 1953.

The city was bombed by U.S. forces due to its strategic position on the vital North Korean supply line, and the old Yalu River Bridge was destroyed. Renamed "Broken Bridge," it became a war relic and tourist attraction in its own right.

In the center of Dandong, overlooking the old Broken Bridge and the nearby Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, a smaller piece of infrastructure that facilitates cross-border rail and one-lane road traffic with the North Korean city of Sinuiju, local businesses sell Korean outfits along with trinkets and souvenirs, cashing in on Chinese fascination with the neighbors.

Grocery stores sell liquor in bottles that look like grenades, mortars and bullets, while hotels positioned along the river, facing North Korea, offer telescopes and binoculars in bedrooms for guests to peer across the Yalu into apartments and farmland on the far side. On some sections of the river, North Korea is only about 1,000 feet away.

Using our own long lens, CBS News was able to see people in North Korean apartments at night. At first light, the North Korean side became a hive of activity as people headed out to the fields and greenhouses to work.
George, a 16-year-old student, said he was visiting Dandong because of his passion for Chinese and North Korean history.

"North Korea is trying to get better connections with China, and China is opening to Western countries more and more, and if those things continue to happen, maybe North Korea will be opening to Western countries the same as China," he said.
As for the increasing tension on the Korean Peninsula, George dismissed the concerns.
Kim Jong Un, he said, is just "trying to tell the Western countries and the whole world that the DPRK is powerful enough to join the global stage right now."

While in Dandong, CBS News visited a restaurant and met a North Korean waitress who said she had been living in China for a year — one of as many as 80,000 North Koreans living and working in the city, all of whom are strictly monitored and not permitted to assimilate with the local Chinese population.
She told CBS News she missed home and hopes to return one day to North Korea, and she praised Kim Jong Un as a father to her country.

title: Women in U.K. are getting automatic pardons for past abortion convictions
summary: Women who have received a caution from police will also be pardoned, and women arrested or investigated for ending their own pregnancy will have those details removed from their criminal records.
story: Women in the United Kingdom who were convicted of illegally terminating their pregnancies under a Victorian-era law will receive automatic pardons on Monday, the government said.
This follows the passage of a landmark vote by Parliament last year to decriminalize abortion by repealing a section of the 1861 Offences Against the Person Act.

Women who have received a caution from police will also be pardoned, and women arrested or investigated for ending their own pregnancy will have those details removed from their criminal records. They will not have to apply for pardons, and some will be issued posthumously.

The government did not provide the number of women affected. But Tonia Antoniazzi, the Labour member of Parliament who introduced the decriminalization amendment, said police have investigated more than 100 women suspected of illegal abortions in the five years preceding last year's vote. That included some who suffered natural miscarriages and stillbirths.
Antoniazzi described how women suspected of illegally aborting a fetus were once "dragged from hospital beds to police cells" and interrogated when they should have been cared for.

"This trauma cannot be erased, but I hope that this offers some alleviation of the pain these women have endured, enabling them to participate fully in society again, living their lives to the full, working the jobs they've always wanted to," she said.

Under current law, doctors can legally carry out abortions in England, Scotland and Wales up to 24 weeks, and beyond that under special circumstances, such as when the life of the mother is in danger. Abortion in Northern Ireland was decriminalized in 2019.
Under the Crime and Policing Act that took effect this spring, women who terminate a pregnancy at any stage will not face criminal charges.
The measure was opposed by anti-abortion groups that argued it would open the door to abortion on demand at any stage of pregnancy.

"While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognizes the profound harm caused by their criminalization and represents a meaningful step towards justice," said Heidi Stewart, with the British Pregnancy Advisory Service, according to CBS News partner BBC News.
The law was changed after high-profile prosecutions, including the jailing of a mother of three that caused an outcry from abortion rights supporters.

Carla Foster was sentenced to more than two years in prison in 2023 for medically inducing an abortion about eight months into her pregnancy. An appeals court freed her a month later, saying the case called for "compassion, not punishment."

Another woman, Nicola Packer, was acquitted on a charge of unlawfully self-administering poison or a noxious thing with intent to procure a miscarriage. Packer, who took abortion medicine when she was about 26 weeks pregnant, testified that she did not know she had been pregnant for more than 10 weeks, which was the legal limit.
Her friend Helle Tumbridge, with Packer's consent, told BBC News that the whole incident has been "incredibly traumatic."
She said it took five years of investigations before a trial eventually found Packer not guilty.
"Of course, by that point the damage had been done," Tumbridge said, "and she'll live with that trauma for the rest of her life."

title: Drug lord who orchestrated murder of U.S. agent dies at 80
summary: Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, the architect of modern Mexican drug trafficking, was known as "the boss of bosses."
story: Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, the architect of modern Mexican drug trafficking known as "the boss of bosses," who transformed the global cocaine trade and orchestrated the murder of a U.S. agent, died Sunday at age 80, officials said.

The notorious drug kingpin, a former police officer who played a key role in forging alliances with Colombian traffickers, died in a hospital where he had been transferred from prison two days earlier.

"After remaining under observation with a guarded prognosis, he died on November 15 at the medical facility" after "he suffered multiple organ failure," according to a statement from the security ministry of the state of Jalisco, where he was being held.
Felix Gallardo's health had deteriorated markedly in recent years, with conditions including high blood pressure, diabetes and deafness.

In 2022, then-president Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador said he was "in very poor health." A judge granted him house arrest, but technical problems with electronic ankle monitoring prevented his transfer.
One of the founders of the Guadalajara cartel, from which the Sinaloa cartel would later emerge, Felix Gallardo had been incarcerated since 1989 and was serving a 40-year sentence.

He was convicted for the 1985 murder of an undercover U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency officer, Enrique "Kiki" Camarena Salazar, which outraged the United States. Last year, Camarena's alleged killer,  Rafael Caro Quintero, was transferred to the U.S. along with 28 other prisoners requested by the U.S. government.

Camarena, a father of three sons, was living in Guadalajara, Mexico, with his family working as an undercover DEA agent, his son told CBS News in a 2017 interview. He had been stationed there for four years on the trail of the country's biggest marijuana and cocaine traffickers.
A memorial was created in Camarena's honor in Los Angeles in 2014.
His son Enrique, who became a judge in 2014 in San Diego, told CBS News he carries his father's lessons into the courtroom. "He taught us to treat everyone fairly."
Rise of the cartels
Felix Gallardo was a native of Sinaloa state, where he was born on Jan. 8, 1946, according to public records.
His involvement in crime went virtually hand in hand with his career in the state and federal police.
He even served as a bodyguard to a Sinaloa governor, a role that experts say may have helped him secure the complicity and protection of powerful politicians.
He partnered with another veteran kingpin, Rafael Caro Quintero. Together with other crime bosses, they united gangs trafficking drugs to the United States and formed the Guadalajara cartel.
The cartel was formed around a "hegemonic model" and laid "the roots for nearly all of today's drug trafficking activities," according to InSight Crime, a website specializing in the drug trade.
Felix Gallardo "partnered with Colombian traffickers like Pablo Escobar, and became Escobar's most important Mexico associate," the publication said.
The Guadalajara gang controlled the country's underworld, earning Felix Gallardo the nicknames "El jefe de jefes" and "El Padrino" -- which translate to "the boss of bosses" and "the Godfather."
Downfall
Felix Gallardo was convicted for the February 1985 murder of Camarena Salazar, who was kidnapped and tortured.
The agent's death remains an open wound for the United States.
Intense pressure from Washington led to the arrest in 1985 of Caro Quintero, who is now imprisoned in the United States on charges of drug trafficking and the agent's murder.
Felix Gallardo was arrested in April 1989 but continued to control the criminal business from prison, according to experts.
He was serving his sentence at Puente Grande prison in Jalisco state.

The Guadalajara cartel imploded in the 1990s, and its local leaders formed regional cartels, including the Sinaloa cartel, built up by Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman and Ismael "El Mayo" Zambada, both sentenced to life in prison in the United States.

Felix Gallardo remained in the popular imagination through narcocorridos, or drug ballads, such as "El jefe de jefes," which is banned in public spaces, and Netflix dramas about drug trafficking, with Mexican actor Diego Luna portraying the kingpin.

title: Basketball player allegedly had 75 pounds of drugs in luggage
summary: Nigeria's anti-narcotics agency said it had arrested an American professional basketball player with 33.95 kilograms of cannabis in his luggage on arrival at the main airport.
story: Nigeria's anti-narcotics agency on Sunday said it had arrested an American professional basketball player with 33.95 kilograms (about 75 pounds) of cannabis in his luggage on arrival at the main airport.
The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) named the player as 28-year-old Greene Da'monte Khiree, a native of Savannah, Georgia.

He was arrested on Wednesday at the main international airport car park in Lagos after he "was observed abandoning his two checked-in bags before attempting to exit the airport with only his carry-on luggage," NDLEA said in a statement.

The bags bearing his name tags were filled with 16 packs of Loud, described as a "potent strain of cannabis," said NDLEA, which posted several images of the player with suitcases full of the purported drugs.
He had arrived in Lagos from Thailand, where he said he had lived and played professional basketball since October 2025, the agency said.

The agency said he claimed he was visiting Nigeria to "build networks for his basketball career" but examination of his mobile phone showed information suggesting his "knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity."
FIBA lists a player by the name DaMonte Greene, a point guard, one of whose recent appearances was at the Phuket Elite Cup in September.
Greene was the leading scorer for the semiprofessional Georgia Bombers during the 2023-24 season, averaging 26.3 points per game, according to the Basketball Job Market.
Nigeria has been considered a trafficking and production hub for drugs bound for other countries, but researchers say the contraband spills into local markets.
Recent busts of industrial-scale meth production labs have left authorities worrying that Mexican cartels are establishing links in Nigeria to produce and ship meth out of the country.
In a separate incident announced on Sunday, Nigerian officials said a man was arrested at the airport after more than 25 kilograms of meth were found concealed in packs of assorted breakfast cereals.

In September, the agency said it had dismantled a meth lab and arrested a Mexican suspected drug kingpin who was allegedly attempting to flee Nigeria through Lagos, the BBC reported. In August, a social media influencer suspected of links to an international drug trafficking network was arrested after authorities seized cocaine worth nearly $28 million, which was allegedly destined for the U.K.

title: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left company in 2025, denies wrongdoing
summary: The company denies wrongdoing after accusations that it smuggled Nvidia's AI chips into China.
story: The Singapore-based company at the center of the scandal that brought down Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said Sunday that suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang left the company in 2025. It also denied any wrongdoing, saying it "conducts legitimate and lawful business."

In a statement to CBS News, Megaspeed International said Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, left the company in August 2025 and has no current role. It did not comment on the allegations that Alice Huang is a suspected Chinese spy.
"Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters," the company's statement said.

Alice Huang was an executive at Megaspeed and is the woman with whom Jensen Huang was having an affair. She is suspected by U.S. intelligence of being an asset of China's Ministry of State Security, which China denies. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO last week.
U.S. investigators say Alice Huang used industry contacts and a series of shell companies to access 240,000 chips banned for export into China.
In the past three years, Megaspeed has been one of Nvidia's biggest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5 billion in AI chips and advanced hardware, The New York Times first reported.

Now the company, which began as an offshoot of a China-based gaming firm and grew into a juggernaut by gaining access to the Nvidia chips, is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling Nvidia's restricted AI computer chips into China.
In a statement to CBS News on Sunday, the company said that recent assertions about its business, supply chain and global operations are "not supported by verifiable evidence."

"Megaspeed designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate," it said.
It added: "The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation."
President Trump said last week the FBI was investigating the romantic and business ties between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, who are not related.

CBS News reported on Friday that Singaporean authorities seized Alice Huang's passport in June 2025 while trying to engage the U.S. government to support their investigation into the suspected smuggling of Nvidia chips to China, according to a source with knowledge of the matter.
The source added that the Singaporean government received no meaningful help from Washington at the time.

title: Transcript: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 15, 2026
summary: The following is the transcript of the interview with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 15, 2026.
story: The following is the transcript of the interview with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 15, 2026.

MARGARET BRENNAN: For more, we go now to the Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy. Good morning to you, Mr. Secretary. Will the country be back to fully operational with a full flight schedule by the end of today?

SEC. SEAN DUFFY: So we have some delays in the airspace right now, but as we look to the end of the day and into tomorrow, we should be running at full capacity. What happens with a ground stop, like on Friday, we have airplanes and crews that are out of position, so it takes a little bit of time for the airlines to get back and choreographed and at full capacity and operations, but we're well on our way.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So I know that there was a router in El Dorado, Arkansas, as I understand it, that became an issue on Friday. You said on another network this morning there was a second issue at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. Are those two things related? And if so, why did they both become problems on Friday?

SEC. DUFFY: Yeah, so the- the Amarillo facility- that work had been done weeks ago, and so why- when we did the install in El Dorado, did that start to broadcast data into our network? But then also the- the facility in Amarillo- why did that happen? We're investigating that right now. We actually have both routers with L3Harris, who operates and owns our network. FAA is on site as well. FBI is offering support. We're looking at that right now, and when we know what the root cause of this issue was- was it- was it the install from L3Harris? Was it the router? I'm going to tell you and the American people what we find.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, was the issue old infrastructure or was it new equipment?

SEC. DUFFY: So first off, the- the- the telecom in El Dorado, it was an old copper wire that basically was- it was going to be decommissioned. They said it can't be used anymore. So we were forced by the telecom provider to actually update that copper to fiber, and we brought in our routers and did the work, and that's when we saw the- the flooding of the network. So this was- this is part of our maintenance that we do on this really old architecture of a telecom network that was- I mean, this goes back decades. By the way, the rest of the world, every institution, every company, not just in the U.S. but around the world, they've all switched over to digital and fiber. It's just the FAA is still using this really old telecom network that has to be updated, upgraded, and I think built brand new.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So the union that represents aviation safety specialists, PASS, as they're called, said the issue was isolated to two contractor-owned and maintained routers that were being updated in the middle of the day, and they said their technicians were not involved in the upgrades. So I wonder, did the FAA do a risk assessment in advance and know that something like this was- happened, or were you totally caught off guard?

SEC. DUFFY: So let's be clear, the union that works at the FAA, they'll do the work on the radios- our equipment, or the radar- our equipment. They do all of the work on FAA-owned equipment. This union doesn't do any work on telecom, and it's our telecom contractor and providers like L3Harris in this situation. They're the ones that actually do the work. So the FAA lets L3Harris into our- into our sites, and then L3Harris will do the telecom work. But our- this union only works on our equipment. This telecom is not our- is- that's not our equipment. It's L3Harris's network. So just to clarify that, this- this was done appropriately, which by the way, it's been done thousands of times by us, by others, and other companies. This has never happened, and so that's why when you have a remote location like this, we felt comfortable doing it in the middle of the day because it's been done thousands of times. We've never had this situation. We're going to have to reevaluate now when we do this work. Now, normally, if you have a big facility, a Newark or an Atlanta or an LA, we have work to do, we do that at night, but in a remote location, we can do it during the day because the risk historically has been very low. Obviously, on Friday we saw no, it flooded our network, and we had to take the extraordinary step of issuing a ground stop.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So there was not a risk assessment, or there was a risk assessment, and this was just not foreseen as an issue?

SEC. DUFFY: Oh no, no- listen, we do risk assessments on everything, right? And if you want to talk about a risk assessment, the GAO has done a risk assessment on my network, on all of the old equipment, and they'll say, "Hey, this is- this is risky America. Make the investments and fix American air traffic control systems." And by the way, the Congress gave me $12.5 billion dollars.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

SEC. DUFFY: I've- I've got ordered new radar, new radios, new voice switches. We're doing all of that, but it's also risky to say we're operating on a 1980s network with copper wires. So we've done a risk assessment- assessment: How do you switch over from copper to fiber? We keep airplanes safe in the sky. That's our number one priority. We've done that, and which is why it's worked thousands of times when we've made the switch over.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, when--
SEC. DUFFY: --this time it- it didn't- and the- go ahead.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah. So you just mentioned the- the Government Accountability Office. They also, in a September report, concluded that there is a push to modernize quickly, and that the FAA is buying delivery speed at the risk of cost uncertainty and potential disruptions. So, should you have seen this coming?
SEC. DUFFY: Well, first off, with regard to the GAO, my number one priority is safety, which is why we shut down the airspace on Friday, right? We did the closure--
MARGARET BRENNAN: They're saying speed.

SEC. DUFFY: No, I'm going to get to that. But I want to make sure that- that Americans get from point A to point B safely. They get back to their loved ones. I want them to be on time, but I want them to be safe, which is why we issued the ground stop. In regard to speed, we are going I think at the- at the right speed, we- we have to get off old network, old telecom. By the way, that's why I've already switched over 70 percent of copper to fiber without incident, without issue. Almost 470 radios have been switched over. New- new- new electronic flight strips and towers. We're doing incredible work, and just- let's be clear about one thing.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEC. DUFFY: For decades, this work in the FAA has not been done. It hasn't been done because it's hard. I don't want to be dishonest. It's a hard problem to solve. The Trump administration, with my leadership, we are solving the problem. We're building and deploying new technology. One of the problems I have is I need more money to- to build a new--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
SEC. DUFFY: --telecom network. I need new software, but we're doing the right thing by- by way of the American people by fixing this really really old system that was left to us.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But respectfully, the American people have put a lot of money into infrastructure upgrades. In 2021, it was $25 billion for upgrades under Biden. Under your administration, the Trump administration, as you just said, $12.5 billion for upgrades. Democrats say the lion's share of the money that was provided to you- you just have not obligated or spent. Why? And if the White House has allowed for reprogramming of funds, why do you keep saying Congress is stopping you from spending the money they're giving you?

SEC. DUFFY: So first off, there was a lot of money that was given to the FAA in the past, and I can't answer for other secretaries or other FAA administrators. A lot of money was given, not a lot of work was done. So when I asked for a massive amount of money to fix the system, what the Congress did is they said, "Okay, we'll give you a partial funding, $12.5 billion dollars," in One, Big Beautiful Bill. And they were very specific in how we spend it. Now I can't- I can't go buy radar off the shelf. This is a massive order. So we've asked those who won the contract, I want them to build the radar in America. They'll start to deliver those radar to us in the spring. All of them will be deployed by the end of 2028. So all that money hasn't been spent, but it's been obligated to radar. Radio is the same thing. I'm buying radios, but they're not on the shelf. They have to be built. They specifically said how I spend the money, and I've- and I've got it all spent, ready to be deployed by the end of the- the president's tenure in office. But what I don't have money for is a new telecom system. I don't have money for new software. Those- those are critical pieces to the infrastructure, and it's been historically underinvested in. I'm making the case to the American people and the Congress. For the first time, the FAA is taking your money, and we're actually building with your money. Let me continue. Let's finish the job. Let's not see what happened on Friday. Let's not let it happen again
MARGARET BRENNAN: Is $50 billion the total ask?--
SEC. DUFFY: Let's make sure we keep the American people safe- yeah, $50 billion.
MARGARET BRENNAN: All right, Mr. Secretary. I'm told you have to get to another network. Thank you for your time this morning. 'Face the Nation' will be back in one minute. Stay with us.

title: U.S. reportedly floated trading Ukrainian land for NATO membership
summary: The Ukrainian president said he would put the question of a potential exchange to the people if certain guarantees were in place.
story: U.S. negotiators asked Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to consider giving up a part of his country in exchange for NATO membership, the leader claimed.
Zelenskyy told journalists on Friday he had been asked for the first time whether he would withdraw from the eastern region of Donbas in exchange for membership in the military alliance.
"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," the Ukrainian president said.

Zelenskyy said he was discussing a "security package" for Ukraine which included security guarantees from NATO and the European Union, an "adequate number of troops, weapons" as well as financial support. The Ukrainian president said if these measures are offered, he would ask Ukrainians whether to accept the potential exchange.
He did not specify if he meant a referendum, but added, "I have no right to make that decision on my own."
Control over the Donbas region, much of which has been occupied by Russia since the start of the war, has been a recurring sticking point in negotiations to end the conflict.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has previously demanded that Ukraine pull its forces out of the Donbas region as a precondition for a peace agreement.

After staging elections dismissed by most of the world as a sham in occupied parts of the Donbas region, Putin declared in September 2022 that four regions of eastern Ukraine had also been annexed by Russia. None of the annexations have been recognized by the U.S. or the United Nations, and most countries consider them illegal land grabs.

Zelenskyy said he told U.S. negotiators Ukraine would need security guarantees modeled on NATO's Article 5 "as an absolute minimum." That article sets out a key principle for the military alliance, whereby an attack on one of the member states is considered an attack on all other members.
The Ukrainian president added he was "not sure it would necessarily work," and said he needed more specific details on the potential membership.

Russell Brand's recent message from behind prison bars is being "urgently investigated" by authorities as the "appalling" move proves to have "broken the rules."

On Sunday, Brand — who was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison for rape and sexual assault — claimed he is "not guilty" in a message read by his wife, Laura Brand, during an episode of the couple's weekly Sunday Service YouTube vlog.

In the message, Brand claimed his innocence while confirming he is currently being jailed at Littlehey Prison, a prison for individuals who have been convicted of sexual offenses.

"Beloved brothers and sisters in Christ, God bless you for your support. As you know, I am not guilty for the offenses I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening," Laura read from a notebook.

"The good news is that Christ is with us when we choose him, and I do. I am incarcerated in HMP Littlehey. Little as in small, and hey as in, ‘Hey, I’m in the biggest sex offenders’ prison in Europe. story: Speaking at the 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony, the music icon opens up about living on his own, spending "a lot of time in hospital," and working three times a week to stay mobile.
English singer and drummer Phil Collins relies on a full-time nurse during his "enforced" time off from touring.
During an interview with Fox News Digital at the 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Induction ceremony, Collins said that adjusting to not performing has been easy.

"Adjusting is easy. I spent a lot of time in hospital with various things, so that was enforced, you know, time off. But I just sit at home, I live on my own, I got a nurse there all the time to make sure I take medication on time, and I've got my assistant who is always there," Collins began.

"I got a nurse there all the time to make sure I take medication on time, and I've got my assistant who is always there."

title: Robert Pattinson’s James Bond casting could bring 'darker,' 'moodier' twist as fans crave classic 007: expert
summary: Robert Pattinson calls his James Bond casting "the honor of a lifetime," but critics say his brooding Batman past makes him a risky pick for 007.
story: Former Bond girl Alison Papworth shares why she wants the next 007 to stay true to the books as speculation swirls over the role.
James Bond may never miss, but Robert Pattinson's casting as the next iconic British secret agent was positively shocking to fans across the world.

Pattinson, 40, called the role "the honor of a lifetime," in a statement released Monday where "Dune" director Denis Villeneuve was also tapped to bring Bond back to the big screen following Daniel Craig's 15-year reign as 007.
Fox News contributor Raymond Arroyo admitted he was "shaken, not stirred" by the casting choice.
ROBERT PATTINSON NAMED NEXT JAMES BOND
Actor Robert Pattinson at the screening of the film "Primetime" at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival in Italy, on Sept. 5. (Laurent KOFFEL/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images)

"As a huge fan of the Ian Fleming novels, Pattinson isn’t quite what I envisioned or what I think fans were hoping for," Arroyo told Fox News Digital. "After five Bond films with Daniel Craig in the lead, it was probably time to bring back some of the fun and charm that Pierce Brosnan and Roger Moore brought to the franchise."
He noted how Pattinson was known for his "brooding and dark qualities," a contrast to the more masculine qualities a Bond character usually brings to the screen.
FORMER BOND GIRL SAYS NEXT 007 SHOULD BE 'ANOTHER GORGEOUS MAN' AS JAMES BOND DECISION
"As a huge fan of the Ian Fleming novels, Pattinson isn’t quite what I envisioned or what I think fans were hoping for."

"Fun and a light touch is not the first thing that comes to mind when you think of his filmography," Arroyo said. "His Batman was a pretty dreary affair, the sequel of which I could care less about seeing. Bond also requires a certain physicality and strength – he is an assassin after all."
Arroyo believed Henry Cavill "would have been a much better choice all round."
Sean Connery starred as James Bond 007 in the '64 film "Goldfinger." (Screen Archives/Getty Images)

"But it sounds like MGM/Amazon wants to give audiences a darker, moodier Bond – just when the public is craving a good, old-fashioned escape. We’ll see if audiences wish this new Bond to ‘Live or Let Die.’"
Amazon MGM Studios announced Pattinson’s casting on social media with a brief snippet of the actor emerging from the shadows with a gun.
PIERCE BROSNAN BACKS 'FANTASTIC BEASTS' STAR FOR NEXT JAMES BOND, PREDICTS FANS WILL BE 'BLOWN AWAY'

"Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey. We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007," Villeneuve said in a statement.
"I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin."
Daniel Craig starred as the British secret agent from 2006–21. (Greg Williams/Eon Productions via Getty Images)
Adrienne Uthe, founder of Kronus Communications, exclusively told Fox News Digital that Pattinson was a "risk" to the franchise.

"He's going in as the underdog, period," Uthe said. "To win over the Connery people, the Brosnan people, the Craig people, he can’t just be good — he has to do it better than what’s been done before. That’s the bar when you take a role this iconic, you have to prove you’re actually worth it."
Pattinson found global fame years ago as telepathic vampire Edward Cullen in the "Twilight" series, which collectively grossed more than $3.3 billion worldwide.

"He can’t just be good – He has to do it better than what’s been done before. That’s the bar when you take a role this iconic, you have to prove you’re actually worth it."
Uthe noted that while a younger audience already knows his face and therein may show up to watch him as Bond, there's still a risk of "watering down the brand."
Pierce Brosnan stars as 007 opposite Denise Richards as Dr. Christmas Jones in the '99 James Bond film "The World Is Not Enough." (Keith Hamshere/Getty Images)
"Bond is established, seasoned, it’s got pedigree — so he has to bring pedigree to it too," Uthe said. "He has to prove he can be taken seriously in a role like Bond."

She added, "Now, underdogs can win. People forget Daniel Craig got torn apart when he was cast — too blonde, too rough, wrong guy — and then 'Casino Royale' came out and that was the end of that conversation. So it’s doable. But he has to earn it on screen, nobody’s handing it to him."

Seven actors have starred as the legendary British spy over the years, a role which first originated on television with Barry Nelson before Sean Connery was tapped to play the secret service agent in the '62 film "Dr. No."

Brand expert Eric Schiffer explained that the franchise may face a fan exodus with a "painfully boring" 007, a contrast to the previous Bonds played by David Niven, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton and Pierce Brosnan.
English actor Roger Moore poses for a portrait in London, England, on July 20, 1979. Moore portrayed James Bond in the Bond series. (Getty Images)
"Pattinson as Bond is a slap in the face to James, to 007's character, and largely because of his prior history and the Bond character himself," Schiffer told Fox News Digital.
"He failed as Batman. It was a horror show, and prior to that he was the 'Twilight' guy with too much makeup. We're now James Bond? Well, what happened?"

title: Russell Brand’s wife opens up after comedian’s rape conviction, shares message from imprisoned husband
summary: Laura Brand appeared alone on the couple's weekly Sunday Service YouTube vlog, sharing a message Russell Brand asked her to read from prison.
story: Fox News senior foreign affairs correspondent Greg Palkot reports on Russell Brand's sentencing following his convictions for rape and sexual assault in London.
Russell Brand's wife, Laura Brand, broke her silence Sunday, nearly one week after the actor was convicted of rape and sexual assault and sentenced to more than 10 years in prison.
Laura, 39, appeared alone to present the couple's weekly Sunday Service YouTube vlog, which she admitted would look "a little different this week" after his conviction.
"I’m here without Russell, but we’ve decided to keep going," Laura shared of the sermon which was partially recorded during the trial.
BEAR GRYLLS ADDRESSES RUSSELL BRAND'S BAPTISM, CALLS VICTIMS 'HEROES OF THE DAY' AFTER VERDICT
Russell Brand was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison last week after being convicted of rape. (James Manning)

"I open with a reading from Philippians, then share an episode we recorded together during the trial that we’d been holding back. We talk about why some of the coverage sounds like a football match and what it’s like to pray when something has taken over your whole week. I read some of your comments, share a little Brother Lawrence and close with a message Russell asked me to read. Thank you for being here with me."
RUSSELL BRAND FOUND GUILTY OF ONE COUNT OF RAPE AND THREE COUNTS OF SEXUAL ASSAULT
While sitting in front of a window, Laura began the weekly series with the intention to "continue the good work that was being established here in this Sunday service community."
"It may look different, but the ambitions are very much the same, and we trust God, and we trust his plan, and we trust everything he's doing right now," she said.
Russell Brand was found guilty last week of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault following a four-week criminal trial. (Elizabeth Cook/PA Wire via Zuma Press)
Laura Brand appeared in court to support her husband. (Getty Images)

"Even though it's painful and obviously will take some getting used to for me to even sit here and not have my companion and my person with me ... I want to continue, and I'm grateful for the support, and I'm grateful for you, and thank you for your messages."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Laura noted that while Russell was not with her at the moment, she said that "the Holy Spirit is moving, and the Holy Spirit cannot be restrained."

"I'm speaking to Russell. He's OK, and he's praying," Laura said. "Unsurprisingly, he's praying, and we decided for me to continue. He asked if I would read the rest of the Philippians passage, which I will continue to do now, from his Bible."

She then said she had a note from Russell, and read it out loud: "Beloved brothers and sisters in Christ, God bless you for your support. As you know, I am not guilty for the offenses I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening."

Laura continued: "The good news is that Christ is with us when we choose him, and I do. I am incarcerated in HMP Littlehey. Little as in small, and hey as in, ‘Hey, I’m in the biggest sex offenders’ prison in Europe. The good news is that I have already seen that the staff here are strong, they are kind, and they are dedicated. And as for my fellow prisoners, I now know that I am in no position to judge anyone."

"I don’t know which other men here are not guilty, and the ones that are, they are people that Christ died to save, like you and me. Let us all love, pray for, and forgive one another as God forgave us."
"Please support my treasured wife and family. I feel your prayers, your brother in Christ. Russell," she concluded the note.
On Nov. 5, a London jury found Brand, 51, guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault involving four women, stemming from incidents between 2004-09.

He denied the charges and was acquitted of two additional rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault.
Brand was immediately taken into custody following the verdict, according to the BBC. Upon release, the comedian will also be required to register as a sex offender for life.

During sentencing on Monday, Mr. Justice Joel Bennathan said Brand had demonstrated a "casual and arrogant disregard" for women’s right to refuse his sexual advances.

"About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous," Bennathan said. "You were clever — and in many people’s eyes, funny and charismatic. You had also become a sexual predator."

The judge described one of Brand’s sexual assaults as "outrageous and possibly laddish, but also a criminal offense," adding that Brand’s behavior reflected his belief that "fame meant you could act how you liked, when you liked, unhindered by the rules by which decent people live."

title: Ashley Judd claims mom Naomi threatened to pull tuition over what she was learning and her lesbian professor
summary: Ashley Judd reveals Naomi Judd threatened to stop paying her tuition over a lesbian theologian professor on her new podcast "A Table Prepared."
story: Wynonna Judd told Fox News Digital, her and her mom Naomi Judd's shared love of music helped them "bypass the bullcrap" and build a close relationship.
Ashley Judd is opening up about a past rift with her late mother, Naomi Judd, sparked by a lesbian college professor.

On the debut episode of her new podcast, "A Table Prepared," Ashley sat down with her co-host, former Christ Church Nashville Pastor Dan Scott. During their conversation, Ashley claimed that Naomi "threatened to stop paying my tuition at the University of Kentucky" over what she was learning, and also the professor's sexual orientation.

"She didn’t like what I was learning," Ashley said. "She didn’t like [that] I had a lesbian theologian professor that was taking me through Hebrew scripture and looking at the women listed as property after the donkeys."
Ashley Judd spoke about her late mother Naomi Judd in her debut episode of her new podcast, "A Table Prepared." (Getty Images)

Ashley explained that her mother, who died by suicide in 2022, felt pressured to align politically with the country music industry out of fear of "disapproval and retaliation." Behind closed doors, however, Naomi was much more open about expressing her personal and political beliefs "in the home."
WYNONNA JUDD WISHES BOND WITH MOM WAS LIKE THEIR MUSIC, BUT 'THERE WAS A LOT OF DYSFUNCTION'
"She could share all kinds of political and social views that would surprise people if they thought Naomi Judd thought, felt, said that," Ashley said.
"She didn’t like [that] I had a lesbian theologian professor that was taking me through Hebrew scripture and looking at the women listed as property after the donkeys."
As an example of the issues that moved her mother, Ashley noted that Naomi felt "a lot of compassion" for women making headlines for harming their children.
Ashley Judd, Naomi Judd and Wynonna Judd. (Ke.Mazur/WireImage)

title: Beauty queen stripped of Miss USA crown over hidden husband, kids gets unexpected spotlight decades later
summary: Justus Kelley honors Mary Leona Gage, who lost her Miss USA crown in 1957 for being married with children, as she prepares for Miss Universe.
story: Justus Kelley shares how she practiced with her baby in a carrier, squeezed in workouts during nap time and prepared for the stage around motherhood.

Nearly 70 years ago, a beauty queen lost her Miss USA crown after pageant officials learned she was married and had children. In August, Justus Kelley broke that barrier, becoming the first married woman and mother to win the title during the pageant's 75th edition.
Kelley, 31, is a foster mother who founded the nonprofit Foster Footprints to support children and families involved in foster care.
The historic victory came three years after the Miss USA pageant changed its rules to allow married women and mothers to compete.
Kelley is scheduled to compete in the 75th Miss Universe pageant, which is set to take place Nov. 24 in Puerto Rico.
FORMER MISS USA CONTESTANT MADE A LIFE-CHANGING DECISION AT 26 AFTER CANCER DEVASTATED FAMILY

Justus Kelley (left), the first married mom to win Miss USA, is paying tribute to Mary Leona Gage (right), the former Miss USA 1957, who was stripped of her title after it was revealed she was married and had two children. Kelley will be competing in the Miss Universe pageant on Nov. 24, 2026. (Ivan Apfel/Getty Images; Getty Images)
Kelley paid tribute to Gage by wearing a custom black-and-white coat featuring the former beauty queen's image as she traveled to Puerto Rico for the competition.

"Having the opportunity to represent the United States on the Miss Universe stage, I couldn't help but think about Mary Leona Gage and the circumstances under which she represented this organization," Kelley, 31, told People magazine.

"She was a woman who, in many ways, wasn't allowed to be fully herself or embrace all that she was. Her title was ultimately taken away because society wasn't ready to accept who she was as a wife and mother of two."
Justus Kelley and her husband Tyler have been licensed foster parents in the Commonwealth of Virginia for nearly two years. (Ivan Apfel/Getty Images)

On Aug. 27, the Miss USA Organization held the 75th edition of the national pageant in Miami. Kelley, who held the title of Miss Virginia USA 2026, succeeded 2025 winner Audrey Eckert. The pageant began allowing married women and mothers to compete in 2023.
WATCH: MISS USA 2026 REVEALS HOW SHE TRAINED FOR PAGEANT WITH KIDS IN TOW
In 1957, Gage represented Maryland in the Miss USA pageant and won the title, according to People.

Shortly after Gage's win, rumors circulated about her marital status and children. Gage initially denied the reports. However, it was later revealed that she had married at 14 and given birth to her first child soon afterward. She had her second child at 16, The Baltimore Sun reported.

Leona Gage, ex-Miss USA, disqualified from the Miss Universe contest because she was married rather than single, returned to California to do a television show for NBC. She later headed to Las Vegas for an engagement at the Tropicana Hotel. Gage spent the day in Hollywood with Debbie Reynolds at the Brown Derby. (Bettmann Archive)
Gage also misrepresented her age, telling pageant officials she was 21 when she was actually 18.

Mrs. Mary Leona Gage Ennis, the young lady who won the title of Miss U.S.A. in the Miss Universe contest and then lost it when it was discovered she was married and the mother of two children, is shown in this photo made in 1956 with her husband, Gene and their sons David, left, and Gene Jr. at the time she was 17 years old. (Getty Images)
Following an official investigation, Gage was disqualified and stripped of her Miss USA crown. Runner-up Charlotte Sheffield, who represented Utah, assumed the crown and received the prizes.
Gage, who lost the crown about 24 hours after her win, said she received hate mail following her disqualification.
Actress Zsa Zsa Gabor and Mary Leona Gage in Los Angeles, circa 1957. (Getty Images)

Gage had already competed in the Miss Universe preliminary round and secured a spot among the 15 semifinalists before she was disqualified. Although Sheffield inherited the Miss USA crown, she could not replace Gage in the international competition because preliminary judging had already concluded.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Leona Gage of Maryland was crowned Miss USA. (Bettmann Archive)

According to The Baltimore Sun, Gage later worked as a performer at the Tropicana Hotel in Las Vegas and reportedly dated Frank Sinatra and former Mr. Universe Mickey Hargitay. She also pursued a film career but never achieved widespread success.
Despite losing her crown, Gage continued watching the Miss USA pageant every year. She died in 2010 at age 71.
Justus Kelley married her high school sweetheart. (Ivan Apfel/Getty Images)
Kelley told People that Gage has been on her mind as she prepares for the Miss Universe competition.

Miss USA 2026 winner Justus Kelley and Miss Florida Aileen Cerchiara stand on stage during the 2026 Miss USA Final Competition and Coronation at Adrienne Arsht Center for the Performing Arts in Miami, Florida., on Aug. 27, 2026. (Ivan Apfel/Getty Images)

"I think about how much has changed since then, and how grateful I am that today's American women have the opportunity to represent their country while embracing every part of who they are," Kelley said.
"I hope this moment serves as a reminder that we stand on the shoulders of women who dared to challenge what was expected of them, so that we could have the freedom to be exactly who we are today."

Justus Kelley walks the runway at the Michael Cinco show during New York Fashion Week Powered by Art Hearts Fashion at The Angel Orensanz Foundation on Sept. 12, 2026, in New York City. (Getty Images for Art Hearts Fashion)

The Miss USA pageant began in 1952 in Long Beach, California, with New York's Jackie Loughery becoming its first winner. The competition is separate from the Miss America pageant, which traces its history to a 1921 event in Atlantic City, New Jersey.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Miss USA was founded in 1952. (Bettmann Archive)
In an earlier interview with Fox News Digital, Kelley expressed a similar message about motherhood and ambition.
She said she hoped to use her reign as Miss USA to challenge the idea that women must choose between their families, careers and personal dreams.

Designer Marina Safina, Miss USA Justus Kelley and models walk the runway at the Marina Safina show during Los Angeles Fashion Week Powered By Art Hearts Fashion at The Majestic Downtown on Oct. 8, 2026. (Getty Images for Art Hearts Fashion)

"You don't have to choose one part of who you are," Kelley said. "You can be all of who you are. That, to me, is the message. We can embrace every part of who we are. It doesn't take away from the other. It doesn't mean there aren't trade-offs, and there aren't times when we have to lean on our village more heavily to get through all the things that we may be pursuing. But know that we don't have to sacrifice ourselves."

Miss Virginia USA 2026 Justus Kelley is crowned Miss USA 2026 onstage during the 2026 Miss USA Final Competition & Coronation at Adrienne Arsht Center for the Performing Arts on Aug. 27, 2026, in Miami, Florida. (Ivan Apfel/Getty Images)
Kelley said her victory gave her an opportunity to represent mothers and wives who balance family life with their own ambitions.
Miss USA 2026 Justus Kelley wants to raise awareness of providing a loving home to foster children. (Ivan Apfel/Getty Images)

"Knowing that history was made as the first mom, as the first wife, as the first woman in her 30s, my first thought was how amazing it is to get to do this and to represent women from all over the country, from all over the world that resonate with, 'Hey, we're still dreaming,'" she said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Miss USA 2026 Justus Kelley stands on stage during the Miss USA Final Competition and Coronation at the Adrienne Arsht Center for the Performing Arts in Miami, Florida, on Aug. 27, 2026. (Ivan Apfel/Getty Images)
"We're raising our families, but we still have dreams. We still have things that we want to go after and pursue. But what an honor. I get to do this. I get to represent these women. What an honor."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: 'General Hospital' star Cameron Mathison says ‘red flags’ drove him to demand answers before cancer diagnosis
summary: Cameron Mathison opens up to Fox News Digital about kidney cancer, divorce, wildfire loss and how those struggles led him to "A Very Arctic Christmas" with Jill Wagner.
story: The "A Very Arctic Christmas" actor tells Fox News Digital he pushed for an MRI for two years before the scan saved his life and explains how cancer transformed his approach to health.
Cameron Mathison knew something was wrong — and spent two years pushing for answers before an MRI revealed he had cancer.
The "General Hospital" star told Fox News Digital the frightening experience changed how he approaches his health, including knowing when to stop pushing his body.
"I just knew something was wrong," said Mathison, who stars in Great American Media's "A Very Arctic Christmas."
'LIONESS' STAR JILL WAGNER RAISES DAUGHTERS IN TENNESSEE TOWN OF 800, WHERE HORSES AND BUGGIES STILL ROAM
Cameron Mathison told Fox News Digital he knew something was wrong with his health before an MRI revealed kidney cancer. (Christine Bartolucci/Disney via Getty Images)
Mathison was diagnosed with renal cell carcinoma, a type of kidney cancer, in 2019 after an MRI revealed a tumor.

Before his diagnosis, the actor said he had gone to extraordinary lengths to monitor his health, undergoing bloodwork, gut microbiome testing and hormone evaluations. Despite those efforts, he said, troubling results left him searching for an explanation.

"I was a guy trying to do it right, but like I was alluding to, I was very extreme," he said. "And I was doing these extreme things, and I was getting the blood tests, and … things were just off … they were like red flags."

title: Richard Sterban of The Oak Ridge Boys dead at 83
summary: Richard Sterban's iconic bass voice powered The Oak Ridge Boys' "Elvira" to No. 1. His family revealed he battled pancreatic cancer since March.
story: Richard Sterban of Oak Ridge Boys has died. He was 83. (Getty Images)
Richard Sterban, whose unmistakable voice helped make The Oak Ridge Boys’ "Elvira" a country music classic, has died. He was 83.

The singer died Saturday, Nov. 14, in Hendersonville, Tennessee, from complications of bronchitis and pneumonia following a long battle with cancer, according to an announcement from his family and The Oak Ridge Boys.

"We appreciate all of your love, support, and prayers. Please continue to lift us up in this difficult time, we find comfort knowing that he is currently face to face with Jesus," his family said in a statement obtained by Fox News Digital.

Sterban publicly announced his pancreatic cancer diagnosis in September 2025, revealing that doctors had diagnosed him that March. Despite his health struggles, the country music veteran expressed hope that his faith and medical care would help him recover and return to performing.
JOHN ANDERSON, COUNTRY MUSIC HALL OF FAMER, DEAD AT 71
Sterban announced his pancreatic cancer diagnosis last year.  (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

"With the help of the Good Lord above, I believe I will be able to get through this," he said at the time. He also thanked fans for their prayers and said he hoped to return to the road within several months.
NEW PANCREATIC CANCER PILL COULD RESHAPE TREATMENT AS EARLY TRIAL RESULTS STUN RESEARCHERS

After stepping away from touring in May 2025, Sterban returned to the Grand Ole Opry on Jan. 30 and 31, 2026, joining his bandmates for performances of "Elvira" that brought audiences to their feet, according to the announcement.
"Having Richard on stage with us again was one of God’s greatest blessings," fellow Oak Ridge Boys singer Duane Allen said.

Richard Sterban, Tanya Tucker and William Lee Golden attend the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum Class of 2026 Medallion Ceremony in Nashville, Tenn., on Oct. 18, 2026. (Getty Images for Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum)
GEORGE STRAIT PULLS OFF INCREDIBLE CAREER ACCOMPLISHMENT WITH STUNNING CONCERT

Born April 24, 1943, in Camden, New Jersey, Sterban began singing in Sunday school at age 6. His voice transitioned from soprano to bass by eighth grade, setting him on a path that would eventually take him from gospel quartets to some of music’s biggest stages.

Before joining The Oak Ridge Boys, Sterban performed behind Elvis Presley as a member of J.D. Sumner and the Stamps Quartet. He toured and recorded with Presley and appeared in the 1972 concert film, "Elvis on Tour."
Later that year, he left the job to become The Oak Ridge Boys’ bass singer.
"I wanted to be in the best vocal group in the world," Sterban said, according to the announcement.

Alongside lead singer Allen, baritone William Lee Golden and tenor Joe Bonsall, Sterban helped transform the Southern gospel quartet into a country and pop crossover act. Their hits included "Y’all Come Back Saloon," "Bobbie Sue," and "American Made."
The Oak Ridge Boys said it was a "blessing" to share the stage with their bandmate earlier this year.  (Omar Vega/WireImage)

But it was Sterban’s booming bass refrain on the group’s 1981 recording of "Elvira" that became his musical calling card. The song reached No. 1 on the country chart and No. 5 on the pop chart and earned a Grammy Award.
OUTLAW COUNTRY SINGER DAVID ALLAN COE DEAD AT 86
"It’s the song everyone hopes to hear at our concerts," Sterban said on its 40th anniversary, according to the announcement.
The group became Grand Ole Opry members in 2011 and entered the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2015.
DOLLY PARTON DEAD AT 80
Their decades together also forged deep personal bonds.
In January 2021, Allen reflected on his relationship with Sterban, Golden and Bonsall.

LOUISVILLE, KENTUCKY - AUGUST 22: Joe Bonsall, Duane Allen, William Lee Golden, and Richard Sterban of the Oak Ridge Boys performs during the Kentucky State Fair on August 22, 2021 in Louisville, Kentucky. (Photo by Stephen J. Cohen/Getty Images) (Stephen J. Cohen/Getty Images)
"I think the four of us have grown closer than we’ve ever been in our whole career," Allen told Fox News Digital at the time.
RANDY TRAVIS’ WIFE SAYS DOCTORS GAVE COUNTRY LEGEND 1% CHANCE OF SURVIVAL BEFORE MIRACULOUS COMEBACK

The Oak Ridge Boys also developed a lasting friendship with former President George H.W. Bush. At his request, they performed "Amazing Grace" at his funeral in Houston in December 2018, taking an overnight flight after a concert in Washington state to attend.
"There’s no way we wouldn’t do it," Sterban said, according to the announcement.

Away from the stage, Sterban was a devoted baseball fan and a part owner of the Nashville Sounds minor league team for 30 years. He continued recording late in life, contributing to several tracks on The Oak Ridge Boys’ October 2026 album, "Buried Treasures."

Sterban is survived by his wife, Donna; daughters Lauren and Tori; sons Rich, Doug and Chris; eight grandchildren; and three great-grandchildren.
