title: Johnny Depp fled Hollywood spotlight for quiet Bahamas life where 'nobody’s pointing a camera at me'
summary: Johnny Depp opens up about how his 1940s Bahamas wood house with a yurt and painting studio became his sanctuary away from cameras and fame.
story: Johnny Depp says that living in the Bahamas has given him "total peace and quiet." (Getty Images)
Johnny Depp turns to the Bahamas to experience a private life.
During an interview with the Wall Street Journal, Depp opened up about craving privacy and not being able to have it in the United States.

"Today, I live most of the time in the Bahamas. It’s where I’ve found total peace and quiet. Nobody’s pointing a camera at me or staring. I bought my 1940s wood house in 2004 and added a yurt and a painting studio. Art continues to be a sanctuary that lets me process the world around me," Depp told the outlet.
‘GREASE’ STAR STOCKARD CHANNING SAYS SHE’S ‘HAPPY BEING A RECLUSE’ AFTER LEAVING AMERICA
Johnny Depp lives in the Bahamas most of the time these days, he said. (Tim P. Whitby/Getty Images for The Red Sea International Film Festival)

Depp famously purchased his own island in the Bahamas in 2004. In 2009, he told Vanity Fair that "escapism is survival to me," and that, after playing a difficult role, "my head was done in. I needed to escape. So being able to get on the boat and move allowed my head freedom again."

He continued, "Somehow, the mathematics led me here to my island. I don’t think I’d ever seen any place so pure and beautiful. You can feel your pulse rate drop about 20 beats. It’s instant freedom. And that rare beast—simplicity—can be had. And a little morsel of anonymity."
The actor added, "Whenever I was getting frustrated about being ‘novelty boy’ and making movies, I told myself, Calm down. I can come down here and disappear."

Depp told SCMP Style in 2023, "Where I feel the most myself in this world, and where I go to feel absolutely normal, I suppose, is my place in the Bahamas, because it’s an island and nobody’s looking at me. You’ve got to have some sanctuary, a safe place where you can escape the scrutiny and the interest of others, a place where you can just sit on a beach, read, paint, meditate or whatever, that’s freedom to me. That’s the only real freedom."
Johnny Depp has said in the past how much his home in the Bahamas means to him. (Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images)

Making music is also something Depp likes to do on his island. Telling WSJ about how he passes his time there, he said, "I like to grab about four or five books and flop on the couch and read. Or I play guitar in my music studio."
In the 80s, Depp was in a band – music was what originally brought him to Los Angeles in 1983, not acting.

"Soon after, I met actor Nicolas Cage at a friend’s house. Nic came to see my band several times, and we became friends," Depp said. "Six months later, he suggested I try acting. I was up for anything that would help pay the bills."

"There was a great veil lifted when my first child was born. And suddenly, I understood exactly what everything had been for," Depp said. "There were years of that, that I thought, ‘What am I doing? Why am I doing these movies?’ This is what it's all about."

title: Sammy Kershaw accepts CMA apology after country stars speak out over red carpet access
summary: Sammy Kershaw's CMA Awards red carpet denial ignited a firestorm among country music artists who say the industry sidelines legends for influencers.
story: 'Outnumbered' panelists discuss country star Rodney Atkins' advice for young people to avoid social media fads and the impact of social media on America's youth.

Sammy Kershaw and Rodney Atkins spoke out about being denied permission to walk the red carpet at this year’s Country Music Association Awards, prompting criticism over how the organization treats veteran country artists.

Last week, Kershaw, 68, shared a statement on Instagram in which he revealed that the organization rejected his request to walk the carpet at the upcoming ceremony with his wife, Mendy, a decision that he called "extremely hurtful, embarrassing and very disappointing."

Following Kershaw's post, Atkins, 57, announced that he and his wife, Rose Falcon, were also denied red carpet access and would no longer be attending the ceremony, which will be held on Nov. 18 and marks the CMAs' milestone 60th anniversary.
COUNTRY STAR CODY JOHNSON SAYS NASHVILLE WANTED TO CHANGE HIM BEFORE SUCCESS
Country musician Sammy Kershaw spoke out after being denied access to the 2026 CMAs red carpet. (Getty Images)

After facing backlash from other country musicians and fans, the CMA issued a response in which the organization explained that its red carpet criteria helps manage limited space and security needs and apologized to those who "felt excluded by those decisions." The CMA also added that it was speaking with Kershaw's team.
On Tuesday, Kershaw shared a post in which he said that he had accepted an apology from the CMA as well as an invitation for himself and Mendy to walk the red carpet and attend the ceremony.

The controversy sparked an uproar among country artists, who argued that the CMA has welcomed influencers, actors and crossover celebrities onto the red carpet while sidelining veteran performers. In addition, other country musicians raised broader concerns about how the industry as a whole recognizes artists who helped shape the genre.

In his initial post on Nov. 5, Kershaw wrote that the denial of his request to walk the CMAs carpet "really hurts me." He explained that he learned of the rejection just two weeks ahead of the awards show after he and Mendy had already rearranged his touring schedule and booked flights and hotels.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Kershaw said he and his wife, Mendy, pictured at the 2016 CMAs, had already booked flights and hotels.  (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

"My wife, Mendy, and I don't get to attend these events very often, due to touring and schedule conflicts," Kershaw wrote at the time. "She was really looking forward to us sharing a special evening together celebrating country music. Then, to find out I was denied the red carpet two weeks before the show, after being strung along for several months and expecting we would be attending, WTF?"

Kershaw pointed to his decades-long career and longstanding relationship with the CMA to question why he was excluded. He cited his more than 50 years in the music business, millions of records sold, over two dozen Billboard hits, a past CMA Horizon Award nomination and his status as a "lifetime CMA member" since 1992.
The musician also noted that he previously "donated" his time to perform at CMA Fest, and that he hoped he had earned the right to walk the carpet alongside his wife just as they had in the past.

"I’m blessed to still be out on tour every year, performing for the greatest fans in the world doing what I love," Kershaw wrote. "I believe there should be room to recognize the artists who have spent their lives contributing to this organization’s success.

"I love country music, but never in a million years would I think that a successful country music entertainer (and I’m not the only one) would not be able to walk the red carpet. It’s extremely hurtful, embarrassing and very disappointing. I guess the next time I attend the CMA’s, it will be in tribute after I’m gone, if I’m lucky," he concluded.

Two days after Kershaw's post, Atkins shared a video in which he revealed that he and his wife, who is also a longtime CMA member, had also been excluded from the CMAs red carpet and decided to skip the event.
"Well, I found out that Sammy Kershaw and I have something in common this year. Neither one of us got approved to walk the CMA awards red carpet," he began.

"When I heard about Sammy, I thought, 'What a shame. He's a great guy, sweetheart of a dude. Spent his life representing country music.' Then I found out the same thing happened to me," Atkins continued. "And in a way, I get it. I've always been kind of an outsider, maybe a shrub in the landscape of country music."
Rodney Atkins said he and his wife, Rose Falcon, were also denied red carpet access. (Getty Images)
NATALIE MAINES’ ANTI-TRUMP TIRADE, ZACH BRYAN’S FENCE-CLIMBING CLASH FUEL COUNTRY MUSIC’S BIGGEST FEUDS

Atkins went on to emphasize that he was having his strongest touring year, that his album "True South" reached the second round of CMA voting for album of the year and that his latest single could extend his chart presence into a third decade.
In a statement the musician shared alongside the video, Atkins expressed his gratitude to his fans "who made this career possible."
"You've always made me feel welcome in country music, and that's what matters most," he wrote.

"After more than 20 years as a CMA member and countless CMA Fests I’ve played for free, Rose and I were denied red carpet clearance, just like Sammy Kershaw. So we’ve decided not to attend this year’s CMA Awards," Atkins shared. "I also believe the artists who helped build the foundation of country music, like Sammy Kershaw, deserve a place in its celebrations."

The ""She Don’t Know She’s Beautiful" singer‘s post was met with supportive comments from other country stars, including some from the younger generation that paid tribute to Kershaw for his foundational contributions to the industry.
"If you haven’t earned the right to be there then nobody has… disappointing to say the least," Riley Green wrote.
Carly Pearce commented, "Many of us wouldn’t be here without artists like you…"
Jake Owen declared himself "Team Sammy," while Granger Smith added, "So sad for country music. I grieve for the old CMA."
"This is wild! I’ll give you my spot!!," Drew Bainbridge offered. "You paved the way for all of us on that carpet."
Other artists questioned why influencers were invited to walk the carpet while Kershaw was denied.
"Ugh this makes me sad for country music. Can we please bring back the legends and not influencers?" Kylie Morgan wrote.
"They’ll let zero talent influencers walk the red carpet but not Sammy Kershaw? I hate it here," Meghan Patrick commented.
Riley Green was among the country stars who rallied behind Kershaw. (John Nacion/WireImage)

Veteran country star Mark Chesnutt reacted to Kershaw's snub by the CMA in a lengthy statement on Facebook in which he criticized the organization, arguing that it prioritizes celebrities from outside the genre over longtime country artists.
"So Sammy Kershaw won’t be allowed to walk the red carpet at the big CMA Awards," he wrote. "Well that’s about right. The CMA doesn’t care about us old 90s guys any more."

"It’s a shame they don’t respect the stars that dominated the charts in the past thirty years or before that but they sure roll out the welcome mat for pop stars and Hollywood movie stars and even hip hop artists," he continued. "Anything but country music gets the performance spots on the show."
Chesnutt also contrasted the country music industry's treatment of the genre’s history with the recognition received by rock icons.

"Rock n Roll honors its history and respects its legends while country music industry executives seem to ignore its rich history and its legends," he wrote. "Thank God there’s still a lot of people that love traditional country music. They keep coming to our shows and showing their love and respect for the music we’ve made for nearly forty years now and we’ll keep working for them and not for those who don’t matter to US!"
Mark Chesnutt said that the CMA "doesn’t care about us old 90s guys any more." (Rick Diamond/Getty Images for Country Thunder)
Country singer Pam Tillis, who also rose to fame in the 1990s, also addressed Kershaw's red carpet denial, though she clarified that her criticism was not solely directed at the CMA.

"So let’s talk about today’s drama in country music: Sammy Kershaw and the CMAs. I’m not going to single out the CMA, because this happens all the time in our business," she wrote in a post on Instagram. "It’s the nature of our industry that the rising stars get the spotlight, just as we did at one point."
Tillis emphasized the importance of preserving a legacy, pointing to her own experience growing up as the daughter of country icon Mel Tillis.
"I learned early that a legacy doesn’t keep itself," she wrote. "Somebody has to stand up and say, ‘This artist mattered. They made a contribution.’ I’ve done that for Daddy most of my life."
She acknowledged that rising stars naturally receive attention, but argued that established performers still connect with generations of fans.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"And I’ll tell you what I’ve seen: the country audience is a multigenerational audience, and ‘90s country is still very viable, even if it isn’t always visible," she wrote. "A lot of us have three generations of fans showing up to our shows, singing, whooping and hollering for our songs. Many of today’s artists are making it big with their own spin on the ‘90s sound."

"I dare say many of us have felt the sting of being passed over for this, that and the other, in order to create an image that’s only part of the picture," Tillis continued. "I know today’s new artists need all the support they can get in such a crazy, competitive market. But legacy artists who want to show up can be the bridge between where this music came from and where it’s going."
"Many of us never say anything about these slights," she added. "We just keep on doing our thing. As an artist who is a lifetime CMA member, Sammy just spoke out."
Pam Tillis said she had learned early that a "legacy doesn’t keep itself."  (Getty Images for Stagecoach)
On Monday, the CMA released a statement responding to the backlash and citing space and security criteria for red carpet management.

"In recent days, several artists and their fans have spoken out about this year’s CMA Awards red carpet guidelines," the organization wrote. "Like any major televised event, the red carpet has criteria that exists to help manage limited space and the security needs for both the artists and the media. We are deeply sorry anyone felt excluded by those decisions."

"Our organization’s mission is to honor the history and celebrate the excellence of Country Music," it continued. "With this 60th anniversary year, we are working extra hard to simultaneously spotlight the last six decades, while also celebrating what has been a tremendous year in 2026. It’s not easy to do all of that in just one night, but we are up for the challenge."

"We also know this is about more than a red carpet, and we are committed to keep listening and keep finding ways to make sure all artists feel welcome and at home here," the CMA added. "To that point, we are in touch with Sammy Kershaw’s team and look forward to continuing that conversation."

On Tuesday, Kershaw shared a positive update, revealing that CMA leadership had "extended a sincere, heartfelt apology" which he had accepted following a "sincere and meaningful private conversation."

"The CMA has also extended an invitation for my wife, Mendy, and me to walk the red carpet and attend this year's awards alongside our fellow artists," he wrote. "I am grateful for that invitation and appreciate their willingness to listen, acknowledge our concerns, and work toward a positive outcome."

Kershaw also thanked fans, fellow artists and the country music community for their support. He explained that he originally spoke publicly because he was hurt, rather than seeking attention or controversy.
The "Cadillac Style" singer emphasized that the controversy was about more than his personal invitation.

"This was never about the red carpet," he wrote. "It was about recognizing and respecting those who dedicated their lives to this music and preserving the history and legacy that makes country music so special."
Kershaw expressed his hopes that the conversations would produce lasting change in how legacy artists are recognized.
"You cannot celebrate 60 years of country music without celebrating the artists who helped build those 60 years," he wrote.

"Country music has always been about honoring where we’ve come from while embracing where we’re going," Kershaw continued. "I have nothing but respect for the incredible talent carrying country music into the future. Every generation of artists deserves its moment to shine, and I believe there’s room to celebrate all of them."

title: Kathy Ireland’s husband escapes burning boat after engine explodes 20 miles offshore
summary: Kathy Ireland shared dramatic footage of husband Greg Olsen's boat engulfed in flames after an engine explosion 20 miles west of Santa Barbara.
story: Kathy Ireland described the working dynamic between herself and her husband while working together on his commercial fishing boat.
Kathy Ireland is thankful after her husband narrowly escaped a fire that engulfed his boat while he was alone at sea.

In a recent Instagram post, the 63-year-old actress shared video of husband Dr. Greg Olsen's boat, the 4th Watch, engulfed in flames. Ireland said Olsen was out alone on the water while she was away on business.
"Life is really hard and really beautiful. God is great," she wrote. "Engine exploded and a fire quickly melted all navigation equipment and survival raft!"

She then thanked everyone "who prayed and continue to pray" for her husband, as well as all "those who aided in the rescue," including "@towboatus_ventura and the entire community" for their quick response.
KATHY IRELAND REVEALS 'BIG RED FLAG' THAT EXPOSED ALLEGED $100M 'UNCONSCIONABLE' BETRAYAL
Ireland said she is thankful for those who helped her husband survive the ordeal. (Michael Tullberg/Getty Images)
"Most of all, we thank our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ for this miracle of his survival," she added.
Ireland also shared a note she wrote to her husband following the incident, saying her "heart is both heavy and full" because she knows how much "love, sweat and life you poured into this vessel."
Ireland shared a message for her husband in her Instagram post. (Rebecca Sapp/Getty Images for Santa Barbara International Film Festival)
"This vessel brought so much joy and so many blessings to our family and countless others," she continued.

"My heart is heavy with yours. This is more than a boat, there are many implications. My heart is mostly full. Full because of the outpouring of love and support. Multitudes were praying for you! I’m so thankful to all who rushed to pray and come to your rescue."
Ireland credited God with Olsen's survival. (Arturo Holmes/Getty Images)

"I’m so thankful God gifted you with a brilliant mind to navigate this disaster so seamlessly," she added. "I’m eternally thankful to Him for loving and rescuing you. Though the vessel is no more, the 4th Watch is forever. You named that boat so profoundly. He has so much ahead for you! I’m so proud of you."

Fans in the comments section shared well-wishes for Ireland and Olsen, with some recounting their own experiences with losing their belongings due to a fire.
Fans in the comments section sent Ireland and her husband their well-wishes. (Rebecca Sapp/Getty Images for SBIFF)
"Unbelievable!!! I’m SO grateful your husband is ok," one fan wrote. "🙏 And having parents who lost their home in a fire I completely understand your sadness about the loss of the boat. "

"Oh my! I am so glad he is safe," another added. "The boat and gear is replaceable, but the emotions are real. So sorry!!!!" A third follower wrote, "So sorry to hear this, BUT, Thankful to God that he saved your Precious One!"

The TowBoatUS Ventura Instagram account also shared video of the fire and its aftermath, saying the company received a call about the fire around 3 p.m. on Wednesday afternoon, noting the vessel was "20 nautical miles west of Santa Barbara Harbor."

In its post, TowBoatUS Ventura credited Olsen for his quick thinking, noting that he "was prepared and did everything right." They wrote that he initially "attempted to extinguish the fire before ultimately activating his EPIRB and abandoning ship into a kayak."

title: Tom Arnold admits he hasn’t dated in nearly 10 years after calling people his age ‘disgusting’
summary: Tom Arnold reveals he hasn't dated in nearly ten years but says his "My Crazy X-Wife" comedy tour changed his outlook on finding love.
story: Tom Arnold explained that wanting to live a long life and "be present" for his kids motivates him on his health journey.
Tom Arnold shared he's ready to fall in love again after being single for close to a decade.
During a recent interview with Page Six, the 67-year-old actor and comedian went into a deep dive about his love life, telling the outlet that "it would be good to love somebody and be loved."

"I used to say, people are like, because I haven’t had a date for nine and a half years, ‘You should date someone your own age,’" he said. "And I’m like, ‘Dude, have you seen people my age? We are freaking disgusting.'"

He went on to say that since meeting many different women while on his "My Crazy X-Wife" comedy tour, he changed his tune, saying he has "learned there's a lot of funny, smart, sexy 60-something women" out there.
Arnold shared he hasn't been on a date in over nine years. (FREDERIC J. BROWN/AFP via Getty Images)

The "True Lies" star has been married four times. His first marriage was to Roseanne Barr, from 1990 to 1994.

Barr recently defended Arnold in an interview with The Hollywood Reporter after Chuck Lorre claimed in his memoir, "Sitcom," that "Roseanne" writers were encouraged to put Arnold's name on scripts "as if Tom had written them." Arnold later denied these claims to Entertainment Weekly.

title: 'Dallas’ star Patrick Duffy says mother was killed rushing to husband after gunmen opened fire at bar
summary: Patrick Duffy described how his father took a step toward the returning gunmen before they opened fire, killing both parents in their Montana bar.
story: The actors revealed how COVID brought them together over Zoom calls.

Patrick Duffy's mother was doing a crossword puzzle when two armed men returned to the bar she and her husband owned in Montana, and one of them shot her husband. Moments later, she rushed toward him and was shot and killed, too.

The "Dallas" star, 77, recalled the final moments of his parents' lives during an appearance on the "Still Here Hollywood" podcast, revealing how the double murder unfolded and how he found the strength to carry on.
The murders took place nearly 40 years ago, on Nov. 18, 1986.
'DALLAS' STAR PATRICK DUFFY AND LINDA PURL RECALL START OF SURPRISING LOVE STORY: 'BOTH NERVOUS AS TEENAGERS'

Patrick Duffy was starring as Bobby Ewing on the hit television series "Dallas" when his parents, Terence and Marie Duffy, were shot and killed during a robbery at their Montana bar on Nov. 18, 1986. (CBS via Getty Images)

"My parents were murdered when two young men robbed the bar that my parents owned in Montana," the actor told host Steve Kmetko. "My dad had thrown these two boys out because they were drunk and obstreperous. He just threw them out of the bar, and they went somewhere, finished whatever they were drinking, and the anger boiled up and they went back in."
Sean A. Wentz and Kenneth A. Miller were both 19 at the time, People magazine reported. Duffy's parents, Marie and Terence, were the only ones in the bar when the gunmen returned.
From left: Charlene Tilton, Linda Gray, Larry Hagman, Patrick Duffy and Sheree J. Wilson won the TV Land Pop Culture Award for "Dallas." (L. Cohen/WireImage)

"It was very late at night," Duffy said. "There was nobody in the bar except my father and my mother, and they walked in with their shotguns. As soon as my dad saw them, this is in the testimony that came out in the court, my dad turned to them and apparently took a step towards them, saying, 'I told you to ...'"
WATCH: PATRICK DUFFY AND LINDA PURL FELL IN LOVE ONLINE
Duffy's father never finished his sentence.

"... That's when they opened up on him and killed him," Duffy said. "And then my mother was on the other end of the bar doing a crossword puzzle and took a couple steps running towards dad. And they shot her too."
"And then, if that wasn't stupid enough, instead of just running, they jumped over the bar to the cash register, took the money and a couple of bottles of booze and then left."
Patrick Duffy attends a photocall for "The Bold and the Beautiful" during the 62nd Monte-Carlo TV Festival in Monte-Carlo, Monaco, on June 19, 2023. (Getty Images)

The Los Angeles Times previously reported that Terence and Marie's bodies were found by a group of people who had stopped for a drink after finishing their shifts at the nearby Montana Developmental Center. One woman spotted Marie on the floor but initially thought she might have fainted. When she saw blood on Terence, she went outside and flagged down a friend for help.
Linda Gray and Patrick Duffy pose at the launch of "Dallas" on Foxtel's SoHo at The Loft in Sydney, Australia, on Aug. 19, 2014. (WireImage)
Duffy learned of his parents' deaths the following morning.

"... My sister had called she was completely devastated," he recalled. "... She was a police woman, and she was on her way to Montana. By the time I hung up the phone, there were film crews at the gate."

Patrick Duffy (left) is seen here opposite Larry Hagman (right) on the set of "Dallas." (CBS via Getty Images)
Duffy said Lorimar Television, the production company behind "Dallas," arranged transportation and other support for him following the murders.

"Lorimar [Television] called, everybody called, [the] support team got in there and said, 'We have the jet ready. We'll fly you to Montana. We'll take care of everything. We'll send a PR person with you to take care of all that.'"
Patrick Duffy appears as Bobby Ewing in the CBS prime-time soap opera "Dallas," which premiered April 2, 1978. (CBS via Getty Images)
Duffy said his Buddhist faith helped him cope with the loss. It also gave him the strength to tell his sons, Padraic and Conor, that their grandparents had been killed.

Actor Patrick Duffy and his sons Padriac and Conor attend the opening night of "Joan Rivers: A Work in Progress By A Life in Progress" at the Geffen Playhouse in Los Angeles on Feb. 13, 2008. (WireImage)
"The Buddhist philosophy is one of the continuous life cycle of your entity," Duffy explained on the podcast.

"... The first thing I did was, it was just as the boys were getting up to go to school, very young, and I said, '... I'm going to chant with you,' because we always chanted before they went off to school. I said, 'We have to chant for grandma and grandpa because they've both been killed, and we have to chant for them because they're going to understand it and hear it.'"

Actors Julie Gonzalo, Brenda Strong, Jordana Brewster, Larry Hagman, Linda Gray and Patrick Duffy and executive producers Cynthia Cidre and Michael M. Robin speak onstage during the Dallas panel at the 2012 Turner TCA in Pasadena, California, on Jan. 14, 2012. (WireImage)

Miller and Wentz were convicted in connection with the murders and sentenced to prison, according to People magazine. Nine.com.au reported that Miller was released on parole in 2007, and Wentz was granted parole in 2015.

title: Princess Diana’s legendary White House dance with John Travolta almost didn’t happen
summary: Princess Diana danced with Clint Eastwood, Tom Selleck and Ronald Reagan that evening, but it took coaxing to get John Travolta onto the floor.
story: "Princess Diana: Love, Life, Legacy — A Life of Giving," an exhibition at the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library, reveals the story behind Princess Diana's famous dance with John Travolta and showcases her iconic velvet gown.
John Travolta had all the right moves, but when the chance to dance with Princess Diana came along, even Hollywood's smoothest dancer got cold feet.

The Princess of Wales and the actor lit up the White House ballroom in 1985, creating one of the most unforgettable moments in royal and Hollywood history. Diana was attending a White House dinner hosted by President Ronald Reagan and first lady Nancy Reagan when she took a spin with the heartthrob.

More than four decades later, their legendary dance is being celebrated at "Princess Diana: Love, Life, Legacy — A Life of Giving," an exhibition at the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library in Simi Valley, California. More than 700 artifacts connected to Diana's life are on display.
PRINCESS DIANA, HOT DOGS AND A PRESIDENTIAL MATCHMAKING ATTEMPT: ICONIC ROYAL VISITS TO AMERICA
American actor John Travolta dancing with Princess Diana in Cross Hall of the White House, Washington, D.C., on Nov. 9, 1985. (Glasshouse Images)

The collection, presented through a partnership between the Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute (RRPFI) and Renae Plant's Princess Diana Museum, features the velvet gown designed by Victor Edelstein that Diana wore that night.
But the iconic dance nearly didn't happen.

Princess Diana's "Travolta" dress is a highlight of the exhibition dedicated to the late Princess of Wales and her warm friendship with the Reagans. (Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute)

"In preparation for the state dinner, the Marine Band that was going to perform the music during the dinner was told to rehearse music from 'Saturday Night Fever,'" Melissa Giller, chief marketing and cultural programming officer at RRPFI, told Fox News Digital.
WATCH: PRINCESS DIANA'S ICONIC DANCE WITH TRAVOLTA GETS NEW SPOTLIGHT

"The social secretary, Gahl Burt, she orchestrated it after speaking with Mrs. Reagan that after the dancing began, Gahl would walk up to John Travolta and tap him on the shoulder and encourage him to have a dance with Princess Diana," Giller said. "Now through the whole evening, Princess Diana danced with Ronald Reagan. She danced with Clint Eastwood. She danced with Tom Selleck and many others."
But when it came time for Travolta to step onto the dance floor with Diana, he needed some coaxing.
President Ronald Reagan dances with Princess Diana in Cross Hall of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 9, 1985. (Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

"When it was time, Gahl Burt walked up to John Travolta and tapped him on the shoulder," Giller said. "He was actually a bit hesitant. He didn't know if it was something he should do. But after some encouragement, he went up and asked the princess to dance."

Prince Charles and Princess Diana met President Ronald Reagan and First Lady Nancy Reagan at the White House in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 9, 1985, during an official visit to the United States. (Tim Graham Photo Library/Getty Images)
Travolta mustered the courage and approached Diana. The two then waltzed across the checkered floor to music from "Saturday Night Fever."
"They ended up dancing for 15 minutes," Giller said with a smile.
President Ronald Reagan and Nancy Reagan welcome Princess Diana and Prince Charles at the White House in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 9, 1985. (AFP via Getty Images)

"Every presidential library archive has a photo that's the most requested by the public. President Nixon's library is the photo of Elvis meeting President Nixon. And one of our most requested photos is the one of Princess Diana dancing with John Travolta."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Princess Diana is seen here with John Travolta in the Cross Hall of the White House in Washington, D.C., at a dinner for Prince Charles and Princess Diana of the United Kingdom on Nov. 9, 1985. (Alamy Live News.)
Travolta later admitted he was nervous before approaching Diana.

"I didn't think they'd ask me to dance with her," he told Esquire Mexico in 2021. "I had the great privilege and honor of doing so, and I thought, 'There must be a reason for doing this and I better give it my all.’ That meant lead the dance well and make sure we had fun. That was the easy part, but just the fact of greeting Diana appropriately, being confident and asking her to dance was a complicated task."
President and Mrs. Reagan welcome Prince Charles and Princess Diana to the White House on Nov. 9, 1985. (Bettmann Archive)
The "Grease" star also recalled how special it was to dance with Diana.
John Travolta later revealed that dancing with Princess Diana was one of the highlights of his life. (John Shelley Collection/Avalon/Getty Images)

"Think of the setting. We were at the White House. It's midnight. The stage is like a dream. I approach her, touch her elbow, invite her to dance," he said. "She spins around and gives me that captivating smile, just a little sad, and accepts my invitation. And there we were, dancing together as if it were a fairytale."
In the 2021 interview, Travolta also recalled his disbelief over the once-in-a-lifetime encounter.
Princess Diana's childhood keepsakes on display. (Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute)
"Who could imagine that something like this is going to happen to you one day? I was smart enough to register it in my memory as a very special, magical moment."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
John Travolta and Princess Diana danced for 15 minutes. (Pete Souza/The White House via Getty Images)
Travolta also told Dutch television station Één that it was Nancy who told him Diana wanted to dance with him.

"[She] said, 'It is her wish,'" the actor recalled. "At midnight, I had to tap her on her shoulder, and I had to say, 'Would you care to dance?' She turned around and dipped her head in that Lady Diana way, and we were off for 15 minutes dancing."
Princess Diana's Versace dress. (Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute)

"I'll never forget it," he continued. "I'm so honored that I was able to experience this, and I know for a fact that it was her highlight of being in the United States; it was her favorite moment. So I feel I made her life better, she made my life better, and I'm very sorry that she's not here."

Diana, Princess of Wales, wearing a cream lace gown with a scalloped neckline designed by Murray Arbeid and the Lover's Knot diamond and pearl tiara, smiles as she attends a dinner at the British Ambassador's Residence in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 11, 1985. (Getty Images)
During a 2016 appearance on "Good Morning America," Travolta was asked if there was anything from the 1980s that he'd like to bring back to the 2010s. He said he'd love to dance with Diana again.
"That was one of the highlights of my life, so that's probably the best moment of the '80s."
Princess Diana's honeymoon shoes and hat on display. (Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute)
Giller noted that the Prince and Princess of Wales maintained a close friendship with the Reagans.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
The former Prince Charles is seen here attending a dinner with President Ronald Reagan and his wife Nancy at the White House in Washington, D.C. (Jean-Louis Atlan/Sygma)

"When Princess Diana got married to Prince Charles, Ronald Reagan, as President of the United States, could not go because the assassination attempt happened a few months ago and he was [still] recovering," Giller explained. "So, Mrs. Reagan went on behalf of President Reagan, as well as the United States. And I think that sort of bonded her with Princess Diana, although of course, Mrs. Reagan was much older than Princess Diana."
"They shared a kinship, especially once Princess Diana became a mother," Giller said. "You can see that in [their] letters and their relationship."
Princess Diana's "final goodbye" dress was designed for the Princess of Wales but never worn before her tragic death in August 1997. (Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute)
The exhibition features letters Nancy and Diana wrote to each other over the years, as well as gifts the Reagans received from the Prince and Princess of Wales.
Princess Diana with Nancy Reagan at the White House in 1985. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)
Giller said the exhibition aims to show visitors the woman behind the royal title, highlighting Diana's humanitarian work and influence beyond her relationship with the Reagans.
"Diana: Love Life Legacy — A Life of Giving" showcases more than 700 original artifacts from Princess Diana's extraordinary life. (Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute)

"This isn't just an exhibition about dresses and shoes and jewelry," she said. "This is an exhibition about a woman who truly cared about her family, about her people, about all people, not just those in Europe, but around the world."

Princess Diana's famous "Caring Dress" from the Princess Diana Museum is also on display. (Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute)
The exhibition, which opened Nov. 7, runs through May 31, 2027.
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Pancreatic cancer mystery deepens as researchers make unexpected discovery
summary: University of Cincinnati study found Black patients' pancreatic tumors had more B cells and cells tied to drug resistance, pointing to tailored care.
story: Dr. Raymond Wadlow, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Inova Schar Cancer Institute in Virginia, said the surrounding immune cells and tissue may affect how a tumor behaves and responds to treatment.

A University of Cincinnati study found differences in pancreatic tumors that could help explain why that type of cancer affects some patients differently, potentially leading to more personalized treatments.

Researchers examined 22 pancreatic tumors from patients of different racial backgrounds across the U.S., looking for differences in cancer cells and how the immune system responds to them. The study included seven Black patients and 15 non-African American patients.
The findings were published in the journal Cancer Research.
FDA APPROVES ONCE-DAILY PILL FOR DEADLY CANCER AFTER PATIENTS' SURVIVAL RATES NEARLY DOUBLE
Tumors from Black patients had fewer of the most common type of pancreatic cancer cells and more cells with a mix of different characteristics, the researchers found.
Some of those cell characteristics have been associated with drug resistance, but the study did not establish whether they affected patients’ treatment outcomes.
A University of Cincinnati study found differences in pancreatic tumors that could help explain why that type of cancer affects some patients differently. (iStock)

Additionally, tumors from Black patients contained more B cells, a type of immune cell, and larger clusters of immune cells. Researchers found signs that some B cells may suppress the body’s response to cancer, although the significance of these differences is unclear.
PATIENTS REMAIN CANCER-FREE NEARLY 3 YEARS AFTER RECEIVING EXPERIMENTAL IMMUNOTHERAPY

Dr. Raymond Wadlow, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Inova Schar Cancer Institute in Virginia, said that using immunotherapy to help the immune system attack the disease has been particularly challenging in pancreatic cancer.

"That's been very difficult to do in pancreatic cancer because the pancreatic tumor subverts the immune system so that it is fighting for it instead of for the host or the rest of the body," Wadlow, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.

Tumors from Black patients contained more B cells, a type of immune cell, and larger clusters of immune cells. Researchers found signs that some B cells may suppress the body’s response to cancer. (iStock)
The study found no significant differences between groups in the major genetic changes known to drive the disease.
Pancreatic cancer is approximately 20% more likely to develop in Black Americans than in non-African Americans, according to the researchers.
WHERE YOU LIVE COULD SHAPE YOUR RISK OF CANCER MORTALITY, STUDY SUGGESTS

The findings highlight the importance of including patients from different backgrounds in cancer research, according to lead study author Nina Steele, Ph.D., an assistant professor in UC’s College of Medicine.
"This study shows that ignoring diverse ancestry in medical research leaves blind spots in the search for a cure," she told Fox News Digital.
An oncologist (not pictured) encouraged newly diagnosed patients to ask about hereditary genetic testing, which can identify inherited mutations that may also affect relatives. (iStock)
Wadlow noted that pancreatic cancers can share major DNA mutations but can differ considerably in how their cells behave and interact with nearby immune cells and surrounding tissue.
"Those differences may also vary across patient populations, such as between Black and non-Black patients," he told Fox News Digital.
"While intriguing, these findings are still a long way from changing patient care."
"That is potentially important both for understanding disparities in pancreatic cancer and, ultimately, for developing more individualized treatments."
Pancreatic cancer can vary from one tumor to another, and even within the same tumor, Wadlow explained. "The cancer cell itself is only part of the story," he said.
Pancreatic cancer is approximately 20% more likely to develop in Black Americans than in non-African Americans, according to the researchers. (iStock)
The surrounding immune cells and tissue may affect how a tumor behaves and responds to treatment, helping to explain why a single treatment approach may not work for every patient.
The findings have several limitations.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Researchers have not established how the intermediate tumor cells affect survival or whether they respond differently to standard chemotherapy, Steele said.
The team also needs to study pancreatic tissue from people without cancer to better understand when these differences develop.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Wadlow cautioned that race and genetic ancestry do not fully account for the environmental, socioeconomic and biological factors that could explain the findings.
Larger studies involving patients from diverse backgrounds are needed to determine whether these differences affect treatment outcomes or survival, the oncologist said.
Immunotherapy to help the immune system attack cancer has been particularly challenging in pancreatic cancer, an oncologist said. (Aaron Chown/PA Images via Getty Images)
"While intriguing, these findings are still a long way from changing patient care," he added.
Wadlow encouraged newly diagnosed patients to ask about hereditary genetic testing, which can identify inherited mutations that may also affect relatives.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"If we find an inherited mutation, then family members can be tested," he said.
Steele said the findings also underscore the need for clinical trials that represent the patients affected by pancreatic cancer.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"It is also a reminder for the medical system to ensure that clinical trials reflect the entire population at risk, in order to find treatments that can help all patients, not just some patients," she told Fox News Digital.
The research was funded in part by the National Cancer Institute.

title: Widely used antidepressant outperformed by 3 other drugs in major study of 30,000 people
summary: A study of 20 antidepressants and over 30,000 patients found three medications may beat fluoxetine for long-term depression treatment results overall.
story: Dr. Daniel Amen, founder of Amen Clinics, identifies six behaviors people should avoid when experiencing depression, including drinking alcohol, withdrawing from others and consuming highly processed foods.
Three antidepressants may work better than fluoxetine, widely known by the brand name Prozac, at helping people with depression get better and stay well over time, a new study suggests.
The research, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, compared 20 antidepressants to determine how well they eased depression symptoms and helped prevent them from returning over time.
Researchers analyzed 115 previous clinical trials involving more than 30,000 people, according to a news release from Radboud University Medical Center in the Netherlands.
CERTAIN SLEEP HABITS COULD OFFER CLUES TO HIDDEN TYPE OF DEPRESSION, SCIENTISTS SAY

They found that escitalopram, sold under the brand name Lexapro; duloxetine, sold as Cymbalta; and agomelatine performed better over the long term than fluoxetine, which researchers used as the main comparison drug.

Eli Lilly told Fox News Digital that it discontinued manufacturing Prozac in 2024. The company noted that fluoxetine remains available in many FDA-approved generic medicines and that neither the study nor the university’s news release specifically referred to Prozac or any Lilly product.
A new study suggests three antidepressants may work better than fluoxetine at helping people recover from depression and stay well over time. (iStock)
The findings suggest that antidepressants can continue helping people after their symptoms improve, although some medications appeared to work better than others at keeping patients well.
Paul van Haaren, a researcher at Radboud University Medical Center who worked on the study, noted that the three medications have different benefits and drawbacks.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"Escitalopram is already widely used," he said in the release. "Agomelatine works well, but one of its side effects is the risk of liver failure. Duloxetine is less well-known and is prescribed less frequently as a first-line treatment."

Escitalopram belongs to a common group of antidepressants known as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. These medications are often recommended as a first option for treating depression, according to the release.
Researchers compared antidepressant treatments to better understand which medications may help patients maintain improvements and avoid a return of depression symptoms. (iStock)
Among the SSRIs included in the study, escitalopram appeared to work best at helping patients stay well over time.

Eric Ruhé, a professor of difficult-to-treat depression at Radboud University Medical Center, said the findings could eventually influence how doctors choose antidepressants. Still, the researchers stressed that this does not mean everyone with depression should take escitalopram.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"As a prescriber, you consider the balance between a medication's benefits and side effects," Ruhé said in the release. "That balance differs from person to person."
Dr. Carole Lieberman, a board-certified psychiatrist based in Beverly Hills, California, who was not involved in the study, urged caution when interpreting the findings.
Escitalopram, duloxetine and agomelatine appeared to outperform fluoxetine in maintaining improvements in depression symptoms over the long term. (iStock)
She noted that agomelatine is not approved in the U.S.
"The best way to treat someone with depression is not always with antidepressants, and certainly not with antidepressants alone," Lieberman told Fox News Digital.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Psychotherapy or talk therapy can also play an important role in treating depression, according to Lieberman, while some patients may benefit from using medication along with therapy.
There were some limitations to the study, the researchers acknowledged.
Researchers cautioned that the findings cannot predict which antidepressant will work best for a specific patient, emphasizing the need for individualized treatment decisions. (iStock)
Rather than enrolling a new group of patients and following them over time, the researchers combined results from 115 previous clinical trials to compare how the medications performed.

The findings also cannot predict which antidepressant will work best for a specific person. The researchers stressed that doctors and patients should consider both the potential benefits and side effects when choosing a medication.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
People with questions about their antidepressants should speak with their doctor before making any medication changes, according to the release.
Fox News Digital reached out to the researchers and additional drug manufacturers for comment.

title: Woman’s kratom addiction spiraled from 4 capsules to 100 a day: ‘Zombie shell of myself’
summary: Hilary Tesluck shares how kratom capsules led to a spiraling addiction, with her daily intake climbing to 100 capsules before she sought help.
story: Hilary Tesluck, 30, executive director of End Kratom Addiction, shares her journey of dependence and recovery with Fox News Digital.
Kratom-related reports to U.S. poison centers rose about 1,200% from 2015 to 2025, reaching a record high of 3,434 last year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
For Hilary Tesluck, a 30-year-old woman in Michigan, the potential for addiction began well before those numbers emerged.
Tesluck, who now works to raise awareness of kratom addiction and support others in recovery, said she first tried kratom capsules in 2017 at age 21.
KRATOM INDUSTRY WARNS SYNTHETIC OPIOIDS SHOULD NOT BE CALLED 'KRATOM'

Her initial use involved leaf kratom rather than concentrated 7-OH products, she shared. The American Kratom Association argues that 7-OH should be distinguished from natural leaf kratom, while acknowledging that kratom itself can cause dependence.
Hilary Tesluck, who now works to raise awareness of kratom addiction and support others in recovery, said she first tried kratom capsules in 2017 at age 21. (Hilary Tesluck)

"It was introduced to me by a friend who knew that I was someone who suffered from anxiety and took prescription medication for it," Tesluck told Fox News Digital. "I wanted to be more holistic and natural in what I was consuming."
She noted that she doesn’t recall any dosing recommendations on the label. "I didn’t know how much to take, but my friend told me to take four capsules."
WHAT IS KRATOM? RISKS OF POPULAR SUBSTANCE REVEALED AFTER COLLEGE STUDENTS' DEATHS
At first, Tesluck – an undergraduate student at the time, who was also conducting research and tutoring – noticed the substance gave her a boost in energy, confidence and productivity.
Growing dependence
Tesluck's daily intake climbed gradually. "Very slowly, over time, I had to take just one more capsule or just one more dose, and then went all the way up to 100," she said.
Her day-to-day functioning began to suffer, she shared. "I was not doing very well at work. I was getting … written up for performance."
Physically, she had lost nearly 40 pounds and struggled to even stand in the shower "because my body was so wasted away."
Tesluck said a friend introduced her to kratom as a more "holistic and natural" alternative to her anxiety prescription medication. (Hilary Tesluck)
Tesluck’s belief that kratom was natural and legal made her growing dependence difficult to accept, she said.
"About a year and a half into my kratom addiction from just the leaf … I finally realized I needed to do something, and I needed help."
Seeking help
When she first sought treatment in 2020, Tesluck described feeling dismissed, saying that the facility’s urine test did not detect her use and that she had to explain what kratom was to the staff.
"They were confused why I was there," she said. "So I left after just a few days because I felt kind of humiliated, and I went right back to my use."
Tesluck found more help in 2021, when she attended an online recovery meeting.
"I had nothing to lose," she said. "It changed everything for me to hear other people telling my story for the first time."
After years of feeling alone in her addiction, she said, she finally felt surrounded by people who understood.
"It’s one problem at two strengths."

In 2023, Tesluck relapsed following her grandmother’s death. "I was just grief-stricken. She was really close to me," she said. "So I went to the smoke shop just to get a little bit of kratom, just one time."
She later experienced a separate relapse involving 7-OH, which she said followed the death of her cat and the end of a relationship on the same night.
MEN AND WOMEN WHO SMOKE MARIJUANA MAY EXPERIENCE DIFFERENT EFFECTS, STUDY SUGGESTS
7-OH, short for 7-hydroxymitragynine, occurs naturally in trace amounts in kratom. Concentrated 7-OH products contain much higher levels than the leaf itself.
The body converts some of kratom’s main active compound, mitragynine, into 7-OH, research shows. Both compounds act on opioid receptors and can contribute to dependence, according to the FDA.
"The 7-OH was very strong," Tesluck said. "I stayed on that for just a few months because of how intense it was."
At first, Tesluck — an undergraduate student at the time, who was also conducting research and tutoring — noticed that kratom gave her a boost in energy, confidence and productivity. (Hilary Tesluck)
She returned to her recovery group for support. "I had to take a leave of absence, and I got clean from 7-OH again with their help," she said.
Having struggled with both leaf kratom and 7-OH, Tesluck views them as closely connected. "It’s one problem at two strengths," she said.
‘SUPER-DRUG’ 10 TIMES STRONGER THAN FENTANYL LINKED TO DEATHS ACROSS MULTIPLE STATES

Mac Haddow, senior fellow on public policy for the American Kratom Association, disputed this characterization of leaf kratom and concentrated 7-OH. In comments to Fox News Digital, he argued that the body’s conversion of mitragynine into 7-OH does not produce equivalent exposure to concentrated products.
Haddow also raised the possibility that the capsules Tesluck initially consumed may have contained ingredients beyond natural leaf kratom.
Varying regulations
Kratom rules vary widely across the country, with states taking different approaches to age restrictions, product standards and bans.
"It’s really been a patchwork," Tesluck said. "It’s different from state to state. Some states ban it, some states regulate it."
Today, Tesluck describes herself as a "person in long-term recovery from both kratom and 7-OH addiction." (Hilary Tesluck)
Florida, for example, prohibits selling or providing kratom products to anyone under 21.
Washington’s health department says unscheduled kratom products remain largely unregulated there, without age restrictions, labeling standards or ingredient-testing requirements.
Texas law requires kratom product labels to include directions and a recommended serving size.
"We support stronger enforcement across the board."
Haddow also emphasized the need for consumer warnings, adding, "The American Kratom Association supports accurate labeling to warn consumers that kratom can cause dependence."
"We support stronger enforcement across the board, and excise taxes on kratom products to fund that enforcement."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
In an October interview with Fox News Digital, Haddow also backed age restrictions. "Twenty-one and up should be the only people who have access to these products," he said.
Tesluck also raised concerns about how the products are marketed, describing social media ads as looking "very harmless" or "very cool," potentially drawing consumers’ interest.
"It’s something that you might want to try just based on the marketing itself and the packaging," she warned.
Tesluck said her work regularly brings her into contact with parents grieving children whose deaths they attribute to kratom products, including in states with Kratom Consumer Protection Acts.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The FDA says no kratom drugs are approved by the agency, and that kratom cannot legally be marketed as a dietary supplement or added to conventional foods.
In December 2025, federal authorities seized approximately 73,000 concentrated 7-OH products valued at roughly $1 million from three Missouri firms, according to the FDA.
Warning signs
People taking kratom should pay attention to whether their use is beginning to dictate their daily routines, including planning around obtaining it or worrying about running out, Tesluck urged.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Like making sure when the smoke shop closes that you have enough time to get there," she said.

Diminished appetite, weight loss and hair loss were among the effects Tesluck experienced. Other signs of problematic kratom use may include cravings, higher consumption than intended, unsuccessful attempts to stop and continued use despite problems at work or home, according to the National Institute on Drug Abuse.
Kratom rules vary widely across the country, with states taking different approaches to age restrictions, product standards and bans. (Getty Images)

Feeling unable to miss a dose was another concern for Tesluck. "If I took less than what I was taking, I would feel even worse and sicker," she recalled. "So I was kind of stuck at that baseline with kratom."
Haddow acknowledged that consumers can develop dependence or addiction.
"I was kind of like a zombie shell of myself overall."
"Kratom can cause physical dependence, and some consumers have reported they develop addiction to kratom," he told Fox News Digital.
Feelings of sedation, numbness or irritability may also occur, Tesluck said.
"I was kind of like a zombie shell of myself overall," she said. "I wasn’t really the same person, personality-wise. I was irritable. I was mean."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Today, Tesluck describes herself as a "person in long-term recovery from both kratom and 7-OH addiction." She serves as executive director of End Kratom Addiction, a Virginia-based nonprofit that aims to raise awareness of kratom-related risks and advocates for stronger regulation.
"My advocacy looks a lot like meeting one-on-one with families … and coordinating resources for those who are still in addiction," she said.
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Common blood pressure drug helps more stroke survivors reach critical health target
summary: The REDUCE trial found spironolactone lowered blood pressure by nearly eight points in stroke survivors, but key questions about prevention remain.
story: Dr. Jason A. Gluck, vice chair of the Heart & Vascular Institute and system chief of cardiology at AtlantiCare in New Jersey, discusses a recent study that found stroke incidence has more than doubled among young adults.
A low-cost medication could help stroke survivors whose blood pressure remains elevated despite treatment, a new study suggests.

The research, known as the REDUCE trial, looked at whether adding spironolactone, a medication commonly known as a water pill, could help lower blood pressure after a stroke. The findings were presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions, Nov. 6-9, 2026, in Chicago.
Participants were split into two groups. One added spironolactone to their regular treatment, while the other continued with usual post-stroke care.
SIMPLE EXERCISE DONE JUST ONCE A WEEK COULD HELP LOWER BLOOD PRESSURE
Researchers tracked the participants' blood pressure at home over the following six months to determine whether adding the medication made a difference.

After three months, the top blood pressure number was nearly eight points lower on average among people taking spironolactone compared with those receiving usual care – about 126 versus 133, the study said.
Researchers found that adding spironolactone to regular post-stroke care helped lower blood pressure more than usual treatment alone. (iStock)
More patients taking spironolactone also reached the recommended blood pressure goal of less than 130/80. That included 52% of those taking the medication compared with 30% receiving usual care.

"Lowering blood pressure is the most important step in preventing another stroke, yet many survivors struggle to reach recommended blood pressure targets after a stroke," study co-lead author Dr. Jordana Cohen, an associate professor of medicine and epidemiology at the University of Pennsylvania, said in a news release.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"When spironolactone was added to post-stroke care, we saw a meaningful drop in blood pressure that may lower the risk of future strokes and heart attacks," she added.

Dr. Alfred Joshua, a California-based board-certified emergency physician and former chief medical officer who was not involved in the research, said the findings are encouraging, but do not yet show that the medication prevents a subsequent stroke.
Researchers found that 52% of patients taking spironolactone reached the recommended blood pressure goal, compared with 30% receiving usual post-stroke care. (iStock)

"We already know that controlling blood pressure lowers the risk of another stroke," Joshua told Fox News Digital. "This study measured blood pressure, so whether adding spironolactone leads to fewer repeat strokes is still an open question."

Spironolactone works by helping the body get rid of extra salt and water, which can lower blood pressure, according to the U.S. National Library of Medicine. It also causes the body to hold onto potassium, so patients taking it need to have their levels checked, the drug’s prescribing information states.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Joshua warned that high potassium is one of the main safety concerns because it can develop without symptoms. The risk can be higher for people with kidney problems and those taking certain medications or potassium supplements.
The medication can also lower blood pressure enough to cause dizziness, he added.
Spironolactone helps the body eliminate excess salt and water, which can lower blood pressure in patients who need additional treatment. (iStock)
"If your blood pressure is still high after a stroke, bring your home readings to your clinician and ask whether this medication is a good fit," Joshua advised.
Study limitations
The trial ended early with 160 participants instead of the planned 200, and about 15% did not have blood pressure readings available at the three-month mark, the researchers noted.
People taking spironolactone were also taking slightly more blood pressure medications overall than those receiving usual care.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The study was not designed to determine whether spironolactone actually prevents another stroke or heart attack. Larger and longer studies are needed to answer that question, according to the researchers.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital reached out to the researchers for comment.

title: Simple salt substitute could prevent three million deaths a year worldwide, study estimates
summary: A Nature Health study finds potassium salt substitutes could prevent nearly 3 million deaths yearly, but hyperkalemia poses risks for some patients.
story: Christopher Gardner, PhD, a nutrition scientist at Stanford University, says increasing fiber is crucial in a healthy diet and recommends eating more fruits, vegetables and minimally processed foods rather than eliminating an entire food group.

Replacing regular table salt with a potassium-enriched alternative could prevent nearly three million deaths and more than 10 million cases of heart and kidney disease worldwide every year, according to a major study published in Nature Health.

Researchers at the Australia-based George Institute for Global Health analyzed dietary patterns and disease risks among 4.6 billion adults across 193 countries to estimate the potential benefits of the switch.
The study relied on mathematical simulations rather than a clinical trial, using estimates that can vary in accuracy, the researchers acknowledged.
HIGH SALT INTAKE LINKED TO FASTER MEMORY DECLINE IN ONE GROUP, STUDY FINDS
High blood pressure affects roughly 1.4 billion adults worldwide and is a leading cause of strokes, heart attacks and chronic kidney damage, according to the World Health Organization.
Consuming too much salt can contribute to high blood pressure, as its sodium content causes the body to retain water, increasing blood volume and putting added pressure on artery walls.

Replacing regular table salt with a potassium-enriched alternative could prevent nearly three million deaths and more than 10 million new cases of heart and kidney disease worldwide annually, according to a modeling study. (iStock)

Potassium-enriched salt replaces some sodium with potassium while looking, tasting and cooking like regular salt. The swap reduces sodium intake while boosting potassium, which helps relax blood vessels and promotes the removal of excess sodium from the body, according to the researchers.
If households replaced only the salt used in home cooking and at the dining table, the model projected 1.85 million fewer deaths and 6.19 million fewer new cases of heart and kidney disease annually.
ANCIENT CHINESE MOVEMENT SHOWS PROMISE FOR REDUCING BLOOD PRESSURE AT HOME, STUDY SAYS
In another scenario, replacing salt only in restaurant meals and processed foods was projected to prevent about 1.56 million deaths and 5.46 million new disease cases annually.

In a more targeted scenario, researchers projected that switching 80% of adults with diagnosed high blood pressure to potassium-enriched household salt could prevent about 590,000 deaths worldwide each year.

If households replaced only the salt used in home cooking and at the dining table, the model projected 1.85 million fewer deaths and 6.19 million fewer new cases of heart and kidney disease annually. (iStock)

The projected benefits varied by region, depending on population size and sources of dietary sodium. The largest potential benefit was seen in China, with an estimated 1.08 million deaths averted each year under full replacement.
India followed with nearly 400,000 preventable deaths, while the U.S. could potentially avoid roughly 105,000 deaths and 492,000 new disease cases annually.
POPULAR FOOD COULD BOOST HEART HEALTH, BUT THE AMOUNT YOU NEED TO EAT MAY SURPRISE YOU

In many Asian and African countries, most dietary salt comes from home cooking, suggesting that greater awareness and access to potassium-enriched alternatives could encourage healthier habits, according to the researchers.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Broader adoption by food manufacturers and restaurants would be needed to maximize the health benefits in Western countries, where more than 70% of dietary sodium comes from processed and restaurant foods, the study suggested.

"This study shows that small changes have an enormous impact on two prominent diseases globally: cardiovascular disease and kidney disease," Dr. Nathan Goodyear of the Williams Cancer Institute in California told Fox News Digital.
While the study's models suggested that the heart health benefits outweighed the risks for the overall population, experts cautioned that the substitute may not be safe for everyone. (iStock)
Goodyear, who was not involved in the study, said the bigger take-home message is that health is "not something that we’re just born with."
"It’s something that we cultivate. It’s the environment we cultivate," he said. "And this environment influences the potential for disease harvest long before disease is diagnosed."
Potential risks
While the study's models suggested that the heart health benefits outweighed the risks for the overall population, experts cautioned that the substitute may not be safe for everyone.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Potassium-enriched salt substitutes can also pose risks, including hyperkalemia, a condition in which excess potassium builds up in the blood and can trigger dangerous irregular heart rhythms, according to the National Kidney Foundation.

Because extra potassium can trigger dangerous heart rhythms in people whose kidneys cannot filter it properly, individuals with advanced chronic kidney disease or those on certain blood pressure medications should consult a doctor before making the switch. (iStock)
The body normally removes excess potassium through urine, but people with advanced kidney disease or those taking certain blood pressure medications may have difficulty eliminating it.
The World Health Organization advises against potassium-enriched salt substitutes for people with kidney problems that impair potassium removal, unless recommended by a healthcare professional.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"We’re constantly in medicine looking for the magic bullet in causation, magic bullet in disease treatment, [but] that does not exist," said Goodyear.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Chronic diseases such as heart disease, kidney disease, diabetes and cancer often develop over time due to multiple contributing factors, the doctor noted.

Widespread adoption could also face challenges, as potassium-enriched salt costs about twice as much as regular salt on average and would require cooperation from food manufacturers and suppliers, according to the researchers.
