title: Common heart pill under scrutiny for older patients as study weighs risks of stopping
summary: A new clinical trial found 13% of older adults who stopped statins had a heart attack, stroke or died, compared with 9% who continued treatment.
story: Dr. Christopher Kelly, a UNC Health cardiologist, emphasized individualized decisions based on overall health and expected lifespan when deciding whether to continue statin use.
Some older adults may be able to stop taking statins with little added risk over two years, but a new study raises concerns about longer-term safety.

That’s according to a randomized clinical trial that was presented on Nov. 7, 2026, at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions in Chicago, and published in The New England Journal of Medicine.

Statins are prescription medications that lower LDL, or "bad," cholesterol by reducing how much cholesterol the liver makes. They are known to help reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke, according to the National Heart, Lung and Blood Institute.
COMMON CHOLESTEROL DRUG LINKED TO LOWER DEMENTIA RISK WHEN STARTED EARLY

The study — conducted by researchers from the University of Bern in Switzerland, the University of California, San Francisco, and other institutions — included 1,880 adults aged 70 years and older, all of whom were taking statins to prevent a first heart attack or stroke.
Some older adults may be able to stop taking statins with little added risk over two years, but a new study raises concerns about longer-term safety. (iStock)

All participants had at least two chronic medical conditions, but did not have established cardiovascular disease or previous cardiovascular events. Half of the participants stopped taking statins, and the other half continued.
After two years, the added risk from stopping statins was small enough to fall within the limits researchers had set for the study. However, that did not mean stopping carried no added risk.
5 HABITS THAT COULD HELP KEEP YOU OUT OF A NURSING HOME, FROM AN ORTHOPEDIC SURGEON

Over the full follow-up, which lasted about two years for the typical participant and up to four years for some, about 13% of those assigned to stop statins had a heart attack, an ischemic stroke or died from any cause, compared with 9% assigned to continue treatment.

The study’s safety monitoring board also recommended that participants who were assigned to stop statins discuss restarting treatment with their healthcare team, according to the American College of Cardiology.
Statins are prescription medications that lower LDL, or "bad," cholesterol by reducing how much cholesterol the liver makes. (iStock)
For other outcomes, the researchers found no meaningful differences between the two groups in reported quality of life, muscle pain, falls or loss of muscle mass and strength.
Dr. Christopher Kelly, a UNC Health cardiologist, emphasized that continuing statins did not worsen reported muscle pain or quality of life in the trial.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Although guidelines support lowering high cholesterol earlier in life, the benefits of continuing statins in older age are less certain, said study author Dr. Rita F. Redberg, a cardiology professor at the University of California, San Francisco, in a press release.
"This small, increased risk of cardiovascular events means that one cannot make a general recommendation about stopping statins in this patient population."
Earlier studies found no difference in mortality after adults 70 and older stopped statins for primary prevention, she noted.

"One study suggested quality of life improvements after stopping statins," Redberg said, adding that her team explored whether stopping was safe for older adults taking the drugs to prevent a first cardiovascular event.
Study limitations

The study had several limitations. About 14% of participants did not stick with their assigned treatment plan. Some who were told to stop taking statins resumed them, while others assigned to continue treatment stopped taking the drugs, according to the researchers.
The findings also may not apply to all older adults, as the study was limited to people aged 70 and older who had multiple chronic health conditions but no history of heart disease or stroke.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Although some participants were followed for up to four years, the study primarily assessed outcomes over about two years. Longer follow-up is needed to determine how stopping statins affects patients over many years.
Weighing the risks
"This small, increased risk of cardiovascular events means that one cannot make a general recommendation about stopping statins in this patient population," Redberg said.

"There should be shared decision-making between the patient and the healthcare professional to know if it is appropriate for an individual to discontinue the medication," the researcher said. (iStock)

"There should be shared decision-making between the patient and the healthcare professional to know if it is appropriate for an individual to discontinue the medication. In general, however, discontinuation is safe for most people who are in this age group and without a previous CVD event."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Kelly, who was not involved in the study, noted that a healthy 70-year-old could live another 20 years, leaving questions about the effects of stopping treatment over that longer period.
The doctor also emphasized individualized decisions based on overall health and expected lifespan, noting that he "errs on the side of caution" with his own patients.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I typically recommend that they continue taking it unless they have specific concerns about that medication, such as side effects, or if they are taking a lot of medicines, and they're just really eager to stop taking one of them."

title: White House blasts 'Trumpcare for All' pitch from far-left El-Sayed who called president 'unserious fool'
summary: White House slammed Abdul El-Sayed's "Trumpcare for All" pitch, warning the Medicare for All plan would threaten Americans' existing health coverage.
story: Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed references an AI-generated image depicting President Donald Trump as Jesus Christ while sarcastically calling the president "Habibi" to embrace "Medicare for All." (Credit: X @AbdulElSayed)

The White House blasted far-left Michigan Democrat Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed's pitch to President Donald Trump to embrace "Trumpcare for All," warning that the Medicare for All proposal would threaten Americans' existing health coverage.

"The Radical Democrats’ socialist proposal for a government takeover of healthcare should really be called ‘Medicare for None’ as it destroys access to the life-saving care Americans rely on daily," White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster told Fox News Digital.
The sharp response came after El-Sayed, who recently called Trump an "unserious fool," posted a 16-second video Tuesday urging the president to embrace the progressive proposal.
BERNIE SANDERS THINKS MEDICARE FOR ALL BILL COULD PASS, 'NOT ABSOLUTELY CERTAIN' TRUMP WOULD VETO

Democrat Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has said he'll call Medicare for All proposal "Trumpcare for All" if the president agrees to go along with it. (Evan Cobb for The Washington Post via Getty Images, File)

"I think there is a responsibility that we have to engage with [Trump] as the unserious fool that he is," El-Sayed said during a recent appearance on "Pod Save America," according to earlier Fox News Digital reporting.
Despite those remarks, the senator-elect struck a more conciliatory tone in his latest appeal.
"Donald. Habibi. Midterms were rough. I get it," El-Sayed said in the video posted Nov. 17, addressing Trump with the Arabic term "habibi," commonly translated as "my dear" or "my beloved."
"Trumpcare for All. It's really popular. People really want healthcare. You can put your name all over it."
EL-SAYED ADMITS FREE HEALTHCARE MEANS PAYING 'A LITTLE BIT MORE IN TAXES' REGARDLESS OF INCOME
Despite those calling President Trump "unserious," El-Sayed has seemingly struck a more conciliatory tone in his latest appeal. (Asra Q. Nomani/Fox News Digital, File)

The video featured a mock "Trumpcare" card and an AI-generated image depicting Trump as Jesus Christ, which El-Sayed, a Muslim, referenced while urging the president to embrace socialized, taxpayer-funded healthcare.
"Donald, this is your chance to heal the sick (like in that one AI image. You know the one)," El-Sayed said.
The White House instead pointed to Trump's efforts to lower prescription drug prices, contrasting those policies with the single-payer system advocated by El-Sayed.

"President Trump is focused on taking on the special interests that are driving up the costs of healthcare for all Americans including through his historic efforts to ensure American patients never pay more than those in other developed nations for all prescription drugs, which has already saved Americans well over $1 Billion," Schuster said.
MAJORITY OF AMERICANS BROADLY REJECT SOCIALIST IDEOLOGY EVEN AS FAR LEFT SURGES TO POWER
In response to El-Sayed, the White House said, in part, "The President will continue delivering real results that lower costs and put Americans first." (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images, File)

"The President will continue delivering real results that lower costs and put Americans first, while Democrats push ideas that have devastated economies and ruined healthcare quality anywhere they have been implemented."

The administration also cited a U.S. Council of Economic Advisers' analysis estimating that Medicare for All would increase the federal budget deficit by approximately $47.4 trillion between 2027 and 2036 in the absence of additional taxes or revenues.
The White House also cited a CEA projection that Medicare for All would shift large numbers of Americans away from employer-sponsored insurance and into a new government-run coverage system.

Medicare for All, a sweeping single-payer health care proposal championed by Democratic socialists, would replace much of the nation's private health insurance system with federally financed coverage. Supporters argue it would guarantee coverage, while critics warn of substantial tax increases and massive federal spending.

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and other far-left Democrats are in favor of Medicare for All, a single-payer health care proposal that would replace much of the nation's private health insurance system with federally financed coverage. (Erin Kirkland/Bloomberg via Getty Images, File)
El-Sayed's public appeal was not his first attempt to recruit Trump to the idea.
During a CNN appearance earlier this month, the incoming senator suggested that the president could attach his name to a universal health care proposal.
"Donald, if you're watching, we can put your name on it. I know you like to put your name on stuff," El-Sayed said, according to a Nov. 10 social media post by CNN anchor Kaitlan Collins.
The unusual overture follows a contentious Michigan Senate race in which El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Democrat also mocked Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Rogers during his election victory remarks, adding to the contrast between his earlier criticism of the administration and his latest invitation to collaborate.
El-Sayed is scheduled to take office Jan. 3, 2027.
El-Sayed's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
Fox News Digital's Leo Briceno contributed to this reporting.

title: POWs, teens among 6 US soldiers from Korean War identified seven decades later
summary: The DPAA identified six U.S. soldiers missing from the Korean War, including two teenagers, decades after they died as prisoners of war or in action.
story: Modern forensic analysis helped identify six Korean War soldiers, including two 18-year-olds and men who died as prisoners of war.
At least six U.S. soldiers who went missing during the Korean War, including two teenagers, have been identified decades after their deaths.

The soldiers, who ranged in age from 18 to 28, all served in the U.S. Army, the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency (DPAA) said. Five were junior enlisted soldiers or noncommissioned officers, including four corporals and one sergeant. The sixth was a commissioned officer, a first lieutenant.
Officials said the soldiers either died as prisoners of war or were presumed killed in action.

The soldiers identified were Cpl. Jackie Lee Thurman, 18, of Illinois; 1st Lt. Raymond Banker Gilbert, 23, of Ohio; Cpl. Richard Neal Lennox, 18, of Michigan; Cpl. William Reynold Laughlin Jr., 21, of Oregon; Sgt. Joseph Alfred Platzkoester, 28, of Illinois; and Cpl. Andrew R. Tischler, 21, of Celina, Texas.
EXPERTS FINALLY SOLVE MYSTERY OF TEENAGE REVOLUTIONARY WAR SOLDIER 246 YEARS AFTER HIS DEATH

Cpl. Jackie Lee Thurman, 18, (left) went missing while attempting to escort a wounded officer, while 1st Lt. Raymond Banker Gilbert, 23, (right) died as a prisoner of war.  (Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency)

Most of the soldiers had been buried for decades as "Unknowns" at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific, also known as the Punchbowl, in Honolulu, Hawaii. Their remains were later disinterred through DPAA initiatives between 2016 and 2024 and sent to the agency's laboratory for modern forensic analysis.
Gilbert, a member of Battery B, 503rd Field Artillery Battalion, 2nd Infantry Division, was wounded and captured before being reported missing on Dec. 1, 1950.
He died from his wounds as a prisoner of war on Jan. 31, 1951.
His remains were returned in 1954 and buried as an Unknown in Honolulu. They were disinterred in July 2024, and he was officially identified on June 4, 2026.
‘FREEDOMS ARE NEVER FREE’: A JEWISH AMERICAN SOLDIER BURIED WITH NAZIS FINALLY LAID TO REST WITH US TROOPS

Thurman, a member of Battery B, 99th Field Artillery Battalion, 1st Cavalry Division, went missing on Sept. 3, 1950, while attempting to escort a wounded officer under heavy mortar fire near Taegu and Waegwan, South Korea.
His remains were eventually recovered in 1952 and buried as an Unknown in Honolulu. They were disinterred in November 2022, and he was officially identified on May 18, 2026.
Lennox, a member of Company C, 1st Battalion, 7th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division, was reported missing on Nov. 28, 1950, following an enemy attack near Sachang-ni, North Korea.
He was captured and taken to Prisoner of War Camp 1 in Changsong, where he died nearly a year later in October 1951.
His remains were returned in 1954 and buried as an Unknown in Honolulu. They remained there until they were disinterred on June 13, 2016. He was officially identified on Aug. 7, 2025.
Cpl. William Reynold Laughlin Jr., 21, went missing Dec. 2, 1950, during a withdrawal near the Chosin Reservoir. (Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency)
Laughlin Jr., a member of Company D, 1st Battalion, 32nd Infantry Regiment, 7th Infantry Division, went missing on Dec. 2, 1950, during a withdrawal near the Chosin Reservoir.
He was never reported as a prisoner of war, and the Army issued a presumptive finding of death on Dec. 31, 1953.
His remains were returned in 1954 and buried as an Unknown in Honolulu. They were disinterred in July 2022, and he was officially identified on Sept. 28, 2026.
People visit the Korean War Veterans Memorial in Washington, D.C., which honors Americans who served during the conflict. (Bill O'Leary/The Washington Post via Getty Images)
Platzkoester, a member of Company H, 2nd Battalion, 38th Infantry Regiment, 2nd Infantry Division, went missing on May 30, 1951, during a convoy ambush near Inje, South Korea.
The Army issued a presumptive finding of death in December 1953 and declared his remains unrecoverable in January 1956.
Unbeknownst to officials at the time, his remains had already been recovered in the fall of 1951 and later buried as an Unknown in Honolulu in 1956.
They were disinterred in November 2023, and he was officially identified on May 29, 2026.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Tischler, a member of Company F, 2nd Battalion, 15th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division, was reported missing in action on May 25, 1951, during a road march near Taewol Village, South Korea.
The DPAA officially accounted for him on May 5, 2026.
Each soldier is memorialized on both the Courts of the Missing in Honolulu and the Korean War Veterans Memorial Wall in Washington, D.C.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Senior US official undercuts CNN’s alarming Iran ‘dirty bomb’ report: ‘It’s not new’
summary: President Donald Trump warned Iran would pay a price "no country has ever paid" if a dirty bomb threat to Washington, D.C., proves real, amid divided assessments.
story: President Donald Trump warned Iran on Monday that it would face unprecedented retaliation if it were to carry out an attack on Washington, D.C.

A senior U.S. official is challenging a new report on Iran developing plans for a "dirty bomb" attack on Washington, D.C., which drew a warning of overwhelming retaliation from President Donald Trump this week.

The prospect of Iranian-directed violence on American soil has shadowed U.S. security officials for decades. From a plot to bomb a Washington restaurant to assassination schemes targeting former officials and dissidents, Tehran has repeatedly sought ways to reach its enemies inside U.S. borders.
"I’m not sure why this was leaked because it’s not new," a senior U.S. official told Fox News' Jennifer Griffin in response to the report.
"Iran is very aspirational, but not suicidal. If they were to attack D.C. or any other U.S. city it would cause us to have a full out war with them. Their friends would not come to their aid."

CNN reported this week that U.S. intelligence indicated Iran was developing potential plans to target senior Trump administration officials in Washington with a radiological device or chemical weapon.

Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps officers attend a memorial ceremony for IRGC commanders, nuclear scientists and civilians killed in the Iran-Israel war at the Imam Khomeini Grand Mosque in downtown Tehran on July 2, 2025. (Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
BESSENT MOVED TO MILITARY BASE AS IRAN THREATS EXCEED ‘ADVANCED STAGE,’ OFFICIAL SAYS
Sources described the planning as an effort to develop options rather than evidence of an imminent attack, with officials divided over whether Tehran could or would execute it.
"We’re looking into it," Trump said in Manila on Tuesday when asked about the new report.
Pressed on whether Washington faced an imminent threat, he warned: "Well, if there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before."
"I hope it’s not, but we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," the president added.
White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said, "We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland."

Iran could make a dirty bomb, but would need someone inside the United States with the expertise to handle the materials and carry out an attack, said Andrea Stricker, deputy director of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies’ nonproliferation program.
A dirty bomb combines conventional explosives with radioactive material, spreading contamination without producing a nuclear explosion.
The White House is seen from the Washington Monument on Nov. 4, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)
U.S. authorities have spent nearly two decades building defenses against that possibility.
DHS launched its Securing the Cities program in 2007 to help local agencies detect and deter nuclear and radiological threats, including dirty bombs, beginning in the New York City region.
"Making a radiological dispersal device would be within Iran’s know-how, as well as a chemical weapon," Stricker told Fox News Digital.
Iran’s chemical weapons program dates back to the 1980s. "More recently, they've been looking at how to weaponize chemical weapons like fentanyl and disperse them through the air," Stricker said.
Fentanyl can suppress breathing to the point of respiratory arrest.
"I think for an attack using chemical weapons like this, they would probably want to go with something rudimentary. Industrial scale chemicals like chlorine would be easy to obtain," she added.
President Donald Trump. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)
IRAN-BACKED TERROR SUSPECTS PLOTTED ATTACK ON US TROOPS USING VANS PACKED WITH FUEL, DOJ SAYS
Rather than risk transporting hazardous materials into the country, Tehran could look to obtain them here, she said.
"They may want to simply try to steal them or procure them from inside the United States. That would probably ease their task," Stricker said.
But the technical demands would complicate Iran’s reliance on hired criminals to execute its operations.
"In the past, they've used sort of everyday criminals for hire to execute some of their other plots, and luckily we foiled a lot of these," she said.

Fox News’ Jennifer Griffin contributed to this report.

title: Judge fires back at Fani Willis' office in courtroom clash over Trump case: 'Due process doesn't apply to you'
summary: A Georgia appeals judge grilled Fani Willis' office over its bid to challenge nearly $17 million in legal-fee requests from Trump and other ex-defendants.
story: Willis’ office argued it should be allowed to defend its budget as President Donald Trump and other former defendants seek nearly $17 million in legal-fee reimbursements, but an appeals judge said the office was not entitled to due process.

A Georgia appellate judge pressed Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis’ office Tuesday as it pushed for permission to fight millions in legal-fee requests from President Donald Trump and other former defendants in her collapsed election interference case.

Before a three-judge panel, Willis’ office argued it should be allowed to protect its budget from payments stemming from a prosecution she and her office were disqualified from handling in December 2024.

"What process are you entitled to? You’re the government. Due process doesn’t apply to you," Judge J. Wade Padgett told Donald Wakeford, a chief senior assistant district attorney representing Willis’ office.

Trump and other former defendants are seeking nearly $17 million under a Georgia law passed last year, with Trump alone requesting more than $6 million. The law allows defendants to recover legal fees if their prosecutor is removed for improper conduct and their charges are later dismissed.
MIKE DAVIS: CALIFORNIA'S HIGHEST COURT DISGRACES ITSELF BY UPHOLDING DISBARMENT OF JOHN EASTMAN

President Donald Trump (left) and Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis (right). Prosecutors in Georgia are seeking more time to appoint a new attorney after Willis was disqualified from handling Trump’s election interference case. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images; Alex Slitz-Pool/Getty Images)
Tuesday’s hearing focused on whether Willis’ office could participate in challenging those requests.

The state is represented in the reimbursement fight by Pete Skandalakis, executive director of the Prosecuting Attorneys’ Council of Georgia, who took over after Willis’ disqualification and moved to dismiss the charges in November 2025.

Willis’ office argued he cannot adequately protect its financial interests because his own decision to drop the case opened the door to the reimbursement requests. Wakeford also argued that Skandalakis’ authority in the case ended when the prosecution did.
"This statute has created a mess and that is no secret," Wakeford said of the new Georgia law allowing defendants to seek reimbursement for their legal fees.
The judges pressed him on whether Willis’ disqualification still bars her office from participating.
MIKE DAVIS: DISGRACED GEORGIA JUDGE MUST LEAVE THE BENCH OVER SEX SCANDAL

Special prosecutors Nathan Wade, left, and Daysha Young talk amongst themselves during a hearing on the Georgia election interference case, on March 1, 2024, in Atlanta, Georgia.  (Alex Slitz / Getty Images)
"So let’s talk about the elephant in the room then," Padgett said, pointing to the court’s earlier ruling declaring the district attorney wholly disqualified.
"The criminal prosecution has ended," Wakeford responded, arguing that the fee dispute is a separate matter.
"Is the disqualification over? Is she no longer wholly disqualified?" Judge Ken Hodges asked.
Wakeford said that Willis’ disqualification applied to the criminal prosecution, arguing it did not bar her office from participating in the separate legal-fee dispute.
But the panel also questioned whether that finding satisfies the new law’s requirements for reimbursement.
CALIFORNIA HIGH COURT ORDERS DISBARRING OF FORMER TRUMP ATTORNEY OVER EFFORT TO DISPUTE 2020 ELECTION RESULTS
Fani Willis, Fulton County District Attorney, at the Fulton County Courthouse in Atlanta, Georgia, US, on Friday, March 1, 2024.  (Alex Slitz/AP/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"The trial judge found an appearance of impropriety and found that actual misconduct had not been established," Padgett said.

Willis and her office were removed from the case after an appeals court found that her romantic relationship with Nathan Wade, the special prosecutor she appointed, created an appearance of impropriety.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

In March, Fulton County Superior Court Judge Scott McAfee denied Willis’ request to intervene, finding that Skandalakis could adequately represent her office’s interests. Her office is asking the appeals court to overturn that decision.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The court announced no ruling during Tuesday’s hearing, leaving unresolved whether Willis’ office can directly challenge the fee requests.
Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: Dems campaign promise to freeze energy costs faces glaring reality check
summary: Sam Romain of Americans for Energy Dominance says Democrats' energy price controls, from Gina Hinojosa's Texas rate freeze to state caps, can't fix supply.
story: Sam Romain, chairman of Americans for Energy Dominance, believes Democrats will have no choice but to grapple with supply-side policy challenges once their commitments stall

Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa is preparing her first step into left-leaning policies in the historically deep red state by implementing an emergency utility rate freeze — but one expert worries the proposal will become a failed attempt to address the affordability crisis.

More Democratic-led states are looking to impose similar plans to Hinojosa's after she said on Day One of being governor that she will freeze residential electricity rates, an idea that many warn clashes with Texas’ uniquely competitive energy sector and could inadvertently create energy shortages.

"It's a campaign promise they made on the trail," Sam Romain, chairman of the free market group Americans for Energy Dominance, told Fox News Digital. "But they don't have the power to just freeze the rates. You can't just wave a magic wand and freeze the rates."
DEMOCRAT GINA HINOJOSA STUNS ABBOTT, MAKES HISTORY AS FIRST LATINA TEXAS GOVERNOR
Gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa speaks to members of the media during a block walk campaign event in San Antonio, Texas, on Nov. 1, 2026. (Christopher Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Romain believes it’s only a matter of time before Democrats across the country have to wrestle with ways to increase energy production — even as they are currently exploring a variety of energy price controls.
"We know that price works based on supply and demand, right? It's basic, basic economics," Romain said.

"And what you're seeing across the nation is this Democratic price control scheme that's dressed up as an emergency. The problem is you can't necessarily freeze your way out of the supply problems," Romain added.
Some Democratic-led strategies aim to lock down energy prices while others look to subsidize them. Some plans call for both.

In one such case, Democrat Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, who took office in January, is demanding a six-year rate freeze as a Florida company looks to buy Virginia’s largest energy supplier. She has also called for "a tripling of monthly bill credits for ratepayers."

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill promised to declare a state of emergency to cap energy rates at the outset of her term in January 2026, but has since pivoted to implement a credit system to offset electricity costs using executive orders.

Among the newly elected Democrats, California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra promised to "institute a freeze on utility rates… while the state investigates long-term solutions to bring these costs under control," a strategy he framed as a priority.

In Wisconsin, Democratic Gov.-elect David Crowley will lead a legislature that last year entertained a proposal to cap gas and electricity bills at 4% of a qualifying household’s annual income. Crowley himself has also proposed a similar "fair deal" plan that would cap annual rent increases at 7%.
DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT
Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger pushed her party to pass the ballot initiative. (Maxine Wallace/The Washington Post/Getty Images)
And in Ohio, Democratic state leadership led by House Minority Leader Dani Isaacsohn has proposed a 12-month freeze on utility rates as Amy Acton prepares to take the gubernatorial mansion.
To Romain, these proposals deal a twofold blow.

In addition to failing to build out supply, he believes they also discourage additional production. "A freeze in and of itself doesn't actually build anything. Actually, it does almost the opposite. It discourages developers from building. They don't know if they're going to be able to recoup their profit margin on their construction," Romain said.

Questions also remain about the legality of some of the plans. In Texas, for instance, experts have noted that Hinojosa’s planned use of an emergency declaration may quickly run into legal resistance.

Nick Loris, the president of C3 Solutions, a conservative coalition for climate solutions that focuses on energy, environment and agriculture policy, questioned the emergency powers Hinojosa says she plans to use.

"The Texas Disaster Act lets the governor declare disasters and suspend the regulatory laws and statutes that are in existence. But I think there is a high degree of skepticism, both from courts, but also from state policymakers, that this warrants such a claim — and that it is such a disaster," Loris said.

Romain believes Democrats will face similar legal hurdles in other states. But even though he expects price-control strategies to stall, Romain believes that creates an opportunity: fertile ground for a bipartisan affordability strategy as Democrats look to keep their commitments.
"Democrats know there's a supply-side issue," Romain said.
LIZ PEEK: DEMOCRATS’ AFFORDABILITY SCAM COLLAPSES IN STATES THEY ACTUALLY RUN
Gov. Mikie Sherrill speaks in the Assembly Chamber of the New Jersey State House in Trenton on March 10, 2026. (Heather Khalifa/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"Their solution to it is different than the Republicans'… And the solution is quite simply to just let American companies build and compete. The problem is to unleash American innovation. This country was built by builders, right? And so let our companies build the tools they need, let them build the generation sites, let them build the power plants," Romain said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Permitting reform is one area in particular he believes may soon turn into an area for cooperation, a deregulation of the rules that govern energy production.
"I'm actually really optimistic… that we're going to have a massive permit reform package done very quickly, very soon, actually," Romain said.
"I think that we have a massive opportunity in front of us."
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Warren grills Trump Navy secretary on cost of Iran war: 'You don't have any idea?'
summary: Elizabeth Warren pressed acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao on the Iran war blockade's cost as he dodged questions and urged funding to reach 355 ships.
story: Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., grilled acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao over the cost of the Iran war during his confirmation hearing on Tuesday.
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., grilled acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao over the cost of the Iran war during his confirmation hearing on Tuesday.

Warren repeatedly pressed Cao on how much U.S. taxpayers were spending to support the U.S. Navy's blockade on Iranian ports as well as recovering from damage sustained in the conflict. Cao dodged multiple questions, stating that assessments were ongoing or he simply didn't have access to the data.
"Acting Secretary Cao what is the daily cost of the U.S. naval blockade on Iranian ports?" Warren asked.
TRUMP'S $88B IRAN WAR BILL COLLIDES WITH SENATE OPPOSITION
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, speaks during a Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing in Washington, Jan. 14, 2025. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"Senator, I do not know the daily cost, ma'am," Cao responded.
"You don't have any idea. You've been running this thing since April and you don't have any idea what that costs," Warren pressed.
IRAN WAR'S PRICE TAG HITS $80B — MORE THAN DOUBLE WHAT CONGRESS WAS TOLD
"Well, senator, I know the rough cost of how much it's costing us so far. But again, the cost of losing the strait–," Cao said.
Warren cut him off, "I'm not asking you that. I just want to have the dollars here. Independent estimates are about $32.5 million a day. Does that sound about right to you?"

Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao testifies during the Senate Armed Services Committee hearing titled "The Posture of the Department of the Navy in review of the Defense Authorization Request for FY2027 and the Future Years Defense Program," in Dirksen building on Tuesday, May 19, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
BLOCKADE 101: AMERICAN SEA POWER ON DISPLAY AS TRUMP CORNERS IRAN AND WARNS OFF CHINA
"Senator, let me do some quick Asian math in my head. But yes, it's about $30 billion so far," he confirmed.
"So you you confirm that number, and that means the American taxpayers are spending about $1 billion a month just on this blockade," she said.
RO KHANNA PITCHES $1,700 CHECKS FOR AMERICANS TO OFFSET IRAN WAR COSTS: 'A CHANCE TO DELIVER'
Warren then moved on to the Iranian attack on the U.S. Navy's base in Bahrain, but Cao once again said he did not know the cost, saying the assessment is still ongoing.
The Senator referenced an estimate from the Wall Street Journal placing the cost at roughly $400 million. When asked if it was accurate, Cao said simply, "I'll find out."
COST OF IRAN WAR EXPLODES AS TOLL ON US AIR FLEET NEARLY DOUBLES
The USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72), a Nimitz-class nuclear-powered aircraft carrier, is shown at Naval Air Station North Island in San Diego, Calif., on Aug. 11, 2025. (Mike Blake/Reuters)
Warren went on to say that the U.S. should not "spend another cent" on the war in Iran, noting the total estimated cost of the war provided by the Pentagon is over $47 billion.
Cao urged lawmakers to approve further funding for the Navy throughout Tuesday's hearing. He argued that the U.S. is in a "1939 moment," and must "be able to build like we did back in World War II."
THIRD US AIRCRAFT CARRIER ARRIVES IN MIDDLE EAST AS IRAN RULES OUT UN NUCLEAR INSPECTIONS
He said the U.S. Navy currently has roughly 280 active vessels, but he said the country needs to surge up to 355.
U.S. Central Command released this photo on Feb. 24, saying, "Sailors and Marines aboard USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN 72) regularly perform maintenance to keep aircraft mission-ready." (CENTCOM)

Several lawmakers shared concerns about reports of poor morale and mental health among sailors due to long deployments for the Iran war. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., highlighted eight suicide attempts aboard vessels in the USS Abraham Lincoln's carrier strike group, blasting Cao's characterization that there had been eight "mitigated" suicides.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Cao argued that the long deployments seen in the Iran war are due to a lack of available vessels, once again urging lawmakers to approve funding to bolster U.S. fleets.
Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

title: Obama-appointed judge paves way to unseal Ilhan Omar search warrant in blow to Trump's DOJ
summary: A federal judge in Washington, D.C., paved the way to unseal the criminal search warrant and related documents against Rep. Ilhan Omar.
story: White House 'border czar' Tom Homan joins 'America Reports' to discuss federal probes into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., the threat of migrant caravans and more.

A federal judge in Washington, D.C. who has often ruled against the Trump administration dealt a blow to the Justice Department Tuesday, paving the way to unseal the criminal search warrant and related documents against Rep. Ilhan Omar.

Judge James Boasberg, who was appointed to the bench by former President Barack Obama in 2011, asked the DOJ's attorneys to submit proposed redactions to the documents, excluding the main affidavit, by Friday. Unless a higher court intervenes, the court will publish the redacted documents online Monday beginning at 5 p.m. after consulting with prosecutors.
After its release, the groups seeking the documents have until Nov. 30 to challenge any blacked-out sections.

While criminal warrants aren't typically unsealed until after charges are filed, 15 media organizations and watchdog group Judicial Watch sued to obtain the warrant. They have argued that releasing the contents of the warrant is in the public interest.
Rep. Ilhan Omar poses for a portrait in her office on Capitol Hill on Dec. 10, 2025. (Demetrius Freeman/The Washington Post via Getty Images)
'RADICAL LEFT LUNATIC' JUDGE TRUMP WANTED IMPEACHED TAKES UP ILHAN OMAR WARRANT FIGHT
The plaintiffs argued specifically that it should be made public which statutes federal investigators think Omar may have broken.
Boasberg signaled that he would not release the warrant application, which is a sworn statement submitted to a judge explaining facts and evidence that establish probable cause for issuing a warrant.
The DOJ did not immediately return Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Omar is facing a probe related to whether she or her father fraudulently filled out immigration paperwork in order for her to obtain citizenship. The Somali-born congresswoman said last week that she wasn't privy to what exactly the DOJ is investigating.

During the raid, which was conducted by Homeland Security Investigations (HIS), Omar's personal cellphone, computer and passport were seized. Her DNA has also been obtained, and her sister, Sahra Noor, was questioned by investigators the week of the raid.
FEDERAL AGENTS SEIZE PHONE OF REP ILHAN OMAR IN RAID TIED TO IMMIGRATION FRAUD PROBE

Homeland Security Investigations police search the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on Oct. 12, 2026, in Washington, D.C. According to reports, the search is part of an ongoing criminal investigation. (Andrew Leyden/Getty Images)

In a motion seeking to prevent the federal search warrant for the congresswoman’s home from being unsealed, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia referred to Omar as "Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar…" and sources later told Fox News Digital that Ilhan Omar is not the congresswoman's "real name."
That news caused speculation that Omar married her brother, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, to resurface. The pair married in 2009, and officially divorced in 2017.
ILHAN OMAR APPEARS CLUELESS ON BASIS FOR FEDERAL PROBES: ‘YOU PROBABLY HAVE MORE DETAILS ON THAT’

Omar has not been charged with a crime and has repeatedly and categorically denied any wrongdoing. She has characterized the investigation as politically motivated, saying President Donald Trump is targeting her.

But the DOJ under former President Barack Obama opened an investigation into Omar's marriage with Nur Said Elmi in 2016 — suggesting the nonpartisan nature of some of the inquiries into the Minnesota lawmaker.
Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., and Rep. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., speak during a news conference on Capitol Hill on Jan. 25, 2023, in Washington, D.C. (Jabin Botsford/The Washington Post via Getty Images)
OBAMA BACKS ILHAN OMAR AMID PROBE, ACCUSES TRUMP ADMIN OF 'APPALLING' TARGETING IN LENGTHY STATEMENT

The New York Times first reported that Obama's FBI and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) began the probe in the summer of 2016, and that officials "found some evidence that [the marriage] was fraudulent." The Times reported that the investigation concluded when officials decided the potential felony crime was past the statute of limitations.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
That probe, an official told Fox News Digital, remained open until 2021, when it was closed under the Biden administration.
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Sen Rand Paul and Sen-elect Andy Barr back Rep James Comer for Kentucky governor
summary: Sen. Rand Paul and Rep. Andy Barr both backed Rep. James Comer for Kentucky governor after the congressman announced a gubernatorial bid.
story: Rep. James Comer, R-Ky., discusses Democrats’ calls to impeach and investigate their political opponents and President Donald Trump on ‘The Ingraham Angle.’
Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., and Sen.-elect Andy Barr, R-Ky., are both backing Rep. James Comer, R-Ky., for Kentucky governor.
"I’m proud to endorse my friend @JamesComer to be Kentucky’s next Governor! Please help him to get there!" Paul declared in a Monday night post on X.
Barr, a House Republican who just won a U.S. Senate contest during the midterms, also threw his support behind Comer's candidacy.
JAMES COMER LAUNCHES BID FOR KENTUCKY GOVERNOR
Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. (Pete Kiehart/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"No one will fight harder for Kentucky families, Kentucky farmers, and Kentucky's future than my friend James Comer. Kentucky conservatives have built a strong legislature, and now we need a Governor who will work with them, not against them," Barr said in a Tuesday statement.

"With James Comer in the Governor's mansion, we'll finish the job on eliminating the state income tax and unleash Kentucky energy producers to lower costs and create jobs. I'm proud to stand with James Comer for Governor," he added.
MASSIE'S PUSH TO IMPEACH HEGSETH SPLITS CONSTITUENTS IN HIS OWN BACKYARD: 'PURE SPITE'
Rep. Andy Barr, R-Ky., leaves the House Republican Conference caucus meeting in the U.S. Capitol on Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Comer, who has served in the House of Representatives for a decade, just won re-election during the midterms. The lawmaker, who chairs the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, announced a Bluegrass State gubernatorial bid on Monday.
He previously ran for Kentucky governor in 2015, but lost the GOP gubernatorial primary by only 83 votes.
The state's 2027 race for governor will take place in slightly less than a year, and the primary is set for May 18.
GOP FISCAL HAWK SOUNDS ALARM ON 'OUT OF CONTROL' FEDERAL SPENDING, SAYING 'BOTH PARTIES HAVE FAILED US'

From right, then-Senate candidate Rep. Andy Barr, R-Ky., then House candidate Ralph Alvarado, Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., and KC Crosbie, co-chair of the RNC, attend a Get Out the Vote rally hosted by the Republican Party of Kentucky in Lexington, Ky., on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Current Gov. Andy Beshear, a Democrat who is currently serving his second term, is ineligible to serve a third-consecutive term. Kentucky's state constitution stipulates, "The Governor shall be ineligible for the succeeding four years after the expiration of any second consecutive term for which he shall have been elected."
Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Sherrill commits $20.2M to deportation defense while condemning Rutgers over Border Patrol speaker
summary: Mikie Sherrill condemned Rutgers College Republicans over a Gregory Bovino event while pouring $20.2 million into New Jersey's deportation defense program.
story: Chief Border Patrol Agent Greg Bovino addresses the status of Kilmar Abrego Garcia and of operations in New Orleans on ‘Jesse Watters Primetime.’

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill put her money where her mouth was this week as the Democrat criticized Rutgers University’s College Republican chapter for hosting a top former Border Patrol leader around the same time her administration allocated millions to a program meant to help illegal immigrants and others in the state fight deportation.

Sherrill’s condemnation of the Rutgers students’ event drew criticism on X from observers who said it fueled protests outside the New Brunswick building where retired Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino spoke. Protests erupted inside the room as well, with video from inside showing Bovino responding to shouting protesters before he was briefly led out of the forum.

"Everyone in this country is entitled to due process and a fair hearing under the law — regardless of where they were born," Sherrill said Friday in announcing a total of $20.2 million to fund the Detention Deportation Defense Initiative within Trenton’s Office of New Americans.
NJ TAXPAYERS ON THE HOOK FOR $12M MORE AS DEM GOVERNOR PROTECTS ILLEGAL ALIENS BATTLING DEPORTATION

Some of the funds will help migrants held at Delaney Hall in Essex County, where nightly protests have erupted since May. The governor previously visited the facility in solidarity with the detainees inside, while Sherrill ally Sen. Andy Kim, D-N. J., drew widespread attention online after being caught in a cloud of pepper spray dispersed by ICE toward surrounding protesters.

"With the Trump Administration ramping up ICE activity and creating impossible obstacles for people facing detention and deportation to navigate alone, New Jersey is stepping up to connect residents with qualified legal counsel and equip more attorneys to take on this vital work," Sherrill said Friday, adding that the state’s immigrant community should not have to face a "complex" legal system alone.

Commissioner Stephen Cha, head of Sherrill’s Department of Human Services, where the Office of New Americans sits, added in a statement that access to legal representation upholds due process and promotes a more "efficient" immigration system.

The $20.2 million will be spread among 10 service providers and continue the Murphy-era initiative’s mission to offer legal expertise and representation for "low-income residents facing detention and deportation."
EXCLUSIVE VIDEO: DEMS SLAMMED FOR DEMANDING ‘FIVE-STAR ACCOMMODATIONS’ FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS AT ICE FACILITY

Protesters yell at then-U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino and federal agents during an earlier immigration enforcement operation in Minnesota. Protests also erupted inside and outside a Rutgers University building when Bovino spoke there Monday. (Armando L. Sanchez/Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)
Sherrill’s new cash infusion nearly tripled the initiative’s most recent budget allocation.

After Sherrill announced plans in June to increase the deportation defense initiative’s funding, Republicans in the state warned that the money could be better spent elsewhere, including on New Jersey residents.

"New Jersey families are being crushed by some of the highest electric bills, property taxes, and costs of living in the entire country, and Governor Sherrill's answer is to spend more than $20 million defending illegal immigrants," said outgoing Rep. Jeff Van Drew, R-N.J., who was unseated by Cape May Mayor Zachary Mullock in this month’s blue wave.

"It is a complete insult to every hardworking taxpayer in this state. New Jersey citizens should come first. If they can find $20 million for immigration lawyers, they can find money to lower utility delivery charges or provide relief to the people who actually live, work and pay taxes here."
Van Drew said in June that every dollar Trenton spends on an illegal immigrant is a dollar that could have helped keep a New Jersey family from leaving the state.

A DHS spokesperson said Sherrill has "consistently shown more concern for criminal illegal aliens who've broken our laws and destroyed any possibility of ever remaining in our country than she ever has for Rachel Morin, Laken Riley, Jocelyn Nungaray and the true victims of illegal alien crimes in America," while adding it does not comment specifically on matters involving former personnel like Bovino.
Fox News Digital reached out to Sherrill for comment.
Sherrill had publicly condemned Bovino and Rutgers’ College Republicans for holding the event.

Rutgers is New Jersey’s state university, and the governor appoints some of its board members. Delaware Valley radio host Rich Zeoli said the state gives the New Brunswick school about $1.4 billion annually, adding the argument can be made she is "using a classic intimidation tactic to silence speech she doesn't like."
MARKWAYNE MULLIN GOES OFF ON DEMS’ 'GARBAGE' MEMORIAL DAY ‘POLITICAL STUNT’ AT ICE FACILITY

A file photo shows a Rutgers University campus in New Jersey. Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill criticized the university’s College Republican chapter for hosting retired Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino in New Brunswick. (Eduardo Munoz/Reuters)

Sherrill urged attendees to press Bovino on why he chooses "cruelty over humanity" and what he thinks of the November election results and the argument that they represent a collective rebuke of his enforcement approach.
The North Carolina native shot back at Sherrill, saying her statement was "spoken like a true lib who puts illegal aliens before her own citizens."
"Gubner, I am deeply disappointed in your penchant for using the Governor’s Office to limit Constitutional rights of Americans," Bovino said in a statement.

"This coming from someone who cheated at the Naval Academy (you weren’t allowed to walk), and enriched yourself via insider trading in defense stocks as a Congressgirl — priceless." Sherrill has said she was barred from walking at the graduation not because she was involved in cheating but because she declined to identify classmates involved.

New Jersey State Assemblyman Paul Kanitra, R-Point Pleasant Beach, said Sherrill’s criticism of Bovino contrasts with her silence over Democrats electing a candidate in the state who was once acquaintances with the mastermind behind the 1993 World Trade Center bombing.
"The thought-police strike again," Kanitra said.

"I didn’t see you weighing in when any Adam Hamawy said some pretty heinous things recently? That didn’t seem to warrant a tweet," he said, referring to the Mercer County doctor and former defense trial witness for the Blind Sheikh who won the race to succeed retiring Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, D-N.J.

Hamawy was never charged with any wrongdoing in connection with Abdel-Rahman, and his campaign previously told Fox News Digital related criticisms amount to "guilt-by-association" shaming and that Republicans and right-wing press are simply concerned that Hamawy will be "Donald Trump's worst nightmare."
Bovino later challenged Sherrill to attend his event, which the governor did not attend.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
"Tell you what, come on down to Rutgers and put your insider-trading money where your mouth is. You won’t be able to cheat your way through this one."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Sherrill’s 2025 gubernatorial campaign previously denied the stock-trading allegation raised by Bovino, which stemmed from Republican challenger Jack Ciattarelli’s claim that she "cash[ed] in to the tune of $7 million" by "flipping stocks" while in Congress.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: Mamdani takes swipe at Trump administration's response to tech outages: 'Far from what many wanted to hear'
summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Tuesday blasted the federal government's response to multiple technical outages that impacted Americans.
story: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani takes a swipe at the Trump administration following multiple technical issues that halted flights, email services and online banking platforms across the U.S.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani took a swipe at the Trump administration Tuesday following days of tech outages sweeping the nation, saying that "the response that we heard from federal officials was far from what many wanted to hear."
Mamdani spoke after the U.S. experienced a slew of technology disruptions that halted flights, email services and online banking platforms across the country.

"What I will say to New Yorkers is both an understanding of their frustration, we are speaking about New Yorkers who had made plans for months, some of them years, about going on a trip with their family or coming home from a trip with their family. And frankly, the response that we heard from federal officials was far from what many wanted to hear," Mamdani said.

"And it did not leave many New Yorkers with any greater sense of confidence about our national capabilities in case of this occurring again," he continued. "And I'm looking forward to seeing Democratic majorities in the House and the Senate utilize that power to also ensure that we're delivering more answers at a national level, because what we were hearing from some of the secretaries that day was in no way confidence building."
DUFFY VOWS TO MODERNIZE AGING AIR TRAFFIC SYSTEM AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP
The White House, when asked by Fox News Digital for comment, referred to remarks that Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton made to FOX Business on Tuesday.
"We do not see the indicia of a coordinated cyberattack — let me just be clear about that — and we do not see the indicia of state-sponsored activity here," Clayton said on "The Claman Countdown."
"And we can be fairly confident in that because we know those things exist and we have been looking for them in the past," Clayton continued.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said two routers from Federal Aviation Administration facilities in Texas and Arkansas are undergoing extensive testing as investigators examine whether faulty equipment or an installation problem triggered the nation's longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years this past Friday.
The shutdown occurred as contractor L3Harris was replacing aging copper wiring with fiber-optic technology in the FAA's communications system.

Duffy then said during an appearance on Fox News' "Hannity" Monday that he plans to modernize America’s aging air traffic control system and build new architecture that is "worthy of America." The secretary also said intelligence agencies found no evidence of a cyberattack.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks during a press conference at Athens Square Park on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, in New York City. (Getty Images)
DHS CHIEF TELLS AMERICANS TO 'BREATHE' AMID TECH OUTAGES, INSISTS HOMELAND IS 'SECURE'

The roughly five-hour ground stop affected more than 1.5 million passengers whose flights were scheduled to depart on Friday afternoon and evening. More than 12,000 flights were canceled that day, according to the FAA, while delays and cancellations continued through the weekend.
Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin also said Monday on "Hannity" that "the homeland is secure.
"Our banking system is secure and when something like this happens, we’re able to react and react fast," Mullin continued.

Mullin’s remarks came as customers Monday reported trouble accessing online services of major U.S. banking platforms, including Wells Fargo, Chase, U.S. Bank and Bank of America. United Airlines also faced a widespread system outage on Monday that briefly affected departing flights.

Passengers wait at boarding gates at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Washington, D.C., on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) had issued a ground stop at all U.S. airports due to a communications problem. (Zina Desmazes/AFP via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Mullin maintained that the incidents were not a result of cyberattacks and described the disruptions as "individually unrelated."
Fox News Digital's Nora Moriarty, Stephen Sorace and Landon Mion contributed to this report.
Greg Norman is a reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: NSA's highly classified communications network disrupted by widespread outage
summary: The National Security Agency's classified NSA Net faces an intermittent outage, with staggered arrivals preventing tens of thousands of logins at once.
story: 'Fox & Friends' examines major technology outages disrupting services nationwide after consecutive system failures hit Chase Bank and United Airlines during a 90-minute ground stop. Theresa Payton, the Fortalice Solutions CEO, joins the program to analyze the critical infrastructure concerns. The national security expert outlines essential preparedness steps following multiple high-profile tech disruptions.

The National Security Agency's internal classified communications network is experiencing an "intermittent outage," but critical communications remain intact, a person familiar with the matter told Fox News Digital on Tuesday.
The disruption affects a highly classified network known as NSA Net, which agency personnel use to communicate classified information internally.

The latest impact at one of the nation's most sensitive intelligence agencies also comes amid a string of technology outages affecting major U.S. institutions, from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to Microsoft and major banks, raising fresh concerns about the reliability of critical communications infrastructure.
DHS CHIEF TELLS AMERICANS TO 'BREATHE' AMID TECH OUTAGES, INSISTS HOMELAND IS 'SECURE'

The NSA logo is displayed on a smartphone screen with the American flag in the background in Creteil, France, on April 21, 2026. (Photo by Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images) (Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images))
CNN first reported the outage Tuesday, citing five people familiar with the matter.

The agency has implemented staggered arrival times for personnel at NSA to prevent tens of thousands of employees from attempting to log into their computers simultaneously as officials work to address the disruption, the person familiar with the matter said.
The issue appears to be technical in nature, according to the source, though the precise cause has not been established.
Despite the disruption, the agency has not lost critical communications capabilities and has numerous backup facilities available to maintain operations, the source said.
Image shows entrance to the NSA headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
DUFFY: INVESTIGATORS EXAMINING 2 ROUTERS AFTER NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP, NO SIGNS OF FOREIGN CYBERATTACK
The NSA, which is responsible for collecting and analyzing foreign signals intelligence, plays a central role in supporting U.S. intelligence and military operations.
It remains unclear when the outage began or how long it will take to fully restore the affected network.
Fox News Digital reached out to the NSA for comment.
The disruption comes amid a string of high-profile technology outages over the last week affecting government systems and major businesses.

On Friday, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop after a telecommunications failure disrupted aircraft communications and radar feeds. The agency said instability spread to 17 of its 22 air route traffic control centers before flights resumed later that evening.

The disruption was attributed by the FAA to excessive data flooding its aging telecommunications network, potentially originating from two facilities in Texas and Arkansas. Officials said they had found no indication of a cyberattack.
Sign depicts entrance to the NSA  (SAUL LOEB/AFP via Getty Images)

Federal authorities are separately warning of increasingly sophisticated cyber threats. In a Nov. 13 advisory, the FBI warned that hackers are exploiting an artificial intelligence-powered penetration testing framework known as ARTEX to automate attacks against organizations worldwide.

The FBI said the technology has allowed some attackers to move from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours. Microsoft previously linked the framework to a China-aligned hacking group's exploitation of a ConnectWise supply-chain compromise, which involved attempts to access more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 customer environments.

There is no evidence linking the NSA disruption to the ARTEX activity or the other recent outages.

title: Bush-appointed judge torpedoes Trump immigration rule, rips DHS for overstepping its authority
summary: A federal judge appointed by President George W. Bush ruled DHS overstepped its authority on the F-1 student visa, blocking fixed time limits.
story: A federal judge in Boston has blocked the Trump administration's $100,000 H-1B visa fee, stating it is an unauthorized tax without congressional approval. The policy, enacted last year, drastically increased the fee from $2,000-$5,000 to prioritize U.S. citizens. The White House plans to appeal the decision.
An immigration rule drafted by the Trump administration to plug an alleged gap in the visa system has met its end at the hands of a federal judge appointed by former President George W. Bush.

District Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV of Massachusetts ruled Monday that the Department of Homeland Security overstepped its authority by promulgating a rule that placed greater restrictions on visas for international students, exchange visitors and foreign journalists. His ruling represents a victory for the labor unions and university presidents that challenged the rule, and another loss in the Trump administration’s legal crusade to crack down on immigration.

The DHS rule would have replaced a longstanding policy by only allowing international students to study in America for a fixed timeframe, generally capped at four years, requiring them to apply for an extension if they wish to continue their studies. Previously, there was no fixed time limit for international students so long as they remained enrolled in a university and otherwise maintained legal status. The rule also would have imposed new restrictions on transferring schools, changing academic programs and pursuing additional degrees, while subjecting students to additional immigration reviews intended to combat fraud and national security threats.
TRUMP ADMIN SUED OVER VISA TIME RESTRICTIONS FOR FOREIGN STUDENTS, JOURNALISTS
The Trump administration says foreign student visa vetting will be a continued process, not a one-time check. (iStock)

"DHS acknowledges that there are legitimate reasons why a student may pursue another academic degree at the same or lower level as the one he or she has completed — for example, pursuing an M.B.A. after a J.D.," the judge wrote. "But the Final Rule would effectively prohibit such a student from entering the United States to pursue those studies. And the purported reasons given by DHS for doing so — protecting national security and preventing fraud — are not reasonably related to the nature and purpose of the F-1 visa program."

"Put bluntly, DHS is seeking to prevent or discourage the very activity — providing educational opportunities for foreign students in the United States — that Congress sought to permit and encourage," Saylor continued. "The statute simply does not grant DHS such broad and open-ended authority to undermine the F-1 visa program."
US STATE DEPARTMENT HAS YANKED MORE THAN 175K VISAS UNDER TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SO FAR
Students pass by Sather Gate on the campus of University of California, Berkeley on Thursday, February 19, 2026. (Christina House / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
Saylor had already blocked the rule from taking effect in September, but Monday's ruling went further by striking it down entirely after finding that DHS violated federal administrative law.

Lawyers representing the department disagreed with the judge’s characterization, arguing that indefinite admission periods prevent immigration officials from periodically reassessing whether foreign nationals are complying with the conditions of their visas. Mandatory extensions, in the telling of the agency, would create additional opportunities to identify fraud, security risks and immigration violations — risks it says are substantiated by past cases of fraud and abuse in the student visa system.

"The performative outrage is incredible. Where was the outrage when foreign nationals were abusing the system, violating the terms of their student visas, and making a mockery of our immigration laws? If the media really cared about legitimate international students, they would be thanking President Trump for cracking down on the rampant fraud to ensure only those truly intending to study in the United States are given the privilege," a DHS spokesperson told Fox News Digital.
Saylor, however, further argued that DHS failed to establish how its new rule would constitute an improvement over existing systems meant to catch visa fraud.

"But DHS has not adequately explained how implementing an unreviewable, completely discretionary renewal system — after a foreign student has already been in the country for four years — meaningfully enhances the ability of DHS to root out cases of fraud, or how the benefits of such a system outweigh the immense costs of abandoning the existing system," he wrote.
DHS PROPOSES MASSIVE $70K FEE FOR FOREIGN STUDENTS SEEKING WORK AUTHORIZATION

The "Trump Gold Card" is a visa program that allows foreign nationals permanent residency and a pathway to U.S. citizenship for a $1 million investment in the United States. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Currently, DHS relies on the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) to monitor student visa fraud. SEVIS is a federal database that monitors international students and exchange visitors, tracking their enrollment, immigration status and compliance with visa requirements through information reported by schools and program sponsors. The agency argued that the system is a "data-reporting system for schools" that is "not designed for performing all relevant fraud and security screening."

Saylor was identified as a Republican in a 2014 profile piece. The same piece noted Saylor had close ties to former Massachusetts Gov. Mitt Romney and that he was reportedly considered for a position in the Bush administration. He was confirmed by a bipartisan vote in the Senate, even winning the support of Democratic Sen. Ted Kennedy, a noted liberal, who praised him for his fair-mindedness and independence.
