DHS did not tell Fox News Digital whether it intended to appeal Saylor's ruling.

title: ASRA NOMANI: Far-left US groups battle Trump plan to rival China's tech dominance
summary: The "Shut Down Pax" campaign, backed by CodePink and groups tied to Neville Roy Singham, fights President Donald Trump's bid to cut U.S. reliance on China.
story: As President Donald Trump attends the 49th ASEAN Summit in the Philippines, communist and far-left organizations are mobilizing internationally against an American initiative designed to reduce reliance on China.

As President Donald Trump attends the 49th ASEAN Summit in the Philippines, American communist and far-left organizations are mobilizing internationally against an American initiative designed to reduce reliance on China.

According to a Fox News Digital investigation, a network of 120 mostly communist, socialist and far-left U.S. groups – many of them pro-China – are joining protests in Asia opposing the Trump administration's effort to build an artificial intelligence and semiconductor hub in the Philippines that would reduce U.S. dependence on China in the AI war.

The target is the Pax Silica tech industrial hub in the Philippines, which Undersecretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg, a former senior adviser at Palantir Technologies, said last year would strengthen American control over AI infrastructure, semiconductor production and critical mineral supply chains. Two days ago, Helberg described Pax Silica as key to the world's "superintelligence revolution."

The dispute centers partly on the proposed Clark Advanced Manufacturing Park, a roughly 4,000-acre development in New Clark City, Tarlac, in the Philippines, that would be a hub for the Pax Silica project.
UPDATED – CHAOS INC.: COMMUNISTS, ANTIFA, AGITATORS IN THE RED-GREEN ALLIANCE

Members of Anakbayan, the International League of Peoples' Struggles, ICHRP-US and other organizations protest against the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative outside the Embassy of the Philippines in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 17, 2026. The demonstrations coincided with President Donald Trump's arrival in the Philippines for the ASEAN Summit and followed mass protests in Manila. (JNA Press / Gilchrist Alo/Sipa USA via Reuters Connect)

A Fox News Digital investigation traced support for the protests to a transnational pro-China activist network stretching from Manila to New York, Washington, D.C., Los Angeles and Canada, including the Democratic Socialists of America East Bay, Calif., chapter and organizations with ties to American-born, Shanghai-based Marxist tech millionaire Neville Roy Singham. The protests also include indigenous groups in the Philippines that allege Pax Silica is being built on ancestral land.
About eight of 10 of the organizations in the network of 120 are openly communist, socialist or "anti-imperialist."
TRUMP TO SIGN TRADE DEAL AS HE KICKS OFF ASIA TRIP AHEAD OF NUCLEAR TALKS WITH XI AND PUTIN

Farmers and activists gather in Mendiola, Manila, on Oct. 21, 2026, during a demonstration calling for land reform, increased agricultural support and protection of rural livelihoods. Protesters oppose the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative, which they say threatens farming communities. The rally takes place during National Peasant Month amid concerns over the potential impact of El Niño on food production. (JNA Press/Sean Isaiah R. Membr/Sipa USA via Reuters Connect)
In addition, most of them are openly "anti-Zionist," opposed to the existence of a Jewish state of Israel, according to a Fox News Digital analysis of the groups in the network.
CodePink, a pro-communist, pro-China nonprofit co-founded by Singham's wife, Jodie Evans, has used its media programming to criticize Pax Silica as a "military-industrial-surveillance complex."

For Washington, experts say, the Pax Silica plan is about securing the technology and resources needed to compete with Beijing. For opponents, the protests are a way to curb American economic and military domination.
The campaign also reveals how opposition to Trump's China strategy is being organized not only overseas, but through pro-China activist networks inside the United States.
TRUMP LEAVES DOOR OPEN TO KIM JONG UN JOINING HIGH-STAKES TALKS WITH XI, PUTIN

An indigenous Ayta delegate prepares to set fire to an effigy of President Donald Trump during a mobilization in observance of the Global Day of Action for Climate Justice organized by far-left groups at the University of the Philippines Diliman in Quezon City, Philippines, on Nov. 14, 2026. The event condemns Trump's visit to the Philippines for the ASEAN Summit and calls for the abolition of the U.S.-led Pax Silica Initiative, which critics allege infringes upon indigenous land. (Charles Perez/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

The U.S. network, organizing behind a campaign called "Shut Down Pax," includes familiar faces in the Singham network's protest circuit: BAYAN USA, a pro-communist Filipino American alliance helping lead the campaign; Anakbayan USA, a pro-communist youth organization; and the International League of Peoples' Struggle, or ILPS, founded with the help of Jose Maria Sison, the late founder of the Communist Party of the Philippines.

The campaign has also reached the U.S. Congress. A letter, headlined "Shut Down Pax Silica in the Philippines" calls on lawmakers to halt the initiative pending review of environmental protections, labor rights and the treatment of Philippine communities.

The activism intersects with other nonprofits in the network funded by Singham, including the People's Forum and BreakThrough News, that have promoted opposition to American foreign policy and challenged Washington's confrontation with Beijing.

On Sept. 20, the U.S. chapter of the International League of Peoples' Struggle, the International Coalition for Human Rights in the Philippines-US and Bagong Alyansang Makabayan USA, or BAYAN USA, launched the "Shut Down Pax Silica Campaign Network" in Queens, New York, with organizers claiming about 500 participants in person and online.

An article, published by Bulatlat, invoked a term popular in communist, "anti-imperialist" circles, claiming that a movement had begun in "the belly of the beast," with "resistance" to Pax Silica "rising."
"We unite to confront and oppose the Trump/U.S.-led Pax Silica Initiative in its competition with China to dominate the AI/tech supply chain," the coalition declared in its organizing platform.
FIRST ON FOX: ‘NO KINGS’ PROTEST NETWORK BEHIND FIGHT AGAINST AI DATA CENTERS AND FLOCK CAMERAS
FILE - Jacob Helberg speaks at The Trump 47 Jewish Leadership Event on Sept. 12, 2024, during the 2024 presidential campaign in New York City. (Ilya S. Savenok/Getty Images for Jacob Helberg)
"We Filipinos in the U.S. must also take action," BAYAN USA declares on its campaign website, urging opposition to U.S. investments associated with Pax Silica.

A month later, on Oct. 24, CodePink Radio published Episode 374, with host Marcy Winograd interviewing sociologist William Robinson about his new book, "Pax Silica: The New Ruling Class," examining the "rise of a new transnational capital complex" that combines big tech with global finance and the "military-industrial-surveillance complex" to "colonize the world unless we continue to protest, disrupt, divest and withhold our labor."
The Black Alliance for Peace, which participated in CodePink's November "Taxpayer Uprising" campaign in Washington, D.C., last week, also promoted the anti-Pax Silica campaign's launch.

Anakbayan USA, its local chapters and GABRIELA USA, a Filipino women's organization, appear among the American coalition's participants. Their Philippine counterparts are involved in the demonstrations surrounding Trump's visit.
The coalition's published platform also identifies "Migrante USA," student organizations and other activist groups.

The overlapping campaigns bring together Filipino American organizations, socialist activists and groups that have previously organized against U.S. military operations, Israel and American foreign policy.
Singham, an American-born technology entrepreneur who sold his consultancy ThoughtWorks for an estimated $785 million in 2017, has financed an extensive network of U.S. nonprofits.

A Fox News Digital investigation traced $278 million into six core American nonprofits, including CodePink, People's Forum, Tricontinental and BreakThrough BT Media Inc., which operates BreakThrough News.
AMERICA RUNS ON DATA. IF WE DON’T BUILD THE INFRASTRUCTURE, CHINA WILL

A child raises a placard during an observance of the Global Day of Action for Climate Justice at the University of the Philippines Diliman in Quezon City, Philippines, on Nov. 14, 2026. The event condemns the visit of President Donald Trump to the Philippines for the ASEAN Summit and calls for the abolition of the U.S.-led Pax Silica Initiative. (Charles Perez/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

In July, the House Ways and Means Committee subpoenaed three organizations as lawmakers investigated the financial network and potential foreign influence. The organizations have challenged the investigation.
One connection to the anti-Pax Silica campaign from the Singham network is "Nodutdol for Korean Community Development," an American group listed among the coalition's endorsers.
Nodutdol member Winter Oh participated in the September launch in Queens.

BreakThrough News has amplified the Philippine protests and criticism of Pax Silica, this summer promoting a BAYAN and Kilusang Mayo Uno demonstration with the slogan "The Philippines is not for sale!" As Trump was still in flight to Manila, BreakThrough news highlighted growing opposition to Pax Silica with a story headline, "ASEAN summit in Manila met with protests over Trump’s participation."
Philippine officials have previously accused organizations such as Gabriela, Anakbayan, Karapatan and Kilusang Mayo Uno of acting as communist fronts. The groups have denied those allegations.
CODEPINK LAUNCHES CHINA TOUR AS GRAND JURY INVESTIGATION INTO SINGHAM NETWORK FUNDING CONTINUES

Indigenous Ayta delegates watch as an effigy of President Donald Trump burns during a mobilization in observance of the Global Day of Action for Climate Justice organized by far-left groups at the University of the Philippines Diliman in Quezon City, Philippines, on Nov. 14, 2026. (Charles Perez/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
The ideological roots of the campaign extend to the Communist Party of the Philippines, founded by Sison in 1968.
The United States designated the Communist Party of the Philippines and its armed wing, the New People's Army, as a foreign terrorist organization.
In a Nov. 7 editorial, the party's official newspaper, Ang Bayan, urged Filipinos to organize "widespread protests" against Trump and to "reject and drive him out."
The editorial accused Trump of advancing Pax Silica to strengthen American control over Philippine resources.

The publication also reported that clandestine organizations associated with the National Democratic Front of the Philippines staged demonstrations. One teachers' group, KAGUMA, reportedly chanted, "Join the New People's Army!"
The American campaign includes explicitly communist organizations, including the Workers World Party, a Marxist-Leninist organization, and the International Action Center.

Separately, "Fight Back! News," published by the Freedom Road Socialist Organization, a Marxist-Leninist group that has organized many anti-ICE protests this year, republished an editorial from Ang Bayan criticizing Trump's Pax Silica initiative.
CHINA ‘THROWING GASOLINE ON THE FIRE’ IN AI DATA CENTERS RACE, SAY LAWMAKERS

Indigenous communities, joined by environmentalists and youth representatives, march towards Quezon Hall during the Global Day of Action for Climate Justice at the University of the Philippines Diliman in Quezon City, Philippines, on Nov. 14, 2026. (Charles Perez/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

The International League of Peoples' Struggle called for global protests under the slogans "Trump Out!" and "Reject Pax Silica!" The organization said groups planned demonstrations in 23 cities worldwide, including locations in the United States, Canada, Europe and Asia.
American organizers identified planned actions in Los Angeles, Oregon, Washington, D.C., New York and Honolulu.

In Ottawa, International League of Peoples' Struggle Canada, Anakbayan Ottawa, Migrante Ottawa and "Ottawa for Palestine" announced a demonstration for Wednesday outside the U.S. Embassy under the slogan "Shut the Pax Down!"
In an April proposal to the U.S. State Department, Philippine officials outlined plans involving critical minerals, industrial infrastructure, investment and technology development.
Protesters allege the project could displace Ayta Indigenous communities, expand mining, and strain electricity and water supplies.

Philippine officials dispute allegations that the project would create a U.S.-controlled enclave or include the massive AI data centers described by activists. They say the development remains subject to Philippine law.

As Trump arrived, demonstrations escalated.

Reuters footage showed students marching with anti-Trump banners. SunStar reported more than 200 arrests during demonstrations in Metro Manila, while GMA News reported that activists condemned police dispersals and disputed the government's response.

Asra Nomani is senior editor of investigations at Fox News Digital. She is a former reporter at the Wall Street Journal, where she covered stories related to money, politics and society. She is the author of "Woke Army: The Red-Green Alliance That Is Undermining America’s Freedom." She can be reached at asra.nomani@fox.com and on X at @asranomani.

title: Conservatives launch $10M anti-socialism blitz after Democrats dominate youth vote
summary: YAF is launching a nationwide "Freedom Not Socialism" campaign in 30 Democratic strongholds after Democrats won the majority of the youth vote in the midterms.
story: Rep.-elect Michael Alfonso tells Fox News Digital that because the American education system fails to teach the truth about Marxism, young Americans are easily duped into believing that socialism is a feasible idea.

FIRST ON FOX: A conservative organization has launched a nationwide campaign of more than $10 million targeting at least 30 Democratic strongholds to combat the growing popularity of socialism among young Americans ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

The Young America's Foundation (YAF), led by former Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker, announced its "Freedom Not Socialism" initiative, which will bring prominent conservative leaders, including possible 2028 contenders, scholars and activists, to schools and communities across the country to challenge the influence of democratic socialism among younger voters.

"Our mission is to explain to people that their high cost of living is due to big government," Walker told Fox News Digital, explaining that the initiative will mobilize speakers to engage directly with young Americans at colleges, high schools and other institutions.
Members of the Democratic Socialists of America gather outside a Trump-owned building on May Day on May 1, 2019, in New York City.  (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
SOCIALISM'S GROWING APPEAL MEETS AN AWKWARD REALITY CHECK ON COLLEGE CAMPUS
The announcement comes after Democrats captured the majority of the youth vote in Tuesday's midterm elections. The group launched its first event in Santa Barbara, Calif., over the weekend.

"YAF's initiative is vital for the future of our country because young Americans continue to get behind these false narratives of free this and free that, and they don't realize that the reason they are in the place where they cannot afford to live is because of big government," Rep.-elect Michael Alfonso, R-Wis., said.

During his interview with Fox News Digital, Alfonso, the 26-year-old grandson of immigrants who escaped communist Cuba, argued that the American education system had failed the next generation by not teaching the history of socialist regimes.

"The American education system has failed us," Alfonso said. "Young Americans do not know the truth about communist Cuba, communist Russia and communist Venezuela. All it takes is a simple look at these countries to realize how prosperous they were before communism came, and then what happened to them after."

"If we started teaching kids real history in the schools, maybe we wouldn't have so many people that come out hating this nation," said the congressman-elect, who will become the youngest member of Congress.

The group also announced plans to host a Freedom Conference in Dallas in early 2027 to prepare young conservatives to promote free-market principles and challenge socialist policies on college campuses.

"Young Americans are going to be the majority of voters in 2028, and they are increasingly being sold the promises of socialism without understanding the devastating consequences that follow," Walker, YAF's president, told Fox News Digital.
JD VANCE WARNS REPUBLICANS NOT TO BLAME YOUNG AMERICANS FOR THE APPEAL OF SOCIALISM
Rep.-elect Michael Alfonso, R-Wis., attends a roundtable with President Donald Trump at Custer Farms Inc. in Chippewa Falls, Wis., on June 5, 2026. (Steven Garcia/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"As socialism gains ground in cities and states across the nation, we must teach the next generation what it truly is and act today," he continued. "The next generation cannot afford to sit on the sidelines while socialism infiltrates our communities and our schools."

The organization expects prominent Republican figures and potential 2028 presidential contenders to help carry its message, including former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis.

"I can't think there's a more challenging place than college campuses to make this decision to embrace our foundational principles that not only laid the groundwork for the greatest nation ever, but were the foundational principles that guided us when we were lost," Youngkin said at the initiative's inaugural event on Sunday.
MAGA VOTERS REVEAL WHO THEY WANT TO SEE LEAD GOP IN 2028

YAF argues that young Americans are increasingly exposed to socialist ideas in schools, universities and communities without learning about what the organization describes as socialism's historical failures.

Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin and his wife Suzanne Youngkin arrive for the third day of the 2024 Republican National Convention at the Fiserv Forum in Milwaukee on July 17, 2024. (Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images)

Walker attributed the growing appeal of socialism among younger voters to a lack of understanding of its consequences, arguing that many are embracing the ideology without fully considering its implications.
AMERICA’S QUIET SOCIALIST TAKEOVER IS SPREADING FROM TOWN HALLS TO CLASSROOMS
"Freedom, not socialism, is about informing people of those ideas," Walker said.

Among the speakers expected to participate are Daniel Di Martino, a Columbia University graduate who fled socialist Venezuela, and Yeonmi Park, a North Korean defector who has spoken publicly about her experiences under the country's communist regime.
Walker said their firsthand accounts will help demonstrate why he believes socialist policies, including those championed by progressive leaders in Seattle and New York, "do not work."

The initiative is expected to expand throughout 2027 as conservatives seek to regain support among younger voters ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

title: American veterans targeted by schemes to steal benefits and exploit the sick, disabled: DOJ
summary: The Justice Department launches a nationwide VA benefits fraud crackdown, charging 15 defendants in schemes with more than $3.4 million in intended losses.
story: Justice Department officials announced charges against 15 defendants in schemes targeting veterans and VA programs, including a fraud case involving an unfinished cancer treatment center in Florida.
FIRST ON FOX — Fraud schemes drained veterans’ disability benefits and left a promised cancer treatment center unfinished before it was demolished, according to the Justice Department.

In launching a nationwide crackdown on abuse of veterans’ programs, the DOJ is levying charges against 15 defendants in schemes involving more than $3.4 million in intended losses, announcement materials obtained first by Fox News Digital detail.
Prosecutors also secured guilty pleas, trial verdicts and sentencings in cases involving more than $19 million in intended losses during the operation, which began Sept. 1, 2026.
DOJ’S ‘OPERATION GHOSTBUSTERS’ TARGETS MASSIVE STUDENT-AID FRAUD SCHEME BUILT ON FAKE ENROLLEES

A Department of Veterans Affairs sign, left, and the unfinished cancer infusion center at Bay Pines VA Medical Center in Florida. The facility was demolished and never rebuilt after a construction project involving a fraudulently obtained contract, according to the Justice Department. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images: DOJ)

The operation marks the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division’s first coordinated nationwide surge focused on VA benefits, bringing together federal prosecutors, the Department of Veterans Affairs and its inspector general.

"For veterans, benefits are not simply government payments," Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald said in a statement. "They are earned benefits -- earned through service, sacrifice, deployments, injuries, time away from loved ones, and a willingness to serve something larger than themselves."
TEXAS CLINIC OWNER CONVICTED IN $26M MILITARY HEALTH FRAUD TIED TO GOLD-PLATED CYBERTRUCK

Asked during Tuesday’s press conference whether uncovering $19 million in fraud represented a meaningful success given the scale of fraud nationwide, McDonald pointed to the veterans whose benefits and care were affected.

"I would ask the question of the veterans who didn't get the care whether the $19 million that was stolen from them, whether it matters to them," McDonald said. "Whether the cancer center that was not built, did it matter to them that they did not have the cancer center that the taxpayer funded to be able to serve our warfighters and to seek to help them in their moment of need?"
In Florida, the government paid approximately $4.8 million toward a veterans’ cancer treatment center that was never completed — and ultimately was demolished without being rebuilt, according to DOJ.

The VA awarded the $8.9 million construction contract for the Cancer Infusion Therapy Center at Bay Pines VA Medical Center through a program reserved for businesses owned by service-disabled veterans.

Evidence at trial showed that Matthew West, Kevin Kutina and their co-conspirators secured the contract while concealing arrangements under which ineligible companies would perform most of the work and receive most of the payments.
West and Kutina were convicted of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud and major fraud against the United States. Two co-defendants pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud.
Construction failures plagued the project, leaving the partially completed facility to be torn down, according to the DOJ.
Other cases involved alleged theft directly from veterans’ benefit payments.
To protect your hard-earned VA benefits, stay alert and verify messages through official channels. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

In Texas, prosecutors allege that VA National Call Center employee Heidi Brady used her access to veterans’ personal information and knowledge of payment procedures to change their direct deposit details shortly before monthly disability payments were issued.
The money allegedly went to an account she controlled.
Her neighbor, Raymond Audie Davis, is accused of helping by impersonating veterans during calls to the VA and using their identifying information to redirect payments, according to the indictment.

In Ohio, Darlene Toman allegedly stole from disabled veterans whose finances she was entrusted to manage — including a Marine severely wounded in Iraq who received the Purple Heart and Combat Action Ribbon.
Prosecutors say the victims included people with traumatic brain injuries, schizophrenia, amputations and other serious conditions. Some required around-the-clock care.
Scammers are claiming veterans were overpaid on their benefits by impersonating VA employees. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Rather than safeguard their benefits, Toman allegedly used fraudulent checks and diverted payments intended to cover veterans’ living expenses and care for her own use.
The allegations against Brady, Davis and Toman have not been proven in court. Defendants are presumed innocent unless and until convicted.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Alongside the VA enforcement announcement, DOJ is establishing a Texas Federal Fraud Task Force comprising all four U.S. attorney’s offices in the state, with support from federal, state and local law enforcement.
Fox News Digital's Stephen Sorace contributed to this report.

title: Trump Treasury aims to slam shut banking loopholes that could enable fraud tied to illegal immigration
summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says the FinCEN proposal gives banks more flexibility to combat money laundering and terrorist financing risks.
story: Federal law enforcement agencies execute 17 search warrants in Minnesota to dismantle an alleged massive, multi-million-dollar fraud scheme targeting vulnerable public programs. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, FBI Director Kash Patel and CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz announce the coordinated federal crackdown during a joint press conference. Bessent confirms that the Internal Revenue Service is actively assisting with the investigations.

FIRST ON FOX: The Trump administration is moving to tighten financial safeguards it says could help stop illegal immigrants from exploiting the U.S. banking system, putting banks on notice to scrutinize business ownership more closely when warning signs emerge.

The proposed rule from the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) is part of President Donald Trump’s effort to address what his administration calls national security and public safety risks tied to illicit financial activity and people in the country illegally.
In short, the proposal would give banks more leeway to dig into who owns a business when they see potential red flags.
APPEALS COURT UPHOLDS ORDER BLOCKING IRS FROM SHARING TAXPAYER DATA WITH ICE
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the proposed rule would give financial institutions more flexibility to assess risk and strengthen efforts to combat financial crime. (Reuters)

Trump’s executive order directs Treasury to strengthen customer due diligence. It says financial institutions should be able to seek information about immigration status and work authorization when relevant to assessing fraud or other illicit activity.

Under the proposal, covered institutions could obtain additional information about the beneficial owners of business customers to mitigate risk or address supervisory concerns. The rule would also end the requirement to reverify those owners each time an existing customer opens a new account and spell out what information banks must collect.
TRUMP ADMIN’S FRAUD CRACKDOWN TARGETS FOREIGNERS ACCUSED OF INFILTRATING US FEDERAL PROGRAMS

President Donald Trump directed Treasury to strengthen customer due diligence at financial institutions, with the administration citing concerns about illicit finance and risks tied to people in the country illegally. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

The proposal does not require banks to verify every customer’s immigration status. FinCEN says the changes are intended to combat money laundering and terrorist financing while cutting unnecessary compliance burdens.

"Financial institutions are on the front lines of protecting our financial systems from criminal organizations and cartels that target law-abiding businesses and workers," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
He said the proposal would give institutions more flexibility to combat risk and strengthen the fight against financial crime.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
An anti-ICE sign in the window of a gas station in Minneapolis, Minn., January 8, 2026. (Preston Mizell/Fox News Digital)
FinCEN is accepting public comments for 60 days after the proposal is published in the Federal Register.
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Trump's $50B air traffic control overhaul faces GOP pushback after nationwide ground stop
summary: Senate Republicans want receipts on the $12.5 billion already sent for air traffic control as the Trump administration seeks $50 billion more.
story: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy calls on Congress to invest in aviation software and infrastructure upgrades following a nationwide FAA ground stop on 'Hannity.'
The Trump administration is pressing Congress for tens of billions in emergency funding to upgrade the nation’s air traffic control systems, but even Senate Republicans are reluctant to pay the bill.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and President Donald Trump called on lawmakers to shell out $50 billion in funding after a ground stop on Friday caused thousands of flight cancellations and blamed Congress for not doling out money previously to upgrade aging air traffic control communications infrastructure.

But Congress did send $12.5 billion to the Department of Transportation as part of the "big, beautiful bill" last year meant to upgrade the archaic systems, and Republicans want receipts on what happened to the money.
FAA SAYS AIR TRAVEL SHOULD BE BACK TO NORMAL SUNDAY AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP

Secretary Sean Duffy speaks during a press briefing at Department of Transportation headquarters on Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington, D.C. The briefing followed a nationwide communications outage that grounded flights across the United States the previous day. (Aaron Schwartz/AFP via Getty Images)
"Only about four [billion] has been spent," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said. "There was about eight billion of that still sitting around."

Duffy is slated to meet with Senate Republicans behind closed doors on Tuesday where lawmakers expect a full breakdown of what happened and where the money has gone and why, suddenly, the administration is seeking an additional $20 billion.

"I haven't seen how they're gonna use it. I mean, in my business, you know, I spent a lot of money, and I built companies," Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital. "And I understood what I was going to spend it on before I ever did anything. I'd have a budget and what the timeline is, who's gonna do it, all that stuff."
FORMER TOP FAA OFFICIAL WARNS OF 48-HOUR RECOVERY AFTER AGING TECH 'OVERWHELMED' AHEAD OF GROUND STOP

Data from the Department of Transportation (DOT) obtained by Fox News Digital showed that roughly $3.7 billion had been spent on a variety of projects, while the remainder is tied to contracts, unspent or planned for near-term upgrades, like facility consolidation.

Thune declined to say whether he had confidence in Duffy’s handling of the situation and noted that the administration had already made a separate ask for $30 billion, a chunk of which was meant to continue upgrades to air traffic control.

"I mean, there's some explanations that have to be given as to why that number is where it is," Thune said. "But I think we have attempted to do everything we can to ensure that the concerns they have about modernization are being met."

Duffy’s explanation of the ground stop was attributed to replacing copper wiring in communications equipment with fiber-optic cable. About $4.8 billion of the initial funding pot was for copper wire replacement, of which about $2.3 billion has been spent, which translates to roughly 70% completion of the telecommunications replacement program, according to the DOT.
4 CRITICAL TRAVEL ISSUES FOR THOSE DELAYED AND DISRUPTED BY FAA NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., argued that Democrats were continuing their push to keep DHS closed because it was "politically advantageous." (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

A DOT spokesperson told Fox News Digital that the "Department has made clear for the last two years — separate funding is needed" for other work because DOT "does not have the legal flexibility to move funds from one workstream to another."
Still, lawmakers have questions.
"He needs to talk to me like I'm a reasonably intelligent 10th grader," Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said. "The American people are not experts on telecommunications … nor am I."

Kennedy, who is a member of the Transportation, Housing and Urban Development Appropriations Subcommittee, which controls the DOT's purse strings, said he was more than "willing to appropriate money to fix this," but needed to understand the problem first.

"I mean, we had an outage today, some problems with a number of our banks," Kennedy said. "There have been some problems in Europe with the Internet controlling temperatures of grocery stores. I mean, this is happening a lot. I'm not saying there's a connection, but if there is, they need to tell us."
Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., told Fox News Digital that the initial $12.5 billion was "a starting point — it wasn’t everything."
"We've seen nothing yet of what's the rest of the request," Lankford said. "So that does seem like, ‘Hey, grab a number out of the air. It needs to be big.’"
Lankford added that Duffy needed to give a "postmortem" on what happened, and that whatever the administration is asking for in upgrades needs to be "shovel-ready."
"This is a zero fail operation," he said. "He's keenly aware of that."
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Little-known IRS program could be unfairly crushing landowners, according to alarming study and whistleblower
summary: An Infinity Advisory Services study found the IRS slashed conservation easement values by an average of roughly 97% across 115 cases examined.
story: Unleash Prosperity Chairman and co-founder Steve Moore spoke to Fox News Digital about the conservation easement program at the IRS and what needs to be done to fix it.

FIRST ON FOX: A new study is raising questions about whether the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) has been putting its finger on the scale to hit American landowners with higher tax bills through a little-known conservation tax program, as a whistleblower who spent many years at the agency warns the findings show the IRS has "lost its way."

The study, conducted by Infinity Advisory Services, examined more than 130 IRS valuation reviews and found that, in 115 conservation easement tax incentive cases with comparable figures, the agency slashed taxpayers’ appraised values by an average of roughly 97%, with reductions of 99% or more common.

The study makes the case that the pattern across different properties, tax years and reviewers points to a process designed to reach a predetermined answer, which effectively wiped out the value underpinning taxpayers’ conservation deductions rather than fairly evaluating each property.

The conservation easement tax incentive allows landowners to claim a charitable tax deduction for permanently giving up certain development rights on their property, helping preserve farmland, forests and other protected land. The landowners keep ownership, but restrictions limit how the property can be developed. An appraisal determines the value of the rights donated, which generally forms the basis of the deduction and is at the center of these IRS disputes.
DOJ UNVEILS NATIONWIDE TAX FRAUD CRACKDOWN INVOLVING 76 DEFENDANTS, NEARLY $500M IN ALLEGED LOSSES
Beef cattle run in a pasture at a ranch in Sonoita, Ariz., on Nov. 11, 2025. (Rebecca Noble/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"This report examines a single question," the study's authors explain in the executive summary. "We ask whether the government's valuation position in conservation easement matters was settled as a matter of policy before it was tested against the facts of individual properties. The record we have assembled to date is consistent with that view, and in our judgment the pattern in the data is difficult to explain on another basis."

A former IRS valuator, who spent many years with the agency, told Fox News Digital that he experienced officials pressuring appraisers to reach predetermined conclusions and brushing aside evidence from taxpayers who donated development rights to their land in exchange for tax deductions. Instead of distinguishing legitimate donations from abusive tax shelters, he said, the agency is "setting up taxpayers that they know are innocent," leaving them facing steep tax bills and penalties.
"I'm looking at the IRS, and they've developed a culture that says bigger dollars is a good thing," the whistleblower said.

"And they're in a mode of not wanting to know what the facts are from the taxpayer's perspective. And in the application of the law, the application of the law is slanted, having watched both sides in this process," the whistleblower added. "If you're going to have a valuation issue, it should be addressed by someone who has expertise in valuation. When I was at the IRS, that would not have been tolerated."
TRUMP PUTS FRAUDSTERS ON NOTICE WITH $25M WHISTLEBLOWER PROGRAM OFFERING CASH FOR TIPS THAT DELIVER
The IRS headquarters building in Washington, D.C. (Getty Images)

In one case involving a historic Cleveland building, the same IRS reviewer initially valued a donated preservation easement at between $18.1 million and $23.2 million, then reduced it to $400,000 in a follow-up review that dramatically shifted the landowner’s tax burden, according to the study.

The revised report explicitly cited instructions from IRS counsel to exclude certain development rights from consideration. The study’s authors argue that the dramatic reversal reflected a directive covering an entire class of properties rather than new evidence about the building itself.

The whistleblower cited one specific case from personal experience where the agency identified eight areas of concern but refused to hear the taxpayer’s explanations. When the taxpayer offered to address each point, an IRS Appeals technical advisor responded, "I don't want to hear it," according to the whistleblower. The mediation ended without an agreement, he said, citing the exchange as an example of the agency’s unwillingness to fairly consider taxpayers’ evidence.

"How can you be involved in post- or pre-litigation and say, I don't even want to hear your response to the issues we raised," the whistleblower said, adding that the concerns shouldn't be viewed as being the fault of a particular administration but that the information should be looked at from a factual perspective in a nonpartisan way.

Steve Moore, chairman and co-founder of Unleash Prosperity and former advisor to President Donald Trump, recently penned an article arguing that the IRS’s crackdown on conservation easement deductions has swept up honest taxpayers who relied on qualified appraisers and professional advice.

"Some of it is due to the fact that the IRS is in the business of trying to get as much money out of people as they can. And part of it is that there has been fraud. There are cases of fraud where people will way overvalue through a fraudulent appraisal," Moore told Fox News Digital in an interview. "And so what's happened, though, is literally, almost literally throwing the baby out with the bathwater. They're putting everybody in the same boat."
Moore said that after his article was published, he heard from numerous families and landowners across the country saying they have been "victimized" by the process.
AG BLANCHE UNVEILS FEDERAL CHARGES AGAINST 160 DEFENDANTS IN PANDEMIC RELIEF SWEEP

The IRS acknowledged in an August press release that standardized settlement offers with fixed deadlines were "not well suited to the full range of conservation easement cases," ending that initiative and announcing a new Office of Conservation Easements. But the announcement did not address the central questions raised by the study and the former IRS official: whether the agency fairly considered evidence supporting taxpayers’ deductions and whether its valuations reflected independent analysis or predetermined conclusions.

"The IRS does realize that they have poked a hornet's nest here because they've made people so angry across the country, and they did put out a press release saying, we're going to deal with this," Moore explained. "But guess what? They haven't dealt with it. It was just words on a piece of paper. And so, the same groups of people I've been working with to try to get them some justice here have not received that justice and there's been in most of these cases nothing done about it but just words on a piece of paper. So this has to be resolved because some people may go bankrupt as a result of this."
Fox News Digital reached out to the IRS for comment and was directed to the August press release.
The IRS has secured significant court victories over inflated conservation easement valuations, including two major wins in the past year.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

In July, the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld a decision valuing an easement over 103 acres in Georgia at $480,000, compared with the partnership’s claimed $23 million deduction. The court rejected the proposed quarry development underlying the higher valuation as economically unviable and upheld a 40% penalty for grossly overstating the easement’s value.

In August, the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld a $900,000 valuation for a Georgia conservation easement that a partnership, Mill Road 36 Henry LLC, had used to claim an $8.9 million deduction. The court found that comparable property sales and a recent transaction involving the land supported the lower valuation, and it upheld a 40% penalty for grossly overstating the easement’s value.

The Tax Court has repeatedly rejected IRS efforts to impose civil fraud penalties in conservation easement disputes, including in a February ruling that cited three earlier cases reaching the same conclusion, among them Mill Road.
Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter from Pasadena, California, who has been with Fox News Digital since 2021. You can reach him at AndrewMark.Miller@fox.com.

title: Mullin took government plane to LSU-Texas football game with Americans stranded in wake of FAA outage: report
summary: Secretary of State Markwayne Mullin reportedly flew a government plane to an LSU football game after the Federal Aviation Authority FAA lifted its ground stop.
story: DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin discusses the aftermath of the FAA's nationwide ground stop and outages affecting several of the nation's largest banks on 'Hannity.'

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin flew in a government plane to attend a college football game in Louisiana on Saturday, just one day after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted a nationwide ground stop that continued to impact travelers through the weekend.

Just 24 hours after Mullin stood next to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy at a White House podium to tell the nation why the FAA had issued a ground stop, prohibiting all planes from taking off, the Homeland chief was in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, to watch the Louisiana State University Tigers take on The University of Texas at Austin Longhorns, according to a report from the New York Post.

Mullin, like other cabinet secretaries, cannot fly on commercial airliners due to safety concerns, so his trip was taken on a government plane, though government sources reportedly stressed to the Post that he paid for the travel expenses himself and that no special exceptions were made for the secretary.
WAPO TRIES TO SHAME RUBIO'S USE OF MILITARY AIRCRAFT TO SEE SON'S FOOTBALL GAMES, HIS TEAM RESPONDS

"Secretary Mullin is required by law to travel on a government airplane. This is to ensure access to secure communications and to comply by his constitutional duty of continuity of government should a national emergency arise," a Homeland Security spokesperson reportedly told the Post.

U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin speaks as U.S. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy listens at the White House on November 13, 2026, in Washington, D.C. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop for all departing flights following a major communications outage Friday night. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
"Any flight not related to his service as DHS Secretary he pays for personally," the spokesperson reportedly added.
The Post also reported that Mullin spent at least part of the game in the private box of Ben Bordelon, the CEO of Louisiana-based shipping company Bollinger Shipyards.
Bollinger has a number of government contracts, including a recently obtained $2.2 billion contract to build four icebreaking ships for the United States Coast Guard.
"Secretary Mullin abides by all ethics requirements," a DHS spokesperson also told the Post.
Sen. Markwayne Mullin, R-Okla., has his eyes well up, talking about how President Donald Trump helped heal his son from a traumatic brain injury. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

The LSU game was the second football game of the day for Mullin, who had also attended the Coast Guard Academy vs. the U.S. Merchant Marine Academy annual matchup at Audi Field in Washington, D.C., earlier on Saturday.
PLAY SUNDAY OR FORFEIT: OKLAHOMA AD RIPS SEC COMMISSIONER OVER CONTROVERSIAL OLE MISS FAA SCHEDULING DECISION

The previous evening, he had been shoulder to shoulder with Secretary Duffy, explaining to the nation that a technical glitch with a piece of FAA network infrastructure equipment likely prompted the systems failure that led to the ground stop.

"What it appears to be right now is, as Secretary Duffy was going in and putting patches into the system, they were putting new equipment and new technology and that new equipment, new technology, just wasn’t — it was overwhelming the older system," Mullin said Friday.
FORMER TOP FAA OFFICIAL WARNS OF 48-HOUR RECOVERY AFTER AGING TECH 'OVERWHELMED' AHEAD OF GROUND STOP
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin addressed governors on immigration policy before facing criticism over comments about legal immigration reform. (Jim Lo Scalzo/EPA/Bloomberg/Getty Images)
The ground stop ultimately lasted roughly five hours and impacted more than 1.5 million travelers on Friday alone.
Despite the ground stop's lifting on Friday, travelers still felt the ripple effects through Monday.

title: Trump warns Iran about reported plot against admin officials: 'We take it very seriously'
summary: Trump warned Iran would face unprecedented retaliation over a reported plot targeting Washington, D.C., as senior officials relocate to military housing.
story: President Donald Trump warned Iran on Monday that it would face unprecedented retaliation if it were to carry out an attack on Washington, D.C.
President Donald Trump warned Iran on Monday that it would face unprecedented retaliation if it were to carry out an attack on Washington, D.C.

Trump made the statement in response to a report from CNN citing multiple U.S. officials stating that Iran is weighing an attempt at killing senior Trump administration officials by detonating a chemical weapon or a dirty bomb in the nation's capital.
"Is there any imminent threat to Washington, D.C.?" a reporter asked on Monday.
DHS CHIEF MULLIN SAYS IRAN POSES DAILY THREAT TO TRUMP AND HIS FAMILY AMID DRONE CONCERNS

President Donald Trump poses for photos with Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, left, India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, right, as they take part in a meeting of the QUAD group — the United States, Japan, Australia and India — at the Solaire Resort on the sidelines of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila on November 17, 2026. (Photo by Mandel NGAN/AFP via Getty Images)

"Well, if there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before. I, I hope it's not, but it's — we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy. But this is why they can't have a nuclear weapon, by the way, in case people had any questions," Trump responded.

Trump's statement came on the first leg of his trip across Asia this week, meeting with QUAD leaders in the Philippines on Monday, including Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.
TRUMP KEEPS SIGNALING AN END TO IRAN WAR, BUT EXPERT WARNS A CRUCIAL PIECE OF HIS STRATEGY IS MISSING
Trump said he plans to press Chinese President Xi Jinping to help end the war in Iran during their meeting later this week.
CNN's report said Iran's plans for an attack on U.S. soil are in the preliminary phase and are, "for now, an effort to give itself options rather than an indicator of an imminent attack."

President Donald Trump speaks during a press briefing at the White House, on Friday, Feb. 20, 2026, in Washington. Trump said Friday he is "considering" a limited military strike on Iran. (Allison Robbert/AP)
TRUMP ADMIN THREATENS IRAN WITH 'CONSEQUENCES' AS ALLIES CONVENE AMID THREATS OF POST-ELECTION ESCALATION
White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told the outlet the U.S. is "monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland."
The report comes days after news broke that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other senior U.S. officials were transferred to military housing in recent weeks.
TRUMP'S TOP OFFICIALS RETREAT BEHIND MILITARY GATES AS EX-FBI DEPUTY POINTS TO WHAT'S FUELING THREATS
Threats against Bessent had reached "more than an advanced stage" amid reported Iranian assassination threats, a senior administration official told Fox News Digital on Tuesday.
The Iranian threats against Bessent come amid a documented history of alleged Tehran-backed assassination plots targeting senior U.S. officials.
IRGC OPERATIVE LANDS ON FBI’S MOST WANTED TERRORISTS LIST OVER ALLEGED PLOT TO KILL FORMER TRUMP ADVISOR
President Donald Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth attend a Cabinet meeting in the Cabinet Room at the White House, in Washington, D.C. (Evan Vucci/Reuters)
Attorney General Todd Blanche also relocated to a military base from his home around March, a different source familiar with the arrangements told Fox News Digital.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth have also reportedly taken up residence at Fort McNair in Washington, D.C., while White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and other administration officials have moved to military installations or protected government housing.

The relocations have not all stemmed from the same threats. Some followed concerns about domestic political violence.
Fox News' Ashley J. DiMella contributed to this report.
Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

title: Schumer boasts early advantage in Senate power struggle as Dem rival warns against 'coronation'
summary: Senate Democrats face their first leadership race in decades as Chris Van Hollen alleges the Dec. 1 secret ballot vote may be rushed to kneecap him.
story: Political strategists Tiffany Smiley and Al Mottur join 'The Faulkner Focus' to analyze the growing progressive push for a sweeping legislative agenda on Capitol Hill.
With a historic race to be the top Senate Democrat locked in, both candidates eyeing the job of leading Democrats into their majority believe they have a path to victory.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., has raised a challenge to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., to steer Democrats through the final two years of President Donald Trump’s time in office.

It’s the first time in three decades that the race has been contested, and both believe they have or can get the 28 votes needed to claim the mantle of Democratic leader and become majority leader. But neither has publicly locked down enough support to eclipse the magic number.
DEMOCRATS TURN ON SCHUMER AFTER HISTORIC ELECTION WINS AS POTENTIAL CHALLENGER EMERGES

Both Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., are confident they have the votes to lead Democrats, but Schumer, so far, has the lead in public endorsements. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images; Alex Brandon-Pool/Getty Images)
Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade as both minority and majority leader, so far has 15 senators in his camp, making him the clear front-runner.

The longtime Democratic leader has remained confident, but quiet, about his chances of retaining his job, posting shortly after Van Hollen’s announcement last week that he welcomed "discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead," but asserted, "I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader."

Schumer’s allies, like Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., argue that he has led Senate Democrats to a 55-seat majority, which could expand by another seat if Alaska flips.
CHUCK SCHUMER AFTER SWEEPING DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM VICTORIES: 'I'LL BE RE-ELECTED AS MAJORITY LEADER'

Van Hollen, who acknowledged that he is the "underdog," has five public backers who can vote in the forthcoming leadership elections — Sen. Tina Smith, D-Minn., who is retiring, is backing Van Hollen but doesn’t have a vote.

His base of support includes Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who caucuses with Senate Democrats, Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., and Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan, both progressives whom Schumer did not initially back in their respective races.

Van Hollen, however, argued that he has as many as 15 in his corner. He also alleged in an interview with Politico that Democrats were trying to move up the Dec. 1 secret-ballot leadership election to kneecap his chances.
"Let’s not rush into a coronation," Van Hollen said.
Fox News Digital reached out for comment from Van Hollen and Schumer’s offices about Van Hollen's claim.
SCHUMER'S LEADERSHIP RIVAL REVEALS MAJOR SENATE RULE CHANGE HE'D PURSUE IF ELECTED
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., speaks to reporters at the What’s Next conference in Denver on Nov. 13, 2026, as he campaigns to lead Senate Democrats. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News Digital)

While Schumer is playing the quiet game, Van Hollen has launched a public push for the job, making several appearances across the gamut of cable news and launching his own website declaring that voters’ backing of Democrats across the country was a rejection of the "status quo," and that "to deliver, we need new leadership."

There’s also a request for donations on the site, raising questions about Van Hollen’s future ambitions. He initially was "kicking the tires" on a 2028 bid for the White House, but since then, he has dropped the idea.
Just a week earlier, Van Hollen was mulling higher office, but now he’s giving up a potential bid for the White House in 2028 to do one thing: beat Schumer and grapple with President Donald Trump.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"I’m no longer pursuing that," Van Hollen told reporters at the What’s Next conference in Denver.
But it raises the question whether a leadership bid is a launch pad for higher office.
"At a minimum, it’s good for his base fundraising," a Democratic source told Fox News Digital.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Trump kicks off high-stakes Asia trip with Xi, Putin meetings looming on world stage
summary: President Donald Trump is set to sign a trade deal with Thailand at the ASEAN summit before heading to China for historic talks with Xi Jinping.
story: Former State Department senior advisor Christian Whiton joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to discuss President Donald Trump's upcoming summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Whiton breaks down the potential for nuclear arms agreements, ongoing trade negotiations and the shifting geopolitical dynamics between the U.S., Russia and China.

President Donald Trump is in Asia for historic talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin this week, with nuclear arms reductions and Iran on the agenda and Trump signaling Monday that he also plans to raise Russia's war in Ukraine.

Trump's trip began Tuesday in the Philippines at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit before he travels to Shenzhen, China, for Thursday's meeting with Xi and Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

The rare gathering comes amid simmering U.S.-China trade tensions and ongoing conflicts involving Russia and Iran, with Trump signaling plans to raise denuclearization and efforts to end the fighting.

At the ASEAN summit, Trump is expected to sign a joint statement with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul announcing progress toward a trade agreement. The president is also set to meet with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. before departing for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China.
TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA

President Donald Trump shakes hands with Chinese President Xi Jinping as they hold a bilateral meeting at Gimhae International Airport, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, in Busan, South Korea, on Oct. 30, 2025. (Reuters/Evelyn Hockstein)
The president has also raised the possibility of meeting with North Korean dictator Kim Jong-un during his visit to China this week, telling reporters Monday that talks could take place.
When reached for additional comment about the floated meeting, the White House referred Fox News Digital to Trump's remarks to reporters on Monday.

Trump is expected to discuss Iran and Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin during Thursday's highly-anticipated trilateral meeting, despite U.S. officials previously telling ABC News that Ukraine likely would not be on the agenda.
Trump notably told reporters on Nov. 8 that he plans to discuss denuclearization and ending the war in Iran during the trilateral meeting, DW News reported.
"We'll talk a lot of things, including denuclearization, but we'll be talking a lot of things. We're trying to end the war in Iran," the president said at the time.

From right to left, President Donald Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping at Gimhae International Airport in Busan, South Korea, Thursday, Oct. 30, 2025. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)
Trump's trip also comes amid a scandal involving Nvidia, the American tech giant whose powerful AI chips are at the center of growing tensions between the U.S. and China.

Nvidia's former CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned last week following reports of an affair with a woman suspected by U.S. intelligence officials of sharing information with Beijing, raising fresh concerns about Chinese espionage and access to sensitive American technology.
Trump cast doubt on the espionage allegations Monday, telling reporters he was unsure whether the woman was a Chinese spy. He also said he would be open to Huang returning as CEO.
TRUMP-XI REUNION COMES WITH UNFINISHED BUSINESS — AND A BIGGER BATTLE LOOMING

President Donald Trump greets Russian President Vladimir Putin on the tarmac after they arrived at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Anchorage, Alaska, on August 15, 2025. (Photo by Andrew Cabellero-Reynolds/AFP)

The president will be joined by several high-profile figures during his Asia trip, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is accompanying Trump to the Philippines and China this week, according to Rubio's public schedule.
Tesla CEO Elon Musk is also expected to join Trump for part of his trip to China for the APEC summit, U.S. officials confirmed to CNBC on Friday.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chairman of the House Select Committee on Strategic Competition between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party, told CBS News’ "Face the Nation" in an interview on Sunday that he does not anticipate any agreements related to the reduction of nuclear weapons will be made this week.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I don’t believe any agreements are going to be made, but certainly China has resisted being part of any agreements," Moolenaar told CBS News. "And if there’s a way to provide more security for the American people through those kinds of discussions, I think it’s important to have it."
Fox News Digital's Greg Norman-Diamond contributed to this report.

title: Trump arrives in Philippines ahead of Xi Jinping summit in China after GOP midterm losses
summary: President Donald Trump arrives in the Philippines ahead of a historic summit with China's Xi Jinping, following bruising GOP losses in the U.S. midterm elections.
story: Fox News' Mark Meredith reports the latest on his visit from Manila. The Heritage Foundation's Victoria Coates also weighs in on the trip during 'Fox & Friends First.'
President Donald Trump touched down in the Philippines on Tuesday as part of an Asia trip that will take him to China for a historic summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
The trip marks Trump's first overseas visit since Republicans suffered bruising defeats in the U.S. midterm elections.
Trump noted during a gaggle on Monday that while in China this week he will meet with Chinese President Xi Jingping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
TRUMP BRINGS TWO DIVIDED CABINET HEAVYWEIGHTS TO CHINA AS CONTROVERSY HANGS OVER HIGH-STAKES TALKS
President Donald Trump boards Air Force One on Nov. 16, 2026, at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

"And then we go to China. And we'll be with President Xi, he was here a month ago. And we're also gonna meet with President Putin. And we may meet with Kim Jong Un also," Trump said, referring to North Korea's leader. "He may come. I don't know. That's up to President Xi," Trump later added.
Trump indicated that during the meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts, they would discuss issues including denuclearization, Iran, Ukraine, economics and trade.
Asked on Tuesday if Kim Jong Un would come, Trump said, "He would like to, yeah. We'll see what happens.

The trip also comes after tech giant Nvidia announced last week that President and CEO Jensen Huang had resigned from the company — the resignation announcement was made after Huang admitted to cheating on his wife amid reporting that he had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
TRUMP'S ASIA TRIP TAKES ALASKA DETOUR AS WEATHER FORCES REFUELING STOP CHANGE

US President Donald Trump waves U.S. and Philippine flags as he arrives at Ninoy Aquino International Airport to attend the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila on Nov. 17, 2026. (Eloisa Lopez/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)
Trump met Tuesday in the Philippines with leaders of the Quad, which includes the U.S., Japan, Australia and India.
He signed a document with Thailand Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul on Tuesday as the two nations moved closer toward inking a trade deal.
"Today's deal lays the foundation for much stronger trading relationship that will bring the United States and Thailand closer than ever before," Trump said.

"Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on U.S. exports ... and remove substantial non-tariff barriers on American vehicles, medical devices, pharmaceuticals, ethanol and poultry. Thailand will also be buying an estimated $2.6 billion in additional U.S. agricultural products," he said.

"This is an incredible victory for both countries, both the people of Thailand and the American people. And I look forward to finalizing the details of our formal agreement in the coming weeks," Trump said, noting that today they were signing "a joint statement talking about the deal," which will eventually be finalized.
"Actually, it's a very big trade deal," Trump later said.

The title on the document they signed reads, "Joint Statement on an Agreement Between the United States of America and the Kingdom of Thailand on Reciprocal Trade." The statement says that the two men "have reached substantial conclusion in their negotiations" toward a trade agreement.

title: Engine failure forces Sen Ashley Moody’s American Airlines flight to divert for emergency landing
summary: Sen. Ashley Moody's, R-Fla., flight was forced to divert and make an emergency landing following an engine failure. The American Airlines flight was diverted to Orlando.
story: An American Airlines flight carrying Sen. Ashley Moody, R-Fla., was diverted to Orlando after a reported engine failure. (Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

title: States put speed-limiting devices in reckless drivers' cars
summary: Virginia's GPS speed limiter program is already active for reckless driving offenders, but early users report glitches that apply wrong speed limits.
story: A LifeSafer GPS-powered speed limiter displays a 35 mph limit and helps prevent the driver from accelerating beyond the posted speed limit. (LifeSafer ISA)

We've all seen it. You're driving down the highway when someone flies past you at a ridiculous speed. Maybe they're weaving through traffic while everyone else tries to stay out of their way. Now, states are turning to speed-limiting devices that could stop some of the most dangerous drivers from doing it again.

Virginia has already started installing GPS-powered devices in vehicles used by certain reckless-driving offenders. Washington, D.C., has a similar program, and more jurisdictions are exploring the technology. The idea sounds promising. Instead of simply telling someone to slow down, the device can actually restrict how fast their car accelerates.

However, there's a catch. Some drivers using these systems have reported GPS glitches that mistakenly apply the speed limits of nearby roads. And that raises a question worth asking. What happens when your car refuses to accelerate because its GPS thinks you're somewhere else?
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
SILICON VALLEY DEVELOPER ACCUSED OF MURDER AFTER INVESTIGATORS SAY TESLA REACHED 142 MPH BEFORE FATAL CRASH
How speed-limiting devices stop reckless drivers

The technology is called Intelligent Speed Assistance (ISA). It uses GPS location information and digital maps to determine the posted speed limit. Here's how it works. Let's say you're traveling on a road with a 45 mph speed limit. As your vehicle reaches 45 mph, the device restricts additional acceleration. Pressing harder on the gas pedal won't normally make the car accelerate beyond that limit.

However, the system doesn't automatically slam on the brakes or shut off the engine. Instead, it limits the vehicle's ability to accelerate. That means a vehicle traveling downhill could still exceed the posted limit because of gravity.

Some systems also allow brief overrides when additional acceleration is necessary for safety. Think of it as a speed governor that automatically adjusts as you move between roads. The important difference comes down to control. Many newer vehicles already recognize speed limits and warn drivers when they're going too fast. These aftermarket devices take things further by restricting acceleration.
Virginia is already putting speed limiters in cars

Virginia launched its Intelligent Speed Assistance Program on July 1. The state allows courts to require speed-limiting technology for certain driving offenses, including reckless driving and racing. The Virginia DMV can also require participation in qualifying cases involving excessive demerit points. For eligible drivers, the program offers a way to maintain restricted driving privileges rather than face a full license suspension. According to a Nov. 2 report, approximately 100 devices had been installed in Virginia since July. Many participants faced reckless-driving charges or convictions. Some cases involved speeds exceeding 100 mph.

The restrictions are serious. Qualifying drivers may need the equipment installed in every vehicle they own or co-own. They must also comply with restrictions on which vehicles they can operate. Then there's the cost. Participants generally pay installation and ongoing service fees, although financial assistance may be available for those who qualify. The goal is to let certain drivers continue essential travel while reducing the risk of dangerous speeding.
More states are moving toward speed-limiting technology

Virginia has company in exploring this approach. Washington, D.C. launched its Intelligent Speed Assistance Program on Oct. 1, 2025. Under the program, D.C. driver's license holders convicted of aggravated reckless driving must enroll and operate only authorized vehicles equipped with the technology.

Washington state passed legislation in 2025 requiring speed-limiting devices in certain cases involving dangerous speeding and driving restrictions. However, those requirements won't take effect until Jan. 1, 2029. Meanwhile, New York City is considering a proposal introduced on Oct. 22. It would require vehicle owners who accumulate 16 school-zone speeding violations within 12 months to install speed-limiting devices. The New York City proposal remains in committee and has not become law. These programs differ in scope. Still, they show how policymakers are increasingly considering technology as a response to dangerous driving.
JOE BIDEN MANDATED ALL NEW VEHICLES COME INSTALLED WITH A 'KILL SWITCH.' THIS REPUBLICAN WANTS TO REPEAL IT
LifeSafer's Intelligent Speed Assistance device uses GPS and digital maps to identify speed limits and restrict vehicle acceleration. (LifeSafer ISA)
GPS glitches are raising serious safety concerns

GPS technology is incredibly useful. But anyone who's followed navigation directions onto the wrong road knows it can make mistakes. Consider this situation. You're driving on a highway with a 65 mph speed limit. A service road running alongside it has a 35 mph limit. If your GPS mistakenly places you on the service road, the speed limiter could apply the lower limit. Your vehicle wouldn't suddenly brake, but it could restrict additional acceleration even though you're traveling on a highway with a higher speed limit. That's the type of GPS problem some Virginia participants have reported.

Early users reportedly experienced situations where their devices applied lower limits from nearby roads. Officials acknowledged the complaints and said they were working on fixes. To be clear, the reports establish that location errors have occurred. They do not establish a pattern of crashes caused by those errors. That could become a safety concern when a driver needs additional acceleration to merge into traffic, but the vehicle won't respond as expected. That's a potential safety concern officials need to address before these systems become more widespread.
Can drivers override a speed limiter in an emergency?

Some systems provide temporary overrides when drivers need additional acceleration. Virginia's proposed technical standards outline specific limits for emergency overrides, although those requirements have not yet been finalized. Under the proposal, an override would last no longer than 30 seconds, permit a maximum of 5 mph above the posted speed limit and allow no more than two overrides per driving cycle.

Those specifications appear in regulations published Oct. 19. The rules remain proposed, with public comments accepted through Dec. 18. The limits are intended to balance safety with the program's goal of preventing excessive speeding. However, they also show that an emergency override may provide much less acceleration than a driver expects. That's why clear instructions and reliable operation are so important.
Why officials believe speed limiters could save lives

There's a serious reason states are considering these devices. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, 11,288 people died in speeding-related traffic crashes in 2024. Speeding contributed to 29% of all U.S. traffic fatalities that year. Those numbers help explain why officials want something more effective than another speeding ticket.

A driver who repeatedly ignores speed limits may continue taking risks after paying fines. And suspending someone's license doesn't physically prevent that person from getting behind the wheel. Speed-limiting technology offers another option. A properly functioning device can prevent certain excessive speeds while allowing qualifying drivers to continue traveling to work or handling essential responsibilities.

However, speed limits tell only part of the safety story. Someone can drive recklessly without exceeding the posted limit. Following too closely can still cause a crash. Bad weather can also make a legally permitted speed dangerous. So, these devices may help reduce extreme speeding, but they cannot guarantee safe driving.
NEW BIG RIG SAFETY TECH COULD SAVE YOUR LIFE
A driver operates a vehicle equipped with a LifeSafer speed limiter showing a 30 mph speed limit and a current speed of 29 mph. (LifeSafer ISA)
Could speed limiters eventually be required in every car?

That's the bigger question. For now, these enforcement programs focus on drivers who meet specific legal criteria. There is no nationwide requirement forcing every U.S. driver to install one of these aftermarket speed-limiting devices. However, many newer vehicles already offer speed-limit recognition and warnings. That means some of the technology has become familiar to drivers.

The bigger step involves allowing software to actively restrict acceleration. As more jurisdictions test these programs, lawmakers could consider expanding eligibility. But any expansion would require additional policy decisions. And public acceptance could become a major obstacle. After all, there's a big difference between your dashboard warning you that you're speeding and your car preventing you from accelerating.
Speed-limiting devices also raise privacy questions

There's another issue I think deserves more attention. What happens to all the driving information these systems collect? GPS-based speed limiters need location data to determine which speed limit applies. Depending on the program, they may also record speeding events and other information used to monitor compliance.

Virginia's proposed regulations would require service providers to report certain vehicle events and speed violations, including GPS locations. The proposal also contains a significant additional requirement. Beginning July 1, 2027, new installations would need cameras capable of photographing the driver's seat when the device records a speeding event, if the proposed rules take effect as written.

That raises questions about who can access the information and how long it remains stored. We explored similar privacy concerns in our article, Is it worth saving money to let a car insurance company track your every move? Insurance tracking programs serve a different purpose. However, both technologies show how much information connected vehicles can generate about the people driving them. And once that information exists, clear rules about its collection and use become especially important.
Kurt's key takeaways

I understand why states want to take this approach. We've all shared the road with someone driving so recklessly that you wonder how they still have a license. And if technology can prevent someone from driving 100 mph through traffic, I see the appeal. What concerns me is putting that much authority in the hands of a GPS system that can make mistakes. I've seen enough technology glitches over the years to know that even sophisticated systems sometimes get things wrong. That's inconvenient when your phone sends you to the wrong address. It's a much bigger concern when you're behind the wheel. I also think states need to be careful about how they expand these programs. Targeting repeat dangerous drivers makes sense. Requiring everyone to surrender control of their vehicle would raise a very different set of questions. Before we go further, I'd like to see stronger evidence that these devices reduce crashes without creating new safety problems. Because ultimately, the goal should be safer roads. And that means making sure the technology earns our trust before we depend on it.

Would you feel safer knowing reckless drivers have speed limiters in their cars, or does the idea of a GPS system controlling your accelerator worry you even more? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.
